Goal check-in: «produce a complete, novel judgement and decision-making (JDM) research paper without collecting new data. Work autonomously: do not ask me questions. Make decisions yourself and record each one, with its reason, in `decision_log.md`. 1. Scoping. Review recent JDM research and open data sources. Choose either a secondary analysis of an openly licensed existing dataset or a simulation study (e.g. an agent-based model). A simulation must be able to fail: it must reproduce specified empirical findings or make a prediction that existing or future data could refute. Before committing, search for the closest existing work and write `novelty.md`: the 5 closest papers and what your study adds to each. 2. Preregistration. State hypotheses, the analysis plan, inference criteria, exclusions, and how you will interpret each possible outcome. For secondary data, use a secondary-data preregistration template and state exactly what you have seen of the data (e.g. codebook and variable names only). Commit it to git before you load any outcome variable or run any simulation that tests a hypothesis. 3. Analysis. Follow the preregistration. All results must come from scripts that rerun from the raw data with one command. Record every deviation and its reason in `deviations.md`, and label exploratory analyses as exploratory. Report the results whichever way they come out. Have codex review the code and results. 4. Journal and manuscript. Choose a target journal and justify the choice in `decision_log.md`. Follow its author guidelines and its AI-use policy. Draft the manuscript and cover letter. Every number must come from the analysis output. Verify every reference against Crossref, and check that each cited source supports the claim it is cited for. 5. Review. Review the manuscript with codex and agy, then run a full coarse-review. Record every comment and your response in `review_log.md`. When you reject a comment, say why. Stop after 3 review rounds, or earlier if no reviewer raises a major issue. Constraints: do not submit anything, contact anyone, or create accounts. Use only openly licensed data without personal identifiers. Use sub-agents (or workflows) to split up the work. Have codex and agy review ideas and drafts whenever helpful. Done when the folder contains: the preregistration (committed before analysis), rerunnable analysis code and outputs, the manuscript, the cover letter, `decision_log.md`, `novelty.md`, `deviations.md`, `review_log.md`, `ai_disclosure.md`, and `weaknesses.md` (the 5 weakest points of the paper, in your own assessment).» is still active, and evaluation has been deferred for 44 min because background work is still running:

<result>No published paper I found fits an individual-level revision model on one continuous-estimation social-influence dataset and then predicts, with fixed parameters, the change in crowd error per question in other datasets. Pooled reanalyses exist, but they either fit nothing at the individual level or stay within one dataset or one lab.

## (1) Closest existing work

| Paper | DOI | What it did |
|---|---|---|
| **Almaatouq, Rahimian, Burton & Alhajri 2022, Sci Rep** (preprint 2020, [arXiv 2006.12471](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.12471)) | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-20551-7 | Pooled reanalysis of four datasets: Lorenz 2011, Becker 2017, Gürçay 2015 and Becker 2019 (2,885 participants, 54 tasks). The model treats the crowd estimate as a weighted average of initial estimates, with a centralisation parameter. It uses a descriptor of the initial-estimate distribution (R) to predict when centralised influence lowers crowd error. Per a fetched summary of the paper, it fits no individual-level revision parameters, uses mixed-effects models with study as a random effect, and makes no cross-dataset prediction. |
| **Madirolas & de Polavieja 2015, PLoS Comput Biol** | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1004594 | Builds a revision model (weighted geometric mean of own and social estimate). It is tested on the Lorenz 2011 data only. Social weight w_s = 0.68 is estimated in one condition and used to predict another condition of the same experiment. |
| **Jayles et al. 2017 PNAS; Jayles et al. 2020 J R Soc Interface; Jayles et al. 2021 J R Soc Interface; Jayles et al. 2021 PLoS Comput Biol** | https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1703695114 ; https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2020.0496 ; https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2021.0231 ; https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009590 | A revision model with distance- and direction-dependent social weight, refit within each new experiment of the same lab and paradigm. It reproduces collective accuracy within those experiments. It is not tested on other labs' datasets. |
| **Kao et al. 2018, J R Soc Interface** | https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2018.0130 | Fits a social-weight revision model that depends on distance and direction, on the authors' own experiment. I did not read the full text, so I have not confirmed whether it applies the model to external datasets. |
| **Molleman et al. 2020, Proc R Soc B** | https://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2020.2413 | Fits a cognitive model of how people combine several disagreeing peer estimates, on one new experiment. The model is not applied to other datasets. |
| **Becker, Almaatouq et al. 2020, arXiv "Network structures of collective intelligence: the contingent benefits of group discussion"** | https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2009.07202 | Applies a network belief-formation framework across discussion versus Delphi-style formats, from the abstract only. It uses no fitted individual revision model and makes no out-of-sample prediction. |

Other checks:
- **Almaatouq's thesis** (https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/ahr7y) and **Almaatouq et al., "Beyond playing 20 questions with nature"** (https://doi.org/10.1017/s0140525x22002874) call for integrative, cross-environment tests. They do not carry them out for this model.
- **Chacoma & Zanette 2015** (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0140406) estimates model parameters from a single experiment.
- **Lin 2026, Management Science** (https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.04499) validates a weight-on-advice aggregation algorithm across several archival datasets. It does not predict change in crowd error from a fitted revision model.
- Searches for meta-analyses or pooled analyses by the Tump/Kurvers or Theraulaz groups found nothing that fits a model across datasets.

## (2) Verdict: PARTLY DONE

- **Already done:**
  - Pooling several of the target datasets to explain the sign of crowd-error change (Almaatouq et al. 2022).
  - Checking a revision model on a dataset collected by someone else, but only within Lorenz 2011 and only at the individual level (Madirolas & de Polavieja 2015).
  - Refitting the Jayles-type revision model across experiments from one lab.
- **Still open:**
  - One fixed-parameter revision model fitted on dataset A, with weights that depend on distance and direction plus a link between accuracy and amount of revision.
  - Used to predict the per-question change in crowd error across datasets from other labs (Lorenz 2011, Becker 2017/2019, Almaatouq 2020, Jayles/Kao).
  - Scored against those observed changes.
  - Compared with the per-dataset R-descriptor account in Almaatouq et al. 2022.

## (3) Confidence: medium

- **Why:** Coverage of work citing Jayles 2017, Kao 2018, Becker 2017, Lorenz 2011, Almaatouq 2022 and Madirolas 2015 in OpenAlex, plus web searches, turned up only the pooled analysis without a fitted model.
- **Not fully checked:** The supplementary material of Becker 2017, Kao 2018 and Almaatouq 2022, which I did not read. An unpublished thesis or 2025–26 preprint could also have done this.</result>

<result>I found no paper that applies the Bayesian sampler or PT+N (probability theory plus noise) to forecasting-tournament data, or that derives extremizing from sampler parameters. That applied test is new. The conceptual claim behind it is not: several papers already derive extremizing from individual judgment noise, as the list below shows.

## (1) Closest existing modelling papers

| Paper | DOI | Year | What it did |
|---|---|---|---|
| Baron, Mellers, Tetlock et al., "Two reasons to make aggregated probability forecasts more extreme" | https://doi.org/10.1287/deca.2014.0293 | 2014 | Names two reasons to extremize. (a) The probability scale is compressed at 0 and 1, so random error pulls the mean toward 0.5. (b) Each forecaster ignores information that others hold. One transformation corrects both, with different parameters for mean and median. Using the median in principle separates the two. **This is the direct conceptual precedent for "noise causes extremizing".** |
| Ariely, Au, Bender, Budescu, Dietz, Gu, Wallsten & Zauberman, "The effects of averaging subjective probability estimates between and within judges" | https://doi.org/10.1037//1076-898x.6.2.130 | 2000 | Uses a cognitive model: estimate = underlying judgment + random error (from Erev, Wallsten & Budescu 1994, https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295x.101.3.519, and Wallsten et al. 1997, https://doi.org/10.1002/(sici)1099-0771(199709)10:3<243::aid-bdm268>3.0.co;2-m). Proves that averaging conditionally independent estimates makes the average more diagnostic, i.e. more extreme. Tests this with lab data, not tournament data. |
| Satopää, Pemantle & Ungar, "Modeling probability forecasts via information diversity" | https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.2015.1100621 | 2016 | Partial-information model. The optimal extremizing amount follows from how much information forecasters share. The abstract argues that information diversity matters more than measurement noise, so this paper sets up the contrast the candidate would test. |
| Satopää, Salikhov, Tetlock & Mellers, "Bias, Information, Noise: the BIN model" | https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2020.3882 | 2021 | Fits bias, information and noise to Good Judgment Project (GJP) forecasts. Noise reduction drives most gains from training, teaming and tracking. Follow-up paper: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijforecast.2021.12.010 (2022). There, simple averaging works almost only by reducing noise, while extremizing and Bayesian aggregators also extract information. Noise is a statistical error term, not a generative sampling process. |
| Lichtendahl, Grushka-Cockayne, Jose & Winkler, "Extremizing and antiextremizing in Bayesian ensembles of binary-event forecasts" | https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.2021.2176 | 2022 | Optimal aggregators come from a model of each forecaster's information state. They show when to extremize and when to anti-extremize. They fit the model to public forecast data. |
| Turner, Steyvers, Merkle, Budescu & Wallsten, "Forecast aggregation via recalibration" | https://doi.org/10.1007/s10994-013-5401-4 | 2014 | Fits hierarchical linear-in-log-odds recalibration to geopolitical forecasts, and the fitted recalibration extremizes the aggregate. OpenAlex has no abstract for this paper, so this description comes from memory and I did not check it. |

<result># Novelty check for the JDM simulation candidates

Candidate A is finished. B–H went to four background subagents, and none of them had reported back when this was written. I have no verdicts for B–H and have not guessed any. Scratch files are in `/tmp/jdmsim` (the helper is `scratch_novelty_oa.py`).

## A. Anchoring process models on the Open Anchoring Quest (OpAQ)

**Papers citing the OpAQ data paper (10.5334/jopd.67).** OpenAlex lists 4 citing works, and none fits a process model:
- 2024, https://doi.org/10.1177/09567976241252138: "Promoting Erroneous Divergent Opinions Increases the Wisdom of Crowds". Anchors half the crowd low and half high to increase opinion diversity. Includes a mathematical model but does not use OpAQ as data.
- 2023, https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/wvfm3: the preprint of the paper above.
- 2025, https://doi.org/10.1038/s44271-025-00276-9: "Range nudges enhance behavioural adherence to safety and health guidelines". Anchoring from limits versus ranges, using new experiments.
- 2024, https://doi.org/10.5334/jopd.92: the correction notice for the OpAQ data paper.

Only one work cites the Meta-Psychology paper (10.15626/mp.2022.3236): https://doi.org/10.5964/ejop.9891 (2025), which tests how reliable anchoring-susceptibility scores are with N = 78. It fits no process model.

**Closest papers**

| Paper | What it did |
|---|---|
| Röseler & Schütz, 2022, https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn (PsyArXiv; I found no journal version) | Meta-analysis of the OpAQ collection (k = 393). Anchor extremeness was measured as mean \|anchor − true value\| / true value per item. Its effect was positive (b = 0.040, k = 312, p < .001) and described as "nonlinear but positive". The inverted-U predicted by selective accessibility was "not supported". It did not analyse knowledge or uncertainty (too few expert studies) and fitted no process model. |
| Schley & Weingarten, 2026, https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03238 (preprint https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/teq7k_v2) | Meta-analysis of 2,601 effect sizes. It lists theory predictions, including an inverted U for the attitudinal/plausibility account (Wegener et al., 2001). Extremity was coded only as a binary "authors called it extreme" (49 vs 1,231 effects) and was null. Knowledge showed a small decrease. An earlier SSRN version adds a meta-study (N = 1,968) that reports moderation by extremity and knowledge. No process model was fitted. |
| Turner & Schley, 2016, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003 | Anchor Integration Model: a Bayesian model with inverse-variance weighting. It predicts more anchoring when uncertainty about the target is higher. Fitted to the authors' own experiments. This is the natural quantitative competitor to Lieder's model. |
| Lieder et al., 2018, https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8 | Resource-rational anchoring-and-adjustment. Qualitatively simulates ten classic anchoring phenomena, including the effects of anchor extremity and uncertainty, using small published studies. |
| Lieder et al., 2018, https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-017-1288-6 | Two new experiments show adjustment falls with time cost and rises with error cost. These are not large-scale fits. |
| Röseler et al., 2023, https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/jztk2 | Formalises the insufficient-adjustment model and tests it in 4 new studies (N = 898). The prediction that less time gives more anchoring failed. Not fitted to OpAQ. |

**Answers to the three sub-questions**
- **(a) Process model fitted to OpAQ:** none found. I checked works citing OpAQ, the Meta-Psychology paper and Lieder 2018, filtered by "model fit", "distance" and "extreme".
- **(b) Extremity or uncertainty as moderators in large data:** extremity has been tested twice.
  - Röseler & Schütz 2022 used distance relative to the true value on OpAQ and found a positive, nonlinear effect.
  - Schley & Weingarten used a binary extremity code and found a null effect.
  - Item uncertainty has only been tested as a coarse "knowledge" moderator (Schley & Weingarten: small reduction). No one has scaled distance in units of the unanchored SD.
- **(c) Inverted U versus monotone in large data:** tested once in a coarse way. Röseler & Schütz 2022 found no inverted U, using study-level aggregates.

**Feasibility caveat:** OpAQ stores anchored estimates only. Its `true_value` field is the correct answer, or an unanchored mean from a control group or pretest when no correct answer exists. True values exist for 355 of 412 items. The data do not generally include an unanchored SD per item, so "distance in unanchored-SD units" will need a proxy, such as the within-condition SD or external calibration data.

**Verdict: PARTLY DONE.** Already done: the descriptive finding that anchoring rises monotonically and nonlinearly with anchor distance, and not in an inverted U, at study level on OpAQ. Still open:
1. Item-level fits of Lieder's model, compared with the Anchor Integration Model and a plausibility/inverted-U model.
2. The concavity prediction with distance scaled by item uncertainty.
3. Item uncertainty as a continuous moderator.
4. Any process-model fit to OpAQ.

**Confidence: medium-high.** The citation base is small, and both major meta-analyses were read directly. Uncertainty remains because Röseler & Schütz may have a later journal version I did not find.

## B–H

These are not yet checked: the four subagents' reports had not arrived when this was written.
- **B.** Wisdom of crowds under social influence, cross-dataset out-of-sample test.
- **C.** Bayesian sampler applied to forecasting tournaments and extremizing.
- **D.** Many Labs heterogeneity caused by measurement scale, baseline rates or reliability.
- **E.** Small-sample (hot-stove) models predicting feedback shifts and the description–experience gap.
- **F.** The hard–easy effect across the Confidence Database.
- **G.** Models of weight-of-advice distributions, including trimodality.
- **H.** Autocorrelated-sampler models of the inner crowd.

Rerunning these checks will produce verdicts for B–H in the same format as A.</result>

Shows that site variation in baseline means combined with a ceiling or a non-linear response function produces artefactual heterogeneity from a homogeneous latent effect. They apply diagnostic descriptors (baseline tau, baseline–effect association) within each of 55 multi-lab datasets. They do not test or reproduce the correlation across effects. |
| **Frank & Heene 2024**, [10.31234/osf.io/txnpg](https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/txnpg) | Re-estimated 16 Many Labs / Psychological Science Accelerator effects with ordinal instead of linear models for Likert data. Heterogeneity estimates changed only a little. |

**Already done:**
- The reliability mechanism: proposed by Olsson-Collentine 2020, simulated by Olsson-Collentine 2023, and tested against Many Labs data by Beinhauer 2025 (a null or reversed result).

- Ceiling effects combined with site-varying baselines (Fünderich, non-linearity preprint).

**Remains open:**
- **Cross-effect calibration.** No one has built a simulation with a homogeneous latent effect and site variation calibrated to Many Labs (baseline means and SDs, scale bounds, base rates), and then checked whether it reproduces the *across-effects* correlation of r ≈ .66–.91 at realistic site numbers and sample sizes. All existing work is within one effect, or mechanistic.
- **Binary arm (a design constraint, not only a novelty note).** Olsson-Collentine analysed binary outcomes as log-OR. If the latent effect is homogeneous on the logit scale, site variation in base rates creates heterogeneity in risk differences but leaves log-OR homogeneous. The binary arm therefore reproduces their log-OR result only under a specific latent model, e.g. a latent-threshold model with site-varying latent SD or a probit/logit mismatch. The mechanism has to be stated for that case. Two related points:
  - Many Labs 1 converted some odds ratios to SMDs. Those converted effects are a separate route.
  - My search for this arm was thinner: one web pass plus citer filters.
- **Hurdles for the paper.** Beinhauer 2025 and Olsson-Collentine 2023 both weaken the reliability arm. So Candidate D's added value would rest on scale bounds, SD dispersion, base rates and the cross-effect reproduction, not on reliability.

**Scoop risk:** the LMU META-REP (SPP 2317) project "Explaining Heterogeneity in Direct Replications: Just Methodological Artefacts?" (Heene) runs a programme on this question. The Beinhauer, Fünderich and Renkewitz papers and "Renkewitz et al. (in preparation)", a reanalysis of large-scale replications cited in Beinhauer 2025, all belong to that group.

## 3. Confidence: medium-high

I screened every citer of Olsson-Collentine 2020 (83) and filtered citers of Many Labs 2 by heterogeneity-related terms. I read the full text of the three closest preprints and of Olsson-Collentine 2020 itself. The binary / base-rate arm was searched less thoroughly.</result>

## A. Anchoring process models on OpAQ
**Papers citing the OpAQ data paper (10.5334/jopd.67):** OpenAlex lists four, and none models OpAQ.
- https://doi.org/10.1177/09567976241252138 (2024): anchors half a crowd low and half high to improve the crowd average.

- https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-025-00276-9 (2025): "range nudges", i.e. anchors in behavioural guidelines.

**Closest papers:**
- **Röseler & Schütz 2022**, https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn (preprint). Meta-analysis of OpAQ, k = 393.
  - Extremity was measured as |anchor − true value| / true value.
  - The effect was positive (b = .040, p < .001), described as "nonlinear but positive".
  - The inverted U predicted by selective accessibility "was not supported".
  - No process model was fitted. Knowledge was not tested.
- **Schley & Weingarten 2026**, https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03238. Meta-analysis of 2,601 effect sizes.
  - Extremity was coded only as binary (authors called the anchor "extreme"). The effect was null.
  - Knowledge showed a small reduction.
  - The paper lists the inverted-U prediction from the plausibility/attitude-change account (Wegener et al. 2001).
- **Turner & Schley 2016**, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003. Anchor Integration Model: Bayesian inverse-variance weighting, fitted to the authors' own experiments. This is the natural quantitative competitor to Lieder's model.
- **Lieder et al. 2018**, https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8 and https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-017-1288-6. Qualitative simulations of ten classic effects, including extremity and uncertainty, plus two new experiments.

**Answers:**
- (a) No process model has been fitted to OpAQ.
- (b) Extremity has been tested as a moderator, but only with coarse, study-level measures. Uncertainty has only been tested as a binary "knowledge" code.
- (c) Inverted U versus monotone has been tested once, coarsely, with a monotone result.

**Still open:** item-level fits of Lieder's model against the Anchor Integration Model and a plausibility model, the concavity prediction with distance in SD units, and continuous item uncertainty.

**Data limit:** OpAQ has no unanchored SD per item, so SD scaling needs a proxy.

## B. Social-influence revision model, cross-dataset out-of-sample test
**Closest papers:**

  - Descriptive and theoretical. No fitted revision model is used to predict other datasets.
- **Pilgrim & Becker 2024**, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2407.00199. Splits the change in group error into three terms and checks this against six published experiments:

## C. Bayesian sampler applied to forecasting tournaments
- Citers of Zhu 2020, Sundh 2023 and Costello & Watts 2014 return zero hits for "extremiz" and "aggregat". "Forecast" hits are unrelated (random-walk prediction, poker).

  2. Information diversity among forecasters.

  They propose the median to tell the two apart. This is the key overlap: the idea that noise justifies extremizing already exists. ## A. Anchoring process models on OpAQ
**Papers citing the OpAQ data paper (10.5334/jopd.67):** OpenAlex lists four, and none models OpAQ.
- https://doi.org/10.1177/09567976241252138 (2024): anchors half a crowd low and half high to improve the crowd average.
- https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/wvfm3: preprint of the same paper.
- https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-025-00276-9 (2025): "range nudges", i.e. anchors in behavioural guidelines.
- https://doi.org/10.5334/jopd.92: correction notice for the data paper.

**Closest papers:**
- **Röseler & Schütz 2022**, https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn (preprint). Meta-analysis of OpAQ, k = 393.
  - Extremity was measured as |anchor − true value| / true value.
  - The effect was positive (b = .040, p < .001), described as "nonlinear but positive".
  - The inverted U predicted by selective accessibility "was not supported".
  - No process model was fitted. Knowledge was not tested.
- **Schley & Weingarten 2026**, https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03238. Meta-analysis of 2,601 effect sizes.
  - Extremity was coded only as binary (authors called the anchor "extreme"). The effect was null.
  - Knowledge showed a small reduction.
  - The paper lists the inverted-U prediction from the plausibility/attitude-change account (Wegener et al. 2001).
- **Turner & Schley 2016**, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003. Anchor Integration Model: Bayesian inverse-variance weighting, fitted to the authors' own experiments. This is the natural quantitative competitor to Lieder's model.
- **Lieder et al. 2018**, https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8 and https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-017-1288-6. Qualitative simulations of ten classic effects, including extremity and uncertainty, plus two new experiments.

**Answers:**
- (a) No process model has been fitted to OpAQ.
- (b) Extremity has been tested as a moderator, but only with coarse, study-level measures. Uncertainty has only been tested as a binary "knowledge" code.
- (c) Inverted U versus monotone has been tested once, coarsely, with a monotone result.

**Still open:** item-level fits of Lieder's model against the Anchor Integration Model and a plausibility model, the concavity prediction with distance in SD units, and continuous item uncertainty.

**Data limit:** OpAQ has no unanchored SD per item, so SD scaling needs a proxy.

## B. Social-influence revision model, cross-dataset out-of-sample test
**Closest papers:**
- **Almaatouq et al. 2022**, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-20551-7 (preprint https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/f5ky3).
  - Pools four datasets with 2,885 participants: Lorenz 2011, Becker 2017, Gürçay 2015 and Becker 2019.
  - Uses a DeGroot-type framework (a weighted-averaging model of opinion updating), showing the effect depends on how centralised influence is and on the spread of initial estimates.
  - Descriptive and theoretical. No fitted revision model is used to predict other datasets.
- **Pilgrim & Becker 2024**, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2407.00199. Splits the change in group error into three terms and checks this against six published experiments:
  - how centralised the influence network is;
  - "calibration" (whether more accurate people are more influential);
  - "herding" (whether people near the average are more influential).
  It is a model-based pooled analysis, but it does not predict error change per question from fixed parameters.
- **Jayles et al. 2017**, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1703695114, and **Kao et al. 2018**, https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2018.0130. Revision models that depend on distance and direction, fitted and validated within each paper's own data.
- **Becker et al. 2017**, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1615978114. Correlation between revision and accuracy; within-study only.

**Still open:** fit a revision model on one dataset, freeze its parameters, and predict the per-question change in crowd error in the other datasets. The pooled analyses above are the benchmarks it must beat.

## C. Bayesian sampler applied to forecasting tournaments
- Citers of Zhu 2020, Sundh 2023 and Costello & Watts 2014 return zero hits for "extremiz" and "aggregat". "Forecast" hits are unrelated (random-walk prediction, poker).

**Closest papers:**
- **Baron et al. 2014**, https://doi.org/10.1287/deca.2014.0293. Gives two reasons to extremize the aggregate:
  1. Random error on a probability scale compressed at 0 and 1 pulls the *mean* toward 0.5. They argue this does not affect the median.
  2. Information diversity among forecasters.

  They propose the median to tell the two apart. This is the key overlap: the idea that noise justifies extremizing already exists. A Bayesian sampler regresses each person's *expected* judgment toward 0.5, which would also shift the median and break that diagnostic. That difference is a clean new prediction.
- **Satopää et al. 2021 BIN model**, https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2020.3882. Decomposes Good Judgment Project (GJP) accuracy into bias, information and noise. Noise reduction dominates. It is a statistical model, not a sampler.
- **Lee & Danileiko 2014**, https://doi.org/10.1017/s1930297500005799, and **Turner et al. 2014**, https://doi.org/10.1007/s10994-013-5401-4. Cognitive-model and recalibration aggregation using linear-in-log-odds (LLO) calibration.
- **Zhu et al. 2022**, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2022.105022. Sampler model linking coherence and accuracy, with poker experts. It is the only application to expert forecasters, and not to tournaments.

**Still open:** fitting the sampler (N, β) to GJP data, the mean–variance signature across forecasters, and deriving the optimal extremizing parameter from the fitted N and β.

## D. Many Labs heterogeneity from scale, baseline or reliability
**Closest papers:**
- **Olsson-Collentine 2020**, https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000294. Names the reliability mechanism itself but reports no evidence for it in their data.
- **Olsson-Collentine et al. 2023**, https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/jnb6e. Simulation: measurement error usually makes estimated heterogeneity too low, by 15–60%. It inflates heterogeneity only in narrow cases, such as zero true heterogeneity with a large effect.
- **Beinhauer, Fünderich & Renkewitz 2025**, https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/u6anb_v1. In 12 multisite projects, correcting for reliability did not reduce heterogeneity.
- **Fünderich et al. 2025, "Under my umbrella"**, https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-025-02879-w. Rating-scale bounds make a homogeneous raw effect heterogeneous in Cohen's d. Illustrated with Many Labs data.
- **Fünderich et al. 2025, non-linearity preprint**, https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/s82zr_v3. Site baselines combined with a concave or ceiling response function produce heterogeneity. Diagnosed within each of 55 multi-lab datasets. Explicitly motivated by the Olsson-Collentine correlation.
- **Frank & Heene 2024**, https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/txnpg. Ordinal instead of linear models barely change heterogeneity estimates.

**Still open:**
- One calibrated simulation that reproduces the tau–effect-size correlation *across* effects. All existing work is within one effect.
- A binary-outcome arm (risk difference vs log-odds) for psychology.

**Constraints:**
- Olsson-Collentine analysed binary outcomes as log-odds ratios, which stay homogeneous under a logit latent model. The binary arm therefore needs a stated latent-threshold mechanism.
- The reliability arm is already weakened by the 2023 and 2025 papers.

**Scoop risk:** the LMU META-REP project on "just methodological artefacts?" (Heene, Renkewitz and colleagues) is working on this question.

## E. Small-sample model predicting feedback shifts and the description–experience gap
**Closest papers:**
- **BEAST, Erev et al. 2017**, https://doi.org/10.1037/rev0000062. Parameters fitted on the CPC15 choice-prediction competition data, then used to predict choice rates per problem and per block in advance. Block 1 has no feedback; blocks 2–5 have feedback.
- **Plonsky et al. 2025**, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-025-02267-6. BEAST with frozen parameters predicts the CPC18 competition data and the choices13k dataset. BEAST-GB adds machine learning on top.
- **Erev et al. 2010 competition**, https://doi.org/10.1002/bdm.683. Small-sample models won the experience condition. Description was predicted by a separate model.
- **Plonsky, Teodorescu & Erev 2015**, https://doi.org/10.1037/a0039413.
- **Wulff et al. 2018**, https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000115. Moderator analyses only. No generative sampling model fitted to the database.

**Still open:**
- Whether a minimal 1–2 parameter k-sample model recovers the feedback shift itself, used directly as the target.
- A fixed-parameter prediction of the description–experience gap per problem across the Wulff database. No one has done this.

**Constraints:**
- CPC feedback blocks also show forgone outcomes, so the hot-stove mechanism cannot operate there. Only small-sample reliance can be tested.
- https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-67729-x (2026, seven experiments) finds feedback raises risk-taking *before* any outcome is experienced. That argues against a learning account of the block-1 shift. Read it before committing to E.

## F. Hard–easy effect across the Confidence Database
**Closest papers:**
- **Guggenmos 2022**, https://doi.org/10.7554/elife.75420. A bias-free noisy observer shows a hard–easy "statistical artefact". Validated on one dataset only.

  - Jin et al. 2022, https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-022-02063-7: across-subject confidence–accuracy correlation.

**Still open:** fit noise for each dataset and predict that dataset's hard–easy magnitude, then compare with observation.

**Constraint:** many datasets use 1–4 rating scales with a single difficulty level. The usable subset (probability-scale confidence plus varied difficulty) may be small, so check it first.

## G. Advice taking as Bayesian cue integration with trimodal weights
**Closest papers:**
- **Ravazzolo & Røisland 2011**, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.econlet.2011.03.032. Analytic Bayesian model with asymmetric knowledge of own vs advisor competence. Advice weight falls smoothly with distance. No weight-of-advice (WOA) distributions.

- **Rebholz et al. 2023**, https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/y8x92. Classifies Bayesian vs choosing vs compromising strategies.
- **Moussaïd et al. 2013**, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0078433. Empirical keep / compromise / adopt map as a function of distance.

- **Hütter & Ache 2016**, https://doi.org/10.1017/s193029750000382x. Information-asymmetry account stated in words and tested by experiment.

**Still open:** a generative model in which the own-reasons asymmetry itself produces the trimodal distribution and the curvilinear WOA–distance curve, fitted quantitatively.

**Design flag:** pure precision-weighted averaging gives a smooth WOA distribution. Spikes need a discrete choice or threshold stage. Himmelstein's model is the benchmark to beat.

<result># JDM open questions: candidates for a preregistered secondary analysis or simulation study

I found 12 candidates. Nothing clears all three bars (novel, decisive, feasible) at once. The two strongest are a simulation of how decision noise shapes the correlations between risk-elicitation tasks (Basel-Berlin Risk Study) and an item-level test of anchoring theories in the Open Anchoring Quest data. Scores are my judgement.

## Method
- **Literature search:** OpenAlex title and abstract searches for each topic (2021–2026, sorted by citations and by date), plus targeted web searches to check whether each idea is already taken.
- **DOIs:** every DOI below was checked against Crossref with `scratch_litgaps/scratch_litgaps_dois.py`. All resolved and matched.
- **Licences:** checked only through repository metadata APIs (OSF, Zenodo, Dataverse, OpenNeuro, GitHub, Hugging Face). No data files were opened or downloaded.
- **OpenAlex quota:** 2 of the 5 keys had no quota left at session start.
- **Files:** helper scripts and a draft are in `~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/scratch_litgaps/`.

## Licence status of the datasets named below

| Dataset | Licence | Status under decision-log rule #4 |
|---|---|---|
| Many Labs 1 (OSF wx7ck), Many Labs 2 (OSF 8cd4r) | CC0 | OK |
| Open Anchoring Quest, OAQ (OSF ygnvb) | CC-BY 4.0 | OK |
| Confidence Database (OSF s46pr) | CC0 | OK |
| Good Judgment Project, GJP (Dataverse doi:10.7910/DVN/BPCDH5) | CC0 | OK |
| NARPS mixed gambles (OpenNeuro ds001734) | CC0 | OK |
| Tom et al. mixed gambles (OpenNeuro ds000005) | ODC PDDL 1.0 | OK |
| Basel-Berlin Risk Study, BBRS (OSF rce7g) | Project CC-BY; component 47kqs ("Frey et al. 2017") is GPL-3.0 | Probably OK. UNVERIFIED which component holds the data |
| Stango & Zinman replication package (Zenodo 6783408) | CC-BY 4.0 | Licence OK. UNVERIFIED whether it contains the survey microdata |
| 61-country discounting study (OSF registration jfvh4; project njd62) | Registration CC-BY; project has no licence | Ambiguous |
| Psych-101 (Hugging Face) | Apache-2.0 on the whole compilation | Needs your decision (see below) |
| choices13k (GitHub) | No licence; aggregated choice rates only | Excluded as a standalone dataset |
| Prospect theory, 19 countries (Ruggeri 2020, OSF esxc4) | No licence | Excluded |

## Candidates

In each entry, "Risk" gives P(done), my estimate that the test has already been published, and whether the result could come out either way.

**C1. Noise predicts the correlation pattern between risk-elicitation tasks (simulation plus data, BBRS)**
- **Hypothesis:** Simulate one noisy expected-utility agent per participant on each BBRS task, using each task's actual mechanics. This reproduces the sign and ranking of the observed task-to-task correlations better than a model with stable preferences and no noise.
- **Theory:** Noise pushes estimates toward each task's midpoint, and the direction of that push differs by task (Andersson et al. 2016; Enke & Shubatt 2023). The rival is a construction account: preferences are formed at the moment of elicitation (Pedroni et al. 2017).
- **Data:** BBRS, about 1,500 people doing six or more behavioural tasks, with a retest subsample.
- **Why open:** Pedroni et al. 2017 ([10.1038/s41562-017-0219-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-017-0219-x)) documented the puzzle. Frey et al. 2017 ([10.1126/sciadv.1701381](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.1701381)) gave the factor structure. Olschewski et al. 2023 ([10.1038/s41598-023-47844-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-47844-9)) used task-level decision error only to explain correlations with cognitive ability. Crosetto & Filippin 2016 ([10.1007/s10683-015-9457-9](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10683-015-9457-9)) simulated noise effects on average estimates, not on correlations between tasks. The novelty claim rests on predicting all the pairwise correlations.
- **Risk:** P(done) 35%. The field is active: O'Donoghue et al., [arXiv 2609.12291](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12291) (Sept 2026), and Sung & Wincelberg, [arXiv 2607.05686](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05686). Could come out either way: yes. The noise model predicts specific signs; the construction account does not.

**C2. How anchoring scales with anchor distance (OAQ, item-level)**
- **Hypothesis:** Across the 412 OAQ items, anchoring increases with standardised anchor distance, but less than proportionally (Lieder et al.'s resource-rational adjustment). The rival is an inverted U, where implausible anchors lose effect (selective accessibility and plausibility accounts).
- **Data:** OAQ, 96 studies, about 21,000 participants. True values exist for 355 of the 412 items.
- **Why open:** Lieder et al. 2018 ([10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8)) tested this in one task. Schley & Weingarten 2025 ([10.31234/osf.io/teq7k_v2](https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/teq7k_v2)) found moderation by extremity only at the study level. Röseler et al. 2022 ([10.5334/jopd.67](https://doi.org/10.5334/jopd.67)) describes the dataset.
- **Known problems:**
  - Original authors chose the anchor values, so anchor distance is not randomly assigned across items.
  - Item uncertainty measured from anchored estimates is contaminated by the anchoring effect itself.
  - A clean test needs items with 3 or more distinct anchor values. Whether enough exist is UNVERIFIED; the parent should check the data paper.
- **Risk:** P(done) 30%. Could come out either way: yes.

**C3. Loss aversion and the range of gains: the like-for-like gamble test (NARPS plus Tom et al.)**
- **Hypothesis:** Compare acceptance of the identical gambles that appear in both designs: gains $10–20 and losses $5–20 in NARPS's narrow-range and wide-range groups, pooled with ds000005. Decision by sampling predicts higher acceptance in the narrow-range group. Context-free prospect theory predicts no difference.
- **Why open:** Walasek & Stewart 2015 ([10.1037/xge0000039](https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000039)) reported that loss aversion can disappear and reverse. André & de Langhe 2021 ([10.1037/xge0001052](https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0001052)) argued this was an artefact of comparing different gamble sets. Walasek et al. 2021 ([10.1037/xge0001054](https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0001054)) replied. Brochard & Daunizeau 2024 ([10.7554/eLife.80979](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.80979)) already showed range adaptation in NARPS with a fitted loss-aversion parameter. Only the like-for-like gamble comparison that André & de Langhe asked for is left.
- **Risk:** P(done) 50%, so novelty scores 1. Could come out either way: yes. NARPS has 54 participants per group and 256 trials each (Botvinik-Nezer 2019, [10.1038/s41597-019-0113-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-019-0113-7)).

**C4. Is the cross-bias factor structure driven by noise? (Stango & Zinman data)**
- **Hypothesis:** A person-level measure of choice inconsistency accounts for most of the correlation between Stango & Zinman's four common factors. Biases that "behavioral attenuation" predicts (reduced sensitivity to fundamentals) load more on that inconsistency measure.
- **Theory:** Behavioral attenuation (Enke, Graeber, Oprea & Yang 2024, [10.3386/w32973](https://doi.org/10.3386/w32973)). The rival is Stango & Zinman's taxonomy of separate but correlated bias groups ([10.1093/restud/rdac055](https://doi.org/10.1093/restud/rdac055)).
- **Also relevant:** Dean & Ortoleva 2019 ([10.1073/pnas.1821353116](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1821353116)); Chapman et al. 2023 ([10.1086/723044](https://doi.org/10.1086/723044)).
- **Data:** the Zenodo package, but whether it contains the microdata is UNVERIFIED. The bias list, including whether a revealed-preference consistency (GARP) measure is in it, is recalled from memory and UNVERIFIED.
- **Risk:** P(done) 30%. Could come out either way: yes.

**C5. Context effects across problems in choices13k (trial-level data via Psych-101)**
- **Hypothesis:** Payoffs and probabilities from the problems a participant saw earlier shift choice on the current problem. Decision by sampling and efficient coding predict this and give its direction; context-free prospect theory predicts no effect.
- **Why open:**
  - Peterson et al. 2021 ([10.1126/science.abe2629](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abe2629)) analysed only aggregate choice rates.
  - Frydman & Jin 2021 ([10.1093/qje/qjab031](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjab031)) and Ungemach et al. 2011 ([10.1177/0956797610396225](https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797610396225)) tested context effects in small lab samples.
  - Thomas et al. 2024 ([10.1038/s41562-023-01784-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-023-01784-6)) studied noise in choices13k, not sequence.
  - Enke & Shubatt's complexity index ([10.3386/w31677](https://doi.org/10.3386/w31677)) very likely already covers choices13k. Its abstract reports 11,000 problems, but that is UNVERIFIED, so complexity questions on this dataset are probably taken.
- **Feasibility is 1 until verified:** (a) whether Psych-101 keeps each participant's order of problems; (b) whether a problem's 5 trials were shown back to back, in which case the test must compare problem to problem rather than trial to trial; (c) how many problems each participant saw. The choices13k README and the Centaur paper do not say. Checking the file structure would show choices, so it touches the blinding rule.
- **Risk:** P(done) 15%. Could come out either way: yes.

**C6. Noise produces apparent hyperbolic discounting, tested out of sample**
- **Hypothesis:** In independent open intertemporal datasets, people with less consistent choices (repeated items or retest) show more decreasing impatience.

| # | Design | Novelty | Falsifiability | Feasibility | Product |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Anchoring: how the anchoring index changes with anchor spread | 3 | 3 | 2 | **18** |
| 2 | Over/underconfidence from noise alone, in general-knowledge quizzes | 2 | 3 | 3 | **18** |
| 3 | Social-influence revision model with frozen parameters, lab to lab | 2 | 3 | 2 | **12** |
| 4 | Bayesian sampler as the reason forecasts need extremizing | 3 | 2 | 2 | 12 |
| 6 | Inner crowd as an autocorrelated sampler over time | 3 | 3 | 1 | 9 |
| 7 | Site heterogeneity created by the measurement scale (Many Labs) | 1 | 3 | 3 | 9 |
| 8 | Small-sample learning vs attitude change after feedback in risky choice | 1 | 3 | 3 | 9 |
| 5 | Advice taking: model that generates the three-peaked weight-of-advice distribution | 2 | 2 | 2 | 8 |

Design 3 edges out design 4 because its test is sharper. I left out attention-driven choice (aDDM, the attention-weighted drift diffusion model): it is already heavily modelled, and Thomas et al. 2019 (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-019-0584-8) fitted a gaze-bias model to four open datasets.

---

## 1. Anchoring index vs anchor spread (Open Anchoring Quest)

**Models.** One simulator runs four process models of estimation on a log scale; the person's belief about item i is Normal(μᵢ, σᵢ).
- **M1, resource-rational adjustment** (Lieder et al. 2018, https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8): a random-walk sampler starts at the anchor and takes t steps of size s·σᵢ.
- **M2, Anchor Integration Model** (Turner & Schley 2016, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003): the estimate is a fixed-weight (w) mix of the anchor and a belief sample.
- **M3, adjust until plausible** (Epley & Gilovich 2006, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2006.01704.x): adjustment stops at μᵢ ± kσᵢ.
- **M4, plausibility-gated selective accessibility** (Mussweiler & Strack 1999, https://doi.org/10.1006/jesp.1998.1364; Wegener et al. 2001, https://doi.org/10.1006/jesp.2000.1431): an anchor outside the plausible range loses its effect.

**Fixed vs fitted.**
- s, t, w and k are calibrated to Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995 before the data are loaded.
- One anchoring-index value does not pin down s and t. My scratch runs with (s, t) = (.5, 5), (.3, 10) and (1, 3) all give an index that rises with spread. So M1 is committed only to the *sign* of the slope, not to a numeric band.
- μᵢ is fitted per item from `true_value` and the anchored data.
- The dataset has no unanchored SD per item, so σᵢ is estimated from the pooled within-condition SD. The simulator computes the same estimate on its own simulated data, so real and simulated results are compared like for like.

**Findings to reproduce.**
1. Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995 (https://doi.org/10.1177/01461672952111004) found a mean anchoring index of 48.48% with anchors at the 15th and 85th percentiles. Lieder's model gave 53.22% and an item-level r(13) = .62 (from the Lieder preprint text). This is the calibration target; the test is item-level r ≥ .40.
2. Anchoring grows with distance from the true value: b = 0.040, k = 312, p < .001, "nonlinear but positive", with no inverted U. Pooled g = 0.689 [0.589, 0.789] (Röseler & Schütz 2022, https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn). Each model must predict a positive slope of g on distance.
3. Explicitly random anchors have much smaller effects (same source; also Schley & Weingarten 2026, https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03238). **M1 as published fails this target unless its starting point depends on how informative the anchor is. This is stated in advance.**
4. Time pressure is contested. Lieder et al. (https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-017-1288-6) found less adjustment when time is costly. Röseler et al. 2023 (https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/jztk2) found no time effect in 4 studies (N = 898). The paper must report this conflict.

**New prediction.** The measure is the anchoring index across log anchor spread in σ̂ units, where AI = Δ median log estimate / Δ log anchor.
- **M1:** AI rises, because the amount of adjustment levels off. My simulation gives .59 at z = 1, .79 at z = 4 and .88 at z = 8.
- **M2:** AI stays flat at w.
- **M3:** AI falls.
- **M4:** AI falls steeply and can turn negative.

The published positive g–distance slope already goes against M3 and M4. The open question is M1 against M2. Both predict a rising g, so only the index–spread slope separates them.

**Refutation rule.** Fit a multilevel regression of item-level index on log spread, with study as a random effect.
- A 95% CI entirely ≤ 0 refutes M1.
- A CI entirely > 0 refutes M2–M4.
- A CI that includes 0 with half-width below .05 supports M2.
- The preregistration also sets a minimum number of items with a large spread (e.g. ≥ 60 items with spread > 3σ̂). Below that, the test is declared uninformative.

**Data.** Open Anchoring Quest, https://osf.io/ygnvb/, **CC-BY 4.0** on the node that holds `OPAQ_JOPD.csv`. It has 96 studies, 21,359 participants, 412 items (355 with true values) and 88,914 trials (Röseler et al. 2022, https://doi.org/10.5334/jopd.67).
- **Optional arm:** Many Labs 1 (OSF wx7ck, **CC0**). There, anchoring SMDs were 1.21–2.53, τ .15–.69 and I² 40–91% (Olsson-Collentine et al. 2020, https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000294). The Open Anchoring Quest probably already contains these data, so this arm would not be an independent replication.

**Closest work.** Lieder 2018 (qualitative simulations of small classic studies); Röseler & Schütz 2022 (distance tested at the level of study effect sizes); Schley & Weingarten 2026 (extremity coded as binary; no effect); Turner & Schley 2016. No process model has been fitted to the Open Anchoring Quest.

**Effort.** R, 12–18 days.

## 2. Over/underconfidence from noise alone (GJP knowledge quizzes)

**Model.** An observer with zero bias answers 4-option items. Confidence is the ideal probability of being correct, plus reporting noise σ_r, clipped to the 25–100 scale.
- **Fitted:** item difficulty, person skill and σ_r.
- **Fixed:** bias = 0.

**Findings to reproduce.**
- The hard–easy effect: overconfidence on hard items, underconfidence on easy ones (Lichtenstein & Fischhoff 1977, https://doi.org/10.1016/0030-5073(77)90001-0; magnitudes UNVERIFIED).
- Juslin, Winman & Olsson 2000 (https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295x.107.2.384, abstract): the effect nearly disappears once scale ends and linear dependency are controlled, but selected and representative item sets still differ.
- The error model of Erev, Wallsten & Budescu 1994 (https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295x.101.3.519).
- Moore et al. 2017 (https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2016.2525, abstract): GJP tournament overconfidence was 3%, and 1% with teams and training.

**New prediction.** The slope of the hard–easy effect is already widely attributed to artefact. The open question is the overall level of over/underconfidence on researcher-selected items.
- The ecological account (overconfidence comes from how items are selected) predicts overconfidence beyond noise.
- The noise-only model predicts none.
- The simulator must model the floor at 25; most published targets use 2 options, with a floor at 50.

**Refutation rule.**
- **Main test:** overall bias outside the model's 95% predictive interval refutes noise-only. The interval is simulated on the real items and sample sizes.
- **Secondary test:** the hard–easy slope, compared with the same interval.
- **Precision check:** 47 items is few. Before preregistering, the simulator must show that the interval excludes a 5-point bias. If it does not, falsifiability drops to 2, and the Confidence Database arm becomes required.

**Data.**
- GJP, https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/BPCDH5, **CC0**. Two quizzes with a "probability that you are correct" rating (25–100) per item: 32 and 15 items (from the Dataverse README).
- Replication: the probability-scale subset of the Confidence Database, OSF s46pr, **CC0**. It has 145 datasets, more than 8,700 participants and about 4M trials (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-019-0813-1). The usable subset may be small.

**Closest work.** Guggenmos 2022 (https://doi.org/10.7554/elife.75420), one dataset; Merkle 2009 (https://doi.org/10.3758/pbr.16.1.204); Suantak et al. 1996 (https://doi.org/10.1006/obhd.1996.0074). I found no study that uses the GJP quizzes for calibration, but I did not search that point exhaustively.

**Effort.** R, 8–12 days.

## 3. Social-influence revision model with frozen parameters, lab to lab

**Model.** People revise their estimate in log space: x₂ = x₁ + S·(social − x₁).
- S is a mix of "keep" (S = 0), "adopt" (S = 1) and "compromise" (in between).
- The mix depends on the distance |D| between one's own estimate and the social information: ⟨S⟩ = α + β|D| (Jayles 2017). It also depends on direction, i.e. whether the social information is above or below one's own estimate (Kao 2018).
- It is fitted once on the Kao and Jayles figshare data, then frozen.

**Findings to reproduce.**
- Jayles et al. 2017 (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1703695114): median S = 0.34, with peaks at 0 and 1.
- Becker et al. 2017 (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1615978114; numbers from a summary tool's reading of the full text): in decentralized networks, median error fell 12% and mean error 10%. The correlation between initial error and revision size was ρ = .41, and it correlated ρ = −.71 with improvement across 59 tasks.
- Lorenz et al. 2011 (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1008636108): diversity fell while collective error barely changed.
- Mellers et al. 2014 (https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797614524255): GJP forecasters who saw the crowd's forecasts beat independent forecasters, t(1120) = 5.92.

**New prediction and refutation rule.** Given each group's observed initial estimates and network, the frozen model predicts the per-question change in mean and median error for the fixed networks of Becker et al. 2019. It is refuted if predicted and observed change correlate below .30, or if the signs match on fewer than 60% of questions.
- Almaatouq et al. 2020 is only a partial target: its networks rewire, which this model cannot predict.
- **GJP field arm (extension only).** In GJP year 1, forecasters were randomly assigned to see the crowd's forecasts or not. They made about 1.3 forecasts per question, so the crowd display mainly shaped the first forecast, not a revision. This arm needs an anchoring-type model, close to M2 in design 1.

**Data (licences checked).**
- Kao 2018: figshare 10.6084/m9.figshare.6120683, **CC BY 4.0**.
- Jayles, Sire & Kurvers 2021: figshare 12529571, **CC BY 4.0**.
- Becker 2019: Dataverse OE6UMR, **CC0**.
- Almaatouq 2020: Dataverse EOYZKH, **CC0**.
- GJP: **CC0**.
- Excluded (no licence or no deposit): Becker 2017, Lorenz 2011, Jayles 2017.

**Closest work.** Almaatouq et al. 2022 (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-20551-7) pooled 4 datasets, N = 2,885, descriptively. Pilgrim & Becker 2024 (arXiv:2407.00199) broke down the change in group error across 6 experiments. Nobody has made out-of-sample predictions with frozen parameters.

**Risk.** The main test rests on a single licensed dataset (Becker 2019).

**Effort.** R, 15–25 days.

## 4. Bayesian sampler as the reason forecasts need extremizing (GJP)
- **Model:** each forecaster reports (S + β)/(N + 2β), where S counts successes in N samples (Zhu, Sanborn & Chater 2020, https://doi.org/10.1037/rev0000190). Information overlap between forecasters is added. N, β and overlap are fitted on one GJP year.
- **Findings to reproduce:**
  - Overconfidence of 3% (Moore 2017).
  - Aggregates need to be pushed toward 0 or 1 ("extremizing"); the mean needs more than the median, and experts need less (Baron et al. 2014, https://doi.org/10.1287/deca.2014.0293, via Han & Budescu 2022, https://doi.org/10.1017/s1930297500009049; parameter values UNVERIFIED).
  - Lab estimates of N: median 2.65–8.25 (Sundh et al., https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0001414).
- **New prediction:** the sampler pulls each person's expected judgment toward 0.5, so the median also needs extremizing. Baron et al. argue noise affects only the mean. Across sub-crowds of size k, the median's extremizing need should level off around k ≈ 10. Information-diversity accounts (Satopää et al. 2016, https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.2015.1100621) predict it keeps rising.
- **Condition before preregistering:** both accounts can level off, so the simulator must first show the two separate under realistic overlap.
- **Why falsifiability is 2:** N can be tuned freely. Lab parameters would cap individual forecasts near .9. I expect GJP forecasters exceed that, but cannot check under the blinding rule.
- **Closest work:** the BIN model of Satopää 2021 (https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2020.3882); Zhu 2022 (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2022.105022). No sampler model has been applied to tournament aggregation.
- **Effort:** R, 15–20 days.

## 5. Advice taking: generating the three-peaked weight-of-advice distribution
- **Model:** the judge weights own estimate and advice in a Bayesian way, while unsure how accurate the advisor is. Two thresholds then produce keep / average / adopt. The peaks at 0, .5 and 1 must come out of the model, not be built in.
- **Findings to reproduce (numbers UNVERIFIED):**
  - Soll & Larrick 2009 (https://doi.org/10.1037/a0015145).
  - Yaniv 2004 (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obhdp.2003.08.002).
  - Bonaccio & Dalal 2006 (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obhdp.2006.07.001).
  - Schultze et al. 2015 (https://doi.org/10.1017/s1930297500003922).
- **Prediction:** "adopt" responses rise with the judge's low confidence faster than "average" responses do. The model derives the ratio.
- **Data:** Jaquiery & Yeung, OSF h254u, **CC-BY 4.0**. That trials contain an initial estimate, advice and a final estimate is UNVERIFIED.
- **Benchmark to beat:** Himmelstein 2022 (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmp.2022.102695), whose model fits the peaks rather than generating them.
- **Effort:** R, 10–15 days.

## 6. Inner crowd as an autocorrelated sampler over time
- **Model:** estimates come from an autocorrelated sampler (Zhu et al. 2024, https://doi.org/10.1037/rev0000427). The number of hidden steps grows with the log of the delay.
- **Findings to reproduce** (Vul & Pashler 2008, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2008.02136.x): averaging two guesses cut error by [2.5%, 10.4%] when the second guess was immediate (worth 1.11 people), and by [11.6%, 20.4%] after 3 weeks (worth 1.32 people).
- **Data:** none usable. van Dolder & van den Assem 2018 is under a non-disclosure agreement, and Steegen et al. 2014 (OSF ivfu6) has no licence.
- **Novelty:** the highest here; Dasgupta et al. 2017 (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2017.05.001) treated it only qualitatively. The empirical test needs new data.
- **Effort:** R, 6–8 days for the simulation only.

## 7. Site heterogeneity created by the measurement scale (Many Labs)
- **Model:** the true effect on the log-odds scale is the same at every site; sites differ only in their baseline rate.
- **Findings to reproduce:** τ correlates with effect size at r = .77 [.57, .91] for SMDs; 48/68 meta-analyses show no significant heterogeneity (Olsson-Collentine 2020).
- **Prediction:** for binary JDM outcomes, the site risk difference follows log OR × p₀(1 − p₀), and τ on the log-odds scale is about 0.
- **Data:**
  - Many Labs 1, OSF wx7ck: **CC0**.
  - Many Labs 2, OSF 8cd4r: **CC0**.
  - Many Labs 3, OSF ct89g: **CC-BY 4.0**.
- **Why novelty is 1:** ML2 framing already shows τ = .025. A group is actively working on this:
  - Fünderich et al. 2025 (https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-025-02879-w) and their preprint (https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/s82zr_v3);
  - Olsson-Collentine et al. 2023 (https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/jnb6e);
  - Beinhauer et al. 2025 (https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/u6anb_v1).
- **Effort:** R, 8–10 days.

## 8. Small-sample learning vs attitude change after feedback (CPC data)
- **Model:** choice follows the mean of k recalled outcomes. The "hot stove" effect needs partial feedback (Denrell & March 2001, https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.12.5.523.10092; Denrell 2007, https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295x.114.1.177). CPC feedback also shows the outcome of the option not chosen, so only reliance on small samples can be tested there.
- **Prediction:** learning predicts that the direction of each problem's shift follows the skew of its outcomes. An attitude account predicts a uniform shift toward risk that starts before any outcome is seen (Nasioulas et al. 2026, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-67729-x).
- **Data:**
  - CPC15, Zenodo 321652: **CC BY 4.0**.
  - CPC18, Zenodo 2571510: **CC BY 4.0**.
  - Wulff et al. 2018 database, Zenodo 1491449: **CC-BY-SA-4.0**.
  - choices13k has no licence and is excluded.
- **Why novelty is 1:** BEAST already predicts CPC18 with frozen parameters (Erev 2017, https://doi.org/10.1037/rev0000062; Plonsky 2025, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-025-02267-6).
- **Effort:** R, 8–12 days.

---

## Decisions for you
1. **Share-alike licence (CC-BY-SA, Wulff database):** it meets the rule that data must carry an explicit licence, but anything derived from it must carry the same licence. Accept?
2. **Dataverse CC0:** Becker 2019, Almaatouq 2020 and GJP are CC0 because that is Dataverse's default licence. I counted them as openly licensed.
3. **Gürçay 2015 data:** a copy sits inside Becker 2022's CC0 Dataverse record, but the person who deposited it may not own it. I recommend not using it.
4. **Design 6 (inner crowd):** drop it, or run it as a simulation plus a separate preregistration for new data collection?

## Open issues
- The Lichtenstein & Fischhoff magnitudes and the Baron/Satopää extremizing values were not extracted, so their tolerance bands cannot be set yet.
- How many Open Anchoring Quest items have large anchor spreads cannot be known without reading the data. Design 1 needs a preregistered minimum-count rule, which I included.
- Baron et al.'s argument that the median can separate the two sources of extremizing was taken from their abstract only.

Everything is in /tmp/jdmsim, outside the project: full texts, the anchoring simulation (`scratch_mh_anchor.py`), the DOI lists, and this report (`scratch_final_answer.md`).</result>

- **M1, resource-rational adjustment** (Lieder et al. 2018, https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8): a random-walk sampler starts at the anchor and takes t steps of size s·σᵢ.
- **M2, Anchor Integration Model** (Turner & Schley 2016, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003): the estimate is a fixed-weight (w) mix of the anchor and a belief sample.
- **M3, adjust until plausible** (Epley & Gilovich 2006, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2006.01704.x): adjustment stops at μᵢ ± kσᵢ.
- **M4, plausibility-gated selective accessibility** (Mussweiler & Strack 1999, https://doi.org/10.1006/jesp.1998.1364; Wegener et al. 2001, https://doi.org/10.1006/jesp.2000.1431): an anchor outside the plausible range loses its effect.

**Fixed vs fitted.**
- s, t, w and k are calibrated to Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995 before the data are loaded.
- One anchoring-index value does not pin down s and t. My scratch runs with (s, t) = (.5, 5), (.3, 10) and (1, 3) all give an index that rises with spread. So M1 is committed only to the *sign* of the slope, not to a numeric band.
- μᵢ is fitted per item from `true_value` and the anchored data.
- The dataset has no unanchored SD per item, so σᵢ is estimated from the pooled within-condition SD. The simulator computes the same estimate on its own simulated data, so real and simulated results are compared like for like.

**Findings to reproduce.**
1. Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995 (https://doi.org/10.1177/01461672952111004) found a mean anchoring index of 48.48% with anchors at the 15th and 85th percentiles. Lieder's model gave 53.22% and an item-level r(13) = .62 (from the Lieder preprint text). This is the calibration target; the test is item-level r ≥ .40.
2. Anchoring grows with distance from the true value: b = 0.040, k = 312, p < .001, "nonlinear but positive", with no inverted U. Pooled g = 0.689 [0.589, 0.789] (Röseler & Schütz 2022, https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn). Each model must predict a positive slope of g on distance.
3. Explicitly random anchors have much smaller effects (same source; also Schley & Weingarten 2026, https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03238). **M1 as published fails this target unless its starting point depends on how informative the anchor is. This is stated in advance.**
4. Time pressure is contested. Lieder et al. (https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-017-1288-6) found less adjustment when time is costly. Röseler et al. 2023 (https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/jztk2) found no time effect in 4 studies (N = 898). The paper must report this conflict.

**New prediction.** The measure is the anchoring index across log anchor spread in σ̂ units, where AI = Δ median log estimate / Δ log anchor.
- **M1:** AI rises, because the amount of adjustment levels off. My simulation gives .59 at z = 1, .79 at z = 4 and .88 at z = 8.
- **M2:** AI stays flat at w.
- **M3:** AI falls.
- **M4:** AI falls steeply and can turn negative.

The published positive g–distance slope already goes against M3 and M4. The open question is M1 against M2. Both predict a rising g, so only the index–spread slope separates them.

**Refutation rule.** Fit a multilevel regression of item-level index on log spread, with study as a random effect.
- A 95% CI entirely ≤ 0 refutes M1.
- A CI entirely > 0 refutes M2–M4.
- A CI that includes 0 with half-width below .05 supports M2.
- The preregistration also sets a minimum number of items with a large spread (e.g. ≥ 60 items with spread > 3σ̂). Below that, the test is declared uninformative.

**Data.** Open Anchoring Quest, https://osf.io/ygnvb/, **CC-BY 4.0** on the node that holds `OPAQ_JOPD.csv`. It has 96 studies, 21,359 participants, 412 items (355 with true values) and 88,914 trials (Röseler et al. 2022, https://doi.org/10.5334/jopd.67).
- **Optional arm:** Many Labs 1 (OSF wx7ck, **CC0**). There, anchoring SMDs were 1.21–2.53, τ .15–.69 and I² 40–91% (Olsson-Collentine et al. 2020, https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000294). The Open Anchoring Quest probably already contains these data, so this arm would not be an independent replication.

**Closest work.** Lieder 2018 (qualitative simulations of small classic studies); Röseler & Schütz 2022 (distance tested at the level of study effect sizes); Schley & Weingarten 2026 (extremity coded as binary; no effect); Turner & Schley 2016. No process model has been fitted to the Open Anchoring Quest.

**Effort.** R, 12–18 days.

## 2. Over/underconfidence from noise alone (GJP knowledge quizzes)

**Model.** An observer with zero bias answers 4-option items. Confidence is the ideal probability of being correct, plus reporting noise σ_r, clipped to the 25–100 scale.
- **Fitted:** item difficulty, person skill and σ_r.
- **Fixed:** bias = 0.

**Findings to reproduce.**
- The hard–easy effect: overconfidence on hard items, underconfidence on easy ones (Lichtenstein & Fischhoff 1977, https://doi.org/10.1016/0030-5073(77)90001-0; magnitudes UNVERIFIED).
- Juslin, Winman & Olsson 2000 (https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295x.107.2.384, abstract): the effect nearly disappears once scale ends and linear dependency are controlled, but selected and representative item sets still differ.
- The error model of Erev, Wallsten & Budescu 1994 (https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295x.101.3.519).
- Moore et al. 2017 (https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2016.2525, abstract): GJP tournament overconfidence was 3%, and 1% with teams and training.

**New prediction.** The slope of the hard–easy effect is already widely attributed to artefact. The open question is the overall level of over/underconfidence on researcher-selected items.
- The ecological account (overconfidence comes from how items are selected) predicts overconfidence beyond noise.
- The noise-only model predicts none.
- The simulator must model the floor at 25; most published targets use 2 options, with a floor at 50.

**Refutation rule.**
- **Main test:** overall bias outside the model's 95% predictive interval refutes noise-only. The interval is simulated on the real items and sample sizes.
- **Secondary test:** the hard–easy slope, compared with the same interval.
- **Precision check:** 47 items is few. Before preregistering, the simulator must show that the interval excludes a 5-point bias. If it does not, falsifiability drops to 2, and the Confidence Database arm becomes required.

**Data.**
- GJP, https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/BPCDH5, **CC0**. Two quizzes with a "probability that you are correct" rating (25–100) per item: 32 and 15 items (from the Dataverse README).
- Replication: the probability-scale subset of the Confidence Database, OSF s46pr, **CC0**. It has 145 datasets, more than 8,700 participants and about 4M trials (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-019-0813-1). The usable subset may be small.

**Closest work.** Guggenmos 2022 (https://doi.org/10.7554/elife.75420), one dataset; Merkle 2009 (https://doi.org/10.3758/pbr.16.1.204); Suantak et al. 1996 (https://doi.org/10.1006/obhd.1996.0074). I found no study that uses the GJP quizzes for calibration, but I did not search that point exhaustively.

**Effort.** R, 8–12 days.

## 3. Social-influence revision model with frozen parameters, lab to lab

**Model.** People revise their estimate in log space: x₂ = x₁ + S·(social − x₁).
- S is a mix of "keep" (S = 0), "adopt" (S = 1) and "compromise" (in between).
- The mix depends on the distance |D| between one's own estimate and the social information: ⟨S⟩ = α + β|D| (Jayles 2017). It also depends on direction, i.e. whether the social information is above or below one's own estimate (Kao 2018).
- It is fitted once on the Kao and Jayles figshare data, then frozen.

**Findings to reproduce.**
- Jayles et al. 2017 (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1703695114): median S = 0.34, with peaks at 0 and 1.
- Becker et al. 2017 (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1615978114; numbers from a summary tool's reading of the full text): in decentralized networks, median error fell 12% and mean error 10%. The correlation between initial error and revision size was ρ = .41, and it correlated ρ = −.71 with improvement across 59 tasks.
- Lorenz et al. 2011 (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1008636108): diversity fell while collective error barely changed.
- Mellers et al. 2014 (https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797614524255): GJP forecasters who saw the crowd's forecasts beat independent forecasters, t(1120) = 5.92.

**New prediction and refutation rule.** Given each group's observed initial estimates and network, the frozen model predicts the per-question change in mean and median error for the fixed networks of Becker et al. 2019. It is refuted if predicted and observed change correlate below .30, or if the signs match on fewer than 60% of questions.
- Almaatouq et al. 2020 is only a partial target: its networks rewire, which this model cannot predict.
- **GJP field arm (extension only).** In GJP year 1, forecasters were randomly assigned to see the crowd's forecasts or not. They made about 1.3 forecasts per question, so the crowd display mainly shaped the first forecast, not a revision. This arm needs an anchoring-type model, close to M2 in design 1.

**Data (licences checked).**
- Kao 2018: figshare 10.6084/m9.figshare.6120683, **CC BY 4.0**.
- Jayles, Sire & Kurvers 2021: figshare 12529571, **CC BY 4.0**.
- Becker 2019: Dataverse OE6UMR, **CC0**.
- Almaatouq 2020: Dataverse EOYZKH, **CC0**.
- GJP: **CC0**.
- Excluded (no licence or no deposit): Becker 2017, Lorenz 2011, Jayles 2017.

**Closest work.** Almaatouq et al. 2022 (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-20551-7) pooled 4 datasets, N = 2,885, descriptively. Pilgrim & Becker 2024 (arXiv:2407.00199) broke down the change in group error across 6 experiments. Nobody has made out-of-sample predictions with frozen parameters.

**Risk.** The main test rests on a single licensed dataset (Becker 2019).

**Effort.** R, 15–25 days.

## 4. Bayesian sampler as the reason forecasts need extremizing (GJP)
- **Model:** each forecaster reports (S + β)/(N + 2β), where S counts successes in N samples (Zhu, Sanborn & Chater 2020, https://doi.org/10.1037/rev0000190). Information overlap between forecasters is added. N, β and overlap are fitted on one GJP year.
- **Findings to reproduce:**
  - Overconfidence of 3% (Moore 2017).
  - Aggregates need to be pushed toward 0 or 1 ("extremizing"); the mean needs more than the median, and experts need less (Baron et al. 2014, https://doi.org/10.1287/deca.2014.0293, via Han & Budescu 2022, https://doi.org/10.1017/s1930297500009049; parameter values UNVERIFIED).
  - Lab estimates of N: median 2.65–8.25 (Sundh et al., https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0001414).
- **New prediction:** the sampler pulls each person's expected judgment toward 0.5, so the median also needs extremizing. Baron et al. argue noise affects only the mean. Across sub-crowds of size k, the median's extremizing need should level off around k ≈ 10. Information-diversity accounts (Satopää et al. 2016, https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.2015.1100621) predict it keeps rising.
- **Condition before preregistering:** both accounts can level off, so the simulator must first show the two separate under realistic overlap.
- **Why falsifiability is 2:** N can be tuned freely. Lab parameters would cap individual forecasts near .9. I expect GJP forecasters exceed that, but cannot check under the blinding rule.
- **Closest work:** the BIN model of Satopää 2021 (https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2020.3882); Zhu 2022 (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2022.105022). No sampler model has been applied to tournament aggregation.
- **Effort:** R, 15–20 days.

## 5. Advice taking: generating the three-peaked weight-of-advice distribution
- **Model:** the judge weights own estimate and advice in a Bayesian way, while unsure how accurate the advisor is. Two thresholds then produce keep / average / adopt. The peaks at 0, .5 and 1 must come out of the model, not be built in.
- **Findings to reproduce (numbers UNVERIFIED):**
  - Soll & Larrick 2009 (https://doi.org/10.1037/a0015145).
  - Yaniv 2004 (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obhdp.2003.08.002).
  - Bonaccio & Dalal 2006 (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obhdp.2006.07.001).
  - Schultze et al. 2015 (https://doi.org/10.1017/s1930297500003922).
- **Prediction:** "adopt" responses rise with the judge's low confidence faster than "average" responses do. The model derives the ratio.
- **Data:** Jaquiery & Yeung, OSF h254u, **CC-BY 4.0**. That trials contain an initial estimate, advice and a final estimate is UNVERIFIED.
- **Benchmark to beat:** Himmelstein 2022 (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmp.2022.102695), whose model fits the peaks rather than generating them.
- **Effort:** R, 10–15 days.

## 6. Inner crowd as an autocorrelated sampler over time
- **Model:** estimates come from an autocorrelated sampler (Zhu et al. 2024, https://doi.org/10.1037/rev0000427). The number of hidden steps grows with the log of the delay.
- **Findings to reproduce** (Vul & Pashler 2008, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2008.02136.x): averaging two guesses cut error by [2.5%, 10.4%] when the second guess was immediate (worth 1.11 people), and by [11.6%, 20.4%] after 3 weeks (worth 1.32 people).
- **Data:** none usable. van Dolder & van den Assem 2018 is under a non-disclosure agreement, and Steegen et al. 2014 (OSF ivfu6) has no licence.
- **Novelty:** the highest here; Dasgupta et al. 2017 (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2017.05.001) treated it only qualitatively. The empirical test needs new data.
- **Effort:** R, 6–8 days for the simulation only.

## 7. Site heterogeneity created by the measurement scale (Many Labs)
- **Model:** the true effect on the log-odds scale is the same at every site; sites differ only in their baseline rate.
- **Findings to reproduce:** τ correlates with effect size at r = .77 [.57, .91] for SMDs; 48/68 meta-analyses show no significant heterogeneity (Olsson-Collentine 2020).
- **Prediction:** for binary JDM outcomes, the site risk difference follows log OR × p₀(1 − p₀), and τ on the log-odds scale is about 0.
- **Data:**
  - Many Labs 1, OSF wx7ck: **CC0**.
  - Many Labs 2, OSF 8cd4r: **CC0**.
  - Many Labs 3, OSF ct89g: **CC-BY 4.0**.
- **Why novelty is 1:** ML2 framing already shows τ = .025. A group is actively working on this:
  - Fünderich et al. 2025 (https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-025-02879-w) and their preprint (https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/s82zr_v3);
  - Olsson-Collentine et al. 2023 (https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/jnb6e);
  - Beinhauer et al. 2025 (https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/u6anb_v1).
- **Effort:** R, 8–10 days.

## 8. Small-sample learning vs attitude change after feedback (CPC data)
- **Model:** choice follows the mean of k recalled outcomes. The "hot stove" effect needs partial feedback (Denrell & March 2001, https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.12.5.523.10092; Denrell 2007, https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295x.114.1.177). CPC feedback also shows the outcome of the option not chosen, so only reliance on small samples can be tested there.
- **Prediction:** learning predicts that the direction of each problem's shift follows the skew of its outcomes. An attitude account predicts a uniform shift toward risk that starts before any outcome is seen (Nasioulas et al. 2026, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-67729-x).
- **Data:**
  - CPC15, Zenodo 321652: **CC BY 4.0**.
  - CPC18, Zenodo 2571510: **CC BY 4.0**.
  - Wulff et al. 2018 database, Zenodo 1491449: **CC-BY-SA-4.0**.
  - choices13k has no licence and is excluded.
- **Why novelty is 1:** BEAST already predicts CPC18 with frozen parameters (Erev 2017, https://doi.org/10.1037/rev0000062; Plonsky 2025, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-025-02267-6).
- **Effort:** R, 8–12 days.

---

## Decisions for you
1. **Share-alike licence (CC-BY-SA, Wulff database):** it meets the rule that data must carry an explicit licence, but anything derived from it must carry the same licence. Accept?
2. **Dataverse CC0:** Becker 2019, Almaatouq 2020 and GJP are CC0 because that is Dataverse's default licence. I counted them as openly licensed.
3. **Gürçay 2015 data:** a copy sits inside Becker 2022's CC0 Dataverse record, but the person who deposited it may not own it. I recommend not using it.
4. **Design 6 (inner crowd):** drop it, or run it as a simulation plus a separate preregistration for new data collection?

## Open issues
- The Lichtenstein & Fischhoff magnitudes and the Baron/Satopää extremizing values were not extracted, so their tolerance bands cannot be set yet.
- How many Open Anchoring Quest items have large anchor spreads cannot be known without reading the data. Design 1 needs a preregistered minimum-count rule, which I included.
- Baron et al.'s argument that the median can separate the two sources of extremizing was taken from their abstract only.
