Schütz, Dolling, et al., 2020).

       As most anchoring questions assess only two anchors, and each participant is presented

with only one of them (one is larger and one is smaller than the correct answer), we

operationalized anchor extremeness that was based on the true value as the mean relative

anchoring distance from the true value per anchoring item. That is, we computed the mean of the

absolute distance between the anchor and the true value (in cases where a true value existed)

divided by the true value such that a value of 1 indicated that the anchors were equal to the true

values and a value of 2 meant that anchors were on average 2 (or 1/2) times the true value.

Description of Stimuli

       For anchoring effects, a property of a stimulus (e.g., height of the Eiffel tower) has to be

estimated. In most studies, researchers simply ask participants whether the Eiffel tower is taller
 ANCHORING EFFECTS META-ANALYSIS                                                             12



other than the Random-Effects Multilevel Model, data had to be aggregated by study.

Moderator Analyses

       We conducted independent tests of moderators using multilevel random-effects models

and significance tests (Viechtbauer, 2010). Among continuous moderators (Table 2), only the

anchor distance had an effect on the anchoring effect size, which was positive. Among

categorical moderators (Table 3), type of anchor (no effects for subliminal or random anchors

and large effects for fixed and relevant anchors), type of task (e.g., largest effect for predicted

happiness, no effect for price estimates), comparative questions (small effect for paradigms

without comparative questions, large effect for those with comparative questions), and type of

stimulus (no effect for audio/visual/image, large effect for brief written descriptions) affected

anchoring effect size.

Table 2

Overview of Continuous Moderator Effects
 ANCHORING EFFECTS META-ANALYSIS                                                        21




 Moderator                  M          SD         Min          Max           b           k         p

 Relative distance
 between anchor and        1.25       1.86        -1.03       13.96        0.040        312      < .001
 true value

 Proportion of female
                           0.60       0.15        0.29         0.92        0.056        292      .868
 participants


characteristics), others had the potential to nullify the effect (e.g., type of response scale). We

next explain how our findings (see Table 4) are related to previous research.

Moderators of Anchoring Effects

       The relative distance between anchors and true values was strongly associated with the

size of anchoring effects, with more extreme anchors leading to larger effect sizes. The

proportion of female participants, the sample mean age, the publication year, and monetary

incentives for participation or for accuracy did not affect anchoring effect size. Note that

incentives for accurate estimation not reducing anchoring is only partly consistent with past

knowledge questions in that they are scalable. Participants can even receive two stimuli with the

same true value (e.g., 42 dots) and different anchors (e.g., 21 and 84) without even noticing that

they have already seen the stimulus.

        We believe that future research would benefit from exploring more precise measures than

effect sizes such as Cohen’s d or Hedges’s g. For example, the relative strength of adjustment

could be used because it provides a unitless and general metric. Standardized measures could

help to formalize the relationship between anchor distance and adjustment strength as has been

done in similar fields (e.g., Schultze et al., 2015).

Anchoring Research as a Poster Child for Open Science

        As we found almost as many preregistered studies (k = 182) as nonpreregistered studies

(k = 211), we are optimistic that the field of anchoring is adopting new standards of open

content.thinking: Scoping's complete — two of three agents converged on the same top pick: an item-level test of anchoring process models using the Open Anchoring Quest data, which its own meta-analysis explicitly calls for. Now I'll run a targeted novelty check and have codex and agy critique the shortlist in parallel.

input.command:
mkdir -p ~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/reviews/scoping && cd ~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/reviews/scoping && cat > prompt_shortlist.txt <<'EOF'
You are a senior judgement-and-decision-making (JDM) researcher and methodologist acting as a critical second opinion. We must choose ONE study for a preregistered paper that uses no new data: either a secondary analysis of an openly licensed dataset or a simulation study that can fail against open data. Do NOT open or download any data files (blinding: the preregistration must precede any contact with outcome variables). You may search the literature.

Shortlist:

A. ANCHORING PROCESS MODELS vs ANCHOR EXTREMITY (simulation + secondary data). Data: Open Anchoring Quest (OpAQ; Röseler et al. 2022, J Open Psychol Data, doi 10.5334/jopd.67; OSF ygnvb, CC-BY 4.0): 96 studies, ~21,000 participants, 412 items (355 with true values), 88,914 trial-level estimates, with anchor value, anchorhigh (high/low), anchortype (random/fixed/relevant/self-generated), comparative question, incentive, scale type, task type. Four process models make different predictions for how the *proportional* anchoring index (AI = difference in central tendency of high-anchor vs low-anchor estimates divided by the difference between anchors, on a log or raw scale) changes as the anchors become more extreme relative to the uncertainty of the quantity: (M1) resource-rational adjustment from the anchor with a limited number of steps (Lieder et al. 2018, Psychon Bull Rev) -> AI rises with extremity (adjustment saturates); (M2) anchor integration / constant-weight averaging (Turner & Schley 2016) -> AI flat; (M3) insufficient adjustment until the edge of the plausible range (Epley & Gilovich 2006) -> AI falls; (M4) plausibility-gated selective accessibility (Mussweiler & Strack; Wegener et al. 2001) -> AI falls steeply, can reverse. The meta-analysis on the same data (Röseler & Schütz, PsyArXiv wf2tn) found Hedges' g rises with relative anchor distance (b = 0.040, k = 312) and explicitly called for "relative strength of adjustment ... a unitless metric ... to formalize the relationship between anchor distance and adjustment strength". Plan: item-level (item x study) AI regressed on log anchor extremity with random effects for study; simulate each model through the same estimator to get predictions.

B. DECISION NOISE AND THE RISK-ELICITATION PUZZLE (simulation + secondary data). Basel-Berlin Risk Study (Frey et al. 2017, OSF rce7g, CC-BY): simulate one noisy expected-utility agent per person through each task's mechanics and test whether noise alone reproduces the observed pattern of between-task correlations better than stable preferences. Risks: active 2026 literature (arXiv 2609.12291; 2607.05686), possible DOB fields.

C. NOISE-ONLY OVER/UNDERCONFIDENCE in Good Judgment Project general-knowledge quizzes (CC0): a zero-bias noisy observer; test whether observed overall over/underconfidence falls outside the model's predictive interval. Only 32 + 15 items.

D. FROZEN-PARAMETER SOCIAL-INFLUENCE REVISION MODEL fitted on Kao 2018 / Jayles 2021 (CC-BY) and used to predict per-question change in crowd error in Becker et al. 2019 (CC0). Main test rests on one dataset.

Questions:
1. For each option: can it actually fail (what result would refute it, and is that result plausible)? Has it essentially been done already (name papers)? What is the most serious threat to validity?
2. For option A specifically: (a) What is the right way to define "anchor extremity" when the person's uncertainty about the quantity is unknown? Options: log(anchor/true value); distance in units of the SD of estimates (which are themselves anchored); or distance in units of the between-person SD of the pooled estimates. Which is defensible and outcome-free enough? (b) What confounds threaten an across-item regression (anchors chosen by original authors, item types, scale bounds, closed scales, regression-to-the-mean, outliers, truncation)? (c) Is there a mechanical/artefactual reason AI would fall or rise with extremity regardless of process (e.g., bounded response scales, skew, log transformation)? How should the analysis guard against it? (d) Would a within-item comparison (items presented with more than two anchor values, e.g. moderate vs extreme) be much stronger, and how could it be preregistered when we don't yet know how many such items exist?
3. Which option would you choose, and what would make it publishable in a good JDM journal (e.g., Judgment and Decision Making, J Behav Decis Making, Decision, Psychonomic Bull Rev)?
End with your final answer under a heading "## Answer".
EOF
cp prompt_shortlist.txt prompt_shortlist_agy.txt && echo "End your response with the answer itself under a heading \`## Answer\`." >> prompt_shortlist_agy.txt; echo ok

input.prompt:
Task: a thorough novelty/crowding check for a planned preregistered study, and a list of the 5 closest papers with exact details. Write results to ~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/scoping/anchoring_novelty_check.md and return a summary.

Planned study: Using the Open Anchoring Quest (OpAQ) dataset (Röseler et al. 2022, J Open Psychol Data, doi 10.5334/jopd.67; OSF ygnvb; 412 anchoring items, 96 studies, 88,914 trial-level estimates), test how the PROPORTIONAL anchoring index (AI = difference between high-anchor and low-anchor central estimates / difference between the anchors; Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995 style) changes with anchor extremity (anchor distance relative to the true value and/or to uncertainty about the quantity), at the item level, and compare against predictions simulated from four process models: resource-rational adjustment (Lieder, Griffiths, Huys & Goodman 2018, Psychon Bull Rev, two papers), anchor integration model (Turner & Schley 2016, Cogn Psychol), insufficient adjustment to plausible range (Epley & Gilovich 2006), selective accessibility / plausibility (Mussweiler & Strack 1999; Wegener, Petty et al. 2001; Strack & Mussweiler 1997). Background: the meta-analysis on OpAQ (Röseler & Schütz, "Hanging the anchor off a new ship", PsyArXiv doi 10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn) regressed Hedges' g on mean relative anchor distance and found a positive nonlinear relationship; it called for a unitless relative-adjustment metric. A full text is at /tmp/jdmsim/hanging.txt and the OpAQ data paper at /tmp/jdmsim/opaq.txt.

Do NOT download or open any data files (blinding rule). Read papers only.

Check specifically:
1. Has Röseler & Schütz been published in a journal since (find the version of record and whether the distance analysis changed)? Are there 2023–2026 papers reusing OpAQ (OpenAlex: works citing 10.5334/jopd.67 and citing the meta-analysis preprint; OpenAlex keys: run `set -a; source ~/.claude/api_keys.env; set +a`; use `&api_key=$OPENALEX_API_KEY`; rotate across `$OPENALEX_API_KEYS` if you hit quota)? Summarise what each did.
2. Has anyone tested the anchoring INDEX (proportional adjustment) as a function of anchor extremity across many items, or fitted process models to multi-study anchoring data? Check: Schley & Weingarten (Management Science 2026?, doi 10.1287/mnsc.2023.03238; and PsyArXiv teq7k); Bystranowski et al. 2021 (anchoring in legal judgments meta-analysis); Chapman & Johnson 1994 "The limits of anchoring"; Thorsteinson 2011; Wegener et al. 2001 & 2010; Mussweiler & Strack 2001; Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995; Lieder et al. 2018a/b; Turner & Schley 2016; Schultze, Rakotoarisoa & Schulz-Hardt 2015 (distance between initial estimate and advice); Simmons, LeBoeuf & Nelson 2010; Frederick & Mochon 2012 (scale distortion); Townson 2019; Bahník & Strack; Harris et al. 2019; Shanks et al. 2020; Röseler et al. 2023/2024 papers; any 2024–2026 computational anchoring model papers (search "anchoring" + "computational model" / "Bayesian" / "resource-rational" / "sampling" 2022–2026).
3. For each of the 5 closest papers: full citation, DOI verified via https://api.crossref.org/works/<DOI> (title and first author must match), what they did precisely (design, measure, key numeric result), and what our planned study would add relative to it.
4. Any direct quantitative predictions in the literature for how the anchoring index varies with extremity (e.g., Jacowitz & Kahneman found AI ~ .49 with 15th/85th percentile anchors; any studies with very extreme/implausible anchors reporting AI or proportional adjustment — e.g., Strack & Mussweiler 1997 implausible anchors, Chapman & Johnson 1994, Wegener 2001, Mussweiler & Strack 2000 — give numbers).
Verdict at the end: NOT DONE / PARTLY DONE / DONE, with confidence and what is still open.

# Download the Open Anchoring Quest (OpAQ) trial-level data and verify its hash.
# Writes only the header row to data/variables_seen.txt; no data values are read here.

source_url <- "https://osf.io/download/s4zgw/"   # opaq_70a.csv, OSF ygnvb, CC-BY 4.0
expected_sha256 <- "18ec245c45427f43"            # prefix of the SHA-256 listed by the OSF API
raw_path <- file.path("data", "raw", "opaq_70a.csv")

sha256_file <- function(path) {
  out <- system2("shasum", c("-a", "256", shQuote(path)), stdout = TRUE)
  strsplit(out, " ")[[1]][1]
}

dir.create(dirname(raw_path), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
if (!file.exists(raw_path) || !startsWith(sha256_file(raw_path), expected_sha256)) {
  tmp <- paste0(raw_path, ".part")
  download.file(source_url, tmp, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
  file.rename(tmp, raw_path)
}
hash <- sha256_file(raw_path)
stopifnot(startsWith(hash, expected_sha256))

writeLines(readLines(raw_path, n = 1, warn = FALSE), file.path("data", "variables_seen.txt"))
writeLines(c(
  "# Provenance",
  "",
  paste0("- Source: ", source_url, " (opaq_70a.csv, OSF project ygnvb, dated 2023-02-10)"),
  "- Licence: CC-By Attribution 4.0 International (OSF node licence field)",
  "- Dataset paper: Röseler et al. (2022), Journal of Open Psychology Data, https://doi.org/10.5334/jopd.67",
  paste0("- SHA-256: ", hash),
  paste0("- Size (bytes): ", file.size(raw_path))
), file.path("data", "provenance.md"))
message("OpAQ data present, hash verified: ", hash)

### 1. Comparative Evaluation of the Four Shortlisted Options

---

#### Option A: Anchoring Process Models vs. Anchor Extremity (OpAQ)
* **Can it fail, and is that result plausible?**
  * **Yes, it can decisively fail.** The four candidate models make qualitatively distinct predictions for the slope of the Anchoring Index ($AI = \frac{\Delta \text{Estimates}}{\Delta \text{Anchors}}$) across anchor extremity:
    * **$M_1$ (Resource-Rational Adjustment; Lieder et al., 2018):** Adjustment steps are cost-penalized. At extreme anchors, adjustment terminates early relative to the distance required, causing estimates to remain pulled far toward the anchor; thus, proportional $AI$ is predicted to rise or remain elevated.
    * **$M_2$ (Anchor Integration Model; Turner & Schley, 2016):** Constant-weight averaging predicts that the anchor’s proportional weight $w$ is invariant to extremity; thus, the slope is flat ($d(AI)/d(\text{extremity}) = 0$).
    * **$M_3$ (Insufficient Adjustment to Plausible Boundary; Epley & Gilovich, 2006):** Search terminates at the nearest boundary of a subjective credibility range $[L, U]$. Once an anchor lies beyond this range, the estimate stops at the boundary ($U$ or $L$), leaving $\Delta \text{Estimates} \le U - L$ fixed while $\Delta \text{Anchors} \to \infty$. Thus, $AI$ must strictly fall toward 0.
    * **$M_4$ (Plausibility-Gated Selective Accessibility; Strack & Mussweiler, 1997; Wegener et al., 2001):** Highly extreme or implausible anchors fail to activate target-consistent features, causing $AI$ to collapse steeply or produce contrast.
  * **Plausibility:** Highly plausible. Classical experimental papers (e.g., Chapman & Johnson, 1994; Jacowitz & Kahneman, 1995; Sleeth-Keppler, 2013) demonstrate that while *absolute* mean differences often grow with anchor distance, the *proportional* effect ($AI$) reliably decays for extreme anchors. Rejecting $M_1$ or $M_2$ is empirically likely.
* **Has it essentially been done already?**
  * **No.** Key components exist, but they have never been synthesized into a competitive computational model test on open meta-analytic data:
    * Jacowitz & Kahneman (1995) introduced $AI$, but only evaluated 15th vs. 85th percentile anchors.
    * Wegener et al. (2001) tested extreme vs. moderate anchors, but focused on absolute effect sizes in small bespoke experiments.
    * Turner & Schley (2016) and Lieder et al. (2018) formulated their respective models, but Lieder et al. tested theirs on synthetic numerical dot-estimation tasks rather than semantic general-knowledge corpora.
    * Röseler & Schütz (2022, PsyArXiv `wf2tn`) conducted a meta-analysis on OpAQ, but modeled standardized mean differences (**Hedges' $g$**, finding $g$ increases with distance, $b = 0.040$) rather than the Anchoring Index ($AI$). They explicitly called for a unitless metric to model the adjustment-extremity relationship.
* **Most serious threat to validity:**
  * **Severe cross-item and design confounding.** In OpAQ, anchor extremity was not randomly assigned across items. Researchers chose anchors idiosyncratically; items with high underlying uncertainty were assigned wider anchors. Furthermore, items with bounded scales (percentages, ratings) mechanically truncate responses near the boundary, compressing $AI$ regardless of psychological process.

---

#### Option B: Decision Noise and the Risk-Elicitation Puzzle (Basel-Berlin Risk Study)
* **Can it fail, and is that result plausible?**
  * **Yes, but it sets up a known strawman.** If a pure-noise agent cannot reproduce the observed low-to-moderate positive correlations among lottery tasks ($r \approx 0.15 - 0.30$) or fails out-of-sample likelihood tests against a model with heterogeneous risk preferences, it fails. That it will fail is virtually certain: pure noise models predict zero correlation across structurally distinct tasks unless driven by shared choice-set mechanics.
* **Has it essentially been done already?**
  * **Yes, extensively.** Decomposing decision noise versus preference heterogeneity on the Basel-Berlin Risk Study (BBRS; Frey et al., 2017) has already been published by the original team (Pedroni, Frey, Bruhin, Dutilh, Hertwig, & Rieskamp, 2017, *eLife*) and followed up by structural econometrics literature (e.g., Enke & Graeber, 2023; Beauchamp et al., 2020; Vieider, 2021). Furthermore, recent preprints (e.g., arXiv:2607.05686, arXiv:2609.12291) directly benchmark stochastic choice models and decision noise against cross-task risk correlations.
* **Most serious threat to validity:**
  * **Total lack of novelty and extreme competition.** The paper would enter a heavily saturated field where the baseline hypothesis ("noise alone explains all cross-task variance") is already widely rejected in favor of joint latent-trait plus cognitive-uncertainty models. Additionally, BBRS raw files contain potentially sensitive demographic fields.

---

#### Option C: Noise-Only Over/Underconfidence (Good Judgment Project)
* **Can it fail, and is that result plausible?**
  * **Yes.** If empirical confidence-accuracy calibration falls outside the posterior predictive interval of a zero-bias noisy observer (e.g., persistent overconfidence on easy items or severe skew), the model fails.
* **Has it essentially been done already?**
  * **Yes, repeatedly for 30 years.** The "noise/error model" of overconfidence and the hard-easy effect is one of the oldest debates in JDM (Erev, Wallsten, & Budescu, 1994, *Psychol Rev*; Soll, 1996; Juslin, Winman, & Olsson, 2000, *Psychol Rev*; Moore & Healy, 2008). Re-running this on GJP quizzes is a routine re-demonstration.
* **Most serious threat to validity:**
  * **Fatal sample size ($32 + 15 = 47$ items).** Item-sampling variance in calibration research is notoriously high. With only 47 items, statistical power to distinguish true epistemic overconfidence from response-scale noise is inadequate; posterior predictive intervals will be too wide to draw rigorous theoretical conclusions.

---

#### Option D: Frozen-Parameter Social-Influence Revision Model
* **Can it fail, and is that result plausible?**
  * **Yes.** Out-of-sample predictions on Becker et al. (2019) could correlate $\le 0$ with observed question-level error changes or perform worse than an unweighted mean.
* **Has it essentially been done already?**
  * **Yes.** Jayles et al. (2017, 2020), Becker et al. (2017, 2019), and Almaatouq et al. (2020, 2021) have systematically cross-fitted linear and non-linear revision functions (e.g., French-Harary-DeGroot, distance-weighted averaging) across crowd estimation paradigms.
* **Most serious threat to validity:**
  * **Single-dataset target with severe interface confounds.** The out-of-sample test rests on exactly one dataset with few questions. Differences in user interface (e.g., displaying peer medians vs. full distributions vs. network neighbor avatars) alter social weighting, meaning a frozen-parameter model will likely fail due to task-display idiosyncrasies rather than psychological validity.

---

### 2. Methodological Blueprint for Option A

#### (a) Defining "Anchor Extremity" Without Knowing Individual Uncertainty
* **Why Options 2 and 3 are fundamentally invalid:**
  * *Option 2 (SD of within-condition anchored estimates):* Contaminated by the treatment. Anchoring can induce consensus or bi-modality, directly altering variance post-treatment.
  * *Option 3 (Between-person SD of pooled estimates):* **Mathematically fatal collider/endogeneity.** The pooled variance across high and low anchor conditions contains the treatment effect:
    $$\text{Var}(\text{Pooled}) = \frac{\text{Var}(Y_H) + \text{Var}(Y_L)}{2} + \frac{(\bar{Y}_H - \bar{Y}_L)^2}{4}$$
    Items with large anchoring effects automatically have larger pooled SDs. Dividing anchor distance by this pooled SD creates a mechanical negative correlation between extremity and effect size.
* **The Defensible, Outcome-Free Solution:**
  1. **Primary Metric (Relative Design Distance on Log Scale):** For open-scale positive ratio items (355 of 412 items in OpAQ), define anchor extremity relative to the true value:
     $$\text{Extremity}_A = |\ln(A) - \ln(\text{True})| \quad \text{or} \quad \Delta \ln(A) = \ln(A_{\text{high}}) - \ln(A_{\text{low}})$$
     This relies solely on experimental design parameters ($A$) and factual ground truth ($\text{True}$), preserving strict outcome blinding.
  2. **Controlling for Item-Level Uncertainty:** Because an anchor of $3 \times \text{True}$ is plausible for national populations but absurd for human body temperature, item uncertainty must be accounted for without using anchored responses. Two preregisterable strategies:
     * *Normative Anchor-Percentile Coding:* Many studies in OpAQ used the Jacowitz & Kahneman (1995) protocol, where anchors were established as specific percentiles (e.g., 15th vs. 85th) of a pilot calibration sample. The design metadata (where recorded) provides a standardized uncertainty metric.
     * *Hierarchical Item Random Intercepts:* Include random intercepts and random slopes for item ID ($\sim (1 + \text{Extremity} \mid \text{Item})$). This isolates the extremity slope within items that share the same underlying uncertainty distribution.

---

#### (b) Confounds Threatening an Across-Item Regression
1. **Endogenous Anchor Selection:** Experimenters set wider anchor intervals for items they intuitively knew had higher uncertainty, confounding anchor distance with item ambiguity.
2. **Scale Boundedness and Closed Scales:** Items assessing percentages ($0-100\%$), probabilities, or bounded Likert scales constrain estimates. If an extreme anchor lies near or beyond a boundary (e.g., $95\%$ or $110\%$), participant estimates cannot exceed $100\%$, artificially capping the numerator of $AI$.
3. **Format and Anchortype Heterogeneity:** OpAQ combines provided anchors (selective accessibility; Strack & Mussweiler) with self-generated anchors (insufficient adjustment; Epley & Gilovich). Pooling these without an interaction term confounds process mechanisms.
4. **Heavy Tails and Multiplicative Noise:** Estimates of open ratio quantities (e.g., populations) are log-normally distributed. Outliers in raw space can dominate arithmetic means, generating unstable $AI$ values.

---

#### (c) Mechanical and Artefactual Drivers of $AI$
* **The Inherent Denominator Explosion:**
  The Anchoring Index is defined as:
  $$AI = \frac{\bar{Y}_{\text{high}} - \bar{Y}_{\text{low}}}{A_{\text{high}} - A_{\text{low}}}$$
  Because human estimates are naturally constrained by credibility or scale bounds (e.g., $|\bar{Y}_{\text{high}} - \bar{Y}_{\text{low}}| \le B$), as anchor distance $A_{\text{high}} - A_{\text{low}} \to \infty$, the denominator grows indefinitely while the numerator is bounded. **Therefore, $AI$ must mechanically decline toward zero at extreme distances under almost any bounded generative process.**
* **Safeguards Against Mechanical Artifacts:**
  1. **Simulate a Zero-Adjustment / Bounded Null Agent:** Pass a synthetic agent with fixed subjective bounds $[L_i, U_i]$ (who does not adjust from anchors at all, but simply samples from their prior truncated to the scale) through the exact experimental designs. The empirical regression slope must be benchmarked against this mechanical baseline to verify whether human $AI$ drops faster or slower than purely mechanical bounding predicts.
  2. **Reformulate the Estimator as Elasticity:** Instead of regressing the composite ratio $AI$, estimate a trial-level log-log regression:
     $$\ln(Y_{ijk}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \ln(A_{ijk}) + \beta_2 \ln(\text{True}_i) + u_i + v_j + \epsilon_{ijk}$$
     Here, $\beta_1$ represents the direct elasticity of estimates with respect to anchors. A model predicting saturation ($M_1$) predicts $\beta_1$ to increase with extremity, whereas boundary models ($M_3, M_4$) predict $\beta_1 \to 0$ for extreme anchors.
  3. **Restrict Primary Process Tests to Unbounded Ratio Scales:** Filter out closed scales ($0-100\%$, ratings) for the primary model horse race, analyzing bounded items in a dedicated secondary beta/tobit model.

---

#### (d) Within-Item Comparisons and Preregistration Strategy
* **Is a within-item comparison stronger?**
  **Yes, substantially.** Comparing different anchor extremities across the *same* item eliminates all item-level confounds (true value, domain familiarity, scale bounds, prior distribution).
* **How to preregister without unblinding the outcome data:**
  You can inspect and filter design variables (`item_id`, `anchor_value`, `anchor_high`, `study_id`, `scale_type`) without looking at participant estimates (`estimate`).
  * **Preregistered Two-Tier Contingency Protocol:**
    1. **Tier 1 (Within-Item Subset):** Define an automated algorithmic filter: select all unique items that were administered with $\ge 2$ distinct high-anchor values or distinct anchor distances across studies or conditions. Set a preregistered sample threshold:
       > *"If at least $K \ge 20$ items have multiple anchor distances with $N \ge 50$ per condition, Tier 1 is our primary confirmatory test."*
    2. **Tier 2 (Full-Corpus Mundlak Decomposition):** For the full dataset, specify a within-between mixed-effects model (Mundlak / Bell & Jones, 2015). Decompose anchor extremity $E_{ij}$ for item $i$ in study $j$ into:
       * The item-mean extremity: $\bar{E}_i$ (between-item variation)
       * The within-item deviation: $(E_{ij} - \bar{E}_i)$ (pure within-item variation)
       The coefficient on $(E_{ij} - \bar{E}_i)$ isolates the unconfounded within-item causal effect of extremity across the entire corpus.

---

### 3. Recommendation and Path to Publication

## Answer

### Recommended Choice: Option A (Anchoring Process Models vs. Anchor Extremity)

Option A is the strongest, most viable project. Options B, C, and D suffer from critical flaws: Option B is heavily saturated and risks immediate scooping; Option C is fatally underpowered ($N = 47$ items); and Option D relies on a single target dataset with severe interface confounds. 

Option A leverages a massive open dataset (OpAQ: 96 studies, ~21,000 participants, 412 items) to resolve an explicit, unmet demand in the literature (Röseler & Schütz, 2022). It pits four foundational, competing theoretical frameworks against one another in a formal computational simulation.

### Roadmap to a Top-Tier JDM Publication (*Decision*, *Psychonomic Bulletin & Review*, or *Judgment and Decision Making*):

1. **Synthetic-to-Empirical Forward Simulation:**
   * Write explicit generative computational models for all four candidate processes:
     * $M_1$: Resource-rational random walk with step-cost stopping (Lieder et al., 2018).
     * $M_2$: Constant-weight anchor integration (Turner & Schley, 2016).
     * $M_3$: Sequential adjustment to the boundary of subjective plausibility (Epley & Gilovich, 2006).
     * $M_4$: Kernel-density plausibility-gated selective accessibility (Strack & Mussweiler, 1997).
   * Simulate synthetic agents through the exact item-anchor pairs present in OpAQ. Fit the identical statistical regression pipeline to both simulated and empirical data to generate distinctive model-signature curves.
2. **Defensible, Outcome-Free Metrics:**
   * Pre-register relative anchor distance on the log scale ($|\ln(A) - \ln(\text{True})|$) for all positive ratio items as the primary extremity metric.
   * Completely reject pooled or within-condition response SDs to avoid endogeneity.
3. **Mundlak Within-Between Item Decomposition:**
   * Implement a hierarchical mixed-effects model separating within-item extremity deviations from between-item averages. This eliminates cross-item selection bias and guarantees valid causal inference even if multi-anchor items are limited.
4. **Benchmarking Against a Bounded Null Model:**
   * Explicitly account for the mechanical denominator explosion of $AI$ by simulating a zero-adjustment bounded agent, demonstrating whether human adjustment decay exceeds algebraic scaling constraints.
5. **The `anchortype` Moderation Test:**
   * Exploit the `anchortype` variable in OpAQ (self-generated vs. provided anchors). $M_3$ was formulated specifically for self-generated anchors, whereas $M_4$ was formulated for provided anchors. Testing whether the extremity slope interacts with `anchortype` provides an unprecedented empirical test of the dual-mechanism debate of anchoring.

  Because human estimates are naturally constrained by credibility or scale bounds (e.g., $|\bar{Y}_{\text{high}} - \bar{Y}_{\text{low}}| \le B$), as anchor distance $A_{\text{high}} - A_{\text{low}} \to \infty$, the denominator grows indefinitely while the numerator is bounded. **Therefore, $AI$ must mechanically decline toward zero at extreme distances under almost any bounded generative process.**
* **Safeguards Against Mechanical Artifacts:**
  1. **Simulate a Zero-Adjustment / Bounded Null Agent:** Pass a synthetic agent with fixed subjective bounds $[L_i, U_i]$ (who does not adjust from anchors at all, but simply samples from their prior truncated to the scale) through the exact experimental designs. The empirical regression slope must be benchmarked against this mechanical baseline to verify whether human $AI$ drops faster or slower than purely mechanical bounding predicts.
  2. **Reformulate the Estimator as Elasticity:** Instead of regressing the composite ratio $AI$, estimate a trial-level log-log regression:
     $$\ln(Y_{ijk}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \ln(A_{ijk}) + \beta_2 \ln(\text{True}_i) + u_i + v_j + \epsilon_{ijk}$$
     Here, $\beta_1$ represents the direct elasticity of estimates with respect to anchors. A model predicting saturation ($M_1$) predicts $\beta_1$ to increase with extremity, whereas boundary models ($M_3, M_4$) predict $\beta_1 \to 0$ for extreme anchors.
  3. **Restrict Primary Process Tests to Unbounded Ratio Scales:** Filter out closed scales ($0-100\%$, ratings) for the primary model horse race, analyzing bounded items in a dedicated secondary beta/tobit model.

---

#### (d) Within-Item Comparisons and Preregistration Strategy
* **Is a within-item comparison stronger?**
  **Yes, substantially.** Comparing different anchor extremities across the *same* item eliminates all item-level confounds (true value, domain familiarity, scale bounds, prior distribution).
* **How to preregister without unblinding the outcome data:**
  You can inspect and filter design variables (`item_id`, `anchor_value`, `anchor_high`, `study_id`, `scale_type`) without looking at participant estimates (`estimate`).
  * **Preregistered Two-Tier Contingency Protocol:**
    1. **Tier 1 (Within-Item Subset):** Define an automated algorithmic filter: select all unique items that were administered with $\ge 2$ distinct high-anchor values or distinct anchor distances across studies or conditions. Set a preregistered sample threshold:
       > *"If at least $K \ge 20$ items have multiple anchor distances with $N \ge 50$ per condition, Tier 1 is our primary confirmatory test."*
    2. **Tier 2 (Full-Corpus Mundlak Decomposition):** For the full dataset, specify a within-between mixed-effects model (Mundlak / Bell & Jones, 2015). Decompose anchor extremity $E_{ij}$ for item $i$ in study $j$ into:
       * The item-mean extremity: $\bar{E}_i$ (between-item variation)
       * The within-item deviation: $(E_{ij} - \bar{E}_i)$ (pure within-item variation)
       The coefficient on $(E_{ij} - \bar{E}_i)$ isolates the unconfounded within-item causal effect of extremity across the entire corpus.

---

### 3. Recommendation and Path to Publication

## Answer

### Recommended Choice: Option A (Anchoring Process Models vs. Anchor Extremity)

Option A is the strongest, most viable project. Options B, C, and D suffer from critical flaws: Option B is heavily saturated and risks immediate scooping; Option C is fatally underpowered ($N = 47$ items); and Option D relies on a single target dataset with severe interface confounds. 

Option A leverages a massive open dataset (OpAQ: 96 studies, ~21,000 participants, 412 items) to resolve an explicit, unmet demand in the literature (Röseler & Schütz, 2022). It pits four foundational, competing theoretical frameworks against one another in a formal computational simulation.

### Roadmap to a Top-Tier JDM Publication (*Decision*, *Psychonomic Bulletin & Review*, or *Judgment and Decision Making*):

1. **Synthetic-to-Empirical Forward Simulation:**
   * Write explicit generative computational models for all four candidate processes:
     * $M_1$: Resource-rational random walk with step-cost stopping (Lieder et al., 2018).
     * $M_2$: Constant-weight anchor integration (Turner & Schley, 2016).
     * $M_3$: Sequential adjustment to the boundary of subjective plausibility (Epley & Gilovich, 2006).
     * $M_4$: Kernel-density plausibility-gated selective accessibility (Strack & Mussweiler, 1997).
   * Simulate synthetic agents through the exact item-anchor pairs present in OpAQ. Fit the identical statistical regression pipeline to both simulated and empirical data to generate distinctive model-signature curves.
2. **Defensible, Outcome-Free Metrics:**
   * Pre-register relative anchor distance on the log scale ($|\ln(A) - \ln(\text{True})|$) for all positive ratio items as the primary extremity metric.
   * Completely reject pooled or within-condition response SDs to avoid endogeneity.
3. **Mundlak Within-Between Item Decomposition:**
   * Implement a hierarchical mixed-effects model separating within-item extremity deviations from between-item averages. This eliminates cross-item selection bias and guarantees valid causal inference even if multi-anchor items are limited.
4. **Benchmarking Against a Bounded Null Model:**
   * Explicitly account for the mechanical denominator explosion of $AI$ by simulating a zero-adjustment bounded agent, demonstrating whether human adjustment decay exceeds algebraic scaling constraints.
5. **The `anchortype` Moderation Test:**
   * Exploit the `anchortype` variable in OpAQ (self-generated vs. provided anchors). $M_3$ was formulated specifically for self-generated anchors, whereas $M_4$ was formulated for provided anchors. Testing whether the extremity slope interacts with `anchortype` provides an unprecedented empirical test of the dual-mechanism debate of anchoring.

# Design-only inventory of OpAQ: counts of studies, items and anchor configurations.
# Reads design columns only (see R/read_opaq.R); no estimates are loaded.

source(file.path("R", "read_opaq.R"))
d <- read_opaq(include_outcomes = FALSE)
out <- file.path("output", "design_inventory.txt")
sink(out)

cat("Rows:", nrow(d), "\nStudies (reference_short):", uniqueN(d$reference_short),
    "\nItems (anchoring_item text):", uniqueN(d$anchoring_item),
    "\nItem x study cells:", uniqueN(d[, .(reference_short, anchoring_item)]), "\n\n")

for (v in c("anchortype", "scaletype", "comparative_question", "direction", "incentive",
            "experiment_type", "stimulitype", "sampletype", "anchorhigh")) {
  cat("--", v, "(rows)\n"); print(d[, .N, by = v][order(get(v))])
}
cat("-- tasktype (rows, top 40)\n"); print(head(d[, .N, by = tasktype][order(-N)], 40))

d[, anchor_num := suppressWarnings(as.numeric(anchor))]
d[, true_num := suppressWarnings(as.numeric(true_value))]
cat("\nRows with non-numeric anchor:", d[is.na(anchor_num), .N],
    "\nRows with missing/non-numeric true value:", d[is.na(true_num), .N], "\n")

cells <- d[!is.na(anchor_num), .(
  n = .N, n_anchor_values = uniqueN(anchor_num),
  n_high_values = uniqueN(anchor_num[anchorhigh == 1]), n_low_values = uniqueN(anchor_num[anchorhigh == 0]),
  n_high = sum(anchorhigh == 1, na.rm = TRUE), n_low = sum(anchorhigh == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
  anchortype = paste(sort(unique(anchortype)), collapse = "/"),
  scaletype = paste(sort(unique(scaletype)), collapse = "/"),
  tasktype = tasktype[1], true = true_num[1],
  a_low = if (any(anchorhigh == 0)) median(anchor_num[anchorhigh == 0]) else NA_real_,
  a_high = if (any(anchorhigh == 1)) median(anchor_num[anchorhigh == 1]) else NA_real_
), by = .(reference_short, anchoring_item)]

cat("\n-- Item x study cells by anchor configuration\n")
print(cells[, .N, by = .(has_both_sides = n_high > 0 & n_low > 0,
                         two_fixed_values = n_high_values == 1 & n_low_values == 1)])
cat("\n-- Cells by anchortype\n"); print(cells[, .N, by = anchortype][order(-N)])
cat("\n-- Cells by scaletype\n"); print(cells[, .N, by = scaletype][order(-N)])

pair <- cells[n_high_values == 1 & n_low_values == 1 & anchortype %in% c("2", "3")]
pair[, `:=`(pos = a_low > 0 & a_high > 0 & !is.na(true) & true > 0)]
pair[pos == TRUE, `:=`(log_spread = log(a_high / a_low),
                       log_ext_high = log(a_high / true), log_ext_low = log(true / a_low))]
cat("\n-- Classic fixed two-anchor cells (anchortype 2/3):", nrow(pair),
    "; with positive anchors and true value:", pair[pos == TRUE, .N],
    "; open scale:", pair[pos == TRUE & scaletype == "1", .N], "\n")
cat("   n per cell (quantiles):\n"); print(quantile(pair$n, c(0, .1, .25, .5, .75, .9, 1)))
cat("   log(A_high/A_low) quantiles:\n"); print(quantile(pair$log_spread, c(0, .05, .1, .25, .5, .75, .9, .95, 1), na.rm = TRUE))
cat("   log(A_high/true) quantiles:\n"); print(quantile(pair$log_ext_high, c(0, .05, .1, .25, .5, .75, .9, .95, 1), na.rm = TRUE))
cat("   log(true/A_low) quantiles:\n"); print(quantile(pair$log_ext_low, c(0, .05, .1, .25, .5, .75, .9, .95, 1), na.rm = TRUE))
cat("   Cells where true value lies outside [A_low, A_high]:",
    pair[pos == TRUE & (true < a_low | true > a_high), .N], "\n")

cat("\n-- Within-item extremity variation\n")
multi <- cells[n_high_values > 1 | n_low_values > 1]
cat("Cells with >1 distinct anchor value on a side:", nrow(multi), "\n")
print(multi[, .(reference_short, anchoring_item, n_high_values, n_low_values, anchortype, n)][order(-n)][1:min(.N, 40)])
across <- pair[, .(n_studies = .N, n_spreads = uniqueN(round(log_spread, 3))), by = anchoring_item][n_studies > 1]
cat("\nItems (by identical text) appearing in >1 study as classic pairs:", nrow(across),
    "; with >1 distinct spread:", across[n_spreads > 1, .N], "\n")
print(head(across[order(-n_studies)], 30))
cat("\n-- Studies contributing classic pairs:", uniqueN(pair$reference_short), "\n")
print(pair[, .(cells = .N), by = reference_short][order(-cells)])
sink()
fwrite(cells, file.path("output", "design_cells.csv"))
message("Wrote ", out)

The contribution should be a **risky quantitative comparison**, not a new association between distance and effect size. The existing OpAQ meta-analysis and the newer [Schley–Weingarten anchoring meta-analysis](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5893864) already make a broad moderator analysis a thin claim.

Before contact with estimates, I would freeze: model equations and parameter ranges; how any parameters are obtained without using the test outcomes; eligible task and scale strata; the within-item feasibility gate; the estimator and missingness rules; the prediction score and uncertainty procedure; and what magnitude of disagreement counts against each model. Include a simple constant-weight model and explicit **measurement-only null simulations** as benchmarks. Judge success by held-out item or study prediction and by whether each model predicts the observed *shape*, not only an average AI slope. If models make overlapping predictions for the designs OpAQ contains, call the comparison inconclusive.

That package could suit **Judgment and Decision Making** or **Journal of Behavioral Decision Making** even if every proposed process model fails: a carefully diagnosed failure would tell researchers which observable signature their theories do not explain. **Decision** or **Psychonomic Bulletin & Review** would, in my view, require especially clear formal predictions and convincing discrimination between mechanisms. If OpAQ has too little within-item anchor variation, I would still choose A from this shortlist, but describe the resulting paper as a constrained test of **population-level response functions**, not a decisive identification of cognitive process.

content.content:
## Answer

**I would choose A, but I would make it a preregistered test of *how estimates respond to anchor values*, with the across-item analysis as supporting evidence.** The proposed regression of an item-level anchoring index on anchor extremity is too confounded to distinguish four psychological processes by itself. A is worth pursuing if the preregistration makes model predictions specific enough to fail and gives priority to comparisons of different anchors for the *same question*.

I reviewed papers and dataset documentation only. I did not open or download outcome data. The [2024 correction to the OpAQ paper](https://doi.org/10.5334/jopd.92) adds omitted authors; it does not report a change to the data.

### 1. Can each option fail, and what has already been done?

| Option | A plausible result that would refute its central claim | Closest prior work | Most serious validity threat |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Anchor extremity** | A fixed model predicts a rising proportional response, but estimates show a reliably flat or falling response for the same items across anchor levels—or the reverse. A pattern outside *all four* preregistered predictive ranges would refute the proposed model set. | [Röseler and Schütz’s OpAQ meta-analysis](https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn) already examines anchor distance against standardized effects; [Wegener et al. (2001)](https://doi.org/10.1006/jesp.2000.1431) experimentally found that extreme anchors can have *less* influence than moderate ones. [Lieder et al. (2018)](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8) and [Turner and Schley (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003) provide formal accounts. | Anchor values, target questions, and response formats were often chosen together. Across-item slope differences can reflect those choices rather than a process response to extremity. |
| **B. Decision noise** | A noise model calibrated independently predicts a task-correlation matrix or held-out choices that excludes the observed pattern, while a model with stable preference differences predicts it materially better. This is plausible, especially if task families differ in ways noise cannot reproduce. | [Frey et al. (2017)](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.1701381) documented weak correlations between stated and behavioural risk measures and a reliable stated-preference factor. A [September 2026 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12291) already tests stable preferences under noisy measurement and often does not reject them with conventional data. A [July 2026 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05686) shows that standard noisy risk-choice models can themselves generate risk-aversion reversals. Neither is the proposed Basel–Berlin task simulation, but the conceptual space is crowded. | “Noise alone versus stable preferences” is a false split: stable preferences can generate noisy responses. With flexible person- and task-specific noise, the model can absorb nearly any correlation pattern. |
| **C. Noise-only confidence** | The preregistered, zero-bias observer predicts a narrow interval around zero *overall* confidence minus accuracy, and the observed discrepancy lies well outside it. The contribution should be a **risky quantitative comparison**, not a new association between distance and effect size. The existing OpAQ meta-analysis and the newer [Schley–Weingarten anchoring meta-analysis](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5893864) already make a broad moderator analysis a thin claim.

Before contact with estimates, I would freeze: model equations and parameter ranges; how any parameters are obtained without using the test outcomes; eligible task and scale strata; the within-item feasibility gate; the estimator and missingness rules; the prediction score and uncertainty procedure; and what magnitude of disagreement counts against each model. If OpAQ has too little within-item anchor variation, I would still choose A from this shortlist, but describe the resulting paper as a constrained test of **population-level response functions**, not a decisive identification of cognitive process.

input.content:
# Design note (pre-preregistration draft)

## Question
How does the proportional influence of an anchor on numeric estimates change as the anchor becomes more extreme? Four process models predict different shapes of the anchor-to-estimate response function on the log scale.

## Models (generative scale: natural log of the quantity)
Participant p has belief centre mu_p ~ N(m, sigma_b^2) with m = log(true) + bias, internal uncertainty sigma, response noise.
- M0 null: y = mu_p + e.
- M1 resource-rational adjustment (Lieder et al., 2018): Metropolis-Hastings chain starts at the anchor x, t steps with Gaussian proposals (SD s*sigma) targeting N(mu_p, sigma^2); y = final state. Local elasticity rises with |x - mu|.
- M2 constant-weight integration (Turner & Schley, 2016 AIM): y = w x + (1 - w) mu_p + e. Elasticity flat.
- M3 adjust to the edge of the plausible range (Epley & Gilovich, 2006): y = x if |x - mu_p| < k sigma, else mu_p + sign(x - mu_p) k sigma. Elasticity 1 near, 0 far.
- M4 plausibility-discounted integration (selective accessibility with plausibility gate; Wegener et al., 2001): y = mu_p + w (x - mu_p) exp(-(x - mu_p)^2 / (2 c^2 sigma^2)) + e. Elasticity falls and turns negative beyond c sigma.
Each model's parameters are drawn from ranges that reproduce Jacowitz & Kahneman's (1995) anchoring index (about .49 with anchors at the 15th and 85th percentiles), allowing .30-.60. sigma, sigma_b and bias are drawn from wide ranges.

## Data subsets (design-only inventory, output/design_inventory.txt)
- Within-item set (primary): item-study cells with >= 3 distinct exogenous anchor values, positive ratio-scale quantity, known true value, open scale. Bahník (2021a): 13 items, ~500 participants each, random anchors 1-1000. Imhoff & Barker (2022, Study 2): 1 item, 20 fixed anchors, n = 786. Frech et al. (2021): 4 items, 10 high anchors each, n = 104. Yoon et al. (2021): 2 ratio-scale items with random anchors. Excluded: Röseler & Wagner (2021; anchors computed from each participant's unanchored estimates and participants selected on anchored responses); WTP/WTA items without a true value.
- Across-cell set (secondary): classic fixed two-anchor cells (anchortype 2/3), positive ratio-scale quantity, open scale, known true value (about 150 cells, ~70 studies).

## Estimators (applied identically to simulated and real data)
- Within-item: trial-level mixed model on y~ = log(estimate/true) with x~ = log(anchor/true): y~ = a_c + b x~ + g x~|x~| + random intercepts and slopes by cell, random intercepts by participant. g > 0: elasticity rises with extremity (M1); g ~ 0 (equivalence bounds from simulation): M2; g < 0: M3/M4.
- Across-cell: log anchoring index per cell = (median log est_high - median log est_low) / (log a_high - log a_low), meta-regressed on mean |x~| with random effects for study.

## Inference
Compare the observed g (95% CI) with each model's simulated predictive interval on the exact OpAQ design. Decision table for every outcome cell.

- M4 plausibility-discounted integration (selective accessibility with plausibility gate; Wegener et al., 2001): y = mu_p + w (x - mu_p) exp(-(x - mu_p)^2 / (2 c^2 sigma^2)) + e. Elasticity falls and turns negative beyond c sigma.
Each model's parameters are drawn from ranges that reproduce Jacowitz & Kahneman's (1995) anchoring index (about .49 with anchors at the 15th and 85th percentiles), allowing .30-.60. sigma, sigma_b and bias are drawn from wide ranges.

## Data subsets (design-only inventory, output/design_inventory.txt)
- Within-item set (primary): item-study cells with >= 3 distinct exogenous anchor values, positive ratio-scale quantity, known true value, open scale. Bahník (2021a): 13 items, ~500 participants each, random anchors 1-1000. Imhoff & Barker (2022, Study 2): 1 item, 20 fixed anchors, n = 786. Frech et al. (2021): 4 items, 10 high anchors each, n = 104. Yoon et al. (2021): 2 ratio-scale items with random anchors. Excluded: Röseler & Wagner (2021; anchors computed from each participant's unanchored estimates and participants selected on anchored responses); WTP/WTA items without a true value.
- Across-cell set (secondary): classic fixed two-anchor cells (anchortype 2/3), positive ratio-scale quantity, open scale, known true value (about 150 cells, ~70 studies).

## Estimators (applied identically to simulated and real data)
- Within-item: trial-level mixed model on y~ = log(estimate/true) with x~ = log(anchor/true): y~ = a_c + b x~ + g x~|x~| + random intercepts and slopes by cell, random intercepts by participant. g > 0: elasticity rises with extremity (M1); g ~ 0 (equivalence bounds from simulation): M2; g < 0: M3/M4.
- Across-cell: log anchoring index per cell = (median log est_high - median log est_low) / (log a_high - log a_low), meta-regressed on mean |x~| with random effects for study.

## Inference
Compare the observed g (95% CI) with each model's simulated predictive interval on the exact OpAQ design. Decision table for every outcome cell.

input.content:
# Inclusion rules shared by the prediction simulation and the confirmatory analysis.
# build_sets() works on design columns; when `estimate` is present it is carried along.

source(file.path("R", "read_opaq.R"))

ratio_tasktypes <- c("quantity", "quantitity", "number", "price", "length", "height", "distance",
                     "weight", "population", "volume", "speed", "duration", "birth rate",
                     "income", "width", "area", "circumference", "age")
# Studies whose anchors were computed from each participant's own unanchored estimates.
endogenous_anchor_studies <- c("Röseler & Wagner, 2021")

min_levels_within <- 3     # distinct anchor values per cell for the within-item set
min_log_spread <- 0.25     # across-cell set: log(A_high / A_low) of at least 0.25
min_n_side <- 10           # across-cell set: at least 10 estimates per anchor side

build_sets <- function(d) {
  d <- copy(d)
  d[, `:=`(a = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(anchor)), t = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(true_value)))]
  d[, cell := paste(reference_short, anchoring_item, sep = " || ")]
  d[, pid := paste(reference_short, participant_id, sep = " || ")]
  base <- d[anchortype %in% 1:3 & scaletype == 1 & tasktype %in% ratio_tasktypes &
              !is.na(a) & a > 0 & !is.na(t) & t > 0 &
              !reference_short %in% endogenous_anchor_studies]
  base[, t := t[1], by = cell]   # one true value per cell
  base[, x := log(a / t)]        # anchor position relative to truth (log scale)

  lev <- base[, .(n_levels = uniqueN(a), anchortype = min(anchortype)), by = cell]
  within <- base[cell %in% lev[n_levels >= min_levels_within, cell]]

  pairs <- base[anchortype %in% 2:3 & !is.na(anchorhigh)]
  pc <- pairs[, .(study = reference_short[1], item = anchoring_item[1], t = t[1],
                  n_low_values = uniqueN(a[anchorhigh == 0]), n_high_values = uniqueN(a[anchorhigh == 1]),
                  a_low = a[anchorhigh == 0][1], a_high = a[anchorhigh == 1][1],
                  n_low = sum(anchorhigh == 0), n_high = sum(anchorhigh == 1),
                  anchortype = anchortype[1]), by = cell]
  pc <- pc[n_low_values == 1 & n_high_values == 1 & a_high > a_low &

# Generative process models of anchored estimation on the log scale.
# All quantities are log(value / true value); sigma is the item's belief uncertainty,
# and every model parameter is expressed in units of sigma, so the models are scale-free.
#
# Each participant-item row has a belief centre mu = bias + person offset + belief noise.
# Response = model output + response noise; a small share of responses is contaminated
# (unit errors, typing slips) to mimic real estimation data.

belief_sd_share <- 0.6     # SD of belief centres across people, in sigma units
response_sd_share <- 0.3   # response noise SD, in sigma units
contamination_p <- 0.02    # share of responses with gross errors
contamination_sd <- 2      # SD (log units) of gross errors

model_names <- c(M0 = "No anchoring", M1 = "Resource-rational adjustment",
                 M2 = "Constant-weight integration", M3 = "Adjust to plausible boundary",
                 M4 = "Plausibility-discounted integration")

respond <- function(model, x, mu, sigma, par) {
  d <- x - mu
  switch(model,
    M0 = mu,
    M2 = mu + par$w * d,
    M3 = ifelse(abs(d) < par$k * sigma, x, mu + sign(d) * par$k * sigma),
    M4 = mu + par$w * d * exp(-d^2 / (2 * (par$c * sigma)^2)),
    M1 = {
      z <- x
      for (i in seq_len(par$t)) {
        prop <- z + rnorm(length(z), 0, par$s * sigma)
        log_ratio <- ((z - mu)^2 - (prop - mu)^2) / (2 * sigma^2)
        z <- ifelse(log(runif(length(z))) < log_ratio, prop, z)
      }
      z
    })
}

# rows: data.table with x (log anchor / truth), cell, pid. cellpar: data.table with cell, bias, sigma.
simulate_responses <- function(model, rows, cellpar, par, person_sd = 0.15) {
  r <- merge(rows[, .(row_id = .I, cell, pid, x)], cellpar, by = "cell")
  setorder(r, row_id)
  persons <- unique(r$pid)
  u <- setNames(rnorm(length(persons), 0, person_sd), persons)
  mu <- r$bias + u[r$pid] + rnorm(nrow(r), 0, belief_sd_share * r$sigma)
  y <- respond(model, r$x, mu, r$sigma, par) + rnorm(nrow(r), 0, response_sd_share * r$sigma)
  gross <- runif(nrow(r)) < contamination_p
  y[gross] <- y[gross] + rnorm(sum(gross), 0, contamination_sd)
  y
}

# Anchoring index of each model in the Jacowitz & Kahneman (1995) design: anchors at the
# 15th and 85th percentiles of the unanchored response distribution.
jk_index <- function(model, par, n = 20000) {
  sd_unanchored <- sqrt(belief_sd_share^2 + response_sd_share^2)
  a <- qnorm(0.85) * sd_unanchored
  y_of <- function(x) {
    mu <- rnorm(n, 0, belief_sd_share)
    respond(model, rep(x, n), mu, 1, par) + rnorm(n, 0, response_sd_share)
  }
  (median(y_of(a)) - median(y_of(-a))) / (2 * a)
}

# Estimators applied identically to simulated and observed data.
# y is log(estimate / true value); x is log(anchor / true value).

suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(lme4); library(metafor); library(data.table) })

# Within-item response function: y = a_cell + b x + g x|x|, random intercepts and slopes by cell,
# random intercepts by participant. b is the average elasticity at the true value; g > 0 means the
# local elasticity rises with anchor extremity, g < 0 means it falls.
fit_within <- function(dat) {
  dat <- dat[is.finite(y)]
  dat[, xx := x * abs(x)]
  m <- lmer(y ~ x + xx + (1 + x | cell) + (1 | pid), data = dat,
            control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE, check.conv.singular = "ignore"))
  co <- summary(m)$coefficients
  list(model = m, b = co["x", "Estimate"], b_se = co["x", "Std. Error"],
       g = co["xx", "Estimate"], g_se = co["xx", "Std. Error"])
}

# Across-cell anchoring index: log-scale index per two-anchor cell, meta-regressed on extremity
# (mean absolute log distance of the two anchors from the true value).
cell_indices <- function(rows, cells) {
  r <- merge(rows[is.finite(y), .(cell, anchorhigh, y)], cells[, .(cell, study, x_low, x_high, extremity)], by = "cell")
  r[, .(med_high = median(y[anchorhigh == 1]), med_low = median(y[anchorhigh == 0]),
        mad_high = mad(y[anchorhigh == 1]), mad_low = mad(y[anchorhigh == 0]),
        n_high = sum(anchorhigh == 1), n_low = sum(anchorhigh == 0),
        study = study[1], x_low = x_low[1], x_high = x_high[1], extremity = extremity[1]), by = cell][
    , `:=`(ai = (med_high - med_low) / (x_high - x_low),
           ai_se = 1.2533 * sqrt(pmax(mad_high, 1e-3)^2 / n_high + pmax(mad_low, 1e-3)^2 / n_low) / (x_high - x_low))][]
}

fit_across <- function(ci) {
  m <- rma.mv(ai, ai_se^2, mods = ~ extremity, random = ~ 1 | study / cell, data = ci, method = "REML")
  list(model = m, slope = unname(coef(m)["extremity"]), slope_se = unname(m$se[2]),
       intercept = unname(coef(m)["intrcpt"]), mean_ai = weighted.mean(ci$ai, 1 / ci$ai_se^2))
}

# Estimators applied identically to simulated and observed data.
# y is log(estimate / true value); x is log(anchor / true value).

suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(lme4); library(metafor); library(data.table) })

# Within-item response function: y = a_cell + b x + g x|x|, random intercepts and slopes by cell,
# random intercepts by participant. b is the average elasticity at the true value; g > 0 means the
# local elasticity rises with anchor extremity, g < 0 means it falls.
fit_within <- function(dat) {
  dat <- dat[is.finite(y)]
  dat[, xx := x * abs(x)]
  m <- lmer(y ~ x + xx + (1 + x | cell) + (1 | pid), data = dat,
            control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE, check.conv.singular = "ignore"))
  co <- summary(m)$coefficients
  list(model = m, b = co["x", "Estimate"], b_se = co["x", "Std. Error"],
       g = co["xx", "Estimate"], g_se = co["xx", "Std. Error"])
}

# Across-cell anchoring index: log-scale index per two-anchor cell, meta-regressed on extremity
# (mean absolute log distance of the two anchors from the true value).
cell_indices <- function(rows, cells) {
  r <- merge(rows[is.finite(y), .(cell, anchorhigh, y)], cells[, .(cell, study, x_low, x_high, extremity)], by = "cell")
  r[, .(med_high = median(y[anchorhigh == 1]), med_low = median(y[anchorhigh == 0]),
        mad_high = mad(y[anchorhigh == 1]), mad_low = mad(y[anchorhigh == 0]),
        n_high = sum(anchorhigh == 1), n_low = sum(anchorhigh == 0),
        study = study[1], x_low = x_low[1], x_high = x_high[1], extremity = extremity[1]), by = cell][
    , `:=`(ai = (med_high - med_low) / (x_high - x_low),
           ai_se = 1.2533 * sqrt(pmax(mad_high, 1e-3)^2 / n_high + pmax(mad_low, 1e-3)^2 / n_low) / (x_high - x_low))][]
}

fit_across <- function(ci) {
  m <- rma.mv(ai, ai_se^2, mods = ~ extremity, random = ~ 1 | study / cell, data = ci, method = "REML")
  list(model = m, slope = unname(coef(m)["extremity"]), slope_se = unname(m$se[2]),
       intercept = unname(coef(m)["intrcpt"]), mean_ai = weighted.mean(ci$ai, 1 / ci$ai_se^2))
}

  M3 = data.table(k = seq(0.05, 3, by = 0.025)),

# Predicted estimator outcomes for each process model on the exact OpAQ designs
# (anchor values, true values, participants and cell sizes). Reads design columns only.

suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(data.table); library(parallel) })
source(file.path("R", "design_sets.R"))
source(file.path("R", "models.R"))
source(file.path("R", "estimators.R"))

n_reps <- c(M0 = 100, M1 = 200, M2 = 200, M3 = 200, M4 = 200)
sigma_range <- c(0.3, 1.2)      # belief uncertainty per item (log units)
bias_centre_range <- c(-0.3, 0.3)
bias_sd <- 0.3

sets <- build_sets(read_opaq(include_outcomes = FALSE))
within_rows <- sets$within[, .(cell, pid, x, anchortype)]
across_rows <- sets$across_rows[, .(cell, pid, x, anchorhigh)]
cells <- unique(c(within_rows$cell, across_rows$cell))
calib <- fread(file.path("output", "calibration_grid.csv"))[accepted == TRUE]

one_rep <- function(model, rep) {
  set.seed(1e5 * match(model, names(n_reps)) + rep)
  par <- if (model == "M0") list() else {
    g <- calib[model == (..model)]
    as.list(g[sample(.N, 1), intersect(c("s", "t", "w", "k", "c"), names(g)), with = FALSE])
  }
  cellpar <- data.table(cell = cells, sigma = runif(length(cells), sigma_range[1], sigma_range[2]),
                        bias = rnorm(length(cells), runif(1, bias_centre_range[1], bias_centre_range[2]), bias_sd))
  w <- copy(within_rows)[, y := simulate_responses(model, within_rows, cellpar, par)]
  a <- copy(across_rows)[, y := simulate_responses(model, across_rows, cellpar, par)]
  fw <- fit_within(w)
  fr <- fit_within(w[anchortype == 1])
  ff <- fit_within(w[anchortype != 1])
  fa <- fit_across(cell_indices(a, sets$across_cells))
  data.table(model, rep, par = paste(names(par), unlist(par), sep = "=", collapse = ";"),
             b = fw$b, b_se = fw$b_se, g = fw$g, g_se = fw$g_se,
             b_random = fr$b, g_random = fr$g, g_random_se = fr$g_se,
             b_fixed = ff$b, g_fixed = ff$g, g_fixed_se = ff$g_se,
             across_slope = fa$slope, across_slope_se = fa$slope_se, across_mean_ai = fa$mean_ai)
}

jobs <- rbindlist(lapply(names(n_reps), function(m) data.table(model = m, rep = seq_len(n_reps[[m]]))))
res <- rbindlist(mclapply(seq_len(nrow(jobs)), function(i) {
  tryCatch(one_rep(jobs$model[i], jobs$rep[i]), error = function(e) data.table(model = jobs$model[i], rep = jobs$rep[i], error = conditionMessage(e)))
}, mc.cores = 8), fill = TRUE)
fwrite(res, file.path("output", "predictions_raw.csv"))

q <- function(v) paste0(sprintf("%.3f", median(v, na.rm = TRUE)), " [", sprintf("%.3f", quantile(v, .025, na.rm = TRUE)), ", ", sprintf("%.3f", quantile(v, .975, na.rm = TRUE)), "]")
summ <- res[is.na(if ("error" %in% names(res)) error else NA), .(reps = .N, b = q(b), g = q(g), g_random = q(g_random), g_fixed = q(g_fixed),
                                  b_random = q(b_random), b_fixed = q(b_fixed), across_slope = q(across_slope),
                                  across_mean_ai = q(across_mean_ai), share_g_pos = mean(g > 0)), by = model]
fwrite(summ, file.path("output", "predictions_summary.csv"))
print(summ)

input.prompt:
We are preparing a manuscript for a judgement-and-decision-making (JDM) journal: a preregistered secondary analysis of an open multi-study anchoring dataset (Open Anchoring Quest, ~95 studies, trial-level) combined with simulations of four cognitive process models of anchoring (resource-rational adjustment, constant-weight anchor integration, adjustment to the plausible boundary, plausibility-discounted integration), testing how anchor influence changes with anchor extremity. The study was designed, run, and written by an AI system (Claude) under the instruction of a human researcher (Lukas Wallrich, social psychologist / meta-scientist). # Estimators applied identically to simulated and observed data.
# y is log(estimate / true value); x is log(anchor / true value).

suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(lme4); library(metafor); library(data.table) })

# Gross-error rule: drop responses further from the true value (log scale) than both a factor of
# 1,000 and ten times the most extreme anchor used for that cell. A response equal to any anchor
# is always retained, so the rule cannot remove strongly anchored answers.
drop_gross_errors <- function(dat) {
  dat <- dat[is.finite(y)]
  dat[, y_limit := pmax(log(1000), max(abs(x)) + log(10)), by = cell]
  dat[abs(y) <= y_limit][, y_limit := NULL][]
}

# Within-item response function: y = a_cell + b x + g x|x|, with uncorrelated random intercepts,
# slopes and curvatures by cell, and random intercepts by participant. b is the average elasticity at the true value; g > 0 means the
# local elasticity rises with anchor extremity, g < 0 means it falls.
fit_within <- function(dat) {
  dat <- drop_gross_errors(dat)
  dat[, xx := x * abs(x)]
  m <- lmer(y ~ x + xx + (1 + x + xx || cell) + (1 | pid), data = dat,
            control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE, check.conv.singular = "ignore"))

  list(model = m, b = co["x", "Estimate"], b_se = co["x", "Std. Error"],
       g = co["xx", "Estimate"], g_se = co["xx", "Std. Error"])
}

The simulated data pass through the same estimator code as the real data. Predictions are frozen in the preregistration. | Codex and the advisor: predictions must be fixed before data contact, and simulated responses must go through the same bounds, transformations, exclusions and estimator. Calibrating to an external finding keeps the OpAQ outcomes out of the parameter choice. |
| 15 | 2026-09-27 | Add a gate: the shape test is interpreted only if the average elasticity b is credibly positive (95% CI lower bound above 0). Report relative curvature rho = g / b for the equivalence decision. | If anchoring is absent (possible for random anchors), g is near zero for a trivial reason and would be misread as support for constant-weight integration (advisor). rho removes the dependence of g on overall anchoring strength. |
| 16 | 2026-09-27 | Gross-error rule: drop responses whose log distance from the truth exceeds both log(1000) and the cell's largest anchor distance plus log(10). | Removes unit errors and typing slips without removing any response that equals an anchor, so the rule cannot bias the test against strong anchoring. |
