<note>A task-notification fires each time this agent stops with no live background children of its own. The user can send it another message and resume it, so the same task-id may notify more than once.</note>
<result>I found no prior study that does what the planned study does. No paper computes the proportional anchoring index item by item on OpAQ, relates it to anchor extremity scaled by true value or uncertainty, and compares it against simulated predictions from several process models. Three pieces of work come close:

- **Röseler & Schütz (2022, preprint):** used OpAQ, 386 items, extremity measured relative to the true value. Effect size was Hedges g.
- **Schley & Weingarten meta-study (2025 preprint version):** 8 items, anchors at calibration percentiles. Outcome was z-scored estimates.
- **Lieder et al. (2018a):** fitted the anchoring index for 15 Jacowitz & Kahneman items. Never tested how the index changes with extremity.

The first two found larger effects with more extreme anchors. But both measured an absolute or standardized gap, and a constant anchoring index also produces a larger gap when anchors are further apart. So neither result tests whether the proportional index changes. An index-based analysis is the test that tells the models apart.

Evidence tiers: **full text** = read in full; **figure-read** = my estimate from a plot; **abstract only**; **UNVERIFIED** = not read. Closeness to the planned study runs 0–3. I checked every DOI below against Crossref and each one matched. No data files were opened.

## A. Schley & Weingarten

**One paper or two: one paper, in several versions.**
- The Management Science article is doi 10.1287/mnsc.2023.03238: "Fifty Years of Anchoring Effects: A Theoretical Reintegration and Meta-Analysis", Schley & Weingarten. Crossref gives online publication on 2026-05-19, with no volume, issue or pages yet.
- The PsyArXiv version teq7k_v2 (2025-12-09) is marked in Crossref as the preprint of the Management Science article. It has the same abstract as the journal version, and SSRN 10.2139/ssrn.5893864 matches it. I read teq7k_v2 in full (48 pp.). I did not read the journal version itself (UNVERIFIED).
- The 2025-01 version, "…A Meta-Analysis and Meta-Study of Anchoring Effects" (SSRN 10.2139/ssrn.5114456), is the teq7k v1 PDF, revision 5 (88 pp.). I read it in full. It adds a preregistered meta-study (N = 1,968). That meta-study is not in teq7k_v2 and, judging by the abstract, not in the published article.
- SSRN 4605057 (2023) is an earlier version with 1,283 effect sizes (abstract only).

**(1) Data sources**
- Main analysis: 1,280 high-vs-low effect sizes from 482 studies in 178 papers; 2,601 effect sizes across all their databases (v2, abstract and p. 23).
- Searches were run Dec 2017, Feb 2019 and Feb 2024 (v2 pp. 15–16).
- **OpAQ is not used and not cited.** The only Röseler reference is the 2021 subliminal-anchoring paper.

**(2) How extremity was coded**
- In the meta-analysis it is a binary flag: whether the original authors called the anchor "extreme" or "implausible", or whether other anchor levels in the study were more moderate. 49 of 1,280 effect sizes are flagged (Table 2, pp. 20–21).
- There is no measure relative to the true value or to uncertainty. They note that only 8.3% of studies (40 of 482) reported a calibration pretest (p. 39).
- In the meta-study, extremity is defined by calibration percentiles (3rd/97th, 15th/85th, 30th/70th of a Prolific calibration sample), varied within participants over 8 items (2025 version, Table 7, p. 50). This is effectively extremity relative to uncertainty.

**(3) Level of testing and results**
- **Meta-analysis:** tested at the effect-size level in a 3-level model (effect sizes nested in studies) with robust variance estimation (v2 p. 22).
  - Multivariate coefficient for extreme anchors: −0.02 [−0.20, 0.16].
  - Univariate: 0.01. Subset of studies that manipulated extremity: 0.09 [−0.14, 0.31] (Table 5, p. 28).
  - Table 6 (p. 29): 0.84 extreme vs 0.82 not extreme; in the within-study subset, 0.69 (k = 29) vs 0.61 (k = 33).
  - Their interpretation (p. 31): "this coefficient implies not that the anchoring effect is proportional to the anchor extremity but that the total magnitude of the anchoring effect appears no larger or smaller for anchors defined by their study's authors as 'extreme.'" They also say the coding may not capture the construct.
  - No nonlinearity test.
- **Meta-study:** tested at the trial level in a mixed model with item dummies, a linear (−0.5/0/0.5) and a quadratic extremity term (pp. 52–54).
  - The paper gives no numbers in the text. From Figure 4 (p. 55), figure-read: linear interaction about +0.74, quadratic about +0.10, CI above 0.
  - From Figure 3 (p. 53), figure-read: the high-minus-low gap is about 0.2 SD for 30/70, 0.5 SD for 15/85 and 1.0 SD for 3/97.
  - Text (p. 56): "results of the meta-study indicated a large increase in the anchoring effect when the anchors were more extreme."
- **Why this is not a proportional-index result:** the outcome is estimates z-scored within item, and the distance between the two anchors grows several-fold across levels (e.g., African countries 24/48 vs 3/72). The paper gives no way to compute the index.

**(4) Effect-size metric**
- Hedges g only (v2 p. 18).
- Anchor–estimate gaps are analysed separately in Online Appendix H, which I did not read (UNVERIFIED).
- **No anchoring index or other unitless adjustment measure** appears in either version.

**(5) How theories were compared**
- Seven theories get qualitative predictions in Table 1 (p. 7).
- For extremity: anchoring-and-adjustment and selective accessibility predict an increase up to a threshold; the attitudinal view (Wegener et al. 2001) predicts an inverted U; extremeness aversion and noise theory predict an increase (p. 12).
- There is no model fitting. They explicitly declined to tally winners and losers (p. 33).
- They call for formal models, citing Turner & Schley 2016 and Lieder et al. 2018 (p. 39).
- In the 2025 version (p. 70) they say that mapping extremity properly "requires assessing anchor values at each level of a baseline distribution – rather than at just the 3rd/97th, 15th/85th, and 30th/70th percentiles."

**(6) Random or uninformative anchors**
- "Transparently random" coefficient: −0.19** [−0.33, −0.05] multivariate; −0.23** with controls; −0.05 and −0.18 (not significant) in the univariate models (Table 5, p. 28).
- Table 6 (p. 29): g = 0.78 random vs 0.83 not random.
- The 2025 version reports −0.27*** instead (its Table 5, p. 42).
- Primed or incidental anchors: −0.72*** (p. 28).

**Closeness:** meta-analysis 1; meta-study 2 (extremity relative to uncertainty, but 8 items, z-score outcome, no index, no models).

## B. Young et al. 2026, Cognitive Psychology 164, 101796 (doi 10.1016/j.cogpsych.2026.101796)

Full text read (CC-BY, Cambridge repository copy with journal pagination).
- **Design:** 10 studies, N = 1,353 after exclusions (pp. 7–8), plus 953 calibration participants. The anchors are items, not numbers ("torch vs laptop"), in their "High-Low" design.
- **Outcome:** percentile rank of each estimate within the calibration distribution, following Jacowitz & Kahneman, plus an assimilation score (p. 7).
- **Result:** meta-analytic g = 0.25 [0.05, 0.45] (p. 11). Low-value items were anchored more than high-value items.
- **OpAQ:** not used. They cite Röseler & Schütz 2022 only as a meta-analysis (p. 1).
- **Models:** no process models fitted. The only simulation is one validating the rank measure (Supplementary Material 1). They conclude selective accessibility gives the best account (abstract).
- **Extremity:** only a discussion remark. The largest effect was in Study 1, where item values differed by factors of 44–500, "consistent with" Lieder et al. (pp. 15–16). No proportional-adjustment analysis.
- They cite Schley & Weingarten (2025) as d = 0.876 (p. 2) and 0.88 (p. 15), while every Schley & Weingarten version I read reports 0.824/0.825. I did not resolve this.

**Closeness: 0.**

## C. Searches, 2022–2026

**Method:** OpenAlex 2022–2026 citers: 164 for Lieder 2018a, 21 for Lieder 2018b, 54 for Turner & Schley. I also ran OpenAlex keyword searches and web searches. The OpenAlex citer list for OpAQ (jopd.67) is low-recall: it returned only 4 papers and missed two papers that do use OpAQ. **No citer fits models to multi-item anchoring data or relates the proportional index to extremity.**

| Paper (verified DOI) | What it did | Close |
|---|---|---|
| **Röseler & Schütz 2022, "Hanging the Anchor Off a New Ship", PsyArXiv 10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn** (single version, 2022-03; never published) | Full text. Meta-analysis **of OpAQ**: 90 studies, k = 386 items, N = 17,708, Hedges g (pp. 17–18). g = 0.689 [0.589, 0.789] (abstract). Extremity = mean relative distance of anchor from the true value per item (p. 11). "Relative distance" b = 0.040 per unit, k = 312, p < .001 (Table 2, p. 21). They describe the relationship as "positive and nonlinear" (Table 4, p. 29; p. 30), but the PDF shows only a linear coefficient. The nonlinear evidence may be in their online app, which I did not check. They conclude against selective accessibility's prediction that extreme anchors give smaller effects (p. 30). Random anchors: smaller effects that are still above 0 (p. 26). They recommend a unitless "relative strength of adjustment" metric "to formalize the relationship between anchor distance and adjustment strength" (p. 34). That is the planned study's gap, named explicitly. | **2** |
| Röseler et al. 2024, *Meta-Psychology* 8, 10.15626/mp.2022.3236 | Abstract only. OpAQ-based; shows that individual susceptibility-to-anchoring scores are unreliable. No extremity or model analysis. | 1 |
| Röseler, Incerti, Rebholz & Seida, PsyArXiv 10.31234/osf.io/jztk2_v3 (2025) | Abstract only. A formalized insufficient-adjustment model; 4 new studies, N = 898. Less adjustment time did not pull estimates closer to the anchor. No OpAQ or extremity analysis mentioned. | 1 |
| Wu, Farmer, Pready-James & Warren 2026, *Cognitive Science* 50, 10.1111/cogs.70229 | Full text (Europe PMC submitted version, section numbers only). VR height estimation. Exp 2: N = 127, anchor offsets of 2/4/8 m, with no-anchor trials. Subjective anchoring score rises linearly with subjective offset: β = 0.66, t(1904.85) = 42.69. They fit a weighted-linear descriptive model and link it to Turner & Schley's integration model. This is a single perceptual quantity. | 1 |
| Lee & Morewedge 2022, *Psychological Science* 33:60–75, 10.1177/09567976211024254 | Abstract only. 11 preregistered experiments, N = 3,552. Anchoring grows with stimulus magnitude through noise (scalar variability). Relevant to an uncertainty-scaled definition of extremity. | 1 |
| Spicer, Zhu, Chater & Sanborn 2022, *Psychological Science* 33:1395–1407, 10.1177/09567976221089599 | Abstract only. Anchoring and repulsion occur together in perceptual and cognitive judgments (N = 200). Sampling-model background. | 1 |
| Zhu et al. 2024, *Psychological Review* 131:456–493, 10.1037/rev0000427 | Abstract only. The autocorrelated Bayesian sampler, a candidate process model for estimates. No multi-item anchoring fit mentioned. | 0–1 |
| Rebholz, Biella & Hütter 2024, *J Behav Decis Mak* 37, 10.1002/bdm.2369 | Abstract only. Mixed-effects regression weights as an alternative to ratio-of-differences indices, which is a methods point relevant to the index. | 1 (methods) |
| Mayer & Rebholz 2024, PsyArXiv 10.31234/osf.io/69jwr | Abstract only. Expertise manipulation, contrasting insufficient adjustment, selective accessibility and scale distortion. | 0–1 |
| Yasseri & Reher 2022, *J Comput Soc Sci* 5:1001–1021, 10.1007/s42001-021-00158-0 | Abstract only (the PDF fetch returned HTML). Large online experiment; "positive, yet complex relationship between the anchors and the bias." | 1 |
| Honda, Kagawa & Shirasuna 2024, *Cognition* 246, 10.1016/j.cognition.2024.105758 | Abstract only (preprint abstract). Uses two very different anchors to improve wisdom of crowds; simulation plus 2 experiments. | 0 |
| Bixter & Luhmann 2025, *Acta Psychologica* 252, 10.1016/j.actpsy.2024.104646 | Abstract only. Multiple conflicting anchors; primacy effect. | 0 |
| Li, Weigel, Ferraro & Messer 2025, *Economic Inquiry* 63:387–402, 10.1111/ecin.13279 | Abstract only. Power and replication of one willingness-to-pay anchoring study. | 0 |

Several 2025–2026 papers on anchoring in large language models (arXiv, e.g. 2505.15392) report an anchoring index against anchor distance for LLMs. I did not verify these; they are not about humans.

## D. What Lieder 2018 and Turner & Schley 2016 fitted

Lieder page numbers are from the 2017 PsyArXiv preprints (5x2em and zu4pt). I did not check the pagination of the published Psychonomic Bulletin & Review versions.

**Lieder et al. 2018a, PBR 25:322–349, doi 10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8**
- **Jacowitz & Kahneman fit:** Jacowitz & Kahneman's anchoring index across **15 quantities**. Uncertainty σ came from their own elicitation; means were Jacowitz & Kahneman's unanchored medians. Two parameters were fitted by least squares on the index (29 adjustments, step size 22.4; p. 25).
  - Predicted mean index **53.22% vs observed 48.48%**, r(13) = 0.62, p = .0135 (p. 26).
  - Predicted index correlates with σ: Spearman ρ = 0.586. This matches Jacowitz & Kahneman's r(13) = −0.68 between confidence and the index (p. 31).
- **Self-generated anchors:** Epley & Gilovich 2006, 19 quantities. 80.62% vs 80.95% relative adjustment; r(17) = 0.61 (p. 27).
- **Cognitive load:** r(5) = 0.96 (p. 29).
- **Russo & Schoemaker (Attila, anchors 500–1300), plus an MTurk replication (N = 300):** simulated with the Jacowitz & Kahneman parameters. Mean estimates rise linearly with the anchor; the model overshoots at the highest anchor (pp. 30–31). Compared on mean estimates, not the index.
- **Simmons et al. 2010 Study 3b:** incentives affect adjustment only for implausible anchors. Plausible: 0.76 [−0.42, 1.94]; implausible: 17.8 [9.76, 25.91]; ρ(22) = 0.72 (p. 39).
- **Stated prediction on extremity:** bias ≈ (a − x)·rᵗ, so bias grows in proportion to the anchor–truth distance (Eqs. 3–4, p. 20; Table 1, p. 23). For a fixed number of adjustments, that means a constant relative adjustment.
- **Their Figure 4 (p. 19), my reading:** the optimal number of adjustments rises with distance measured in σ units. At intermediate time costs, the remaining bias is non-monotonic in distance. That implies the index could fall with extremity. The authors do not say this in the text.
- They never derived or tested how the index varies with extremity.

**Lieder et al. 2018b, PBR 25:775–784, doi 10.3758/s13423-017-1288-6**
- Bus-delay prediction tasks with time-cost × error-cost incentives. Exp 1: N = 30 recruited, self-generated anchor (p. 6). Exp 2: N = 60, provided low/high anchors (p. 14).
- Bias was modelled as linear in the true value.
- Relative adjustment: 41.3% [38.5, 44.0] in Exp 1 (p. 10). In Exp 2, 29.86% for low anchors and 27.25% for high anchors, not different, z = 1.16 (p. 16).
- One quantity; no extremity manipulation.

**Turner & Schley 2016, Cognitive Psychology 90:1–47, doi 10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003**
- Full text from the author's website copy, journal pagination.
- **Exp 1:** N = 589 across 5 between-participant conditions (unanchored prior, regular, directional, irrelevant, cognitive load; p. 12). 6 items from Simmons et al. and Jacowitz & Kahneman, **one anchor per item** (high for 3 items, low for 3; p. 13). The model was fitted separately per item with Bayesian estimation (p. 14). **No anchoring index is possible with this design, and none is used.**
- **Exp 2:** N = 189, within-person prior and posterior estimates plus confidence ratings, hierarchical model (p. 26).
- **Extremity is an assumption, not a finding.** Anchor influence is mapped from "prior consistency" (the prior CDF at the anchor; p. 21) via a Bézier curve, "producing an inverted U-shaped relationship between anchor extremity and the magnitude of the shift … for simplicity" (p. 23). An asymptote is allowed as a special case. Summary (p. 25): more implausible anchors get "a proportionally smaller influence."
- The curvilinear pattern in Fig. 14 (p. 31) is across participants' prior-to-anchor distance for one fixed anchor per item. It is not a test across anchor levels.

**Closeness: Lieder 2018a 1–2 (source of a model, not a test); Lieder 2018b 0–1; Turner & Schley 1.**

## Not verified

- The Management Science published text and the online appendices at osf.io/d583s (including anchor–estimate gaps in Appendix H).
- Where Röseler & Schütz show the "nonlinear" relationship: it is not in the PDF text, possibly in their online app.
- Full texts of the entries marked abstract only above.
- Published PBR page numbers for both Lieder papers.

Papers I read are in /tmp/jdmsim: scratch_nov_sw_v2.pdf, scratch_nov_sw_ms.pdf, scratch_nov_sw_young.pdf, scratch_nov_sw_turner.pdf and scratch_nov_sw_wu.txt. I also read another agent's files there: scratch_lieder_5x2em.pdf, scratch_lieder_zu4pt.pdf and hanging.txt.</result>

- The 2025-01 version, "…A Meta-Analysis and Meta-Study of Anchoring Effects" (SSRN 10.2139/ssrn.5114456), is the teq7k v1 PDF, revision 5 (88 pp.). I read it in full. It adds a preregistered meta-study (N = 1,968). That meta-study is not in teq7k_v2 and, judging by the abstract, not in the published article.
- SSRN 4605057 (2023) is an earlier version with 1,283 effect sizes (abstract only).

**(1) Data sources**
- Main analysis: 1,280 high-vs-low effect sizes from 482 studies in 178 papers; 2,601 effect sizes across all their databases (v2, abstract and p. 23).
- Searches were run Dec 2017, Feb 2019 and Feb 2024 (v2 pp. 15–16).
- **OpAQ is not used and not cited.** The only Röseler reference is the 2021 subliminal-anchoring paper.

**(2) How extremity was coded**
- In the meta-analysis it is a binary flag: whether the original authors called the anchor "extreme" or "implausible", or whether other anchor levels in the study were more moderate. 49 of 1,280 effect sizes are flagged (Table 2, pp. 20–21).
- There is no measure relative to the true value or to uncertainty. They note that only 8.3% of studies (40 of 482) reported a calibration pretest (p. 39).
- In the meta-study, extremity is defined by calibration percentiles (3rd/97th, 15th/85th, 30th/70th of a Prolific calibration sample), varied within participants over 8 items (2025 version, Table 7, p. 50). This is effectively extremity relative to uncertainty.

**(3) Level of testing and results**
- **Meta-analysis:** tested at the effect-size level in a 3-level model (effect sizes nested in studies) with robust variance estimation (v2 p. 22).
  - Multivariate coefficient for extreme anchors: −0.02 [−0.20, 0.16].
  - Univariate: 0.01. Subset of studies that manipulated extremity: 0.09 [−0.14, 0.31] (Table 5, p. 28).
  - Table 6 (p. 29): 0.84 extreme vs 0.82 not extreme; in the within-study subset, 0.69 (k = 29) vs 0.61 (k = 33).
  - Their interpretation (p. 31): "this coefficient implies not that the anchoring effect is proportional to the anchor extremity but that the total magnitude of the anchoring effect appears no larger or smaller for anchors defined by their study's authors as 'extreme.'" They also say the coding may not capture the construct.
  - No nonlinearity test.
- **Meta-study:** tested at the trial level in a mixed model with item dummies, a linear (−0.5/0/0.5) and a quadratic extremity term (pp. 52–54).
  - The paper gives no numbers in the text. From Figure 4 (p. 55), figure-read: linear interaction about +0.74, quadratic about +0.10, CI above 0.
  - From Figure 3 (p. 53), figure-read: the high-minus-low gap is about 0.2 SD for 30/70, 0.5 SD for 15/85 and 1.0 SD for 3/97.
  - Text (p. 56): "results of the meta-study indicated a large increase in the anchoring effect when the anchors were more extreme."
- **Why this is not a proportional-index result:** the outcome is estimates z-scored within item, and the distance between the two anchors grows several-fold across levels (e.g., African countries 24/48 vs 3/72). The paper gives no way to compute the index.

**(4) Effect-size metric**
- Hedges g only (v2 p. 18).
- Anchor–estimate gaps are analysed separately in Online Appendix H, which I did not read (UNVERIFIED).
- **No anchoring index or other unitless adjustment measure** appears in either version.

**(5) How theories were compared**
- Seven theories get qualitative predictions in Table 1 (p. 7).
- For extremity: anchoring-and-adjustment and selective accessibility predict an increase up to a threshold; the attitudinal view (Wegener et al. 2001) predicts an inverted U; extremeness aversion and noise theory predict an increase (p. 12).
- There is no model fitting. They explicitly declined to tally winners and losers (p. 33).
- They call for formal models, citing Turner & Schley 2016 and Lieder et al. 2018 (p. 39).
- In the 2025 version (p. 70) they say that mapping extremity properly "requires assessing anchor values at each level of a baseline distribution – rather than at just the 3rd/97th, 15th/85th, and 30th/70th percentiles."

**(6) Random or uninformative anchors**
- "Transparently random" coefficient: −0.19** [−0.33, −0.05] multivariate; −0.23** with controls; −0.05 and −0.18 (not significant) in the univariate models (Table 5, p. 28).
- Table 6 (p. 29): g = 0.78 random vs 0.83 not random.
- The 2025 version reports −0.27*** instead (its Table 5, p. 42).
- Primed or incidental anchors: −0.72*** (p. 28).

**Closeness:** meta-analysis 1; meta-study 2 (extremity relative to uncertainty, but 8 items, z-score outcome, no index, no models).

## B. Young et al. 2026, Cognitive Psychology 164, 101796 (doi 10.1016/j.cogpsych.2026.101796)

Full text read (CC-BY, Cambridge repository copy with journal pagination).
- **Design:** 10 studies, N = 1,353 after exclusions (pp. 7–8), plus 953 calibration participants. The anchors are items, not numbers ("torch vs laptop"), in their "High-Low" design.
- **Outcome:** percentile rank of each estimate within the calibration distribution, following Jacowitz & Kahneman, plus an assimilation score (p. 7).
- **Result:** meta-analytic g = 0.25 [0.05, 0.45] (p. 11). Low-value items were anchored more than high-value items.
- **OpAQ:** not used. They cite Röseler & Schütz 2022 only as a meta-analysis (p. 1).
- **Models:** no process models fitted. The only simulation is one validating the rank measure (Supplementary Material 1). They conclude selective accessibility gives the best account (abstract).
- **Extremity:** only a discussion remark. The largest effect was in Study 1, where item values differed by factors of 44–500, "consistent with" Lieder et al. (pp. 15–16). No proportional-adjustment analysis.
- They cite Schley & Weingarten (2025) as d = 0.876 (p. 2) and 0.88 (p. 15), while every Schley & Weingarten version I read reports 0.824/0.825. I did not resolve this.

**Closeness: 0.**

## C. Searches, 2022–2026

**Method:** OpenAlex 2022–2026 citers: 164 for Lieder 2018a, 21 for Lieder 2018b, 54 for Turner & Schley. I also ran OpenAlex keyword searches and web searches. The OpenAlex citer list for OpAQ (jopd.67) is low-recall: it returned only 4 papers and missed two papers that do use OpAQ. **No citer fits models to multi-item anchoring data or relates the proportional index to extremity.**

| Paper (verified DOI) | What it did | Close |
|---|---|---|
| **Röseler & Schütz 2022, "Hanging the Anchor Off a New Ship", PsyArXiv 10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn** (single version, 2022-03; never published) | Full text. Meta-analysis **of OpAQ**: 90 studies, k = 386 items, N = 17,708, Hedges g (pp. 17–18). g = 0.689 [0.589, 0.789] (abstract). Extremity = mean relative distance of anchor from the true value per item (p. 11). "Relative distance" b = 0.040 per unit, k = 312, p < .001 (Table 2, p. 21). They describe the relationship as "positive and nonlinear" (Table 4, p. 29; p. 30), but the PDF shows only a linear coefficient. The nonlinear evidence may be in their online app, which I did not check. They conclude against selective accessibility's prediction that extreme anchors give smaller effects (p. 30). Random anchors: smaller effects that are still above 0 (p. 26). They recommend a unitless "relative strength of adjustment" metric "to formalize the relationship between anchor distance and adjustment strength" (p. 34). That is the planned study's gap, named explicitly. | **2** |
| Röseler et al. 2024, *Meta-Psychology* 8, 10.15626/mp.2022.3236 | Abstract only. OpAQ-based; shows that individual susceptibility-to-anchoring scores are unreliable. No extremity or model analysis. | 1 |

Exp 2: N = 127, anchor offsets of 2/4/8 m, with no-anchor trials. Subjective anchoring score rises linearly with subjective offset: β = 0.66, t(1904.85) = 42.69. They fit a weighted-linear descriptive model and link it to Turner & Schley's integration model. This is a single perceptual quantity. | 1 |
| Lee & Morewedge 2022, *Psychological Science* 33:60–75, 10.1177/09567976211024254 | Abstract only. 11 preregistered experiments, N = 3,552. Anchoring grows with stimulus magnitude through noise (scalar variability). Relevant to an uncertainty-scaled definition of extremity. | 1 |

Several 2025–2026 papers on anchoring in large language models (arXiv, e.g. 2505.15392) report an anchoring index against anchor distance for LLMs. I did not verify these; they are not about humans.

## D. What Lieder 2018 and Turner & Schley 2016 fitted

Lieder page numbers are from the 2017 PsyArXiv preprints (5x2em and zu4pt). I did not check the pagination of the published Psychonomic Bulletin & Review versions.

**Lieder et al. 2018a, PBR 25:322–349, doi 10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8**
- **Jacowitz & Kahneman fit:** Jacowitz & Kahneman's anchoring index across **15 quantities**. Uncertainty σ came from their own elicitation; means were Jacowitz & Kahneman's unanchored medians. Two parameters were fitted by least squares on the index (29 adjustments, step size 22.4; p. 25).
  - Predicted mean index **53.22% vs observed 48.48%**, r(13) = 0.62, p = .0135 (p. 26).
  - Predicted index correlates with σ: Spearman ρ = 0.586. This matches Jacowitz & Kahneman's r(13) = −0.68 between confidence and the index (p. 31).
- **Self-generated anchors:** Epley & Gilovich 2006, 19 quantities. 80.62% vs 80.95% relative adjustment; r(17) = 0.61 (p. 27).
- **Cognitive load:** r(5) = 0.96 (p. 29).
- **Russo & Schoemaker (Attila, anchors 500–1300), plus an MTurk replication (N = 300):** simulated with the Jacowitz & Kahneman parameters. Mean estimates rise linearly with the anchor; the model overshoots at the highest anchor (pp. 30–31). Compared on mean estimates, not the index.
- **Simmons et al. 2010 Study 3b:** incentives affect adjustment only for implausible anchors. Plausible: 0.76 [−0.42, 1.94]; implausible: 17.8 [9.76, 25.91]; ρ(22) = 0.72 (p. 39).
- **Stated prediction on extremity:** bias ≈ (a − x)·rᵗ, so bias grows in proportion to the anchor–truth distance (Eqs. 3–4, p. 20; Table 1, p. 23). For a fixed number of adjustments, that means a constant relative adjustment.
- **Their Figure 4 (p. 19), my reading:** the optimal number of adjustments rises with distance measured in σ units. At intermediate time costs, the remaining bias is non-monotonic in distance. That implies the index could fall with extremity. The authors do not say this in the text.
- They never derived or tested how the index varies with extremity.

**Lieder et al. 2018b, PBR 25:775–784, doi 10.3758/s13423-017-1288-6**
- Bus-delay prediction tasks with time-cost × error-cost incentives. Exp 1: N = 30 recruited, self-generated anchor (p. 6). Exp 2: N = 60, provided low/high anchors (p. 14).
- Bias was modelled as linear in the true value.
- Relative adjustment: 41.3% [38.5, 44.0] in Exp 1 (p. 10). In Exp 2, 29.86% for low anchors and 27.25% for high anchors, not different, z = 1.16 (p. 16).
- One quantity; no extremity manipulation.

**Turner & Schley 2016, Cognitive Psychology 90:1–47, doi 10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003**
- Full text from the author's website copy, journal pagination.
- **Exp 1:** N = 589 across 5 between-participant conditions (unanchored prior, regular, directional, irrelevant, cognitive load; p. 12). 6 items from Simmons et al. and Jacowitz & Kahneman, **one anchor per item** (high for 3 items, low for 3; p. 13). The model was fitted separately per item with Bayesian estimation (p. 14). **No anchoring index is possible with this design, and none is used.**
- **Exp 2:** N = 189, within-person prior and posterior estimates plus confidence ratings, hierarchical model (p. 26).
- **Extremity is an assumption, not a finding.** Anchor influence is mapped from "prior consistency" (the prior CDF at the anchor; p. 21) via a Bézier curve, "producing an inverted U-shaped relationship between anchor extremity and the magnitude of the shift … for simplicity" (p. 23). An asymptote is allowed as a special case. Summary (p. 25): more implausible anchors get "a proportionally smaller influence."
- The curvilinear pattern in Fig. 14 (p. 31) is across participants' prior-to-anchor distance for one fixed anchor per item. It is not a test across anchor levels.

**Closeness: Lieder 2018a 1–2 (source of a model, not a test); Lieder 2018b 0–1; Turner & Schley 1.**

## Not verified

- The Management Science published text and the online appendices at osf.io/d583s (including anchor–estimate gaps in Appendix H).
- Where Röseler & Schütz show the "nonlinear" relationship: it is not in the PDF text, possibly in their online app.
- Full texts of the entries marked abstract only above.
- Published PBR page numbers for both Lieder papers.

Papers I read are in /tmp/jdmsim: scratch_nov_sw_v2.pdf, scratch_nov_sw_ms.pdf, scratch_nov_sw_young.pdf, scratch_nov_sw_turner.pdf and scratch_nov_sw_wu.txt. I also read another agent's files there: scratch_lieder_5x2em.pdf, scratch_lieder_zu4pt.pdf and hanging.txt.</result>

content.text: The novelty check confirms the gap is open. Röseler & Schütz named it explicitly, and Schley & Weingarten's 2026 meta-analysis coded extremity only as a binary flag and used no proportional index. It also flags something that affects my resource-rational model: in Lieder et al. (2018a) the optimal number of adjustments grows with anchor distance. That can reverse the predicted shape. I'm reading their exact specification before freezing predictions.

relative adjustment size is less than one. Therefore, the average estimate usually lies
between the anchor and the correct value. Fourth, because the relative adjustment is
less than one, the anchoring bias increases linearly with the distance from the anchor to
the correct value.

exceed a geometrically decaying function of the number of adjustments as illustrated in

beliefs. Consequently, assuming that the bound is tight, resource-rational

function of the correct value x and the anchor a:

linearly with the distance from the anchor to the correct value as illustrated in Figure 5.

adjustment makes the interesting, empirically testable prediction that the less time and
computation a person invests into generating an estimate, the more biased her estimate
will be towards the anchor. As illustrated in Figure 6a, the relative adjustment (see
Figure 5) increases with the number of adjustments. When the number of adjustments
is zero, then the relative adjustment is zero and the prediction is the anchor regardless
of how far it is away from the correct value. However, as the number of adjustments
increases, the relative adjustment increases and the predictions become more informed
by the correct value. As the number of adjustments tends to infinity, the average guess

of the anchoring bias increases with the distance of the correct value from the anchor
(Panel b).

distribution.

plausible costs of computation, the resource-rational number of adjustments is much
smaller than the number of adjustments required for convergence to the posterior
distribution. This might explain why people’s estimates of unknown quantities are
biased towards their anchor across a wide range of circumstances. Yet, optimal resource
allocation also entails that the number of adjustments increases with the relative cost of
error and decreases with the relative cost of time. Hence, our theory predicts that the
anchoring bias is smaller when errors are costly and larger when time is costly; Figure
6b illustrates this prediction.

property of diminishing returns per additional computation is a universal feature of

many biologically and psychologically plausible mechanisms that share the same
characteristics. We will elaborate on this idea in the General Discussion. In the
following sections, we assess these and other predictions of our model.

1	# Generative process models of anchored estimation on the log scale.
2	# All quantities are log(value / true value); sigma is the item's belief uncertainty,
3	# and every model parameter is expressed in units of sigma, so the models are scale-free.
4	#
5	# Each participant-item row has a belief centre mu = bias + person offset + belief noise.
6	# Response = model output + response noise; a small share of responses is contaminated
7	# (unit errors, typing slips) to mimic real estimation data.
8	
9	belief_sd_share <- 0.6     # SD of belief centres across people, in sigma units
10	response_sd_share <- 0.3   # response noise SD, in sigma units
11	contamination_p <- 0.02    # share of responses with gross errors
12	contamination_sd <- 2      # SD (log units) of gross errors
13	
14	model_names <- c(M0 = "No anchoring", M1 = "Resource-rational adjustment",
15	                 M2 = "Constant-weight integration", M3 = "Adjust to plausible boundary",
16	                 M4 = "Plausibility-discounted integration")
17	
18	respond <- function(model, x, mu, sigma, par) {
19	  d <- x - mu
20	  switch(model,
21	    M0 = mu,
22	    M2 = mu + par$w * d,
23	    M3 = ifelse(abs(d) < par$k * sigma, x, mu + sign(d) * par$k * sigma),
24	    M4 = mu + par$w * d * exp(-d^2 / (2 * (par$c * sigma)^2)),
25	    M1 = {
26	      z <- x
27	      for (i in seq_len(par$t)) {
28	        prop <- z + rnorm(length(z), 0, par$s * sigma)
29	        log_ratio <- ((z - mu)^2 - (prop - mu)^2) / (2 * sigma^2)
30	        z <- ifelse(log(runif(length(z))) < log_ratio, prop, z)
31	      }
32	      z
33	    })
34	}
35	
36	# rows: data.table with x (log anchor / truth), cell, pid. cellpar: data.table with cell, bias, sigma.
37	simulate_responses <- function(model, rows, cellpar, par, person_sd = 0.15) {
38	  r <- merge(rows[, .(row_id = .I, cell, pid, x)], cellpar, by = "cell")
39	  setorder(r, row_id)
40	  persons <- unique(r$pid)
41	  u <- setNames(rnorm(length(persons), 0, person_sd), persons)
42	  mu <- r$bias + u[r$pid] + rnorm(nrow(r), 0, belief_sd_share * r$sigma)
43	  y <- respond(model, r$x, mu, r$sigma, par) + rnorm(nrow(r), 0, response_sd_share * r$sigma)
44	  gross <- runif(nrow(r)) < contamination_p
45	  y[gross] <- y[gross] + rnorm(sum(gross), 0, contamination_sd)
46	  y
47	}
48	
49	# Anchoring index of each model in the Jacowitz & Kahneman (1995) design: anchors at the
50	# 15th and 85th percentiles of the unanchored response distribution.
51	jk_index <- function(model, par, n = 20000) {
52	  sd_unanchored <- sqrt(belief_sd_share^2 + response_sd_share^2)
53	  a <- qnorm(0.85) * sd_unanchored
54	  y_of <- function(x) {
55	    mu <- rnorm(n, 0, belief_sd_share)
56	    respond(model, rep(x, n), mu, 1, par) + rnorm(n, 0, response_sd_share)
57	  }
58	  (median(y_of(a)) - median(y_of(-a))) / (2 * a)
59	}

# and every model parameter is expressed in units of sigma, so the models are scale-free.
#
# Each participant-item row has a belief centre mu = bias + person offset + belief noise.
# Response = model output + response noise; a small share of responses is contaminated
# (unit errors, typing slips) to mimic real estimation data.

belief_sd_share <- 0.6     # SD of belief centres across people, in sigma units
response_sd_share <- 0.3   # response noise SD, in sigma units
contamination_p <- 0.02    # share of responses with gross errors
contamination_sd <- 2      # SD (log units) of gross errors

model_names <- c(M0 = "No anchoring", M1 = "Resource-rational adjustment",
                 M2 = "Constant-weight integration", M3 = "Adjust to plausible boundary",
                 M4 = "Plausibility-discounted integration")

respond <- function(model, x, mu, sigma, par) {
  d <- x - mu
  switch(model,
    M0 = mu,
    M2 = mu + par$w * d,
    M3 = ifelse(abs(d) < par$k * sigma, x, mu + sign(d) * par$k * sigma),
    M4 = mu + par$w * d * exp(-d^2 / (2 * (par$c * sigma)^2)),
    M1 = {
      z <- x
      for (i in seq_len(par$t)) {
        prop <- z + rnorm(length(z), 0, par$s * sigma)
        log_ratio <- ((z - mu)^2 - (prop - mu)^2) / (2 * sigma^2)
        z <- ifelse(log(runif(length(z))) < log_ratio, prop, z)
      }
      z
    })
}

# rows: data.table with x (log anchor / truth), cell, pid. cellpar: data.table with cell, bias, sigma.
simulate_responses <- function(model, rows, cellpar, par, person_sd = 0.15) {
  r <- merge(rows[, .(row_id = .I, cell, pid, x)], cellpar, by = "cell")
  setorder(r, row_id)
  persons <- unique(r$pid)
  u <- setNames(rnorm(length(persons), 0, person_sd), persons)
  mu <- r$bias + u[r$pid] + rnorm(nrow(r), 0, belief_sd_share * r$sigma)
  y <- respond(model, r$x, mu, r$sigma, par) + rnorm(nrow(r), 0, response_sd_share * r$sigma)
  gross <- runif(nrow(r)) < contamination_p
  y[gross] <- y[gross] + rnorm(sum(gross), 0, contamination_sd)
  y
}

# Anchoring index of each model in the Jacowitz & Kahneman (1995) design: anchors at the
# 15th and 85th percentiles of the unanchored response distribution.
jk_index <- function(model, par, n = 20000) {
  sd_unanchored <- sqrt(belief_sd_share^2 + response_sd_share^2)
  a <- qnorm(0.85) * sd_unanchored
  y_of <- function(x) {
    mu <- rnorm(n, 0, belief_sd_share)
    respond(model, rep(x, n), mu, 1, par) + rnorm(n, 0, response_sd_share)
  }
  (median(y_of(a)) - median(y_of(-a))) / (2 * a)
}

5. **Recommendation:** Email the Editor-in-Chief before submitting, since the guidelines invite this when fit is unclear. Describe the AI's role, the authorship line and the meta-scientific framing. <result>1. **Article type:** Regular Article is the fit: 12,000 words excluding references, unstructured abstract of 150–250 words. APA references are optional because the journal accepts "Free Format" submissions (any consistent style; the typesetter reformats). Review is double-anonymised with a separate title page and 4–8 keywords. The Open Materials Policy is mandatory: anonymised code and data at review, then deposit in a repository before acceptance. There is no Registered Report type, badges are retired, and CRediT and a significance statement are not required. The cover letter is required and must argue why the paper suits a multidisciplinary journal and confirm author approval and ethics.
2. **AI policy (journal text, quoted in full in the file):** AI "cannot fulfill the role of, nor be listed as, an author". Any use to "develop any portion of a manuscript" must be described "transparently and in detail, in the Methods or Acknowledgements section". The editor makes the final decision. Wiley's publisher-level guidance adds a disclosure at submission and required Methods content (tool name and version, dates, role, how the author directed and checked the work). It also frames AI as an "assistant at your direction" and says the author must have "maintained intellectual control". Wiley and COPE are quoted verbatim at their own levels. Nothing prohibits a mainly AI-generated manuscript. Wiley's own AI FAQ discloses section drafts "composed by Claude 4 Sonnet" under the authors' direction, which gives a precedent.
3. **Cost:** the journal is hybrid, with no submission fee. The APC is USD 4,200 / GBP 2,780 / EUR 3,470 (Wiley price list updated 2 September 2026). Issues become free to read after a 1-year embargo.
4. **Related articles (Crossref-verified):** 10.1111/cogs.70229 "The Robustness of Anchoring in a Naturalistic VR‐Based Task" (2026) and 10.1111/cogs.70256 "Quantity Estimation by Repeated Comparative Judgments" (2026), which includes an anchoring-and-adjustment model. The searches found no secondary analyses of multi-lab data in this journal; that check is not exhaustive.
5. **Fit:** good if the paper leads with the four-model comparison. It risks a desk rejection if framed as a narrow social-psychology or judgement-and-decision-making paper. The AI-authorship risk is moderate to high because the editor decides and Wiley's "companion, not a replacement" wording fits an AI-run study poorly. I recommend a detailed Methods disclosure and possibly a query to the editor before submission.

The Wiley author-guidelines page blocks scripted downloads, so I read it in a browser session and copied the quotes from the rendered text. One item is UNVERIFIED: whether the Research Exchange submission form has its own AI question. Checking it would mean starting a submission.

input.content:
# Preregistration: How does anchor influence change with anchor extremity? A model-based secondary analysis of the Open Anchoring Quest

Template: Preregistration of secondary data analysis (van den Akker et al., 2021, Meta-Psychology, https://doi.org/10.15626/MP.2020.2625). Question numbers follow the template.

Date: 2026-09-27. This document, the simulation code in `R/`, and the frozen model predictions in `output/predictions_raw.csv` and `output/predictions_summary.csv` are committed to git together, before any outcome variable is read. `R/read_opaq.R` refuses to load the `estimate` column until this file is committed.

## Part 1: Study information

**Q1. Working title.** How does anchor influence change with anchor extremity? Testing five process models of anchoring against 95 studies of open data.

**Q2. Authors.** Lukas Wallrich (Birkbeck, University of London; ORCID [ORCID redacted]), who commissioned and is accountable for the study. The design, code, analyses and text were produced by an AI system (Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic) working autonomously under Lukas Wallrich's instruction, with review by other AI systems (OpenAI Codex CLI, Google Gemini via the Antigravity CLI). See `ai_disclosure.md`.

**Q3. Research questions.**
- RQ1: Within the same item, does the proportional influence of the anchor on estimates (the local elasticity of the estimate with respect to the anchor, on the log scale) rise, stay constant, or fall as the anchor moves further from the true value?
- RQ2: Across item-study cells with a classic high/low anchor pair, does the log-scale anchoring index rise, stay constant, or fall with anchor extremity?
- RQ3: Which of five process models of anchoring, calibrated in advance to an external benchmark, predicts the observed response functions?

**Q4. Hypotheses.** We state competing model predictions rather than one directional hypothesis. All tests use frequentist estimation with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).

Notation. For each estimate, y = ln(estimate / true value) and x = ln(anchor / true value). Within item-study cells we fit y = a_cell + b·x + g·x|x| (plus random effects; Q19). b is the average elasticity at the true value; g is the curvature: g > 0 means the anchor's proportional pull grows with extremity, g < 0 means it shrinks. rho = g / b is the curvature relative to the average elasticity.

Models (full specification in `R/models.R`; all operate on the log scale):
- **M0 No anchoring.** Estimates ignore the anchor.
- **M1 Anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments** (Lieder et al., 2018a, with the number of adjustments held constant): a Metropolis-Hastings chain starts at the anchor and takes t steps towards the belief distribution.
- **M1R Resource-rational anchor-and-adjust** (Lieder et al., 2018a, Eq. 2): as M1, but the number of adjustments minimises expected absolute error plus a time cost per adjustment, so it depends on how far the anchor lies from the belief.
- **M2 Constant-weight integration** (in the spirit of the anchor integration model, Turner & Schley, 2016, with a constant weight): the estimate is a fixed weighted average of anchor and belief.
- **M3 Adjust to the plausible boundary** (Epley & Gilovich, 2006): anchors inside the plausible range are accepted; from anchors outside it people adjust to the nearest edge of the range.
- **M4 Plausibility-discounted integration** (selective accessibility with a plausibility gate; Strack & Mussweiler, 1997; Wegener et al., 2001): the anchor's weight falls smoothly as the anchor becomes implausible.

Predictions (derived by simulation on the exact OpAQ designs; Q20 and `output/predictions_summary.csv`):
- H1 (within-item curvature, pooled): [[PRED_H1]]
- H1a/H1b (within-item curvature, random-anchor and fixed-anchor strata separately): same direction as H1 for each model.
- H2 (across-cell slope of the log anchoring index on extremity): [[PRED_H2]]
- H3 (model adequacy): each model's 95% predictive interval for g, rho, and the across-cell slope, given in Q20. A model is contradicted by the data when an observed statistic lies outside its interval.

## Part 2: Data description

**Q5. Dataset.** Open Anchoring Quest (OpAQ; Röseler et al., 2022, https://doi.org/10.5334/jopd.67; correction https://doi.org/10.5334/jopd.92), file `opaq_70a.csv` (OSF project ygnvb, dated 2023-02-10; SHA-256 18ec245c45427f431c7a01d0b960a7cabf851dffc91ed5f12b10122019966722). Trial-level anchoring data aggregated from openly available and contributed datasets: 95,735 rows, 95 studies, 402 item texts, 466 item-study cells. Each row is one estimate by one participant for one item and one anchor. Cross-sectional; participants mostly lay adults online or in labs, collected 2010-2022 in Europe, Asia and the Americas.

**Q6. Openness.** Publicly available under CC-BY 4.0 (licence field of the OSF project). No registration or agreement needed.

**Q7. Access.** https://osf.io/download/s4zgw/ ; `R/00_fetch.R` downloads it and checks the hash.

**Q8. Date of download.** 2026-09-27 (single analyst).

**Q9. Data collection.** Described in Röseler et al. (2022) and in the source publications listed in the `reference` column; OpAQ harmonised studies that used at least two anchors.

**Q10. Codebook.** Table 1 of Röseler et al. (2022); `labels.xlsx` in the OSF folder "Information for potential contributors" (defines anchortype 5 = incidental/subliminal, which is not in the published table). The file has further columns derived from the estimate (Q18).

**Q11. Manipulated variables.** The anchor value (`anchor`), its side (`anchorhigh`: 1 high, 0 low), and its type (`anchortype`: 1 explicitly random, 2 fixed without explanation, 3 relevant to the target). x = ln(anchor / true value).

**Q12. Measured variables.**
- Outcome: `estimate`, transformed to y = ln(estimate / true value). No other outcome columns are used.
- Design variables and covariates: `true_value`, `reference_short` (study), `anchoring_item` (item), `participant_id`, `tasktype`, `scaletype`, `comparative_question`, `direction`, `incentive`, `experiment_type`.
- Across-cell anchoring index for a cell with one low anchor A_L and one high anchor A_H: AI = [median(y | high) - median(y | low)] / [ln(A_H) - ln(A_L)]. Extremity of the cell: E = (|x_L| + |x_H|) / 2, the mean absolute log distance of the two anchors from the true value.

**Q13. Inclusion and exclusion of units.**
Rows enter only if: `anchortype` is 1, 2 or 3 (excludes self-generated and incidental anchors); `scaletype` = 1 (open response); `tasktype` is a positive ratio-scale quantity (quantity, number, price, length, height, distance, weight, population, volume, speed, duration, birth rate, income, width, area, circumference, age); anchor and true value are numeric and positive; the study is not Röseler & Wagner (2021), whose anchors were computed from each participant's own unanchored estimates. The true value of a cell is the value on its first row.
- Within-item set: cells with at least 3 distinct anchor values. From design columns: 20 cells, 4 studies, 7,952 rows, 1,492 participants. Random-anchor stratum (anchortype 1): Bahník (2021a), 13 cells, 6,578 rows; Yoon et al. (2021, Form C), 2 cells, 172 rows. Fixed-anchor stratum (anchortype 2): Frech et al. (2021), 4 cells, 416 rows (high anchors only, 10 levels); Imhoff & Barker (2022, Study 2), 1 cell, 786 rows (20 levels).
- Across-cell set: cells with anchortype 2 or 3, exactly one low and one high anchor value, ln(A_H / A_L) >= 0.25, at least 10 rows per side. From design columns: 129 cells, 40 studies, 109 items, 24,147 rows. No cell is in both sets.

**Q14. Missing data.** Rows with a missing, non-numeric, zero or negative estimate are excluded (the log is undefined). We will report how many. If a cell loses its eligibility (fewer than 3 anchor values in the within set; fewer than 10 rows on a side in the across set), it is dropped.

**Q15. Outliers.** Gross errors (unit errors, typing slips) are removed with one rule applied identically to simulated and observed data (`drop_gross_errors()` in `R/estimators.R`): a response is dropped when |y| exceeds both ln(1000) and the cell's largest |x| plus ln(10). A response equal to any anchor is always retained. No other trimming. Robustness analysis R1 uses median regression without this rule.

**Q16. Weights.** None.

## Part 3: Knowledge of data

**Q17. Prior work with the dataset.** None by the authors.

**Q18. Prior knowledge.**
- Read before this preregistration: the OpAQ data paper (Röseler et al., 2022); the OpAQ meta-analysis preprint (Röseler & Schütz, 2022, https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn), which reports that Hedges' g increases with the relative distance between anchor and true value (b = 0.040, k = 312) and that explicitly random anchors show smaller effects; Schley & Weingarten (2026) on anchor extremity; Barrera-Lemarchand et al. (2024), whose anchoring weight falls with anchor distance on percentage items; the Röseler & Wagner (2021) analysis script (to check anchor construction). We have not read the results of Bahník (2021a) or Imhoff & Barker (2022) concerning the shape of the estimate-anchor function [[NOVELTY_NOTE]].
- Columns read (design only, via `R/read_opaq.R`): reference_short, reference, id, participant_id, sex, age, nationality, anchoring_item, true_value, anchor, anchorhigh, anchortype, tasktype, direction, incentive, comparative_question, experiment_type, stimulitype, sampletype, scaletype, published, preregistered. Outputs seen: `output/design_inventory.txt`, `output/design_cells.csv`, and the cell and row counts in Q13.
- Never read before this commit: `estimate` and every column derived from it (adjustment, absadjustment, score, restr_score, zestimate, zadjustment, zabsadjustment, zscore, outlier, precision, nchar, precise, zsta).
- A 2026 corrigendum to Weber & Röseler (2025; OSF component sz5b9) reports item-to-effect mix-ups in their study. Weber et al. (2021) contributes 14 cells to the across-cell set. Whether the OpAQ master file is affected is unknown (robustness analysis R6).

## Part 4: Analyses

**Q19. Statistical models.** All code is in `R/estimators.R` (shared with the prediction simulation) and `R/04_confirmatory.R`.

H1 (primary). Within-item set, linear mixed model (lme4, REML):
y ~ x + x|x| + (1 + x + x|x| || cell) + (1 | participant),
with uncorrelated random intercepts, slopes and curvatures by cell and random intercepts by participant. Estimates: b (average elasticity), g (curvature), rho = g / b with a delta-method SE.
H1a/H1b. The same model fitted separately to the random-anchor stratum and the fixed-anchor stratum.
H2. Across-cell set: AI and its SE per cell (SE of each median = 1.2533 × MAD / sqrt(n)); multilevel meta-regression (metafor rma.mv, REML) of AI on E with random intercepts for study and cell within study. Estimate: slope d.
H3. For each model, the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of its simulated g, rho, b and d (Q20), compared with the observed values.

**Q20. Predicted effects and smallest effects of interest.** Model predictions from `R/03_simulate_predictions.R` ([[N_REPS]] replicates per model; each replicate draws model parameters from the set calibrated to Jacowitz & Kahneman's (1995) anchoring index of about .49, allowing .30-.60, and draws item uncertainty sigma ~ U(0.3, 1.2) log units and item bias ~ N(U(-0.3, 0.3), 0.3)):

[[PRED_TABLE]]

Smallest effect of interest for "no curvature": [[SESOI]]

**Q21. Power / precision.** [[POWER]]

**Q22. Inference criteria.**
- Gate G1 (anchoring present): the shape tests for a set or stratum are interpreted only if the lower bound of the 95% CI for b is above 0. If not, we report that set as "no measurable anchoring; shape not testable".
- H1 decision (95% Wald CIs; Satterthwaite degrees of freedom via lmerTest):
  - CI for g entirely above 0: elasticity rises with extremity. Consistent with M1; inconsistent with M1R, M2, M3, M4.
  - CI for g entirely below 0: elasticity falls with extremity. Consistent with M1R, M3, M4; inconsistent with M1 and M2.
  - CI for rho entirely inside the equivalence bounds (Q20): no meaningful curvature. Consistent with M2; inconsistent with M1, M1R, M3, M4.
  - Otherwise: inconclusive.
- H1a/H1b use the same rules within each stratum; if they disagree in sign (both CIs excluding 0 in opposite directions), we report that anchor type moderates the shape and do not pool the conclusion.
- H2 decision: the same three-way rule applied to d, with its own equivalence bounds (Q20).

Date: 2026-09-27. **Q4. Hypotheses.** We state competing model predictions rather than one directional hypothesis. All tests use frequentist estimation with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).

Notation. For each estimate, y = ln(estimate / true value) and x = ln(anchor / true value). Within item-study cells we fit y = a_cell + b·x + g·x|x| (plus random effects; Q19). b is the average elasticity at the true value; g is the curvature: g > 0 means the anchor's proportional pull grows with extremity, g < 0 means it shrinks. rho = g / b is the curvature relative to the average elasticity.

- **M1R Resource-rational anchor-and-adjust** (Lieder et al., 2018a, Eq. 2): as M1, but the number of adjustments minimises expected absolute error plus a time cost per adjustment, so it depends on how far the anchor lies from the belief.
- **M2 Constant-weight integration** (in the spirit of the anchor integration model, Turner & Schley, 2016, with a constant weight): the estimate is a fixed weighted average of anchor and belief.
- **M3 Adjust to the plausible boundary** (Epley & Gilovich, 2006): anchors inside the plausible range are accepted; from anchors outside it people adjust to the nearest edge of the range.
- **M4 Plausibility-discounted integration** (selective accessibility with a plausibility gate; Strack & Mussweiler, 1997; Wegener et al., 2001): the anchor's weight falls smoothly as the anchor becomes implausible.

The true value of a cell is the value on its first row.
- Within-item set: cells with at least 3 distinct anchor values. From design columns: 20 cells, 4 studies, 7,952 rows, 1,492 participants. Random-anchor stratum (anchortype 1): Bahník (2021a), 13 cells, 6,578 rows; Yoon et al. (2021, Form C), 2 cells, 172 rows. Fixed-anchor stratum (anchortype 2): Frech et al. (2021), 4 cells, 416 rows (high anchors only, 10 levels); Imhoff & Barker (2022, Study 2), 1 cell, 786 rows (20 levels).

- Gate G1 (anchoring present): the shape tests for a set or stratum are interpreted only if the lower bound of the 95% CI for b is above 0. If not, we report that set as "no measurable anchoring; shape not testable".
- H1 decision (95% Wald CIs; Satterthwaite degrees of freedom via lmerTest):
  - CI for g entirely above 0: elasticity rises with extremity. Consistent with M1; inconsistent with M1R, M2, M3, M4.
  - CI for g entirely below 0: elasticity falls with extremity. Consistent with M1R, M3, M4; inconsistent with M1 and M2.
  - CI for rho entirely inside the equivalence bounds (Q20): no meaningful curvature. Consistent with M2; inconsistent with M1, M1R, M3, M4.
  - Otherwise: inconclusive.
- H1a/H1b use the same rules within each stratum; if they disagree in sign (both CIs excluding 0 in opposite directions), we report that anchor type moderates the shape and do not pool the conclusion.
- H2 decision: the same three-way rule applied to d, with its own equivalence bounds (Q20).
- H3: a model is contradicted by a statistic when the observed point estimate lies outside that model's 95% predictive interval. A model is retained only if it is not contradicted on g (or rho) and d. We report which models survive; if none survives, we say so.
- The primary conclusion rests on H1 (pooled). H1a/H1b, H2 and H3 are confirmatory secondary tests; we do not correct for multiplicity because each addresses a distinct prediction, and we report all of them.

**Q23. Analytic problems.** If the H1 model fails to converge or is singular, we remove random-effect terms in this order until it converges: curvature variance, slope variance; the participant intercept is kept. If rma.mv fails, we fit a single-level random-effects meta-regression with study-clustered robust SEs (clubSandwich if available, otherwise metafor::robust). Any such change is reported in `deviations.md`.

**Q24. Robustness.**
- R1: median regression (quantreg, tau = .5) of y on cell-specific intercepts and slopes plus a common x|x| term, without the gross-error rule; CI by participant-cluster bootstrap (1,000 draws).
- R2: H1 with the near/far split replacing x|x|: separate slopes for |x| <= 1 and |x| > 1; report the difference.
- R3: H1 without Bahník (2021a).
- R4: H2 with raw-scale anchoring index (Jacowitz & Kahneman, 1995): [median(estimate | high) - median(estimate | low)] / (A_H - A_L).
- R5: H2 adding covariates: anchortype, comparative_question, direction, incentive (0 vs other), experiment_type.
- R6: H2 without Weber et al. (2021).
- R7: H2 with extremity measured as max(|x_L|, |x_H|) and as ln(A_H / A_L).

**Q25. Exploratory analyses (labelled as such in the paper).** Fitting each model's parameters to the observed data (simulation-based estimation) to compare fit; asymmetry between high and low anchors; the relation of Hedges' g to extremity in the across-cell set, for comparison with Röseler & Schütz (2022); plots of binned response functions for each within-item cell.

# Novelty: the five closest papers and what this study adds

Search basis (2026-09-27): OpenAlex, Google Scholar and Semantic Scholar citers of the OpAQ data paper (24 works) and of the OpAQ meta-analysis preprint; OpenAlex citers since 2022 of Lieder et al. (2018a; 164), Lieder et al. (2018b; 21) and Turner & Schley (2016; 54); keyword and web searches for computational models of anchoring and for anchor extremity. Full reports are in `scoping/`. DOIs were checked against Crossref. No work was found that relates the proportional anchoring index to anchor extremity across many items with trial-level data, or that compares process models on OpAQ.

| # | Paper | What it did | What this study adds |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Röseler, L., & Schütz, A. (2022). Hanging the anchor off a new ship: A meta-analysis of anchoring effects. PsyArXiv. https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn | Meta-analysis of the OpAQ data (90 studies, k = 386 items, N = 17,708). Hedges' g rose with the mean relative distance between anchor and true value (b = 0.040 per unit, k = 312). Concluded against the prediction that extreme anchors give smaller effects, and called for a unitless "relative strength of adjustment" metric to formalise how adjustment depends on anchor distance. | g is a standardised mean difference, so it rises with anchor distance even when anchors pull estimates by a constant proportion. We measure the proportional pull directly (log-scale elasticity and anchoring index), separate within-item from across-item variation, and test the pattern against pre-computed predictions of five process models. |
| 2 | Schley, D. R., & Weingarten, E. (2026). Fifty years of anchoring effects: A theoretical reintegration and meta-analysis. Management Science (online 2026-05-19). https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03238 | Meta-analysis of 1,280 high-vs-low effect sizes (482 studies). Extremity was a binary flag (49 of 1,280 effect sizes "extreme"); coefficient -0.02 [-0.20, 0.16]. An earlier version added a meta-study with 8 items and anchors at calibration percentiles; the high-minus-low gap in z-scored estimates grew with extremity. Theories were compared qualitatively; the authors call for formal models. | Continuous, outcome-free extremity (log distance of anchor from truth) instead of a binary author label; a proportional outcome instead of g or z-scores; trial-level data from many studies; formal models whose predictions are simulated on the actual designs and frozen before the data are read. |
| 3 | Barrera-Lemarchand, F., Balenzuela, P., Bahrami, B., Deroy, O., & Navajas, J. (2024). Promoting erroneous divergent opinions increases the wisdom of crowds. Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/09567976241252138 | Modelled the anchored crowd mean as a weighted average of anchor and crowd mean with weight w0·exp(-beta·|A - truth|). In 30 percentage questions with anchors fixed at 5% and 95% (N = 396), the anchoring weight fell with anchor distance (r = -.56). | Their distance varied only through the true value on a bounded 0-100 scale, which can compress responses mechanically. We use open-ended ratio-scale quantities, vary the anchor itself within items (up to 20 anchor levels, and continuous random anchors), and compare this discounting pattern with rival models that predict rising or constant proportional influence. |
| 4 | Lieder, F., Griffiths, T. L., Huys, Q. J. M., & Goodman, N. D. (2018). The anchoring bias reflects rational use of cognitive resources. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 25, 322-349. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8 | Resource-rational anchoring-and-adjustment: a sampling chain starts at the anchor and stops after the number of adjustments that balances error and time cost. Fitted Jacowitz & Kahneman's (1995) anchoring index for 15 quantities (predicted 53.2% vs observed 48.5%). Stated that bias grows in proportion to anchor distance for a fixed number of adjustments; did not derive or test how the proportional index changes with extremity. | We derive the extremity prediction for two variants: a fixed number of adjustments (proportional pull rises with extremity) and an adaptive, resource-rational number (proportional pull falls). We test both on data with many anchor levels per item. |
| 5 | Turner, B. M., & Schley, D. R. (2016). The anchor integration model: A descriptive model of anchoring effects. Cognitive Psychology, 90, 1-47. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003 | Anchor integration model: the anchor shifts the prior belief with a weight that depends on anchor plausibility, mapped with an inverted-U function assumed "for simplicity". Experiment 1 used one anchor per item (N = 589), so the shape across anchor levels was not tested. | We test the shape the model assumes: whether the anchor's weight is constant (M2) or falls with implausibility (M4) across many anchor levels for the same item. |

Further related work: Röseler & Wagner's unpublished OSF project "Absolute versus Relative Adjustment from Anchors" (osf.io/dsyrk, 2020-2021) explored anchor distance and effect strength with anchors built from participants' own estimates; no write-up exists. Röseler et al. (2025, Meta-Psychology, https://doi.org/10.15626/MP.2024.4137) formalised and falsified a time-based insufficient-adjustment model without addressing extremity. Wu et al. (2026, Cognitive Science, https://doi.org/10.1111/cogs.70229) found anchoring scores rising linearly with anchor offset for one perceptual quantity (virtual-reality height estimation).

<result>Psychonomic Bulletin & Review fits the science well, but the AI-authorship question is a high risk that needs your decision.

1. **Article type.** A Brief Report fits: the format explicitly admits "computational model simulations, meta-analyses, or secondary or re-analyses of existing data". Introduction, Results and Discussion may have at most 3,000 words; Methods, references, figures, tables and the abstract are not counted. The abstract limit is 250 words and the style is APA 7. A Theoretical/Review article (no length limit) is a fallback. Judgment and decision making are in scope, and formal models are "particularly welcome".
2. **Required statements.**
   - **Review:** double-anonymous, so the OSF, preregistration and repository links must be anonymised view-only links. A June 2025 announcement called this a one-year pilot. No page I fetched says whether it is now permanent.
   - **Open Practices Statement:** mandatory, placed just before the References. It states where data and materials are and whether the study was preregistered.
   - **Declarations section:** includes Ethics approval. For secondary data, approval "may be required dependent on the law" of the country, so a written exemption from your institution is the safe choice.
   - **Not in use:** no open science badges, no CRediT requirement, no significance statement.
3. **AI policy.** Neither the journal nor the Psychonomic Society has an AI policy of its own, so the Springer / Springer Nature risk framework applies, alongside COPE.
   - **Authorship:** an AI cannot be an author. "Assigning authorship or accountability to AI systems or tools" and "listing AI as an author" are both "Not permitted".
   - **Amber (permitted with disclosure):** AI drafting from author input and AI support for analysis are allowed with human oversight, verification and disclosure.
   - **Red (not permitted):** "Writing results or discussion independently; generating scientific claims or interpretations", and producing analyses or conclusions "without human oversight".
   - **Other constraints:** AI "must not determine conclusions", and "the argument, interpretation, and conclusions must be author-led".
   - **Where to disclose:** Springer asks for "an AI Declaration in your manuscript". COPE asks for disclosure in "the Materials and Methods (or similar section)". I recommend both, plus a mention in the cover letter.
4. **Needs your decision.** Because the work is disclosed and supervised, it sits on the boundary between permitted and not permitted. What decides it is whether you can show real human oversight and author-led interpretation. A manuscript that presents Claude as the one who designed and interpreted the study will probably be read as the not-permitted case and risks desk rejection.
5. **Fees and example papers.** The journal is hybrid. Open access costs £2,590 / $3,890 / €2,990 (plus VAT) under CC BY; the subscription route is free. There is no required cover letter content beyond Springer's rules on re-used material and suggested reviewers. Three recent articles in the journal passed the Crossref DOI check:

<result>Findings are in `~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/scoping/scratch_journals/decision.md`. apa.org blocks curl and WebFetch, so I read the live pages through the r.jina.ai reader and checked the wording against Wayback copies.

1. **Article type:** Decision offers full-length articles (35 pages, "major theoretical contributions") and shorter articles (15 pages). Page limits are double-spaced and exclude tables, figures and references. Choosing between them is your call; the manuscript probably needs the 35-page type. The Registered Report route does not apply, but the Preregistered+Analysis Plan badge does. Other requirements:
   - abstract of at most 250 words, up to 5 keywords, APA 7
   - CRediT roles entered at submission
   - a data/code availability statement in both the author note and the Method section
   - a "Constraints on generality" subsection in the Discussion
   - a consent and ethics-board statement that covers secondary use of data
   - no public significance statement and no stated TOP levels; masked review is optional
2. **AI policy:** Decision has no journal-specific policy and follows APA's. "AI cannot be named as an author on an APA scholarly publication." Use of AI "must be disclosed … and cited", and the authors must verify everything. Nothing bars substantially AI-generated work. The pages disagree on where disclosure goes: the policy page says "in the manuscript", while the Decision guidelines and APA's AI guidance say "in the methods section". APA's guidance table asks for the tool and "number of iterations" in the Method section for code and analysis. COPE matches APA, but I could only read an archived copy (September 2025) because the live COPE page blocked all access.
3. **Main risk:** the real problem is APA's authorship-credit rule, not the ban on AI authors. Ethics Code 8.12a says authors take credit "only for work they have performed or to which they have substantially contributed". So you as sole human author should not claim CRediT roles such as Formal analysis, Software or Writing—original draft. Those roles belong in a detailed disclosure in the Method section. It may also be worth emailing the editor, Tim Rakow, before submitting.
4. **Open access:** it is a hybrid journal. The APC is $3,500 USD under a CC-BY-NC-ND licence. Birkbeck is part of APA's Jisc agreement, which gives CC-BY open access at no cost if the corresponding author is at a participating UK institution. That agreement has a yearly cap on articles, so check with the library first.
5. **Fit:** the scope fits well; the journal favours "large-scale confirmatory tests of theory". But no anchoring paper appears among its roughly 136 research articles since 2021 (checked via Crossref). Two related papers, both checked on Crossref:
   - Kvam et al. (2024), https://doi.org/10.1037/dec0000237, from Decision's AI special issue
   - Hogarth & Soyer (2021), https://doi.org/10.1037/dec0000150

   The rejection rate is 79.5% and the impact factor is 1.6.</result>
