<note>A task-notification fires each time this agent stops with no live background children of its own. The user can send it another message and resume it, so the same task-id may notify more than once.</note>
<result>## Anchoring vs anchor extremity: per-paper quantitative evidence

I checked every DOI below against `api.crossref.org/works/<DOI>` and the title and first author matched, unless the entry says otherwise. "AI" means the two-sided index: (estimate under high anchor − estimate under low anchor) / (high anchor − low anchor). "Local slope" is the change in estimate divided by the change in anchor between two adjacent anchor levels. Where a paper gives means rather than the medians Jacowitz & Kahneman specified, I computed the AI on the means.

All arithmetic is in `/tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_classic_ai.py`. Its output is in `/tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_classic_ai_out.txt`, and working notes are in `/tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_classic_findings.md`. I opened no data files.

**Source quality at a glance:**
- **Full text read:** Strack & Mussweiler 1997; Mussweiler & Strack 2001; Wegener et al. 2001 and 2010; Northcraft & Neale 1987; Bystranowski et al. 2021; Schultze et al. 2015; Turner & Schley 2016; Frederick & Mochon 2012; Smith et al. 2013. Harris et al. 2019, Simmons et al. 2010 and Lieder et al. 2018 are accepted-manuscript or preprint versions, so their page numbers are manuscript pages.
- **Figures only:** Chapman & Johnson 1994. The numbers are read off the figures and are accurate to about ±1.
- **Abstract only:** Townson 2019, Marti & Wissler 2000, Thorsteinson 2011, Lee et al. 2022, Hardt & Pohl 2003.
- **SECONDARY:** Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995, Russo & Schoemaker 1989, and the Hardt & Pohl curve. The source is named in each entry.
- **Not obtained:** see the last list in this section.

### 1. Chapman & Johnson 1994, *JBDM* 7:223–242, [10.1002/bdm.3960070402](https://doi.org/10.1002/bdm.3960070402) (figures only)
- **How I got it:** I could not download the full text (Wiley paywall; the Chrome download route was off). The Exhibit images come from the author-uploaded copy on academia.edu.
- **Design, Experiment 1:** participants gave selling prices for 16 lotteries. Anchors were 0.1, 0.7, 1.3 and 1.9 × the lottery's expected value (EV), crossed with 4 levels of payoff range (Exhibit 2).
- **Result, Exhibit 3 (p.229):** geometric mean prices were about 74, 106.5, 127 and 127.5.
  - I scaled the anchors by the geometric-mean EV (137.6), giving anchors of 13.8, 96.3, 178.8 and 261.4.
  - Local slopes: 32.5/82.5 = **0.39**, then 20.5/82.5 = **0.25**, then 0.5/82.5 = **0.006**.
  - AI for the moderate pair (0.7/1.3) = **0.25**. AI for the extreme pair (0.1/1.9) = 53.5/247.5 = **0.22**.
  - The curve saturates at the high end only. The low anchor still pulls.
- **Result, Exhibit 4 (p.230), by lottery range.** Extremity here is defined relative to the payoff range:

  | Range | Prices at 0.1 / 0.7 / 1.3 / 1.9 | Shape |
  |---|---|---|
  | Very narrow (extreme anchors far outside the range) | ~84 / 104 / 122 / 111 | inverted-U |
  | Narrow | ~67 / 98 / 104 / 132 | monotone |
  | Wide | ~63 / 106 / 143 / 137 | slight downturn |
  | Very wide | ~83 / 117 / 137 / 123 | downturn |

- **Result, Experiment 2, Exhibit 6 (p.234):** monetary anchors spanned 1.08–28.16 × EV. Prices rose monotonically (about 182, 248, 297, 344). I could not compute an AI because the level multipliers and EVs are in the text I could not read.
- **Abstract (read on the Wiley page):** "implausibly extreme anchors had a proportionally smaller effect than anchors close to the expected value."
- **Implication:** the AI falls modestly with extremity overall. Raw effects saturate or turn down at the high end, especially when the anchors sit far outside the plausible range.

### 2. Strack & Mussweiler 1997, *JPSP* 73:437–446, [10.1037/0022-3514.73.3.437](https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.73.3.437)
- **Design, Study 3:** n=67, 8 items, within-subject. Plausible anchors were about 1 SD from the calibration mean (calibration n=151). Implausible anchors were more than 10 SD away (Table 5, p.442).
- **Result, Table 6 (p.443):** the robust figures are z-scores.
  - Plausible: high .04, low −.13, difference **.17 SD**.
  - Implausible: high .25, low −.17, difference **.42 SD**.
  - Interaction F(1,66)=3.55, p<.07.
- **Implied AI:** a raw shift about 2.5× larger across an anchor gap more than 10× wider means the AI falls to roughly a quarter or less. Caveat: the z-scores are standardised on the study's own responses, not the calibration SD.
- **Appendix (p.446), per-item raw means:** median AI is **0.25** for plausible anchors and **0.06** for implausible ones. Implausible anchor gaps were 7–132× wider.
  - At least the Einstein and Gandhi rows and the Da Vinci implausible pair are internally implausible (e.g., Einstein means around 1807 against anchors of 1905/1939). They are probably typographical errors.
  - Do not rely on the per-item values.
- **Implication:** implausible anchors give a larger raw effect but a much smaller AI.

### 3. Mussweiler & Strack 2001, *Social Cognition* 19:145–160, [10.1521/soco.19.2.145.20705](https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.19.2.145.20705)
This paper has 4 anchor levels per item, and both implausible anchors are high.

- **Study 1, Antarctic mean temperature** (true −68°C; Table 1, p.154; n 15–16 per cell):

  | Anchor | −43 | −17 | 700 | 900 |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | Mean estimate | −41.12 | −24.84 | −23.27 | −24.44 |
  | Distance from calibration mean | ~1 SD | ~1 SD | ~56 SD | ~72 SD |

  - AI plausible pair = 16.28/26 = **0.63**.
  - AI implausible pair = −1.17/200 = **−0.006**. The numerator is within noise.
  - AI from the −43 anchor to the 700 anchor = 17.85/743 = **0.024**.
- **Study 2, Gandhi's age at death** (true 78; Table 2, p.156; n 26–28 per cell):

  | Anchor | 61 | 86 | 214 | 271 |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | Mean estimate | 62.92 | 70.36 | 75.26 | 72.86 |
  | Distance from calibration mean | ~1 SD | ~1 SD | ~18 SD | ~26 SD |

  - AI plausible pair = 7.44/25 = **0.30**.
  - AI implausible pair = **−0.04**.
  - AI from the 61 anchor to the 214 anchor = **0.08**.
- **One-sided AI:** I inferred the calibration mean as the midpoint of the plausible pair (−30°C and 73.5 years).
  - Antarctic: 0.86, 0.40, 0.009, 0.006.
  - Gandhi: 0.85, −0.25, 0.013, −0.003.
  - The inference fails in part for Gandhi. The SD implied by the 61/86 anchors (about 12.5) disagrees with the SD implied by the "18 and 26 SD" statement (about 7.7).
- **Implication:** the raw shift plateaus at the plausibility boundary. Estimates under implausible anchors are no higher than under the plausible high anchor, so the AI falls roughly as 1/distance beyond the boundary.

### 4. Wegener, Petty, Detweiler-Bedell & Jarvis 2001, *JESP* 37:62–69, [10.1006/jesp.2000.1431](https://doi.org/10.1006/jesp.2000.1431)
- **Design:** 8 items, each with 6 anchor levels (Appendix, p.68). The design is within-subject 2 (high/low) × 2 (moderate/extreme). Estimates are z-scored per item.
- **Results (pp.65–66):**

  | Study | n | Moderate H/L (difference) | Extreme H/L (difference) | Extreme anchors used |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | Exp 1A | 151 | +.50/−.52 (1.02) | +.37/−.36 (0.73) | "Extremely" low/high (e.g., Washington's age 13/167) |
  | Exp 1B | 145 | +.52/−.41 (0.93) | +.15/−.25 (0.40) | "Very extremely" low/high (e.g., 2/167,054) |
  | Exp 2 (no "random anchor" instruction) | 80 | +.40/−.47 (0.87) | +.26/−.19 (0.45) | Same as 1B |

  - Exp 2 plausibility ratings: 1.28 for extreme vs 4.38 for moderate anchors (9-point scale). Rated plausibility mediated the extremity effect for low anchors.
- **Implied AI ratio, extreme vs moderate (illustrative):** I applied the pooled z-difference ratio to each item's anchor gaps.
  - Exp 1A: median ≈ 0.22 (range 0.05–0.26).
  - Exp 1B: median ≈ 0.0015.
- **Implication:** the raw effect is an inverted U, so the AI falls steeply.

### 5. Wegener, Petty, Blankenship & Detweiler-Bedell 2010, *J Consumer Psych* 20:5–16, [10.1016/j.jcps.2009.12.003](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcps.2009.12.003)
- No new numbers.
- Footnote 1 (p.7) and p.12 cite unpublished raw data (Wegener, Blankenship, Detweiler-Bedell & Petty, 2009): with 3 extremity levels, effects were smaller at low and high extremity than at moderate extremity. The downturn came at lower extremity for high-knowledge participants.
- This claim is UNVERIFIED because the data are unpublished.

### 6. Northcraft & Neale 1987, *OBHDP* 39:84–97, [10.1016/0749-5978(87)90046-x](https://doi.org/10.1016/0749-5978(87)90046-x) (not in the original list; meets the "≥3 anchor levels" criterion)
- **Design:** listing-price anchors at ±4% and ±12% of the true value (Exp 1, p.88) or ±4% and ±11% (Exp 2, p.92). Realtors described deviations over 5% as "obviously deviant".
- **Exp 1, amateurs, appraisal estimates (Table 1, p.89):** anchors 65.9k, 71.9k, 77.9k, 83.9k gave means 63,571; 67,452; 70,423; 72,196.
  - Local slopes: **0.65, 0.50, 0.30**.
  - AI moderate pair **0.50**; AI extreme pair 8,625/18,000 = **0.48**.
- **Exp 1, experts (Table 2, p.90):** only the two extreme anchors were used. AI = 7,379/18,000 = **0.41**.
- **Exp 2 (Tables 3–4, p.93):** the data are noisy.
  - Experts: AI extreme pair 0.49; AI moderate pair −0.17.
  - Amateurs: AI extreme pair 0.92; AI moderate pair 0.33.
  - Hypothesis 2 (distant anchors have less influence) was not supported.
- **Implication:** within the plausible range (about ±12%), the AI is roughly constant at about 0.5, with mild concavity in Exp 1.

### 7. Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995, *PSPB* 21:1161–1166, [10.1177/01461672952111004](https://doi.org/10.1177/01461672952111004) (SECONDARY)
- I could not get the full text (SAGE paywall).
- Lieder et al. 2018 (manuscript p.17) reports the empirical mean AI across 15 items as **48.48%**, with anchors at the 15th and 85th percentiles. It also plots the per-item empirical AIs in Fig. 7.
- Lieder's Table C1 gives Lieder's own belief estimates for each item, not J&K's data.
- I could not verify the per-item AIs or the high/low asymmetry.

### 8. Russo & Schoemaker 1989, *Decision Traps* (book, no DOI; SECONDARY via Lieder et al. Fig. 10, manuscript p.21)
- **Design:** one item (year Attila was defeated; true 451). Anchor bins were 500, 700, 900, 1100 and 1300 (each ±100).
- **Result:** means read off the figure were about 630, 680, 790, 885, 990.
  - Local slopes: 0.25, 0.55, 0.47, 0.53. Overall slope **0.45**.
  - The relation is linear, with no saturation up to about 850 years away from the true value.
- **Lieder's MTurk replication:** means of about 590, 645, 870, 970, 1020. The top slope drops to 0.25.

### 9. Lieder, Griffiths, Huys & Goodman 2018, *PBR* 25:322–349, [10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8) (preprint)
The model predicts two different shapes, depending on which assumption you take.
- **Fixed number of adjustments (Eq. 4, p.13):** E[x̂] = a·rᵗ + (1−rᵗ)·x, so the AI is constant across extremity. Their Russo & Schoemaker simulation uses this and predicts a slope of about 0.95. The data show about 0.45.
- **Optimal number of adjustments (Fig. 4b, p.13).** Distance is measured in σ units of the belief. At a fixed time cost, near anchors are barely adjusted and far anchors are mostly adjusted away. My approximate readings of bias ÷ distance:
  - Time cost ≈ 0.2: about 1.0, 0.85, 0.43, 0.18, 0.03 for anchors 1σ to 5σ away.
  - Time cost ≈ 0.5: about 1.0, 0.98, 0.98, 0.63, 0.26.
- **Implication:** under optimal adjustment the AI falls with extremity measured relative to uncertainty, and the raw bias is non-monotone. This is the prediction to simulate.

### 10. Turner & Schley 2016, *Cognitive Psychology* 90:1–47, [10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003) (PDF from the authors' lab site)
- Section 5.3.2 (pp.23–24) and Fig. 9: the mapping function builds in an inverted-U between anchor extremity and the posterior shift, citing Wegener et al. 2001.
- The model can also produce an asymptote instead, through its maximum-influence parameter.
- Their experiments use one anchor per item, so they give no extremity data.

### 11. Hardt & Pohl 2003, *Memory* 11:379–394, [10.1080/09658210244000504](https://doi.org/10.1080/09658210244000504) (abstract via PubMed; curve SECONDARY)
- **Design:** hindsight-bias paradigm. Anchor distance was scaled to each participant's own range of plausible answers.
- **Abstract:** plausibility fell with distance; bias first rose, then fell beyond some distance; bias was always higher for plausible anchors.
- **Curve:** Fig. 4 is reproduced in Wilson, Arora, Zhang & Griffiths 2021 (CogSci proceedings; [PDF](https://cocosci.princeton.edu/papers/wilson_rational.pdf)), Fig. 1. At distances 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and 7, bias ÷ distance was:
  - Anchor above the original estimate: 0.12, 0.11, 0.14, 0.08, 0.03.
  - Anchor below: 0.38, 0.25, 0.17, 0.11, 0.06.
  - This division assumes the two axes share units.
- **Implication:** the raw shift is an inverted U, and the proportional shift falls with distance measured relative to each participant's own uncertainty.

### 12. Bystranowski, Janik, Próchnicki & Skórska 2021, *Law & Human Behavior* 45:1–23, [10.1037/lhb0000438](https://doi.org/10.1037/lhb0000438)
- **Design:** "anchor value" was coded as a z-score of anchor magnitude between studies, binned at the 25th and 75th percentiles. It is not extremity relative to the true value or to uncertainty.
- **Control vs anchor designs (Table 4, p.12):**

  | Anchor value | k | d |
  |---|---|---|
  | Low | 4 | .43 |
  | Medium | 42 | .59 |
  | High | 5 | .19 |

  - As a continuous moderator: coefficient −.04 (z′) and −.08 (d), not significant.
- **High vs low designs (Table 5, p.13):**

  | Anchor value | k | d |
  |---|---|---|
  | Low | 5 | .82 |
  | Medium | 25 | 1.00 |
  | High | 7 | .77 |

  - The text states the continuous slope was negative in both design types.
- **Authors' summary (p.17):** moderate anchors produced the largest effects, but not significantly so.

### 13. Townson 2019, PhD dissertation, Michigan State University, [10.25335/p9dm-7a29](https://doi.org/10.25335/p9dm-7a29) (verified via DataCite; abstract only)
- Meta-analysis of 84 effect sizes (r), mean r = .401.
- Abstract: "Extremity of the anchor was found to slightly weaken the impact." The size and coding of that effect are not in the abstract, and I could not get past the repository's bot check.

### 14. Harris et al. 2019, *JEP:General* 148:e30–e50, [10.1037/xge0000644](https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000644) (accepted manuscript)
- **Design:** the same two items were tested with different anchor gaps across experiments. Means are in Table 2 (p.23).
- **UK average temperature:**
  - Anchors 8/20°C (p.17): AI = 2.02/12 = **0.17**.
  - Anchors 2/25°C (p.27): AI = **0.225** in Exp 3 and **0.22** in Exp 5.
- **UK new-car price:**
  - Anchors £6,000/£30,000: AI = **0.37**.
  - Anchors £13,000/£200,000: AI = **0.255**.
- **Inconsistency in the manuscript:** the discussion on p.26 describes the Exp 1–2 anchors as 10/18°C and £20,000. With 10/18°C the temperature AI is **0.25**.
- **Implication:** the two items move in opposite directions as the anchor gap widens.

### 15. Simmons, LeBoeuf & Nelson 2010, *JPSP* 99:917–932, [10.1037/a0021540](https://doi.org/10.1037/a0021540) (Penn repository manuscript)
- Single-anchor design with plausible vs implausible anchors (Tables 2–3, manuscript pp.47–48). An AI cannot be computed.
- Note 2 (p.42): implausible anchors left estimates further from the truth on 6 of 8 items.
- The main finding: accuracy incentives increased adjustment only away from implausible anchors.

### 16. Schultze, Rakotoarisoa & Schulz-Hardt 2015, *JDM* 10:144–171, [10.1017/s1930297500003922](https://doi.org/10.1017/s1930297500003922) (advice-taking analogue)
- Exp 1 (Table 1, p.151): weight of advice = −0.093 − 0.003·d + 0.153·ln d, with d as percent distance. This gives about 0.14 at 5%, 0.35 at 40–64%, and 0.34 at 75%. The peak at about 51% is my calculation from the rounded coefficients.
- Pooled across 6 experiments (pp.166–167): B1 = −0.002, B2 = 0.101. The paper states the peak is at **63.84%**. The downturn at far distances is shallow.
- Absolute opinion shift rose roughly in proportion to distance, with no downturn up to 150%.
- **Implication:** the proportional index is an inverted U, driven mainly by advice near one's own estimate being ignored. The linear-plus-log form is a ready template for the AI-vs-distance curve.

### 17. Marti & Wissler 2000, *JEP:Applied* 6:91–103, [10.1037/1076-898x.6.2.91](https://doi.org/10.1037/1076-898x.6.2.91) (abstract only)
- Abstract: awards rose with the plaintiff's request "but decreased with the most extreme request."
- Request levels are SECONDARY (plaintiffmagazine.com): $1.5M, $15M and $25M.
- **Conflict:** Bystranowski et al. (p.6) cite this paper and Chapman & Bornstein 1996 as showing awards rising "even when the anchor is outlandishly high". That contradicts this abstract.

### 18. Other entries
- **Thorsteinson 2011**, *JASP* 41:1774–1792, [10.1111/j.1559-1816.2011.00779.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1559-1816.2011.00779.x) (abstract only): both the high implausible anchor and the extremely high one raised salary offers above control. The abstract gives no comparison between them.
- **Lee, Lee & Kim 2022**, *Korean J Cognitive Science* 33(1):77–93, 10.19066/cogsci.2022.33.1.004: the DOI resolves to the KCI portal but is not in Crossref. From the abstract only: extreme anchors produced smaller anchoring than plausible ones, and difficult items produced larger anchoring.
- **Smith, Windschitl & Bruchmann 2013**, *EJSP* 43:97–108, [10.1002/ejsp.1921](https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsp.1921): Fig. 3 (p.105) only hypothesises a plateau that comes earlier for high-knowledge people. Not tested.
- **Frederick & Mochon 2012**, *JEP:General* 141:124–133, [10.1037/a0024006](https://doi.org/10.1037/a0024006): no extremity manipulation.
- **Quattrone et al. 1984:** unpublished; claims an asymptote. UNVERIFIED; cited by Wegener et al. 2001, p.63.
- **Shanks, Barbieri-Hermitte & Vadillo 2020**, *Collabra* [10.1525/collabra.310](https://doi.org/10.1525/collabra.310): about incidental anchors, not extremity.

**Not obtained (paywalled, no open copy found):**
- **Mussweiler & Strack 2000**, [10.1006/jesp.1999.1414](https://doi.org/10.1006/jesp.1999.1414).
- **Thorsteinson et al. 2008**, [10.1016/j.obhdp.2008.01.003](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obhdp.2008.01.003).
- **LeBoeuf & Shafir 2006**, [10.1002/bdm.535](https://doi.org/10.1002/bdm.535). Note the brief listed 10.1002/bdm.536, which is a different paper. The abstract does not mention extremity.
- **Mussweiler 2001**, [10.1002/ejsp.52](https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsp.52). The abstract does not mention extremity.
- **Chapman & Bornstein 1996**, [10.1002/(sici)1099-0720(199612)10:6<519::aid-acp417>3.0.co;2-5](https://doi.org/10.1002/(sici)1099-0720(199612)10:6<519::aid-acp417>3.0.co;2-5). The download tool returned an unrelated law-review article, which I discarded.

## Synthesis

**Existing quantitative predictions and findings:**
- **Within the plausible range, estimates rise roughly linearly with the anchor, so the AI is roughly flat.**
  - Russo & Schoemaker: slope ≈ 0.45.
  - Jacowitz & Kahneman: mean AI ≈ 0.48.
  - Northcraft & Neale: 0.48–0.50.
  - Mussweiler & Strack 2001 plausible pairs: 0.30–0.63.
  - Chapman & Johnson moderate pair: 0.25.
  - Harris: 0.17–0.37.
- **At and beyond the plausibility boundary, the raw shift plateaus or declines, so the AI falls roughly as 1/distance.**
  - Plateau: Mussweiler & Strack 2001; the high end of Chapman & Johnson.
  - Decline: Wegener 1A/1B/2; the Marti & Wissler abstract; the high bin in Bystranowski; Townson; the Hardt & Pohl curve.
- **Counter-evidence and caveats:**
  - Strack & Mussweiler 1997 found a larger raw effect for implausible anchors, though the implied AI is still smaller.
  - Simmons note 2 found larger anchoring from implausible anchors on 6 of 8 items.
  - The Harris temperature item's AI rose as the anchor gap widened.
  - Chapman & Johnson Experiment 2 kept rising across a 26-fold anchor range.
  - Chapman & Johnson Exhibit 3 shows a high/low asymmetry: saturation at the high end, not the low end.
- **Theoretical curves already stated in the literature:**
  - Linear, diminishing, or "contrast" (inverted-U): Chapman & Johnson Exhibit 1, p.225.
  - Inverted-U by assumption: Turner & Schley.
  - Asymptote: Mussweiler & Strack 2001; Quattrone et al.
  - Constant AI (fixed adjustments) versus falling AI (optimal adjustments): Lieder et al.

**Gaps the planned study would fill:**
- No study reports the proportional AI across three or more extremity levels that span both sides of the plausibility boundary, with per-item means and a calibration SD, on more than two items.
  - The nearest are Chapman & Johnson (lotteries; figures only), Mussweiler & Strack 2001 (two items; implausible anchors all high), Northcraft & Neale (one house per experiment; ±12% only) and Russo & Schoemaker (one item; secondary).
- Only Hardt & Pohl scale distance to each person's own uncertainty, and that is hindsight bias with secondary numbers.
- No study fits the competing models (resource-rational adjustment, anchor integration, insufficient adjustment, selective accessibility) to item-level AI-versus-extremity curves.
- The existing meta-analyses (Bystranowski, Townson) code extremity as raw anchor magnitude or as a crude category, not relative to truth or uncertainty.</result>

<result>## Anchoring vs anchor extremity: per-paper quantitative evidence

I checked every DOI below against `api.crossref.org/works/<DOI>` and the title and first author matched, unless the entry says otherwise. "AI" means the two-sided index: (estimate under high anchor − estimate under low anchor) / (high anchor − low anchor). "Local slope" is the change in estimate divided by the change in anchor between two adjacent anchor levels. Where a paper gives means rather than the medians Jacowitz & Kahneman specified, I computed the AI on the means.

All arithmetic is in `/tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_classic_ai.py`. Its output is in `/tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_classic_ai_out.txt`, and working notes are in `/tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_classic_findings.md`. I opened no data files.

**Source quality at a glance:**
- **Full text read:** Strack & Mussweiler 1997; Mussweiler & Strack 2001; Wegener et al. 2001 and 2010; Northcraft & Neale 1987; Bystranowski et al. 2021; Schultze et al. 2015; Turner & Schley 2016; Frederick & Mochon 2012; Smith et al. 2013. Harris et al. 2019, Simmons et al. 2010 and Lieder et al. 2018 are accepted-manuscript or preprint versions, so their page numbers are manuscript pages.
- **Figures only:** Chapman & Johnson 1994. The numbers are read off the figures and are accurate to about ±1.
- **Abstract only:** Townson 2019, Marti & Wissler 2000, Thorsteinson 2011, Lee et al. 2022, Hardt & Pohl 2003.
- **SECONDARY:** Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995, Russo & Schoemaker 1989, and the Hardt & Pohl curve. The source is named in each entry.
- **Not obtained:** see the last list in this section.

### 1. Chapman & Johnson 1994, *JBDM* 7:223–242, [10.1002/bdm.3960070402](https://doi.org/10.1002/bdm.3960070402) (figures only)
- **How I got it:** I could not download the full text (Wiley paywall; the Chrome download route was off). The Exhibit images come from the author-uploaded copy on academia.edu.
- **Design, Experiment 1:** participants gave selling prices for 16 lotteries. Anchors were 0.1, 0.7, 1.3 and 1.9 × the lottery's expected value (EV), crossed with 4 levels of payoff range (Exhibit 2).
- **Result, Exhibit 3 (p.229):** geometric mean prices were about 74, 106.5, 127 and 127.5.
  - I scaled the anchors by the geometric-mean EV (137.6), giving anchors of 13.8, 96.3, 178.8 and 261.4.
  - Local slopes: 32.5/82.5 = **0.39**, then 20.5/82.5 = **0.25**, then 0.5/82.5 = **0.006**.
  - AI for the moderate pair (0.7/1.3) = **0.25**. AI for the extreme pair (0.1/1.9) = 53.5/247.5 = **0.22**.
  - The curve saturates at the high end only. The low anchor still pulls.
- **Result, Exhibit 4 (p.230), by lottery range.** Extremity here is defined relative to the payoff range:

  | Range | Prices at 0.1 / 0.7 / 1.3 / 1.9 | Shape |
  |---|---|---|
  | Very narrow (extreme anchors far outside the range) | ~84 / 104 / 122 / 111 | inverted-U |
  | Narrow | ~67 / 98 / 104 / 132 | monotone |
  | Wide | ~63 / 106 / 143 / 137 | slight downturn |
  | Very wide | ~83 / 117 / 137 / 123 | downturn |

- **Result, Experiment 2, Exhibit 6 (p.234):** monetary anchors spanned 1.08–28.16 × EV. Prices rose monotonically (about 182, 248, 297, 344). I could not compute an AI because the level multipliers and EVs are in the text I could not read.
- **Abstract (read on the Wiley page):** "implausibly extreme anchors had a proportionally smaller effect than anchors close to the expected value."
- **Implication:** the AI falls modestly with extremity overall. Raw effects saturate or turn down at the high end, especially when the anchors sit far outside the plausible range.

### 2. Strack & Mussweiler 1997, *JPSP* 73:437–446, [10.1037/0022-3514.73.3.437](https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.73.3.437)
- **Design, Study 3:** n=67, 8 items, within-subject. Plausible anchors were about 1 SD from the calibration mean (calibration n=151). Implausible anchors were more than 10 SD away (Table 5, p.442).
- **Result, Table 6 (p.443):** the robust figures are z-scores.
  - Plausible: high .04, low −.13, difference **.17 SD**.
  - Implausible: high .25, low −.17, difference **.42 SD**.
  - Interaction F(1,66)=3.55, p<.07.
- **Implied AI:** a raw shift about 2.5× larger across an anchor gap more than 10× wider means the AI falls to roughly a quarter or less. Caveat: the z-scores are standardised on the study's own responses, not the calibration SD.
- **Appendix (p.446), per-item raw means:** median AI is **0.25** for plausible anchors and **0.06** for implausible ones. Implausible anchor gaps were 7–132× wider.
  - At least the Einstein and Gandhi rows and the Da Vinci implausible pair are internally implausible (e.g., Einstein means around 1807 against anchors of 1905/1939). They are probably typographical errors.
  - Do not rely on the per-item values.
- **Implication:** implausible anchors give a larger raw effect but a much smaller AI.

### 3. Mussweiler & Strack 2001, *Social Cognition* 19:145–160, [10.1521/soco.19.2.145.20705](https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.19.2.145.20705)
This paper has 4 anchor levels per item, and both implausible anchors are high.

- **Study 1, Antarctic mean temperature** (true −68°C; Table 1, p.154; n 15–16 per cell):

  | Anchor | −43 | −17 | 700 | 900 |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | Mean estimate | −41.12 | −24.84 | −23.27 | −24.44 |
  | Distance from calibration mean | ~1 SD | ~1 SD | ~56 SD | ~72 SD |

  - AI plausible pair = 16.28/26 = **0.63**.
  - AI implausible pair = −1.17/200 = **−0.006**. The numerator is within noise.
  - AI from the −43 anchor to the 700 anchor = 17.85/743 = **0.024**.
- **Study 2, Gandhi's age at death** (true 78; Table 2, p.156; n 26–28 per cell):

  | Anchor | 61 | 86 | 214 | 271 |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | Mean estimate | 62.92 | 70.36 | 75.26 | 72.86 |
  | Distance from calibration mean | ~1 SD | ~1 SD | ~18 SD | ~26 SD |

  - AI plausible pair = 7.44/25 = **0.30**.
  - AI implausible pair = **−0.04**.
  - AI from the 61 anchor to the 214 anchor = **0.08**.
- **One-sided AI:** I inferred the calibration mean as the midpoint of the plausible pair (−30°C and 73.5 years).
  - Antarctic: 0.86, 0.40, 0.009, 0.006.
  - Gandhi: 0.85, −0.25, 0.013, −0.003.
  - The inference fails in part for Gandhi. The SD implied by the 61/86 anchors (about 12.5) disagrees with the SD implied by the "18 and 26 SD" statement (about 7.7).
- **Implication:** the raw shift plateaus at the plausibility boundary. Estimates under implausible anchors are no higher than under the plausible high anchor, so the AI falls roughly as 1/distance beyond the boundary.

### 4. Wegener, Petty, Detweiler-Bedell & Jarvis 2001, *JESP* 37:62–69, [10.1006/jesp.2000.1431](https://doi.org/10.1006/jesp.2000.1431)
- **Design:** 8 items, each with 6 anchor levels (Appendix, p.68). The design is within-subject 2 (high/low) × 2 (moderate/extreme). Estimates are z-scored per item.
- **Results (pp.65–66):**

  | Study | n | Moderate H/L (difference) | Extreme H/L (difference) | Extreme anchors used |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | Exp 1A | 151 | +.50/−.52 (1.02) | +.37/−.36 (0.73) | "Extremely" low/high (e.g., Washington's age 13/167) |
  | Exp 1B | 145 | +.52/−.41 (0.93) | +.15/−.25 (0.40) | "Very extremely" low/high (e.g., 2/167,054) |
  | Exp 2 (no "random anchor" instruction) | 80 | +.40/−.47 (0.87) | +.26/−.19 (0.45) | Same as 1B |

  - Exp 2 plausibility ratings: 1.28 for extreme vs 4.38 for moderate anchors (9-point scale). Rated plausibility mediated the extremity effect for low anchors.
- **Implied AI ratio, extreme vs moderate (illustrative):** I applied the pooled z-difference ratio to each item's anchor gaps.
  - Exp 1A: median ≈ 0.22 (range 0.05–0.26).
  - Exp 1B: median ≈ 0.0015.
- **Implication:** the raw effect is an inverted U, so the AI falls steeply.

### 5. Wegener, Petty, Blankenship & Detweiler-Bedell 2010, *J Consumer Psych* 20:5–16, [10.1016/j.jcps.2009.12.003](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcps.2009.12.003)
- No new numbers.
- Footnote 1 (p.7) and p.12 cite unpublished raw data (Wegener, Blankenship, Detweiler-Bedell & Petty, 2009): with 3 extremity levels, effects were smaller at low and high extremity than at moderate extremity. The downturn came at lower extremity for high-knowledge participants.
- This claim is UNVERIFIED because the data are unpublished.

### 6. Northcraft & Neale 1987, *OBHDP* 39:84–97, [10.1016/0749-5978(87)90046-x](https://doi.org/10.1016/0749-5978(87)90046-x) (not in the original list; meets the "≥3 anchor levels" criterion)
- **Design:** listing-price anchors at ±4% and ±12% of the true value (Exp 1, p.88) or ±4% and ±11% (Exp 2, p.92). Realtors described deviations over 5% as "obviously deviant".
- **Exp 1, amateurs, appraisal estimates (Table 1, p.89):** anchors 65.9k, 71.9k, 77.9k, 83.9k gave means 63,571; 67,452; 70,423; 72,196.
  - Local slopes: **0.65, 0.50, 0.30**.
  - AI moderate pair **0.50**; AI extreme pair 8,625/18,000 = **0.48**.
- **Exp 1, experts (Table 2, p.90):** only the two extreme anchors were used. AI = 7,379/18,000 = **0.41**.
- **Exp 2 (Tables 3–4, p.93):** the data are noisy.
  - Experts: AI extreme pair 0.49; AI moderate pair −0.17.
  - Amateurs: AI extreme pair 0.92; AI moderate pair 0.33.
  - Hypothesis 2 (distant anchors have less influence) was not supported.
- **Implication:** within the plausible range (about ±12%), the AI is roughly constant at about 0.5, with mild concavity in Exp 1.

### 7. Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995, *PSPB* 21:1161–1166, [10.1177/01461672952111004](https://doi.org/10.1177/01461672952111004) (SECONDARY)
- I could not get the full text (SAGE paywall).
- Lieder et al. 2018 (manuscript p.17) reports the empirical mean AI across 15 items as **48.48%**, with anchors at the 15th and 85th percentiles. It also plots the per-item empirical AIs in Fig. 7.
- Lieder's Table C1 gives Lieder's own belief estimates for each item, not J&K's data.
- I could not verify the per-item AIs or the high/low asymmetry.

### 8. Russo & Schoemaker 1989, *Decision Traps* (book, no DOI; SECONDARY via Lieder et al. Fig. 10, manuscript p.21)
- **Design:** one item (year Attila was defeated; true 451). Anchor bins were 500, 700, 900, 1100 and 1300 (each ±100).
- **Result:** means read off the figure were about 630, 680, 790, 885, 990.
  - Local slopes: 0.25, 0.55, 0.47, 0.53. Overall slope **0.45**.
  - The relation is linear, with no saturation up to about 850 years away from the true value.
- **Lieder's MTurk replication:** means of about 590, 645, 870, 970, 1020. The top slope drops to 0.25.

### 9. Lieder, Griffiths, Huys & Goodman 2018, *PBR* 25:322–349, [10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8) (preprint)
The model predicts two different shapes, depending on which assumption you take.
- **Fixed number of adjustments (Eq. 4, p.13):** E[x̂] = a·rᵗ + (1−rᵗ)·x, so the AI is constant across extremity. Their Russo & Schoemaker simulation uses this and predicts a slope of about 0.95. The data show about 0.45.
- **Optimal number of adjustments (Fig. 4b, p.13).** Distance is measured in σ units of the belief. At a fixed time cost, near anchors are barely adjusted and far anchors are mostly adjusted away. My approximate readings of bias ÷ distance:
  - Time cost ≈ 0.2: about 1.0, 0.85, 0.43, 0.18, 0.03 for anchors 1σ to 5σ away.
  - Time cost ≈ 0.5: about 1.0, 0.98, 0.98, 0.63, 0.26.
- **Implication:** under optimal adjustment the AI falls with extremity measured relative to uncertainty, and the raw bias is non-monotone. This is the prediction to simulate.

### 10. Turner & Schley 2016, *Cognitive Psychology* 90:1–47, [10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003) (PDF from the authors' lab site)
- Section 5.3.2 (pp.23–24) and Fig. 9: the mapping function builds in an inverted-U between anchor extremity and the posterior shift, citing Wegener et al. 2001.
- The model can also produce an asymptote instead, through its maximum-influence parameter.
- Their experiments use one anchor per item, so they give no extremity data.

### 11. Hardt & Pohl 2003, *Memory* 11:379–394, [10.1080/09658210244000504](https://doi.org/10.1080/09658210244000504) (abstract via PubMed; curve SECONDARY)
- **Design:** hindsight-bias paradigm. Anchor distance was scaled to each participant's own range of plausible answers.
- **Abstract:** plausibility fell with distance; bias first rose, then fell beyond some distance; bias was always higher for plausible anchors.
- **Curve:** Fig. 4 is reproduced in Wilson, Arora, Zhang & Griffiths 2021 (CogSci proceedings; [PDF](https://cocosci.princeton.edu/papers/wilson_rational.pdf)), Fig. 1. At distances 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and 7, bias ÷ distance was:
  - Anchor above the original estimate: 0.12, 0.11, 0.14, 0.08, 0.03.
  - Anchor below: 0.38, 0.25, 0.17, 0.11, 0.06.
  - This division assumes the two axes share units.
- **Implication:** the raw shift is an inverted U, and the proportional shift falls with distance measured relative to each participant's own uncertainty.

### 12. Bystranowski, Janik, Próchnicki & Skórska 2021, *Law & Human Behavior* 45:1–23, [10.1037/lhb0000438](https://doi.org/10.1037/lhb0000438)
- **Design:** "anchor value" was coded as a z-score of anchor magnitude between studies, binned at the 25th and 75th percentiles. It is not extremity relative to the true value or to uncertainty.
- **Control vs anchor designs (Table 4, p.12):**

  | Anchor value | k | d |
  |---|---|---|
  | Low | 4 | .43 |
  | Medium | 42 | .59 |
  | High | 5 | .19 |

  - As a continuous moderator: coefficient −.04 (z′) and −.08 (d), not significant.
- **High vs low designs (Table 5, p.13):**

  | Anchor value | k | d |
  |---|---|---|
  | Low | 5 | .82 |
  | Medium | 25 | 1.00 |
  | High | 7 | .77 |

  - The text states the continuous slope was negative in both design types.
- **Authors' summary (p.17):** moderate anchors produced the largest effects, but not significantly so.

### 13. Townson 2019, PhD dissertation, Michigan State University, [10.25335/p9dm-7a29](https://doi.org/10.25335/p9dm-7a29) (verified via DataCite; abstract only)
- Meta-analysis of 84 effect sizes (r), mean r = .401.
- Abstract: "Extremity of the anchor was found to slightly weaken the impact." The size and coding of that effect are not in the abstract, and I could not get past the repository's bot check.

### 14. Harris et al. 2019, *JEP:General* 148:e30–e50, [10.1037/xge0000644](https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000644) (accepted manuscript)
- **Design:** the same two items were tested with different anchor gaps across experiments. Means are in Table 2 (p.23).
- **UK average temperature:**
  - Anchors 8/20°C (p.17): AI = 2.02/12 = **0.17**.
  - Anchors 2/25°C (p.27): AI = **0.225** in Exp 3 and **0.22** in Exp 5.
- **UK new-car price:**
  - Anchors £6,000/£30,000: AI = **0.37**.
  - Anchors £13,000/£200,000: AI = **0.255**.
- **Inconsistency in the manuscript:** the discussion on p.26 describes the Exp 1–2 anchors as 10/18°C and £20,000. With 10/18°C the temperature AI is **0.25**.
- **Implication:** the two items move in opposite directions as the anchor gap widens.

### 15. Simmons, LeBoeuf & Nelson 2010, *JPSP* 99:917–932, [10.1037/a0021540](https://doi.org/10.1037/a0021540) (Penn repository manuscript)
- Single-anchor design with plausible vs implausible anchors (Tables 2–3, manuscript pp.47–48). An AI cannot be computed.
- Note 2 (p.42): implausible anchors left estimates further from the truth on 6 of 8 items.
- The main finding: accuracy incentives increased adjustment only away from implausible anchors.

### 16. Schultze, Rakotoarisoa & Schulz-Hardt 2015, *JDM* 10:144–171, [10.1017/s1930297500003922](https://doi.org/10.1017/s1930297500003922) (advice-taking analogue)
- Exp 1 (Table 1, p.151): weight of advice = −0.093 − 0.003·d + 0.153·ln d, with d as percent distance. This gives about 0.14 at 5%, 0.35 at 40–64%, and 0.34 at 75%. The peak at about 51% is my calculation from the rounded coefficients.
- Pooled across 6 experiments (pp.166–167): B1 = −0.002, B2 = 0.101. The paper states the peak is at **63.84%**. The downturn at far distances is shallow.
- Absolute opinion shift rose roughly in proportion to distance, with no downturn up to 150%.
- **Implication:** the proportional index is an inverted U, driven mainly by advice near one's own estimate being ignored. The linear-plus-log form is a ready template for the AI-vs-distance curve.

### 17. Marti & Wissler 2000, *JEP:Applied* 6:91–103, [10.1037/1076-898x.6.2.91](https://doi.org/10.1037/1076-898x.6.2.91) (abstract only)
- Abstract: awards rose with the plaintiff's request "but decreased with the most extreme request."
- Request levels are SECONDARY (plaintiffmagazine.com): $1.5M, $15M and $25M.
- **Conflict:** Bystranowski et al. (p.6) cite this paper and Chapman & Bornstein 1996 as showing awards rising "even when the anchor is outlandishly high". That contradicts this abstract.

### 18. Other entries
- **Thorsteinson 2011**, *JASP* 41:1774–1792, [10.1111/j.1559-1816.2011.00779.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1559-1816.2011.00779.x) (abstract only): both the high implausible anchor and the extremely high one raised salary offers above control. The abstract gives no comparison between them.
- **Lee, Lee & Kim 2022**, *Korean J Cognitive Science* 33(1):77–93, 10.19066/cogsci.2022.33.1.004: the DOI resolves to the KCI portal but is not in Crossref. From the abstract only: extreme anchors produced smaller anchoring than plausible ones, and difficult items produced larger anchoring.
- **Smith, Windschitl & Bruchmann 2013**, *EJSP* 43:97–108, [10.1002/ejsp.1921](https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsp.1921): Fig. 3 (p.105) only hypothesises a plateau that comes earlier for high-knowledge people. Not tested.
- **Frederick & Mochon 2012**, *JEP:General* 141:124–133, [10.1037/a0024006](https://doi.org/10.1037/a0024006): no extremity manipulation.
- **Quattrone et al. 1984:** unpublished; claims an asymptote. UNVERIFIED; cited by Wegener et al. 2001, p.63.
- **Shanks, Barbieri-Hermitte & Vadillo 2020**, *Collabra* [10.1525/collabra.310](https://doi.org/10.1525/collabra.310): about incidental anchors, not extremity.

**Not obtained (paywalled, no open copy found):**
- **Mussweiler & Strack 2000**, [10.1006/jesp.1999.1414](https://doi.org/10.1006/jesp.1999.1414).
- **Thorsteinson et al. 2008**, [10.1016/j.obhdp.2008.01.003](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obhdp.2008.01.003).
- **LeBoeuf & Shafir 2006**, [10.1002/bdm.535](https://doi.org/10.1002/bdm.535). Note the brief listed 10.1002/bdm.536, which is a different paper. The abstract does not mention extremity.
- **Mussweiler 2001**, [10.1002/ejsp.52](https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsp.52). The abstract does not mention extremity.
- **Chapman & Bornstein 1996**, [10.1002/(sici)1099-0720(199612)10:6<519::aid-acp417>3.0.co;2-5](https://doi.org/10.1002/(sici)1099-0720(199612)10:6<519::aid-acp417>3.0.co;2-5). The download tool returned an unrelated law-review article, which I discarded.

## Synthesis

**Existing quantitative predictions and findings:**
- **Within the plausible range, estimates rise roughly linearly with the anchor, so the AI is roughly flat.**
  - Russo & Schoemaker: slope ≈ 0.45.
  - Jacowitz & Kahneman: mean AI ≈ 0.48.
  - Northcraft & Neale: 0.48–0.50.
  - Mussweiler & Strack 2001 plausible pairs: 0.30–0.63.
  - Chapman & Johnson moderate pair: 0.25.
  - Harris: 0.17–0.37.
- **At and beyond the plausibility boundary, the raw shift plateaus or declines, so the AI falls roughly as 1/distance.**
  - Plateau: Mussweiler & Strack 2001; the high end of Chapman & Johnson.
  - Decline: Wegener 1A/1B/2; the Marti & Wissler abstract; the high bin in Bystranowski; Townson; the Hardt & Pohl curve.
- **Counter-evidence and caveats:**
  - Strack & Mussweiler 1997 found a larger raw effect for implausible anchors, though the implied AI is still smaller.
  - Simmons note 2 found larger anchoring from implausible anchors on 6 of 8 items.
  - The Harris temperature item's AI rose as the anchor gap widened.
  - Chapman & Johnson Experiment 2 kept rising across a 26-fold anchor range.
  - Chapman & Johnson Exhibit 3 shows a high/low asymmetry: saturation at the high end, not the low end.
- **Theoretical curves already stated in the literature:**
  - Linear, diminishing, or "contrast" (inverted-U): Chapman & Johnson Exhibit 1, p.225.
  - Inverted-U by assumption: Turner & Schley.
  - Asymptote: Mussweiler & Strack 2001; Quattrone et al.
  - Constant AI (fixed adjustments) versus falling AI (optimal adjustments): Lieder et al.

**Gaps the planned study would fill:**
- No study reports the proportional AI across three or more extremity levels that span both sides of the plausibility boundary, with per-item means and a calibration SD, on more than two items.
  - The nearest are Chapman & Johnson (lotteries; figures only), Mussweiler & Strack 2001 (two items; implausible anchors all high), Northcraft & Neale (one house per experiment; ±12% only) and Russo & Schoemaker (one item; secondary).
- Only Hardt & Pohl scale distance to each person's own uncertainty, and that is hindsight bias with secondary numbers.
- No study fits the competing models (resource-rational adjustment, anchor integration, insufficient adjustment, selective accessibility) to item-level AI-versus-extremity curves.
- The existing meta-analyses (Bystranowski, Townson) code extremity as raw anchor magnitude or as a crude category, not relative to truth or uncertainty.</result>

input.content:
# Operating characteristics of the preregistered decision rules, computed on the simulated
# predictions: how often each rule reaches each verdict when each model generated the data.

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(data.table))
r <- fread(file.path("output", "predictions_raw.csv"))[!is.na(b)]

rho_bounds <- c(-0.05, 0.05)     # equivalence bounds for relative curvature (H1)
slope_bounds <- c(-0.03, 0.03)   # equivalence bounds for the across-cell slope (H2)
z <- qnorm(0.975)

verdict <- function(est, se, bounds, rel_est = est, rel_se = se, gate_ok = TRUE) {
  lo <- est - z * se; hi <- est + z * se
  rlo <- rel_est - z * rel_se; rhi <- rel_est + z * rel_se
  fifelse(!gate_ok, "gate failed",
    fifelse(lo > 0, "rising",
      fifelse(hi < 0, "falling",
        fifelse(rlo > bounds[1] & rhi < bounds[2], "flat", "inconclusive"))))
}
r[, gate := b - z * b_se > 0]
r[, h1 := verdict(g, g_se, rho_bounds, rho, rho_se, gate)]
r[, h2 := verdict(across_slope, across_slope_se, slope_bounds)]

tab <- function(v) dcast(r[, .N, by = .(model, v = get(v))][, share := round(N / sum(N), 3), by = model],
                         model ~ v, value.var = "share", fill = 0)
ops <- list(H1 = tab("h1"), H2 = tab("h2"))
q <- function(v) sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", median(v), quantile(v, .025), quantile(v, .975))
intervals <- r[, .(b = q(b), g = q(g), rho = q(rho), g_random = q(g_random), g_fixed = q(g_fixed),
                   across_slope = q(across_slope), across_mean_ai = q(across_mean_ai)), by = model]
bounds <- r[, .(b_lo = quantile(b, .025), b_hi = quantile(b, .975), g_lo = quantile(g, .025), g_hi = quantile(g, .975),
                rho_lo = quantile(rho, .025), rho_hi = quantile(rho, .975),
                slope_lo = quantile(across_slope, .025), slope_hi = quantile(across_slope, .975),
                ai_lo = quantile(across_mean_ai, .025), ai_hi = quantile(across_mean_ai, .975)), by = model]
fwrite(bounds, file.path("output", "predictive_intervals.csv"))
fwrite(intervals, file.path("output", "predictions_summary.csv"))
sink(file.path("output", "decision_properties.txt"))
cat("Equivalence bounds: rho", rho_bounds, "; across-cell slope", slope_bounds, "\n\nH1 verdict shares by generating model\n")
print(ops$H1); cat("\nH2 verdict shares by generating model\n"); print(ops$H2)
cat("\nModel predictive intervals (median [2.5%, 97.5%])\n"); print(intervals)
sink()
cat(readLines(file.path("output", "decision_properties.txt")), sep = "\n")

# Confirmatory analyses as preregistered (prereg/preregistration.md, Q19-Q24).
# Usage: Rscript R/04_confirmatory.R          -> observed OpAQ estimates (after the prereg commit)
#        Rscript R/04_confirmatory.R dry-run  -> estimates replaced by responses simulated from M2,
#                                               to check the pipeline without reading outcomes

suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(data.table); library(lmerTest); library(metafor); library(quantreg) })
source(file.path("R", "design_sets.R"))
source(file.path("R", "models.R"))
source(file.path("R", "estimators.R"))

dry_run <- identical(commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE), "dry-run")
out_dir <- if (dry_run) file.path("output", "dry_run") else file.path("output", "confirmatory")
dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
z <- qnorm(0.975)
rho_bounds <- c(-0.05, 0.05)
slope_bounds <- c(-0.03, 0.03)

# ---- Data -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
sets <- build_sets(read_opaq(include_outcomes = !dry_run))
if (dry_run) {
  set.seed(1)
  cells <- unique(c(sets$within$cell, sets$across_rows$cell))
  cellpar <- data.table(cell = cells, sigma = runif(length(cells), 0.3, 1.2), bias = rnorm(length(cells), 0, 0.3))
  for (nm in c("within", "across_rows")) {
    s <- sets[[nm]]
    s[, estimate := t * exp(simulate_responses("M2", s[, .(cell, pid, x)], cellpar, list(w = 0.45)))]
  }
}
add_y <- function(d) {
  d <- copy(d)
  d[, est := suppressWarnings(as.numeric(estimate))]
  d[, y := fifelse(!is.na(est) & est > 0, log(est / t), NA_real_)]
  d
}
W <- add_y(sets$within)
A <- add_y(sets$across_rows)
cells_A <- copy(sets$across_cells)
exclusions <- rbind(
  data.table(set = "within", rows = nrow(W), invalid_estimate = W[is.na(y), .N],
             gross_error = nrow(W[!is.na(y)]) - nrow(drop_gross_errors(W[!is.na(y)]))),
  data.table(set = "across", rows = nrow(A), invalid_estimate = A[is.na(y), .N],
             gross_error = nrow(A[!is.na(y)]) - nrow(drop_gross_errors(A[!is.na(y)]))))
W <- W[!is.na(y)]
A <- A[!is.na(y)]

# Re-check cell eligibility after exclusions (Q14).
W_ok <- drop_gross_errors(W)[, .(levels = uniqueN(a)), by = cell][levels >= min_levels_within, cell]
W <- W[cell %in% W_ok]
A_ok <- drop_gross_errors(A)[, .(n_low = sum(anchorhigh == 0), n_high = sum(anchorhigh == 1)), by = cell][
  n_low >= min_n_side & n_high >= min_n_side, cell]
A <- A[cell %in% A_ok]
cells_A <- cells_A[cell %in% A_ok]

# ---- H1: within-item response function ----------------------------------------------------------
fit_h1 <- function(dat, formula = y ~ x + xx + (1 + x + xx || cell) + (1 | pid)) {
  dat <- drop_gross_errors(dat)
  dat[, xx := x * abs(x)]
  # Q23: simplify random effects step by step if the fit is singular or fails to converge
  forms <- list(formula,
                update(formula, . ~ . - (1 + x + xx || cell) + (1 + x || cell)),
                update(formula, . ~ . - (1 + x + xx || cell) + (1 | cell)))
  for (i in seq_along(forms)) {
    m <- tryCatch(lmerTest::lmer(forms[[i]], data = dat, REML = TRUE), error = function(e) NULL)
    if (!is.null(m) && !isSingular(m) && length(m@optinfo$conv$lme4$messages) == 0) break
  }
  co <- summary(m, ddf = "Satterthwaite")$coefficients
  V <- as.matrix(vcov(m))[c("x", "xx"), c("x", "xx")]
  b <- co["x", "Estimate"]; g <- co["xx", "Estimate"]
  grad <- c(-g / b^2, 1 / b)
  rho_se <- sqrt(drop(t(grad) %*% V %*% grad))
  ci <- function(term) co[term, "Estimate"] + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, co[term, "df"]) * co[term, "Std. Error"]
  list(model = m, random_structure = i, n_rows = nrow(dat), n_cells = uniqueN(dat$cell), n_participants = uniqueN(dat$pid),
       b = b, b_ci = ci("x"), g = g, g_ci = ci("xx"), g_df = co["xx", "df"], g_p = co["xx", "Pr(>|t|)"],
       rho = g / b, rho_ci = g / b + c(-1, 1) * z * rho_se)
}
shape_verdict <- function(gate_lo, lo, hi, rel_lo, rel_hi, bounds) {
  if (gate_lo <= 0) return("gate failed: no measurable anchoring, shape not testable")
  if (lo > 0) return("rising")
  if (hi < 0) return("falling")
  if (rel_lo > bounds[1] && rel_hi < bounds[2]) return("flat")
  "inconclusive"
}
h1 <- list(pooled = fit_h1(W), random = fit_h1(W[anchortype == 1]), fixed = fit_h1(W[anchortype != 1]))
h1_tab <- rbindlist(lapply(names(h1), function(k) with(h1[[k]], data.table(
  set = k, n_rows, n_cells, n_participants, random_structure,
  b, b_lo = b_ci[1], b_hi = b_ci[2], g, g_lo = g_ci[1], g_hi = g_ci[2], g_df, g_p,
  rho, rho_lo = rho_ci[1], rho_hi = rho_ci[2],
  verdict = shape_verdict(b_ci[1], g_ci[1], g_ci[2], rho_ci[1], rho_ci[2], rho_bounds)))))

# ---- H2: across-cell anchoring index -------------------------------------------------------------
ci_A <- cell_indices(A, cells_A)
fit_h2 <- function(ci, mods = ~ extremity) {
  m <- tryCatch(rma.mv(ai, ai_se^2, mods = mods, random = ~ 1 | study / cell, data = ci, method = "REML"),
                error = function(e) NULL)
  robust_fallback <- is.null(m)
  if (robust_fallback) {   # Q23 fallback
    m <- robust(rma(ai, ai_se^2, mods = mods, data = ci, method = "REML"), cluster = ci$study, clubSandwich = TRUE)
  }
  list(model = m, robust_fallback = robust_fallback)
}
h2_mean <- fit_h2(ci_A, mods = ~ 1)$model
h2 <- fit_h2(ci_A)
h2_coef <- function(m, term = "extremity") {
  i <- which(rownames(m$beta) == term)
  c(est = m$beta[i], lo = m$ci.lb[i], hi = m$ci.ub[i], p = m$pval[i])
}
s2 <- h2_coef(h2$model)
h2_tab <- data.table(n_cells = nrow(ci_A), n_studies = uniqueN(ci_A$study), n_rows = nrow(drop_gross_errors(A)),
                     mean_ai = h2_mean$beta[1], mean_ai_lo = h2_mean$ci.lb, mean_ai_hi = h2_mean$ci.ub,
                     slope = s2[["est"]], slope_lo = s2[["lo"]], slope_hi = s2[["hi"]], slope_p = s2[["p"]],
                     robust_fallback = h2$robust_fallback)
h2_tab[, verdict := shape_verdict(mean_ai_lo, slope_lo, slope_hi, slope_lo, slope_hi, slope_bounds)]

# ---- H3: model adequacy ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
pi <- fread(file.path("output", "predictive_intervals.csv"))
obs <- list(g = h1$pooled$g, rho = h1$pooled$rho, slope = h2_tab$slope)
h3_tab <- pi[, .(model,
                 g_inside = obs$g >= g_lo & obs$g <= g_hi,
                 rho_inside = obs$rho >= rho_lo & obs$rho <= rho_hi,
                 slope_inside = obs$slope >= slope_lo & obs$slope <= slope_hi,
                 b_inside = h1$pooled$b >= b_lo & h1$pooled$b <= b_hi,
                 mean_ai_inside = h2_tab$mean_ai >= ai_lo & h2_tab$mean_ai <= ai_hi)]
h3_tab[, survives := (g_inside | rho_inside) & slope_inside]

# ---- Robustness (Q24) ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
rob <- list()
# R1: median regression without the gross-error rule, participant-cluster bootstrap
{
  d <- copy(W)[, xx := x * abs(x)]
  f <- y ~ 0 + factor(cell) + factor(cell):x + xx
  est <- coef(rq(f, tau = 0.5, data = d))["xx"]
  pids <- unique(d$pid)
  set.seed(20260927)
  boot <- replicate(if (dry_run) 100 else 1000, {
    s <- data.table(pid = sample(pids, replace = TRUE))[, draw := .I]
    bd <- d[s, on = "pid", allow.cartesian = TRUE]
    tryCatch(coef(rq(f, tau = 0.5, data = bd))["xx"], error = function(e) NA_real_)
  })
  rob$R1_median_regression_g <- c(est = unname(est), lo = unname(quantile(boot, .025, na.rm = TRUE)), hi = unname(quantile(boot, .975, na.rm = TRUE)))
}
# R2: piecewise slopes, knot at |x| = 1
{
  d <- drop_gross_errors(W)[, h := sign(x) * pmax(abs(x) - 1, 0)]
  m <- lmerTest::lmer(y ~ x + h + (1 + x + h || cell) + (1 | pid), data = d)
  co <- summary(m)$coefficients
  rob$R2_far_minus_near_slope <- c(est = co["h", "Estimate"], lo = co["h", "Estimate"] - qt(.975, co["h", "df"]) * co["h", "Std. Error"],
                                   hi = co["h", "Estimate"] + qt(.975, co["h", "df"]) * co["h", "Std. Error"])
}
# R3: without Bahník (2021a)
{
  f3 <- fit_h1(W[reference_short != "Bahník, 2021a"])
  rob$R3_without_bahnik_g <- c(est = f3$g, lo = f3$g_ci[1], hi = f3$g_ci[2])
}
# R4: raw-scale anchoring index
{
  r <- merge(drop_gross_errors(A)[, .(cell, anchorhigh, est)], cells_A[, .(cell, study, a_low, a_high, extremity)], by = "cell")
  ci4 <- r[, .(ai = (median(est[anchorhigh == 1]) - median(est[anchorhigh == 0])) / (a_high[1] - a_low[1]),
               ai_se = 1.2533 * sqrt(mad(est[anchorhigh == 1])^2 / sum(anchorhigh == 1) + mad(est[anchorhigh == 0])^2 / sum(anchorhigh == 0)) / (a_high[1] - a_low[1]),
               study = study[1], extremity = extremity[1]), by = cell][ai_se > 0]
  rob$R4_raw_index_slope <- h2_coef(fit_h2(ci4)$model)
}
# R5: covariates
{
  cov <- unique(sets$across_rows[, .(cell, anchortype = factor(anchortype), comparative_question, direction,
                                     incentive_any = as.integer(incentive != 0), experiment_type = factor(experiment_type))], by = "cell")
  ci5 <- merge(ci_A, cov, by = "cell")
  keep <- names(which(sapply(ci5[, .(anchortype, comparative_question, direction, incentive_any, experiment_type)], uniqueN) > 1))
  rob$R5_covariates_slope <- h2_coef(fit_h2(ci5, mods = reformulate(c("extremity", keep)))$model)
}
# R6: without Weber et al. (2021)
rob$R6_without_weber_slope <- h2_coef(fit_h2(ci_A[study != "Weber et al., 2021"])$model)
# R7: alternative extremity measures
{
  ci7 <- copy(ci_A)[, `:=`(ext_max = pmax(abs(x_low), abs(x_high)), ext_spread = x_high - x_low)]
  rob$R7_max_distance_slope <- h2_coef(fit_h2(ci7, mods = ~ ext_max)$model, "ext_max")
  rob$R7_log_spread_slope <- h2_coef(fit_h2(ci7, mods = ~ ext_spread)$model, "ext_spread")
}
rob_tab <- rbindlist(lapply(names(rob), function(k) data.table(analysis = k, est = rob[[k]][1], lo = rob[[k]][2], hi = rob[[k]][3])))

# ---- Save ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
fwrite(exclusions, file.path(out_dir, "exclusions.csv"))
fwrite(h1_tab, file.path(out_dir, "h1_within.csv"))
fwrite(h2_tab, file.path(out_dir, "h2_across.csv"))
fwrite(ci_A, file.path(out_dir, "h2_cell_indices.csv"))
fwrite(h3_tab, file.path(out_dir, "h3_model_adequacy.csv"))
fwrite(rob_tab, file.path(out_dir, "robustness.csv"))
saveRDS(list(h1 = h1, h2 = h2, h2_mean = h2_mean, W = W, A = A, ci_A = ci_A), file.path(out_dir, "fits.rds"))
print(exclusions); print(h1_tab); print(h2_tab); print(h3_tab); print(rob_tab)

saveRDS(list(h1 = h1, h2 = h2, h2_mean = h2_mean, W = W, A = A, ci_A = ci_A), file.path(out_dir, "fits.rds"))

# Confirmatory analyses as preregistered (prereg/preregistration.md, Q19-Q24).
# Usage: Rscript R/04_confirmatory.R          -> observed OpAQ estimates (after the prereg commit)
#        Rscript R/04_confirmatory.R dry-run  -> estimates replaced by responses simulated from M2,
#                                               to check the pipeline without reading outcomes

suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(data.table); library(lmerTest); library(metafor); library(quantreg) })
source(file.path("R", "design_sets.R"))
source(file.path("R", "models.R"))
source(file.path("R", "estimators.R"))

dry_run <- identical(commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE), "dry-run")
out_dir <- if (dry_run) file.path("output", "dry_run") else file.path("output", "confirmatory")
dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
z <- qnorm(0.975)
rho_bounds <- c(-0.05, 0.05)
slope_bounds <- c(-0.03, 0.03)

# ---- Data -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
sets <- build_sets(read_opaq(include_outcomes = !dry_run))
if (dry_run) {
  set.seed(1)
  cells <- unique(c(sets$within$cell, sets$across_rows$cell))
  cellpar <- data.table(cell = cells, sigma = runif(length(cells), 0.3, 1.2), bias = rnorm(length(cells), 0, 0.3))
  for (nm in c("within", "across_rows")) {
    s <- sets[[nm]]
    s[, estimate := t * exp(simulate_responses("M2", s[, .(cell, pid, x)], cellpar, list(w = 0.45)))]
  }
}
add_y <- function(d) {
  d <- copy(d)
  d[, est := suppressWarnings(as.numeric(estimate))]
  d[, y := fifelse(!is.na(est) & est > 0, log(est / t), NA_real_)]
  d
}
W <- add_y(sets$within)
A <- add_y(sets$across_rows)
cells_A <- copy(sets$across_cells)
exclusions <- rbind(
  data.table(set = "within", rows = nrow(W), invalid_estimate = W[is.na(y), .N],
             gross_error = nrow(W[!is.na(y)]) - nrow(drop_gross_errors(W[!is.na(y)]))),
  data.table(set = "across", rows = nrow(A), invalid_estimate = A[is.na(y), .N],
             gross_error = nrow(A[!is.na(y)]) - nrow(drop_gross_errors(A[!is.na(y)]))))
W <- W[!is.na(y)]
A <- A[!is.na(y)]

# Re-check cell eligibility after exclusions (Q14).
W_ok <- drop_gross_errors(W)[, .(levels = uniqueN(a)), by = cell][levels >= min_levels_within, cell]
W <- W[cell %in% W_ok]
A_ok <- drop_gross_errors(A)[, .(n_low = sum(anchorhigh == 0), n_high = sum(anchorhigh == 1)), by = cell][
  n_low >= min_n_side & n_high >= min_n_side, cell]
A <- A[cell %in% A_ok]
cells_A <- cells_A[cell %in% A_ok]

# ---- H1: within-item response function ----------------------------------------------------------
fit_h1 <- function(dat, formula = y ~ x + xx + (1 + x + xx || cell) + (1 | pid)) {
  dat <- drop_gross_errors(dat)
  dat[, xx := x * abs(x)]
  # Q23: simplify random effects step by step if the fit is singular or fails to converge
  forms <- list(formula,
                update(formula, . ~ . - (1 + x + xx || cell) + (1 + x || cell)),
                update(formula, . ~ . - (1 + x + xx || cell) + (1 | cell)))
  for (i in seq_along(forms)) {
    m <- tryCatch(lmerTest::lmer(forms[[i]], data = dat, REML = TRUE), error = function(e) NULL)
    if (!is.null(m) && !isSingular(m) && length(m@optinfo$conv$lme4$messages) == 0) break
  }
  co <- summary(m, ddf = "Satterthwaite")$coefficients
  V <- as.matrix(vcov(m))[c("x", "xx"), c("x", "xx")]
  b <- co["x", "Estimate"]; g <- co["xx", "Estimate"]
  grad <- c(-g / b^2, 1 / b)
  rho_se <- sqrt(drop(t(grad) %*% V %*% grad))
  ci <- function(term) co[term, "Estimate"] + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, co[term, "df"]) * co[term, "Std. Error"]
  list(model = m, random_structure = i, n_rows = nrow(dat), n_cells = uniqueN(dat$cell), n_participants = uniqueN(dat$pid),
       b = b, b_ci = ci("x"), g = g, g_ci = ci("xx"), g_df = co["xx", "df"], g_p = co["xx", "Pr(>|t|)"],
       rho = g / b, rho_ci = g / b + c(-1, 1) * z * rho_se)
}
shape_verdict <- function(gate_lo, lo, hi, rel_lo, rel_hi, bounds) {
  if (gate_lo <= 0) return("gate failed: no measurable anchoring, shape not testable")
  if (lo > 0) return("rising")
  if (hi < 0) return("falling")
  if (rel_lo > bounds[1] && rel_hi < bounds[2]) return("flat")
  "inconclusive"
}
h1 <- list(pooled = fit_h1(W), random = fit_h1(W[anchortype == 1]), fixed = fit_h1(W[anchortype != 1]))
h1_tab <- rbindlist(lapply(names(h1), function(k) with(h1[[k]], data.table(
  set = k, n_rows, n_cells, n_participants, random_structure,
  b, b_lo = b_ci[1], b_hi = b_ci[2], g, g_lo = g_ci[1], g_hi = g_ci[2], g_df, g_p,
  rho, rho_lo = rho_ci[1], rho_hi = rho_ci[2],
  verdict = shape_verdict(b_ci[1], g_ci[1], g_ci[2], rho_ci[1], rho_ci[2], rho_bounds)))))

# ---- H2: across-cell anchoring index -------------------------------------------------------------
ci_A <- cell_indices(A, cells_A)
fit_h2 <- function(ci, mods = ~ extremity) {
  m <- tryCatch(rma.mv(ai, ai_se^2, mods = mods, random = ~ 1 | study / cell, data = ci, method = "REML"),
                error = function(e) NULL)
  robust_fallback <- is.null(m)
  if (robust_fallback) {   # Q23 fallback
    m <- robust(rma(ai, ai_se^2, mods = mods, data = ci, method = "REML"), cluster = ci$study, clubSandwich = TRUE)
  }
  list(model = m, robust_fallback = robust_fallback)
}
h2_mean <- fit_h2(ci_A, mods = ~ 1)$model
h2 <- fit_h2(ci_A)
h2_coef <- function(m, term = "extremity") {
  i <- which(rownames(m$beta) == term)
  c(est = m$beta[i], lo = m$ci.lb[i], hi = m$ci.ub[i], p = m$pval[i])
}
s2 <- h2_coef(h2$model)
h2_tab <- data.table(n_cells = nrow(ci_A), n_studies = uniqueN(ci_A$study), n_rows = nrow(drop_gross_errors(A)),
                     mean_ai = h2_mean$beta[1], mean_ai_lo = h2_mean$ci.lb, mean_ai_hi = h2_mean$ci.ub,
                     slope = s2[["est"]], slope_lo = s2[["lo"]], slope_hi = s2[["hi"]], slope_p = s2[["p"]],
                     robust_fallback = h2$robust_fallback)
h2_tab[, verdict := shape_verdict(mean_ai_lo, slope_lo, slope_hi, slope_lo, slope_hi, slope_bounds)]

# ---- H3: model adequacy ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
pi <- fread(file.path("output", "predictive_intervals.csv"))
obs <- list(g = h1$pooled$g, rho = h1$pooled$rho, slope = h2_tab$slope)
h3_tab <- pi[, .(model,
                 g_inside = obs$g >= g_lo & obs$g <= g_hi,
                 rho_inside = obs$rho >= rho_lo & obs$rho <= rho_hi,
                 slope_inside = obs$slope >= slope_lo & obs$slope <= slope_hi,
                 b_inside = h1$pooled$b >= b_lo & h1$pooled$b <= b_hi,
                 mean_ai_inside = h2_tab$mean_ai >= ai_lo & h2_tab$mean_ai <= ai_hi)]
h3_tab[, survives := (g_inside | rho_inside) & slope_inside]

# ---- Robustness (Q24) ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
rob <- list()
# R1: median regression without the gross-error rule, participant-cluster bootstrap
{
  d <- copy(W)[, xx := x * abs(x)]
  f <- y ~ 0 + factor(cell) + factor(cell):x + xx
  est <- coef(rq(f, tau = 0.5, data = d))["xx"]
  pids <- unique(d$pid)
  set.seed(20260927)
  boot <- replicate(if (dry_run) 100 else 1000, {
    s <- data.table(pid = sample(pids, replace = TRUE))[, draw := .I]
    bd <- d[s, on = "pid", allow.cartesian = TRUE]
    tryCatch(coef(rq(f, tau = 0.5, data = bd))["xx"], error = function(e) NA_real_)
  })
  rob$R1_median_regression_g <- c(est = unname(est), lo = unname(quantile(boot, .025, na.rm = TRUE)), hi = unname(quantile(boot, .975, na.rm = TRUE)))
}
# R2: piecewise slopes, knot at |x| = 1
{
  d <- drop_gross_errors(W)[, h := sign(x) * pmax(abs(x) - 1, 0)]
  m <- lmerTest::lmer(y ~ x + h + (1 + x + h || cell) + (1 | pid), data = d)
  co <- summary(m)$coefficients
  rob$R2_far_minus_near_slope <- c(est = co["h", "Estimate"], lo = co["h", "Estimate"] - qt(.975, co["h", "df"]) * co["h", "Std. Error"],
                                   hi = co["h", "Estimate"] + qt(.975, co["h", "df"]) * co["h", "Std. Error"])
}
# R3: without Bahník (2021a)
{
  f3 <- fit_h1(W[reference_short != "Bahník, 2021a"])
  rob$R3_without_bahnik_g <- c(est = f3$g, lo = f3$g_ci[1], hi = f3$g_ci[2])
}
# R4: raw-scale anchoring index
{
  r <- merge(drop_gross_errors(A)[, .(cell, anchorhigh, est)], cells_A[, .(cell, study, a_low, a_high, extremity)], by = "cell")
  ci4 <- r[, .(ai = (median(est[anchorhigh == 1]) - median(est[anchorhigh == 0])) / (a_high[1] - a_low[1]),
               ai_se = 1.2533 * sqrt(mad(est[anchorhigh == 1])^2 / sum(anchorhigh == 1) + mad(est[anchorhigh == 0])^2 / sum(anchorhigh == 0)) / (a_high[1] - a_low[1]),
               study = study[1], extremity = extremity[1]), by = cell][ai_se > 0]
  rob$R4_raw_index_slope <- h2_coef(fit_h2(ci4)$model)
}
# R5: covariates
{
  cov <- unique(sets$across_rows[, .(cell, anchortype = factor(anchortype), comparative_question, direction,
                                     incentive_any = as.integer(incentive != 0), experiment_type = factor(experiment_type))], by = "cell")
  ci5 <- merge(ci_A, cov, by = "cell")
  keep <- names(which(sapply(ci5[, .(anchortype, comparative_question, direction, incentive_any, experiment_type)], uniqueN) > 1))
  rob$R5_covariates_slope <- h2_coef(fit_h2(ci5, mods = reformulate(c("extremity", keep)))$model)
}
# R6: without Weber et al. (2021)
rob$R6_without_weber_slope <- h2_coef(fit_h2(ci_A[study != "Weber et al., 2021"])$model)
# R7: alternative extremity measures
{
  ci7 <- copy(ci_A)[, `:=`(ext_max = pmax(abs(x_low), abs(x_high)), ext_spread = x_high - x_low)]
  rob$R7_max_distance_slope <- h2_coef(fit_h2(ci7, mods = ~ ext_max)$model, "ext_max")
  rob$R7_log_spread_slope <- h2_coef(fit_h2(ci7, mods = ~ ext_spread)$model, "ext_spread")
}
rob_tab <- rbindlist(lapply(names(rob), function(k) data.table(analysis = k, est = rob[[k]][1], lo = rob[[k]][2], hi = rob[[k]][3])))

# ---- Save ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
fwrite(exclusions, file.path(out_dir, "exclusions.csv"))
fwrite(h1_tab, file.path(out_dir, "h1_within.csv"))
fwrite(h2_tab, file.path(out_dir, "h2_across.csv"))
fwrite(ci_A, file.path(out_dir, "h2_cell_indices.csv"))
fwrite(h3_tab, file.path(out_dir, "h3_model_adequacy.csv"))
fwrite(rob_tab, file.path(out_dir, "robustness.csv"))
saveRDS(list(h1 = h1, h2 = h2, h2_mean = h2_mean, W = W, A = A, ci_A = ci_A), file.path(out_dir, "fits.rds"))
print(exclusions); print(h1_tab); print(h2_tab); print(h3_tab); print(rob_tab)

1	# Confirmatory analyses as preregistered (prereg/preregistration.md, Q19-Q24).
2	# Usage: Rscript R/04_confirmatory.R          -> observed OpAQ estimates (after the prereg commit)
3	#        Rscript R/04_confirmatory.R dry-run  -> estimates replaced by responses simulated from M2,
4	#                                               to check the pipeline without reading outcomes
5	
6	suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(data.table); library(lmerTest); library(metafor); library(quantreg) })
7	source(file.path("R", "design_sets.R"))
8	source(file.path("R", "models.R"))
9	source(file.path("R", "estimators.R"))
10	
11	dry_run <- identical(commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE), "dry-run")
12	out_dir <- if (dry_run) file.path("output", "dry_run") else file.path("output", "confirmatory")
13	dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
14	z <- qnorm(0.975)
15	rho_bounds <- c(-0.05, 0.05)
16	slope_bounds <- c(-0.03, 0.03)
17	
18	# ---- Data -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
19	sets <- build_sets(read_opaq(include_outcomes = !dry_run))
20	if (dry_run) {
21	  set.seed(1)
22	  cells <- unique(c(sets$within$cell, sets$across_rows$cell))
23	  cellpar <- data.table(cell = cells, sigma = runif(length(cells), 0.3, 1.2), bias = rnorm(length(cells), 0, 0.3))
24	  for (nm in c("within", "across_rows")) {
25	    s <- sets[[nm]]
26	    s[, estimate := t * exp(simulate_responses("M2", s[, .(cell, pid, x)], cellpar, list(w = 0.45)))]
27	  }
28	}
29	add_y <- function(d) {
30	  d <- copy(d)
31	  d[, est := suppressWarnings(as.numeric(estimate))]
32	  d[, y := fifelse(!is.na(est) & est > 0, log(est / t), NA_real_)]
33	  d
34	}
35	W <- add_y(sets$within)
36	A <- add_y(sets$across_rows)
37	cells_A <- copy(sets$across_cells)
38	exclusions <- rbind(
39	  data.table(set = "within", rows = nrow(W), invalid_estimate = W[is.na(y), .N],
40	             gross_error = nrow(W[!is.na(y)]) - nrow(drop_gross_errors(W[!is.na(y)]))),
41	  data.table(set = "across", rows = nrow(A), invalid_estimate = A[is.na(y), .N],
42	             gross_error = nrow(A[!is.na(y)]) - nrow(drop_gross_errors(A[!is.na(y)]))))
43	W <- W[!is.na(y)]
44	A <- A[!is.na(y)]
45	
46	# Re-check cell eligibility after exclusions (Q14).
47	W_ok <- drop_gross_errors(W)[, .(levels = uniqueN(a)), by = cell][levels >= min_levels_within, cell]
48	W <- W[cell %in% W_ok]
49	A_ok <- drop_gross_errors(A)[, .(n_low = sum(anchorhigh == 0), n_high = sum(anchorhigh == 1)), by = cell][
50	  n_low >= min_n_side & n_high >= min_n_side, cell]
51	A <- A[cell %in% A_ok]
52	cells_A <- cells_A[cell %in% A_ok]
53	
54	# ---- H1: within-item response function ----------------------------------------------------------
55	fit_h1 <- function(dat, formula = y ~ x + xx + (1 + x + xx || cell) + (1 | pid)) {
56	  dat <- drop_gross_errors(dat)
57	  dat[, xx := x * abs(x)]
58	  # Q23: simplify random effects step by step if the fit is singular or fails to converge
59	  forms <- list(formula,
60	                update(formula, . ~ . - (1 + x + xx || cell) + (1 + x || cell)),
61	                update(formula, . ~ . - (1 + x + xx || cell) + (1 | cell)))
62	  for (i in seq_along(forms)) {
63	    m <- tryCatch(lmerTest::lmer(forms[[i]], data = dat, REML = TRUE), error = function(e) NULL)
64	    if (!is.null(m) && !isSingular(m) && length(m@optinfo$conv$lme4$messages) == 0) break
65	  }
66	  co <- summary(m, ddf = "Satterthwaite")$coefficients
67	  V <- as.matrix(vcov(m))[c("x", "xx"), c("x", "xx")]
68	  b <- co["x", "Estimate"]; g <- co["xx", "Estimate"]
69	  grad <- c(-g / b^2, 1 / b)
70	  rho_se <- sqrt(drop(t(grad) %*% V %*% grad))
71	  ci <- function(term) co[term, "Estimate"] + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, co[term, "df"]) * co[term, "Std. Error"]
72	  list(model = m, random_structure = i, n_rows = nrow(dat), n_cells = uniqueN(dat$cell), n_participants = uniqueN(dat$pid),
73	       b = b, b_ci = ci("x"), g = g, g_ci = ci("xx"), g_df = co["xx", "df"], g_p = co["xx", "Pr(>|t|)"],
74	       rho = g / b, rho_ci = g / b + c(-1, 1) * z * rho_se)
75	}
76	shape_verdict <- function(gate_lo, lo, hi, rel_lo, rel_hi, bounds) {
77	  if (gate_lo <= 0) return("gate failed: no measurable anchoring, shape not testable")
78	  if (lo > 0) return("rising")
79	  if (hi < 0) return("falling")
80	  if (rel_lo > bounds[1] && rel_hi < bounds[2]) return("flat")
81	  "inconclusive"
82	}
83	h1 <- list(pooled = fit_h1(W), random = fit_h1(W[anchortype == 1]), fixed = fit_h1(W[anchortype != 1]))
84	h1_tab <- rbindlist(lapply(names(h1), function(k) with(h1[[k]], data.table(
85	  set = k, n_rows, n_cells, n_participants, random_structure,
86	  b, b_lo = b_ci[1], b_hi = b_ci[2], g, g_lo = g_ci[1], g_hi = g_ci[2], g_df, g_p,
87	  rho, rho_lo = rho_ci[1], rho_hi = rho_ci[2],
88	  verdict = shape_verdict(b_ci[1], g_ci[1], g_ci[2], rho_ci[1], rho_ci[2], rho_bounds)))))
89	
90	# ---- H2: across-cell anchoring index -------------------------------------------------------------
91	ci_A <- cell_indices(A, cells_A)
92	fit_h2 <- function(ci, mods = ~ extremity) {
93	  m <- tryCatch(rma.mv(ai, ai_se^2, mods = mods, random = ~ 1 | study / cell, data = ci, method = "REML"),
94	                error = function(e) NULL)
95	  robust_fallback <- is.null(m)
96	  if (robust_fallback) {   # Q23 fallback
97	    m <- robust(rma(ai, ai_se^2, mods = mods, data = ci, method = "REML"), cluster = ci$study, clubSandwich = TRUE)
98	  }
99	  list(model = m, robust_fallback = robust_fallback)
100	}
101	h2_mean <- fit_h2(ci_A, mods = ~ 1)$model
102	h2 <- fit_h2(ci_A)
103	h2_coef <- function(m, term = "extremity") {
104	  i <- which(rownames(m$beta) == term)
105	  c(est = m$beta[i], lo = m$ci.lb[i], hi = m$ci.ub[i], p = m$pval[i])
106	}
107	s2 <- h2_coef(h2$model)
108	h2_tab <- data.table(n_cells = nrow(ci_A), n_studies = uniqueN(ci_A$study), n_rows = nrow(drop_gross_errors(A)),
109	                     mean_ai = h2_mean$beta[1], mean_ai_lo = h2_mean$ci.lb, mean_ai_hi = h2_mean$ci.ub,
110	                     slope = s2[["est"]], slope_lo = s2[["lo"]], slope_hi = s2[["hi"]], slope_p = s2[["p"]],
111	                     robust_fallback = h2$robust_fallback)
112	h2_tab[, verdict := shape_verdict(mean_ai_lo, slope_lo, slope_hi, slope_lo, slope_hi, slope_bounds)]
113	
114	# ---- H3: model adequacy ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
115	pi <- fread(file.path("output", "predictive_intervals.csv"))
116	obs <- list(g = h1$pooled$g, rho = h1$pooled$rho, slope = h2_tab$slope)
117	h3_tab <- pi[, .(model,
118	                 g_inside = obs$g >= g_lo & obs$g <= g_hi,
119	                 rho_inside = obs$rho >= rho_lo & obs$rho <= rho_hi,
120	                 slope_inside = obs$slope >= slope_lo & obs$slope <= slope_hi,
121	                 b_inside = h1$pooled$b >= b_lo & h1$pooled$b <= b_hi,
122	                 mean_ai_inside = h2_tab$mean_ai >= ai_lo & h2_tab$mean_ai <= ai_hi)]
123	# Shape criteria decide survival; level criteria (b, mean index) depend on the calibration to
124	# Jacowitz & Kahneman and are reported separately. M0 is also contradicted when gate G1 passes.
125	h3_tab[, survives_shape := (g_inside | rho_inside) & slope_inside]
126	h3_tab[model == "M0", survives_shape := survives_shape & h1$pooled$b_ci[1] <= 0]
127	h3_tab[, survives_level := b_inside & mean_ai_inside]
128	
129	# ---- Robustness (Q24) ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
130	rob <- list()
131	# R1: median regression without the gross-error rule, participant-cluster bootstrap
132	{
133	  d <- copy(W)[, xx := x * abs(x)]
134	  f <- y ~ 0 + factor(cell) + factor(cell):x + xx
135	  est <- coef(rq(f, tau = 0.5, data = d))["xx"]
136	  pids <- unique(d$pid)
137	  set.seed(20260927)
138	  boot <- replicate(if (dry_run) 100 else 1000, {
139	    s <- data.table(pid = sample(pids, replace = TRUE))[, draw := .I]
140	    bd <- d[s, on = "pid", allow.cartesian = TRUE]
141	    tryCatch(coef(rq(f, tau = 0.5, data = bd))["xx"], error = function(e) NA_real_)
142	  })

attachment.snippet:
1	# Preregistration: How does anchor influence change with anchor extremity? A model-based secondary analysis of the Open Anchoring Quest
2	
3	Template: Preregistration of secondary data analysis (van den Akker et al., 2021, Meta-Psychology, https://doi.org/10.15626/MP.2020.2625). Question numbers follow the template.
4	
5	Date: 2026-09-27. This document, the simulation code in `R/`, and the frozen model predictions in `output/predictions_raw.csv` and `output/predictions_summary.csv` are committed to git together, before any outcome variable is read. `R/read_opaq.R` refuses to load the `estimate` column until this file is committed.
6	
7	## Part 1: Study information
8	
9	**Q1. Working title.** How does anchor influence change with anchor extremity? Testing five process models of anchoring against 95 studies of open data.
10	
11	**Q2. Authors.** Lukas Wallrich (Birkbeck, University of London; ORCID [ORCID redacted]), who commissioned and is accountable for the study. The design, code, analyses and text were produced by an AI system (Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic) working autonomously under Lukas Wallrich's instruction, with review by other AI systems (OpenAI Codex CLI, Google Gemini via the Antigravity CLI). See `ai_disclosure.md`.
12	
13	**Q3. Research questions.**
14	- RQ1: Within the same item, does the proportional influence of the anchor on estimates (the local elasticity of the estimate with respect to the anchor, on the log scale) rise, stay constant, or fall as the anchor moves further from the true value?
15	- RQ2: Across item-study cells with a classic high/low anchor pair, does the log-scale anchoring index rise, stay constant, or fall with anchor extremity?
16	- RQ3: Which of five process models of anchoring, calibrated in advance to an external benchmark, predicts the observed response functions?
17	
18	**Q4. Hypotheses.** We state competing model predictions rather than one directional hypothesis. All tests use frequentist estimation with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
19	
20	Notation. For each estimate, y = ln(estimate / true value) and x = ln(anchor / true value). Within item-study cells we fit y = a_cell + b·x + g·x|x| (plus random effects; Q19). b is the average elasticity at the true value; g is the curvature: g > 0 means the anchor's proportional pull grows with extremity, g < 0 means it shrinks. rho = g / b is the curvature relative to the average elasticity.
21	
22	Models (full specification in `R/models.R`; all operate on the log scale):
23	- **M0 No anchoring.** Estimates ignore the anchor.
24	- **M1 Anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments** (Lieder et al., 2018a, with the number of adjustments held constant): a Metropolis-Hastings chain starts at the anchor and takes t steps towards the belief distribution.
25	- **M1R Resource-rational anchor-and-adjust** (Lieder et al., 2018a, Eq. 2): as M1, but the number of adjustments minimises expected absolute error plus a time cost per adjustment, so it depends on how far the anchor lies from the belief.
26	- **M2 Constant-weight integration** (in the spirit of the anchor integration model, Turner & Schley, 2016, with a constant weight): the estimate is a fixed weighted average of anchor and belief.
27	- **M3 Adjust to the plausible boundary** (Epley & Gilovich, 2006): anchors inside the plausible range are accepted; from anchors outside it people adjust to the nearest edge of the range.
28	- **M4 Plausibility-discounted integration** (selective accessibility with a plausibility gate; Strack & Mussweiler, 1997; Wegener et al., 2001): the anchor's weight falls smoothly as the anchor becomes implausible.
29	
30	Predictions (derived by simulation on the exact OpAQ designs; Q20 and `output/predictions_summary.csv`):
