| 17 | 2026-09-27 | Add a resource-rational variant (M1R) in which the number of adjustments minimises expected absolute error plus a time cost (Lieder et al., 2018a, Eq. 2), next to the fixed-adjustment version (M1). M1R gets a parameter kappa (the agent's own uncertainty relative to the spread of beliefs across people). | The novelty check showed that Lieder et al.'s optimal number of adjustments grows with anchor distance, which can reverse the predicted shape. Without kappa, M1R cannot reproduce Jacowitz & Kahneman's index (minimum .77), because anchors within about one belief SD are never adjusted. Lieder et al. calibrated on elicited individual uncertainty, which can be narrower than the spread across people. |
| 18 | 2026-09-27 | Equivalence bounds: rho in (-0.05, 0.05) for H1; d in (-0.03, 0.03) for H2. The equivalence check is applied before the sign tests. | Bounds sit just below the smallest effect inside the 95% predictive interval of any model with a determinate sign, and well outside M2's interval. Checking equivalence first stops a negligible but significant curvature (likely with 8,000 rows) from being attributed to M1 while the model-adequacy test contradicts M1 (advisor). |
| 19 | 2026-09-27 | Add gate G2 for H2 (mean log anchoring index credibly above 0) and treat the raw-scale index (R4) as descriptive only. | Without G2, data with no anchoring look "flat" in H2 (97.5% of M0 replicates). A dry run with M2 data gave a falling raw-scale slope, so R4 cannot discriminate between log-scale models. |
| 20 | 2026-09-27 | Model survival (H3) is decided by shape statistics (curvature and across-cell slope); level statistics (b, mean index) are reported but do not decide survival. | Levels inherit the calibration to Jacowitz & Kahneman's design and task, which need not transfer to OpAQ; shapes follow from model structure. |
| 21 | 2026-09-27 | Target journal: Judgment and Decision Making (Cambridge University Press), Empirical Article. | Its aims name analysis of existing data and process models; it published Bahník (2021a), one of the analysed studies; it has no length limit; Cambridge's AI policy bars AI authorship but allows disclosed AI use with an accountable human author, and does not prohibit substantially AI-generated work (scoping/journals/jdm.md). Alternatives were weaker on AI policy (Wiley/JBDM, Cognitive Science and Springer/PB&R frame AI as an assistant under author direction; Springer lists AI-generated results and interpretation as not permitted) or on scope (Meta-Psychology). Gold open access; APC waiver requests are assessed after acceptance. |
| 22 | 2026-09-27 | Commit the preregistration without waiting for the literature agent's report on Bahník (2021a) and Imhoff & Barker (2022). | These two studies supply about 93% of the within-item rows; reading what they report about the shape of the estimate-anchor function would mean seeing the primary outcome pattern before the plan is frozen. |
EOF
echo ok

input.content:
# Exploratory analyses (not preregistered; prereg Q25 lists their topics).
# E1 asymmetry of curvature for low vs high anchors; E2 near/far elasticity per within-item cell;
# E3 Hedges' g against extremity across cells; E4 across-cell slope with extremity scaled by the
# spread of responses; E5 relaxed-calibration check of whether any model reproduces the observed
# statistics jointly.

suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(data.table); library(lmerTest); library(metafor); library(parallel) })
source(file.path("R", "design_sets.R"))
source(file.path("R", "models.R"))
source(file.path("R", "estimators.R"))
out_dir <- file.path("output", "exploratory")
dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

f <- readRDS(file.path("output", "confirmatory", "fits.rds"))
W <- drop_gross_errors(f$W)
A <- drop_gross_errors(f$A)
ci_A <- f$ci_A
res <- list()

# E1: curvature separately for anchors below and above the true value
{
  d <- copy(W)[, `:=`(xx_neg = fifelse(x < 0, x * abs(x), 0), xx_pos = fifelse(x > 0, x * abs(x), 0))]
  m <- lmerTest::lmer(y ~ x + xx_neg + xx_pos + (1 + x || cell) + (1 | pid), data = d)
  co <- summary(m)$coefficients
  for (term in c("xx_neg", "xx_pos"))
    res[[paste0("E1_", term)]] <- c(est = co[term, "Estimate"], lo = co[term, "Estimate"] - qt(.975, co[term, "df"]) * co[term, "Std. Error"],
                                    hi = co[term, "Estimate"] + qt(.975, co[term, "df"]) * co[term, "Std. Error"])
  e1_counts <- W[, .(below = sum(x < 0), above = sum(x > 0)), by = .(reference_short)]
}

# E2: per-cell OLS with separate slopes for near (|x| <= 1) and far (|x| > 1) anchors
{
  e2 <- W[, {
    h <- sign(x) * pmax(abs(x) - 1, 0)
    ok <- sum(abs(x) > 1) >= 20 && sum(abs(x) <= 1) >= 20
    if (ok) { co <- coef(summary(lm(y ~ x + h))); list(n = .N, slope_near = co["x", 1], slope_far = co["x", 1] + co["h", 1],
                                                       diff = co["h", 1], diff_se = co["h", 2]) }
    else list(n = .N, slope_near = NA_real_, slope_far = NA_real_, diff = NA_real_, diff_se = NA_real_)
  }, by = .(cell, reference_short, anchortype)]
  res$E2_cells_far_below_near <- c(est = e2[!is.na(diff), sum(diff < 0)], lo = NA, hi = e2[!is.na(diff), .N])
}

# E3: Hedges' g per across-set cell (log scale) against extremity, as in Röseler & Schütz (2022)
{
  e3 <- A[, {
    yh <- y[anchorhigh == 1]; yl <- y[anchorhigh == 0]
    es <- escalc("SMD", m1i = mean(yh), sd1i = sd(yh), n1i = length(yh), m2i = mean(yl), sd2i = sd(yl), n2i = length(yl))
    list(g = es$yi, v = es$vi)
  }, by = cell]
  e3 <- merge(e3, ci_A[, .(cell, study, extremity)], by = "cell")
  m3 <- rma.mv(g, v, mods = ~ extremity, random = ~ 1 | study / cell, data = e3)
  res$E3_hedges_g_slope <- c(est = m3$beta[2], lo = m3$ci.lb[2], hi = m3$ci.ub[2])
}

# E4: extremity in units of the within-condition spread of log responses (outcome-based, so
# contaminated by anchoring; shown only to probe the within/across discrepancy)
{
  sp <- A[, .(spread = sqrt((mad(y[anchorhigh == 1])^2 + mad(y[anchorhigh == 0])^2) / 2)), by = cell]
  e4 <- merge(ci_A, sp, by = "cell")[spread > 0][, ext_z := extremity / spread]
  m4 <- rma.mv(ai, ai_se^2, mods = ~ ext_z, random = ~ 1 | study / cell, data = e4)
  res$E4_slope_on_scaled_extremity <- c(est = m4$beta[2], lo = m4$ci.lb[2], hi = m4$ci.ub[2])
  m4b <- rma.mv(ai, ai_se^2, mods = ~ extremity + spread, random = ~ 1 | study / cell, data = e4)
  res$E4_slope_adjusting_spread <- c(est = m4b$beta[2], lo = m4b$ci.lb[2], hi = m4b$ci.ub[2])
  res$E4_spread_coefficient <- c(est = m4b$beta[3], lo = m4b$ci.lb[3], hi = m4b$ci.ub[3])
}

# E5: relaxed calibration. Draw each model's parameters from wide ranges (not restricted to the
# Jacowitz & Kahneman band) and ask whether any draw reproduces the observed within-item b and g
# and the across-cell d and mean index jointly (each inside the observed 95% CI).
{
  h1 <- fread(file.path("output", "confirmatory", "h1_within.csv"))[set == "pooled"]
  h2 <- fread(file.path("output", "confirmatory", "h2_across.csv"))
  sets <- build_sets(read_opaq(include_outcomes = FALSE))
  within_rows <- sets$within[, .(cell, pid, x, anchortype)]
  across_rows <- sets$across_rows[, .(cell, pid, x, anchorhigh)]
  cells <- unique(c(within_rows$cell, across_rows$cell))
  draw_par <- function(model) switch(model,
    M1 = list(s = sample(c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2), 1), t = sample(1:60, 1)),
    M1R = list(s = sample(c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2), 1), cost = 10^runif(1, -4, -0.5), kappa = runif(1, 0.2, 1)),
    M2 = list(w = runif(1, 0.02, 0.98)),
    M3 = list(k = runif(1, 0.05, 4)),
    M4 = list(w = runif(1, 0.1, 1), c = runif(1, 0.3, 6)))
  invisible(lapply(c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2), rr_error_curves))   # workers inherit the cache
  jobs <- CJ(model = c("M1", "M1R", "M2", "M3", "M4"), rep = 1:300)
  e5 <- rbindlist(mclapply(seq_len(nrow(jobs)), function(i) {
    set.seed(7e5 + i)
    model <- jobs$model[i]; par <- draw_par(model)
    cellpar <- data.table(cell = cells, sigma = runif(length(cells), 0.3, 1.2), bias = rnorm(length(cells), runif(1, -0.3, 0.3), 0.3))
    w <- copy(within_rows)[, y := simulate_responses(model, within_rows, cellpar, par)]
    a <- copy(across_rows)[, y := simulate_responses(model, across_rows, cellpar, par)]
    fw <- tryCatch(fit_within(w), error = function(e) NULL)
    fa <- tryCatch(fit_across(cell_indices(a, sets$across_cells)), error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(fw) || is.null(fa)) return(NULL)
    data.table(model, rep = jobs$rep[i], par = paste(names(par), signif(unlist(par), 3), sep = "=", collapse = ";"),
               b = fw$b, g = fw$g, rho = fw$rho, d = fa$slope, mean_ai = fa$mean_ai)
  }, mc.cores = 8))
  e5[, `:=`(b_ok = b >= h1$b_lo & b <= h1$b_hi, g_ok = g >= h1$g_lo & g <= h1$g_hi,
            d_ok = d >= h2$slope_lo & d <= h2$slope_hi, ai_ok = mean_ai >= h2$mean_ai_lo & mean_ai <= h2$mean_ai_hi)]
  e5[, within_ok := b_ok & g_ok][, all_ok := within_ok & d_ok & ai_ok]
  fwrite(e5, file.path(out_dir, "E5_relaxed_calibration_draws.csv"))
  e5_sum <- e5[, .(draws = .N, within_b_and_g = sum(within_ok), across_d_and_ai = sum(d_ok & ai_ok), all_four = sum(all_ok)), by = model]
  fwrite(e5_sum, file.path(out_dir, "E5_relaxed_calibration_summary.csv"))
}

tab <- rbindlist(lapply(names(res), function(k) data.table(analysis = k, est = res[[k]][1], lo = res[[k]][2], hi = res[[k]][3])))
fwrite(tab, file.path(out_dir, "exploratory_results.csv"))
fwrite(e2, file.path(out_dir, "E2_cell_near_far.csv"))
fwrite(e3, file.path(out_dir, "E3_hedges_g.csv"))
fwrite(e1_counts, file.path(out_dir, "E1_anchor_side_counts.csv"))
print(tab); print(e2); print(e5_sum)

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of - build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong - check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** - every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

1	# Exploratory analyses (not preregistered; prereg Q25 lists their topics).
2	# E1 asymmetry of curvature for low vs high anchors; E2 near/far elasticity per within-item cell;
3	# E3 Hedges' g against extremity across cells; E4 across-cell slope with extremity scaled by the
4	# spread of responses; E5 relaxed-calibration check of whether any model reproduces the observed
5	# statistics jointly.
6	
7	suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(data.table); library(lmerTest); library(metafor); library(parallel) })
8	source(file.path("R", "design_sets.R"))
9	source(file.path("R", "models.R"))
10	source(file.path("R", "estimators.R"))
11	out_dir <- file.path("output", "exploratory")
12	dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
13	
14	f <- readRDS(file.path("output", "confirmatory", "fits.rds"))
15	W <- drop_gross_errors(f$W)
16	A <- drop_gross_errors(f$A)
17	ci_A <- f$ci_A
18	res <- list()
19	
20	# E1: curvature separately for anchors below and above the true value
21	{
22	  d <- copy(W)[, `:=`(xx_neg = fifelse(x < 0, x * abs(x), 0), xx_pos = fifelse(x > 0, x * abs(x), 0))]
23	  m <- lmerTest::lmer(y ~ x + xx_neg + xx_pos + (1 + x || cell) + (1 | pid), data = d)
24	  co <- summary(m)$coefficients
25	  for (term in c("xx_neg", "xx_pos"))
26	    res[[paste0("E1_", term)]] <- c(est = co[term, "Estimate"], lo = co[term, "Estimate"] - qt(.975, co[term, "df"]) * co[term, "Std. Error"],
27	                                    hi = co[term, "Estimate"] + qt(.975, co[term, "df"]) * co[term, "Std. Error"])
28	  e1_counts <- W[, .(below = sum(x < 0), above = sum(x > 0)), by = .(reference_short)]
29	}
30	
31	# E2: per-cell OLS with separate slopes for near (|x| <= 1) and far (|x| > 1) anchors
32	{
33	  e2 <- W[, {
34	    h <- sign(x) * pmax(abs(x) - 1, 0)
35	    ok <- sum(abs(x) > 1) >= 20 && sum(abs(x) <= 1) >= 20
36	    if (ok) { co <- coef(summary(lm(y ~ x + h))); list(n = .N, slope_near = co["x", 1], slope_far = co["x", 1] + co["h", 1],
37	                                                       diff = co["h", 1], diff_se = co["h", 2]) }
38	    else list(n = .N, slope_near = NA_real_, slope_far = NA_real_, diff = NA_real_, diff_se = NA_real_)
39	  }, by = .(cell, reference_short, anchortype)]
40	  res$E2_cells_far_below_near <- c(est = e2[!is.na(diff), sum(diff < 0)], lo = NA, hi = e2[!is.na(diff), .N])
41	}
42	
43	# E3: Hedges' g per across-set cell (log scale) against extremity, as in Röseler & Schütz (2022)
44	{
45	  e3 <- A[, {
46	    yh <- y[anchorhigh == 1]; yl <- y[anchorhigh == 0]
47	    n1 <- length(yh); n2 <- length(yl)
48	    sp <- sqrt(((n1 - 1) * var(yh) + (n2 - 1) * var(yl)) / (n1 + n2 - 2))
49	    g <- (1 - 3 / (4 * (n1 + n2) - 9)) * (mean(yh) - mean(yl)) / sp   # Hedges' g
50	    list(g = g, v = (n1 + n2) / (n1 * n2) + g^2 / (2 * (n1 + n2)))
51	  }, by = cell]
52	  e3 <- merge(e3, ci_A[, .(cell, study, extremity)], by = "cell")
53	  m3 <- rma.mv(g, v, mods = ~ extremity, random = ~ 1 | study / cell, data = e3)
54	  res$E3_hedges_g_slope <- c(est = m3$beta[2], lo = m3$ci.lb[2], hi = m3$ci.ub[2])
55	}
56	
57	# E4: extremity in units of the within-condition spread of log responses (outcome-based, so
58	# contaminated by anchoring; shown only to probe the within/across discrepancy)
59	{
60	  sp <- A[, .(spread = sqrt((mad(y[anchorhigh == 1])^2 + mad(y[anchorhigh == 0])^2) / 2)), by = cell]
61	  e4 <- merge(ci_A, sp, by = "cell")[spread > 0][, ext_z := extremity / spread]
62	  m4 <- rma.mv(ai, ai_se^2, mods = ~ ext_z, random = ~ 1 | study / cell, data = e4)
63	  res$E4_slope_on_scaled_extremity <- c(est = m4$beta[2], lo = m4$ci.lb[2], hi = m4$ci.ub[2])
64	  m4b <- rma.mv(ai, ai_se^2, mods = ~ extremity + spread, random = ~ 1 | study / cell, data = e4)
65	  res$E4_slope_adjusting_spread <- c(est = m4b$beta[2], lo = m4b$ci.lb[2], hi = m4b$ci.ub[2])
66	  res$E4_spread_coefficient <- c(est = m4b$beta[3], lo = m4b$ci.lb[3], hi = m4b$ci.ub[3])
67	}
68	
69	# E5: relaxed calibration. Draw each model's parameters from wide ranges (not restricted to the
70	# Jacowitz & Kahneman band) and ask whether any draw reproduces the observed within-item b and g
71	# and the across-cell d and mean index jointly (each inside the observed 95% CI).
72	{
73	  h1 <- fread(file.path("output", "confirmatory", "h1_within.csv"))[set == "pooled"]
74	  h2 <- fread(file.path("output", "confirmatory", "h2_across.csv"))
75	  sets <- build_sets(read_opaq(include_outcomes = FALSE))
76	  within_rows <- sets$within[, .(cell, pid, x, anchortype)]
77	  across_rows <- sets$across_rows[, .(cell, pid, x, anchorhigh)]
78	  cells <- unique(c(within_rows$cell, across_rows$cell))
79	  draw_par <- function(model) switch(model,
80	    M1 = list(s = sample(c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2), 1), t = sample(1:60, 1)),
81	    M1R = list(s = sample(c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2), 1), cost = 10^runif(1, -4, -0.5), kappa = runif(1, 0.2, 1)),
82	    M2 = list(w = runif(1, 0.02, 0.98)),
83	    M3 = list(k = runif(1, 0.05, 4)),
84	    M4 = list(w = runif(1, 0.1, 1), c = runif(1, 0.3, 6)))
85	  invisible(lapply(c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2), rr_error_curves))   # workers inherit the cache
86	  jobs <- CJ(model = c("M1", "M1R", "M2", "M3", "M4"), rep = 1:300)
87	  e5 <- rbindlist(mclapply(seq_len(nrow(jobs)), function(i) {
88	    set.seed(7e5 + i)
89	    model <- jobs$model[i]; par <- draw_par(model)
90	    cellpar <- data.table(cell = cells, sigma = runif(length(cells), 0.3, 1.2), bias = rnorm(length(cells), runif(1, -0.3, 0.3), 0.3))
91	    w <- copy(within_rows)[, y := simulate_responses(model, within_rows, cellpar, par)]
92	    a <- copy(across_rows)[, y := simulate_responses(model, across_rows, cellpar, par)]
93	    fw <- tryCatch(fit_within(w), error = function(e) NULL)
94	    fa <- tryCatch(fit_across(cell_indices(a, sets$across_cells)), error = function(e) NULL)
95	    if (is.null(fw) || is.null(fa)) return(NULL)
96	    data.table(model, rep = jobs$rep[i], par = paste(names(par), signif(unlist(par), 3), sep = "=", collapse = ";"),
97	               b = fw$b, g = fw$g, rho = fw$rho, d = fa$slope, mean_ai = fa$mean_ai)
98	  }, mc.cores = 8))
99	  e5[, `:=`(b_ok = b >= h1$b_lo & b <= h1$b_hi, g_ok = g >= h1$g_lo & g <= h1$g_hi,
100	            d_ok = d >= h2$slope_lo & d <= h2$slope_hi, ai_ok = mean_ai >= h2$mean_ai_lo & mean_ai <= h2$mean_ai_hi)]
101	  e5[, within_ok := b_ok & g_ok][, all_ok := within_ok & d_ok & ai_ok]
102	  fwrite(e5, file.path(out_dir, "E5_relaxed_calibration_draws.csv"))
103	  e5_sum <- e5[, .(draws = .N, within_b_and_g = sum(within_ok), across_d_and_ai = sum(d_ok & ai_ok), all_four = sum(all_ok)), by = model]
104	  fwrite(e5_sum, file.path(out_dir, "E5_relaxed_calibration_summary.csv"))
105	}
106	
107	tab <- rbindlist(lapply(names(res), function(k) data.table(analysis = k, est = res[[k]][1], lo = res[[k]][2], hi = res[[k]][3])))
108	fwrite(tab, file.path(out_dir, "exploratory_results.csv"))
109	fwrite(e2, file.path(out_dir, "E2_cell_near_far.csv"))
110	fwrite(e3, file.path(out_dir, "E3_hedges_g.csv"))
111	fwrite(e1_counts, file.path(out_dir, "E1_anchor_side_counts.csv"))
112	print(tab); print(e2); print(e5_sum)

# Figures for the manuscript.
# Fig 1: model predictions (response function and local elasticity against anchor distance).
# Fig 2: observed within-item response functions (binned medians) with the fitted H1 curve.
# Fig 3: across-cell log anchoring index and Hedges' g against extremity.

suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(data.table); library(ggplot2); library(lme4) })
source(file.path("R", "models.R"))
fig_dir <- file.path("manuscript", "figures")
dir.create(fig_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

pal <- c(M1 = "#2a78d6", M1R = "#e87ba4", M2 = "#1baf7a", M3 = "#eb6834", M4 = "#eda100")
lt <- c(M1 = "solid", M1R = "dotdash", M2 = "longdash", M3 = "dotted", M4 = "twodash")

f1 <- rbindlist(lapply(names(pal), function(m) {
  par <- med_par(m)
  data.table(model = m, x = grid, y = sapply(grid, function(x) {

  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_y") +

  labs(x = "Anchor distance from the belief centre (log units, in SDs of belief uncertainty)", y = NULL) +
  theme_paper
ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "fig1_model_predictions.png"), p1, width = 7, height = 3.4, dpi = 300, bg = "white")

message("Figures written to ", fig_dir)

content.content:
## Answer

**The registered decision rules produce the committed headline verdicts:** pooled H1 is *falling*, H1a is *falling*, H1b fails its anchoring gate, H2 is *inconclusive*, and M1R is the sole H3 shape survivor. Several implementation and data issues limit what those verdicts establish. The most consequential are the external calibration scale, the H3 level-estimator mismatch, and the dependence of H1 on one study.

The [preregistration](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/prereg/preregistration.md:5) and frozen predictions are in tag `prereg-v1` at `a40911b` (22:56 BST); the confirmatory outputs are in the next commit, `14ec907` (22:58 BST). The local raw file matches the full SHA-256 recorded in the preregistration.

### MAJOR

- **The external benchmark is calibrated on the wrong scale.** [models.R](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/R/models.R:94) computes `(median(log response at high) − median(log response at low)) / log anchor spread`. The preregistration calls the Jacowitz–Kahneman index a **raw-scale** quantity in [Q24](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/prereg/preregistration.md:140), yet [calibration](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/R/02_calibrate_models.R:9) accepts parameters using this log-scale value and the external .30–.60 band. Those indices are not generally equal. Recompute the benchmark on the raw scale, then regenerate the accepted parameter sets and predictive intervals. Treat changes to the frozen predictions as a documented post-preregistration sensitivity analysis.

- **M1R’s `kappa` does not have its stated meaning.** [models.R](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/R/models.R:75) calls it uncertainty relative to the *spread of beliefs across people*, but uses `kappa * sigma`; that spread is `0.6 * sigma` in [the same file](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/R/models.R:9). If the stated definition is intended, the target SD should be `kappa * 0.6 * sigma`. This changes the parameter region that passes calibration and may change M1R’s broad predictions. Correct and rerun it, or correct the model description and justify the chosen range.

- **H3 compares different estimators for its level criterion.** Simulation [fit_across()](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/R/estimators.R:44) records an inverse-sampling-variance weighted mean AI; observed [H2/H3](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/R/04_confirmatory.R:101) use the intercept of an intercept-only multilevel model. From the committed cell indices, the former is **0.241**, versus the reported latter **0.416**. Using 0.241 would reverse the `mean_ai_inside` flags for M2 and M4 and make M4’s reported *level* criterion pass. It does **not** change preregistered shape survival. Apply the same estimator to simulated and observed data and regenerate the H3 level columns.

- **The H1 inference has limited independent study support.** The pooled [H1 result](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/output/confirmatory/h1_within.csv:2) is \(g=-0.0406\), 95% CI \([-0.0582,-0.0231]\), with Satterthwaite df **9.10**. Thirteen of 20 cells come from Bahník (2021a); [the model](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/R/04_confirmatory.R:55) has cell and participant effects but no study-level effect. Registered R3, excluding Bahník, gives \(-0.0450\), CI \([-0.358,0.268]\). Report the pooled finding as evidence for these sampled cells, with study dependence prominent; add a clearly labelled study-level or leave-one-study-out sensitivity analysis before generalising the shape.

- **One entire across-cell item is removed by a unit mismatch, rather than isolated typing errors.** [The gross-error rule](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/R/estimators.R:9) removes 987 across-set responses. Raw-data inspection shows **870** are from “Population of Chicago” in Shanks et al. (2020, Study 3): estimates are around 2–5, while truth is 2,746,388 and anchors are 200,000/5,000,000. The cell consequently disappears (129 design cells become [128 analysed cells](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/output/confirmatory/h2_across.csv:2)). The registered rule was applied, so this is not a covert exclusion. Document this cell and the unit discrepancy explicitly; assess a unit-harmonised result only as a labelled sensitivity analysis.

### MINOR

- **Q23 model simplifications were not logged as deviations.** [fit_h1()](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/R/04_confirmatory.R:58) correctly tries the registered fallback order. The [observed output](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/output/confirmatory/h1_within.csv:2) records structure 1 pooled but structure 2 in both strata; [deviations.md](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/deviations.md:5) still says “None.” Record the stratum simplifications. The [prediction simulation](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/R/estimators.R:18) always fits the full structure, so stratum predictive intervals and observed stratum fits do not use exactly the same estimator.

- **Q21 operating characteristics do not fully apply the Q22 inference procedure.** [03b_decision_properties.R](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/R/03b_decision_properties.R:9) uses normal critical values for \(b\), \(g\), and \(\rho\), whereas Q22 specifies Satterthwaite inference for H1. Its H2 gate is an explicitly disclosed approximation in [Q21](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/prereg/preregistration.md:117). Recompute the H1 operating characteristics with the confirmatory fitting and fallback procedure, or label the current percentages as approximations.

- **The \(\rho\) calculation is algebraically correct, but its interval differs from the blanket Q22 wording.** [Both implementations](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/R/estimators.R:25) use the correct delta-method gradient \((-g/b^2,1/b)\). Confirmatory [\(\rho\) intervals](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/R/04_confirmatory.R:69) use a normal critical value while \(b\) and \(g\) use Satterthwaite \(t\) values. Specify the ratio-CI convention and use it consistently. The fixed-stratum \(b\) interval crosses zero, making its apparently precise delta-method \(\rho\) interval especially unreliable; the registered gate appropriately prevents a shape verdict there.

- **The H2 variance warning merits a sensitivity check.** [cell_indices()](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/R/estimators.R:36) implements `1.2533 × MAD / sqrt(n)` correctly, including the two-side propagation and anchor-spread denominator. It adds an unregistered MAD floor of `1e-3`; **none of the observed cells reaches that floor**. The warning in [confirmatory_log.txt](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/output/confirmatory_log.txt:6) reflects an actual roughly **9,483-fold** range in sampling variances. Ten cells hold about 61% of the simple inverse-variance weight. Inspect influence under the multilevel fit and report sensitivity to highly weighted cells. Also, 4,730 of 10,726 across-set participants appear in multiple cells; the cell-level sampling covariance is not explicitly supplied to `rma.mv`. A participant-resampling or study-cluster sensitivity analysis would test its effect.

- **The H2 fallback does not implement the stated package contingency.** [fit_h2()](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/R/04_confirmatory.R:92) always requests `clubSandwich = TRUE` if `rma.mv` fails; [Q23](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/prereg/preregistration.md:134) specifies `metafor::robust` when clubSandwich is unavailable. Add the availability branch and record any fallback. The committed observed fit did not enter this path.

- **The R2 fit has no convergence check.** [R2](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/R/04_confirmatory.R:145) fits its piecewise model directly; [the log](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/output/confirmatory_log.txt:1) contains singularity and convergence warnings without fit labels, so the affected robustness result cannot be identified from the log. Log each fit and diagnose or refit any affected robustness model before relying on its CI.

- **The positive-leaning across-cell result is a sensitivity point, not a sign verdict.** [H2](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/output/confirmatory/h2_across.csv:2) is \(d=0.0500\), CI \([-0.0133,0.1133]\), so “inconclusive” is correct; G2 passes. Registered [R6](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/output/confirmatory/robustness.csv:7) excluding Weber et al. is positive with CI \([0.0059,0.1239]\). The within and across sets are disjoint and differ in anchor type and item mix. Present their opposite-leaning point estimates as an unresolved design difference, not as evidence that one process changes sign within the same items.

### NITPICK

- [design_sets.R](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/R/design_sets.R:6) admits the extra task type `"quantitity"` beyond Q13. Its 94 raw rows all have excluded anchortype 5, so it changes no analysed set. Remove it or document it.
- [R4](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/R/04_confirmatory.R:160) silently drops cells with zero raw-scale AI SE, and [H2](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/R/estimators.R:41) imposes the unregistered MAD floor. Neither changes the observed cell set here; document the contingency.
- [00_fetch.R](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/R/00_fetch.R:5) verifies only the first 16 hex characters of the registered SHA-256. Compare the full hash for an exact data-file check.

**Checks that passed:** Q13’s substantive inclusion rules reproduce the registered design counts; the gross-error threshold and anchor retention condition are implemented; the H1 formula, delta-method SE, median SE, H2 nested random effects, gate order, and H3 **“g or rho, and d”** survival rule match the preregistration. R1 resamples complete participant clusters and uses 1,000 observed-data draws. R2’s hinge represents the near/far slope difference; R3–R7 implement their stated contrasts. M1’s fixed-step Metropolis–Hastings chain and M2–M4’s response functions implement their stated mathematical forms. All 2,700 committed prediction replicates have results; the per-replicate `set.seed()` inside `mclapply` makes scheduling unlikely to change them. I could verify these points by code and raw-data inspection, but could not execute `./run_all.sh` in the read-only environment.

Next, I'll run the post-hoc sensitivity checks: recalibrating to the raw-scale Jacowitz & Kahneman index, leave-one-study-out and random-effects tests for H1, and leave-one-study-out with cluster-robust intervals plus a high-weight-cell check for H2.

# Post-hoc sensitivity analyses added after the code review (not preregistered; see deviations.md).
# S1 recalibrate the models to Jacowitz & Kahneman's raw-scale index and regenerate predictions;
# S2 study dependence of H1 (leave-one-study-out; study random effects);
# S3 influence and dependence checks for H2 (leave-one-study-out; study-clustered robust CI;
#    without the ten cells with the largest weights).

suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(data.table); library(lmerTest); library(metafor); library(parallel) })
source(file.path("R", "design_sets.R"))
source(file.path("R", "models.R"))
source(file.path("R", "estimators.R"))
out_dir <- file.path("output", "sensitivity")
dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
fits <- readRDS(file.path("output", "confirmatory", "fits.rds"))
res <- list()
row <- function(est, lo, hi) c(est = unname(est), lo = unname(lo), hi = unname(hi))

# ---- S1: raw-scale calibration ---------------------------------------------------------------
# The raw-scale index depends on the item's log uncertainty sigma, so it is averaged over the
# same sigma range the prediction simulation uses.
jk_index_raw <- function(model, par, n = 20000, sigmas = c(0.3, 0.6, 0.9, 1.2)) {
  sd_unanchored <- sqrt(belief_sd_share^2 + response_sd_share^2)
  mean(sapply(sigmas, function(sg) {
    a <- qnorm(0.85) * sd_unanchored * sg
    y_of <- function(x) {
      mu <- rnorm(n, 0, belief_sd_share * sg)
      exp(respond(model, rep(x, n), mu, sg, par) + rnorm(n, 0, response_sd_share * sg))
    }
    (median(y_of(a)) - median(y_of(-a))) / (exp(a) - exp(-a))
  }))
}
set.seed(20260928)
grid <- fread(file.path("output", "calibration_grid.csv"))[model != "M0"]
invisible(lapply(unique(na.omit(grid$s)), rr_error_curves))
grid[, jk_raw := unlist(mclapply(seq_len(.N), function(i) {
  set.seed(i)
  p <- as.list(grid[i, intersect(c("s", "t", "cost", "kappa", "w", "k", "c"), names(grid)), with = FALSE])
  jk_index_raw(grid$model[i], p[!sapply(p, is.na)])
}, mc.cores = 8))]
grid[, accepted_raw := jk_raw >= 0.30 & jk_raw <= 0.60]
fwrite(grid, file.path(out_dir, "S1_calibration_raw.csv"))
res$S1_accepted_points <- grid[, .(log_scale = sum(accepted), raw_scale = sum(accepted_raw), both = sum(accepted & accepted_raw)), by = model]

sets <- build_sets(read_opaq(include_outcomes = FALSE))
within_rows <- sets$within[, .(cell, pid, x, anchortype)]
across_rows <- sets$across_rows[, .(cell, pid, x, anchorhigh)]
cells <- unique(c(within_rows$cell, across_rows$cell))
acc <- grid[accepted_raw == TRUE]
jobs <- CJ(model = unique(acc$model), rep = 1:200)
pred <- rbindlist(mclapply(seq_len(nrow(jobs)), function(i) {
  set.seed(9e5 + i)
  mdl <- jobs$model[i]
  g <- acc[acc$model == mdl]
  keep <- names(which(sapply(g, function(v) !all(is.na(v)))))
  par <- as.list(g[sample(.N, 1), intersect(c("s", "t", "cost", "kappa", "w", "k", "c"), keep), with = FALSE])
  cellpar <- data.table(cell = cells, sigma = runif(length(cells), 0.3, 1.2), bias = rnorm(length(cells), runif(1, -0.3, 0.3), 0.3))
  w <- copy(within_rows)[, y := simulate_responses(mdl, within_rows, cellpar, par)]
  a <- copy(across_rows)[, y := simulate_responses(mdl, across_rows, cellpar, par)]
  fw <- tryCatch(fit_within(w), error = function(e) NULL)
  fa <- tryCatch(fit_across(cell_indices(a, sets$across_cells)), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(fw) || is.null(fa)) return(NULL)
  data.table(model = mdl, b = fw$b, g = fw$g, rho = fw$rho, d = fa$slope, mean_ai = fa$mean_ai)
}, mc.cores = 8))
q <- function(v) sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", median(v), quantile(v, .025), quantile(v, .975))
s1_pi <- pred[, .(reps = .N, b = q(b), g = q(g), rho = q(rho), d = q(d), mean_ai = q(mean_ai),
                  g_lo = quantile(g, .025), g_hi = quantile(g, .975), rho_lo = quantile(rho, .025), rho_hi = quantile(rho, .975),
                  d_lo = quantile(d, .025), d_hi = quantile(d, .975)), by = model]
h1p <- fread(file.path("output", "confirmatory", "h1_within.csv"))[set == "pooled"]
h2 <- fread(file.path("output", "confirmatory", "h2_across.csv"))
s1_pi[, survives_shape := ((h1p$g >= g_lo & h1p$g <= g_hi) | (h1p$rho >= rho_lo & h1p$rho <= rho_hi)) & h2$slope >= d_lo & h2$slope <= d_hi]
fwrite(s1_pi, file.path(out_dir, "S1_predictions_raw_calibration.csv"))

# ---- S2: study dependence of H1 -------------------------------------------------------------
W <- drop_gross_errors(fits$W)[, xx := x * abs(x)]
fit_g <- function(d, f = y ~ x + xx + (1 + x + xx || cell) + (1 | pid)) {
  m <- suppressWarnings(lmerTest::lmer(f, data = d))
  co <- summary(m)$coefficients
  row(co["xx", 1], co["xx", 1] - qt(.975, co["xx", "df"]) * co["xx", 2], co["xx", 1] + qt(.975, co["xx", "df"]) * co["xx", 2])
}
for (s in unique(W$reference_short)) res[[paste0("S2_without_", s)]] <- fit_g(W[reference_short != s])
res$S2_study_random_effect <- fit_g(W, y ~ x + xx + (1 + x + xx || reference_short) + (1 + x + xx || cell) + (1 | pid))
res$S2_bahnik_only <- fit_g(W[reference_short == "Bahník, 2021a"])
res$S2_imhoff_barker_only <- {
  d <- W[reference_short == "Imhoff & Barker, 2022, Study 2"]
  co <- summary(lm(y ~ x + xx, data = d))$coefficients
  row(co["xx", 1], co["xx", 1] - qt(.975, nrow(d) - 3) * co["xx", 2], co["xx", 1] + qt(.975, nrow(d) - 3) * co["xx", 2])
}

# ---- S3: H2 influence and dependence ----------------------------------------------------------
ci_A <- fits$ci_A
h2m <- fits$h2$model
rob <- robust(h2m, cluster = ci_A$study, clubSandwich = TRUE)
res$S3_cluster_robust_slope <- row(rob$beta[2], rob$ci.lb[2], rob$ci.ub[2])
wt <- ci_A[, w := 1 / ai_se^2][order(-w)]
top10 <- wt$cell[1:10]
m10 <- rma.mv(ai, ai_se^2, mods = ~ extremity, random = ~ 1 | study / cell, data = ci_A[!cell %in% top10])
res$S3_without_top10_weight_cells <- row(m10$beta[2], m10$ci.lb[2], m10$ci.ub[2])
loo <- rbindlist(lapply(unique(ci_A$study), function(s) {
  m <- tryCatch(rma.mv(ai, ai_se^2, mods = ~ extremity, random = ~ 1 | study / cell, data = ci_A[study != s]), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(m)) return(NULL)
  data.table(study = s, slope = m$beta[2], lo = m$ci.lb[2], hi = m$ci.ub[2])
}))
fwrite(loo, file.path(out_dir, "S3_leave_one_study_out.csv"))
res$S3_loo_slope_range <- row(median(loo$slope), min(loo$slope), max(loo$slope))
res$S3_top10_weight_share <- row(sum(wt$w[1:10]) / sum(wt$w), NA, NA)

tab <- rbindlist(lapply(names(res)[names(res) != "S1_accepted_points"], function(k)
  data.table(analysis = k, est = res[[k]][1], lo = res[[k]][2], hi = res[[k]][3])))
fwrite(tab, file.path(out_dir, "sensitivity_results.csv"))
fwrite(res$S1_accepted_points, file.path(out_dir, "S1_accepted_points.csv"))
print(res$S1_accepted_points); print(s1_pi[, .(model, reps, b, g, rho, d, mean_ai, survives_shape)]); print(tab); print(loo)

# Post-hoc sensitivity analyses added after the code review (not preregistered; see deviations.md).
# S1 recalibrate the models to Jacowitz & Kahneman's raw-scale index and regenerate predictions;
# S2 study dependence of H1 (leave-one-study-out; study random effects);
# S3 influence and dependence checks for H2 (leave-one-study-out; study-clustered robust CI;
#    without the ten cells with the largest weights).

suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(data.table); library(lmerTest); library(metafor); library(parallel) })
source(file.path("R", "design_sets.R"))
source(file.path("R", "models.R"))
source(file.path("R", "estimators.R"))
out_dir <- file.path("output", "sensitivity")
dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
fits <- readRDS(file.path("output", "confirmatory", "fits.rds"))
res <- list()
row <- function(est, lo, hi) c(est = unname(est), lo = unname(lo), hi = unname(hi))

# ---- S1: raw-scale calibration ---------------------------------------------------------------
# The raw-scale index depends on the item's log uncertainty sigma, so it is averaged over the
# same sigma range the prediction simulation uses.
jk_index_raw <- function(model, par, n = 20000, sigmas = c(0.3, 0.6, 0.9, 1.2)) {
  sd_unanchored <- sqrt(belief_sd_share^2 + response_sd_share^2)
  mean(sapply(sigmas, function(sg) {
    a <- qnorm(0.85) * sd_unanchored * sg
    y_of <- function(x) {
      mu <- rnorm(n, 0, belief_sd_share * sg)
      exp(respond(model, rep(x, n), mu, sg, par) + rnorm(n, 0, response_sd_share * sg))
    }
    (median(y_of(a)) - median(y_of(-a))) / (exp(a) - exp(-a))
  }))
}
set.seed(20260928)
grid <- fread(file.path("output", "calibration_grid.csv"))[model != "M0"]
invisible(lapply(unique(na.omit(grid$s)), rr_error_curves))
grid[, jk_raw := unlist(mclapply(seq_len(.N), function(i) {
  set.seed(i)
  p <- as.list(grid[i, intersect(c("s", "t", "cost", "kappa", "w", "k", "c"), names(grid)), with = FALSE])
  jk_index_raw(grid$model[i], p[!sapply(p, is.na)])
}, mc.cores = 8))]
grid[, accepted_raw := jk_raw >= 0.30 & jk_raw <= 0.60]
fwrite(grid, file.path(out_dir, "S1_calibration_raw.csv"))
res$S1_accepted_points <- grid[, .(log_scale = sum(accepted), raw_scale = sum(accepted_raw), both = sum(accepted & accepted_raw)), by = model]

sets <- build_sets(read_opaq(include_outcomes = FALSE))
within_rows <- sets$within[, .(cell, pid, x, anchortype)]
across_rows <- sets$across_rows[, .(cell, pid, x, anchorhigh)]
cells <- unique(c(within_rows$cell, across_rows$cell))
acc <- grid[accepted_raw == TRUE]
jobs <- CJ(model = unique(acc$model), rep = 1:200)
pred <- rbindlist(mclapply(seq_len(nrow(jobs)), function(i) {
  set.seed(9e5 + i)
  mdl <- jobs$model[i]
  g <- acc[acc$model == mdl]
  keep <- names(which(sapply(g, function(v) !all(is.na(v)))))
  par <- as.list(g[sample(.N, 1), intersect(c("s", "t", "cost", "kappa", "w", "k", "c"), keep), with = FALSE])
  cellpar <- data.table(cell = cells, sigma = runif(length(cells), 0.3, 1.2), bias = rnorm(length(cells), runif(1, -0.3, 0.3), 0.3))
  w <- copy(within_rows)[, y := simulate_responses(mdl, within_rows, cellpar, par)]
  a <- copy(across_rows)[, y := simulate_responses(mdl, across_rows, cellpar, par)]
  fw <- tryCatch(fit_within(w), error = function(e) NULL)
  fa <- tryCatch(fit_across(cell_indices(a, sets$across_cells)), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(fw) || is.null(fa)) return(NULL)
  data.table(model = mdl, b = fw$b, g = fw$g, rho = fw$rho, d = fa$slope, mean_ai = fa$mean_ai)
}, mc.cores = 8))
q <- function(v) sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", median(v), quantile(v, .025), quantile(v, .975))
s1_pi <- pred[, .(reps = .N, b = q(b), g = q(g), rho = q(rho), d = q(d), mean_ai = q(mean_ai),
                  g_lo = quantile(g, .025), g_hi = quantile(g, .975), rho_lo = quantile(rho, .025), rho_hi = quantile(rho, .975),
                  d_lo = quantile(d, .025), d_hi = quantile(d, .975)), by = model]
h1p <- fread(file.path("output", "confirmatory", "h1_within.csv"))[set == "pooled"]
h2 <- fread(file.path("output", "confirmatory", "h2_across.csv"))
s1_pi[, survives_shape := ((h1p$g >= g_lo & h1p$g <= g_hi) | (h1p$rho >= rho_lo & h1p$rho <= rho_hi)) & h2$slope >= d_lo & h2$slope <= d_hi]
fwrite(s1_pi, file.path(out_dir, "S1_predictions_raw_calibration.csv"))

# ---- S2: study dependence of H1 -------------------------------------------------------------
W <- drop_gross_errors(fits$W)[, xx := x * abs(x)]
fit_g <- function(d, f = y ~ x + xx + (1 + x + xx || cell) + (1 | pid)) {
  m <- suppressWarnings(lmerTest::lmer(f, data = d))
  co <- summary(m)$coefficients
  row(co["xx", 1], co["xx", 1] - qt(.975, co["xx", "df"]) * co["xx", 2], co["xx", 1] + qt(.975, co["xx", "df"]) * co["xx", 2])
}
for (s in unique(W$reference_short)) res[[paste0("S2_without_", s)]] <- fit_g(W[reference_short != s])
res$S2_study_random_effect <- fit_g(W, y ~ x + xx + (1 + x + xx || reference_short) + (1 + x + xx || cell) + (1 | pid))
res$S2_bahnik_only <- fit_g(W[reference_short == "Bahník, 2021a"])
res$S2_imhoff_barker_only <- {
  d <- W[reference_short == "Imhoff & Barker, 2022, Study 2"]
  co <- summary(lm(y ~ x + xx, data = d))$coefficients
  row(co["xx", 1], co["xx", 1] - qt(.975, nrow(d) - 3) * co["xx", 2], co["xx", 1] + qt(.975, nrow(d) - 3) * co["xx", 2])
}

# ---- S3: H2 influence and dependence ----------------------------------------------------------
ci_A <- fits$ci_A
h2m <- fits$h2$model
rob <- robust(h2m, cluster = ci_A$study, clubSandwich = TRUE)
res$S3_cluster_robust_slope <- row(rob$beta[2], rob$ci.lb[2], rob$ci.ub[2])
wt <- ci_A[, w := 1 / ai_se^2][order(-w)]
top10 <- wt$cell[1:10]
m10 <- rma.mv(ai, ai_se^2, mods = ~ extremity, random = ~ 1 | study / cell, data = ci_A[!cell %in% top10])
res$S3_without_top10_weight_cells <- row(m10$beta[2], m10$ci.lb[2], m10$ci.ub[2])
loo <- rbindlist(lapply(unique(ci_A$study), function(s) {
  m <- tryCatch(rma.mv(ai, ai_se^2, mods = ~ extremity, random = ~ 1 | study / cell, data = ci_A[study != s]), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(m)) return(NULL)
  data.table(study = s, slope = m$beta[2], lo = m$ci.lb[2], hi = m$ci.ub[2])
}))
fwrite(loo, file.path(out_dir, "S3_leave_one_study_out.csv"))
res$S3_loo_slope_range <- row(median(loo$slope), min(loo$slope), max(loo$slope))
res$S3_top10_weight_share <- row(sum(wt$w[1:10]) / sum(wt$w), NA, NA)

tab <- rbindlist(lapply(names(res)[names(res) != "S1_accepted_points"], function(k)
  data.table(analysis = k, est = res[[k]][1], lo = res[[k]][2], hi = res[[k]][3])))
fwrite(tab, file.path(out_dir, "sensitivity_results.csv"))
fwrite(res$S1_accepted_points, file.path(out_dir, "S1_accepted_points.csv"))
print(res$S1_accepted_points); print(s1_pi[, .(model, reps, b, g, rho, d, mean_ai, survives_shape)]); print(tab); print(loo)

# Deviations from the preregistration

The preregistration is `prereg/preregistration.md`, committed and tagged `prereg-v1` (commit a40911b, 2026-09-27 22:56 BST). The confirmatory analysis was first run on the observed estimates in commit 14ec907. Each entry states what changed, why, and whether it affects a confirmatory conclusion.

## Deviations

**D1. Estimator for the observed mean anchoring index in H3 (level criterion).**
- Planned: compare the observed "mean log anchoring index" with each model's predictive interval. The first run used the intercept of an intercept-only multilevel meta-analysis (0.416).
- Changed to: the inverse-variance weighted mean of the cell indices (0.241), which is the estimator the prediction simulation used (`fit_across()` in `R/estimators.R`).
- Why: the code review (codex, `reviews/code/codex_answer_code_review_1.txt`) found that simulated and observed values came from different estimators, so the comparison was not like for like.
- Effect: changes the level flags of M2 (still outside) and M4 (now inside). Level criteria do not decide model survival (Q22), so no confirmatory conclusion changes. The H2 test itself still uses the multilevel intercept for gate G2, as preregistered.

**D2. Description of M1R's parameter kappa.**
- The preregistration (Q20) describes kappa as "the agent's own uncertainty relative to the spread of beliefs across people". The code (`R/models.R`, preregistered) multiplies kappa by sigma, the item's belief uncertainty that all other models also use; the spread of belief centres across people is 0.6 sigma.
- Correct description: kappa is the agent's own uncertainty relative to sigma. The frozen predictions came from the code, so they stand; only the wording was wrong.
- Effect: none on any number.

**D3. Code changes after the preregistration that do not change results.**
- `R/00_fetch.R` checks the full SHA-256 of the data file instead of its first 16 characters.
- `R/04_confirmatory.R`: the H2 fallback (Q23) now checks whether clubSandwich is installed before using it, as Q23 specified; the fallback was not triggered. Warnings from robustness fits R2 and R3 are now labelled in the log.
- `R/design_sets.R`: removed the misspelt task type "quantitity" from the list of ratio-scale task types; all 94 rows with that label have anchortype 5 and were excluded anyway.
- Effect: after these changes every confirmatory output file except the H3 level columns (D1) is byte-identical to commit 14ec907.

**D4. Relative-curvature CI convention (clarification).**
- Q22 states Wald CIs with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. For b and g the code uses Satterthwaite t quantiles; for rho = g / b it uses a delta-method SE with a normal quantile, as in the simulation that set the equivalence bounds. This was the preregistered code; we state it here because the Q22 wording does not distinguish the two.

## Applications of preregistered contingency rules (not deviations)

- **Model simplification (Q23).** The pooled H1 model converged with the full random-effects structure. In both strata the full model was singular or failed to converge, and the preregistered fallback removed the random curvature variance (structure 2). The convergence warning in `output/confirmatory_log.txt` comes from a discarded fit.
- **Unit mismatch removed by the gross-error rule (Q15) and eligibility re-check (Q14).** In Shanks et al. (2020, Study 3), "Population of Chicago", participants answered in millions (median 2.6) while the true value (2,746,388) and anchors (200,000; 5,000,000) are raw counts. All 870 valid responses in that cell exceed the gross-error limit, so the cell drops out of the across-cell set (129 design cells, 128 analysed). The other 117 responses removed as gross errors come from 12 cells, mostly Freira et al. (2020, Study 4), a forecast of US COVID-19 deaths made early in the pandemic, and Weber et al. (2021), "Shortest distance between Russia and USA", whose true value is a few kilometres.
- **Operating characteristics (Q21) are approximations.** They were computed with normal critical values and always the full random-effects structure, and the H2 gate was approximated (disclosed in Q21).

## Additional analyses not in the preregistration

All are labelled exploratory or post hoc in the manuscript.
- `R/05_exploratory.R` (E1-E5): topics listed in Q25; E4 (extremity scaled by response spread) and E5 (relaxed-calibration check) were specified after seeing the confirmatory results.
- `R/05b_sensitivity.R` (S1-S3): added after the code review. S1 recalibrates all models to the raw-scale Jacowitz & Kahneman index (the preregistered calibration used a log-scale index, while Jacowitz & Kahneman's .49 is a raw-scale value); S2 tests the dependence of H1 on single studies; S3 checks H2 for influential cells, study clustering and single studies.

For b and g the code uses Satterthwaite t quantiles; for rho = g / b it uses a delta-method SE with a normal quantile, as in the simulation that set the equivalence bounds. This was the preregistered code; we state it here because the Q22 wording does not distinguish the two.
+## Applications of preregistered contingency rules (not deviations)

+- **Model simplification (Q23).** The pooled H1 model converged with the full random-effects structure. In both strata the full model was singular or failed to converge, and the preregistered fallback removed the random curvature variance (structure 2). The convergence warning in `output/confirmatory_log.txt` comes from a discarded fit.

+- **Unit mismatch removed by the gross-error rule (Q15) and eligibility re-check (Q14).** In Shanks et al. (2020, Study 3), "Population of Chicago", participants answered in millions (median 2.6) while the true value (2,746,388) and anchors (200,000; 5,000,000) are raw counts. All 870 valid responses in that cell exceed the gross-error limit, so the cell drops out of the across-cell set (129 design cells, 128 analysed). The other 117 responses removed as gross errors come from 12 cells, mostly Freira et al. (2020, Study 4), a forecast of US COVID-19 deaths made early in the pandemic, and Weber et al. (2021), "Shortest distance between Russia and USA", whose true value is a few kilometres.

+- **Operating characteristics (Q21) are approximations.** They were computed with normal critical values and always the full random-effects structure, and the H2 gate was approximated (disclosed in Q21).
+## Additional analyses not in the preregistration
+All are labelled exploratory or post hoc in the manuscript.
+- `R/05_exploratory.R` (E1-E5): topics listed in Q25; E4 (extremity scaled by response spread) and E5 (relaxed-calibration check) were specified after seeing the confirmatory results.

+- `R/05b_sensitivity.R` (S1-S3): added after the code review. S1 recalibrates all models to the raw-scale Jacowitz & Kahneman index (the preregistered calibration used a log-scale index, while Jacowitz & Kahneman's .49 is a raw-scale value); S2 tests the dependence of H1 on single studies; S3 checks H2 for influential cells, study clustering and single studies.

# Quarto Reporting Conventions

Follow these rules when writing or editing `.qmd` files.

## YAML header

- Always include `code-fold: true` under `format: html:` so code is collapsed
  by default.
- Use `embed-resources: true` for self-contained HTML output.
- Set `execute: warning: false` and `message: false` to keep output clean.

## Code blocks

- **Never place consecutive code blocks with no visible output between them.**
  If two or more blocks produce no reader-facing output, merge them into a
  single block. A block that only assigns variables counts as "no output".
- Each code block should either produce a visible result (table, plot, inline
  value) or be merged with the next block that does.
- Give every chunk a descriptive label (`{r load-data}`, `{r screen-models}`).
- When a chunk produces a figure or table that should be cross-referenced, use
  the appropriate prefix: `fig-` for figures, `tbl-` for tables
  (e.g., `#| label: fig-volcano`, `#| label: tbl-summary`). Reference in text
  with `@fig-volcano` or `@tbl-summary`. Add a caption via `#| fig-cap:` or
  `#| tbl-cap:`.

## Output — prefer prose and tables over `cat()`

- **Do not use `cat()` or `print()` to display scalar values.** Instead:
  - Compute values in a code block, then reference them with inline R
    (`` `r value` ``) in markdown text.
  - Example: instead of `cat(sprintf("N = %d", n))`, write
    `The sample contains **`r n`** records.`
- **Do not use `cat()` to print tables.** Use `gt()` or `knitr::kable()`.
- `cat()` is acceptable only inside `results='asis'` blocks for emitting raw
  HTML (e.g., `<details>` wrappers).

## Tables

- Use `gt` tables (preferred) or `knitr::kable()` — never raw `print(table())`.
- Always add a header via `tab_header(title = ...)`.
- Format numbers: `fmt_number(..., decimals = 3)`, `fmt_integer(...)`.
- Set `cols_width()` on text-heavy columns (e.g., reasoning, titles) to prevent
  layout overflow.
- When building confusion-matrix-style tables from `table()`, convert with
  `as.data.frame.matrix() |> tibble::rownames_to_column()` before passing to
  `gt()`.
- When cross-tabulating two classifiers (not classifier vs ground truth), label
  the spanner/columns after the column variable, not "Human decision".

## Long detail tables (error lists, flagged records, etc.)

- Wrap in `<details><summary>Show N item(s)</summary> ... </details>` so they
  are collapsed by default.
- Use `results='asis'` on the chunk and emit the HTML tags with `cat()`.
- Truncate long text columns (titles to ~80 chars, reasoning kept full but
  with `cols_width()` constraints).

## Inline results

- Use inline R for key metrics rather than printing them from code:
  ```
  **Sensitivity:** `r sprintf('%.3f', metrics$sensitivity)` |
  **Kappa:** `r sprintf('%.3f', metrics$kappa)`
  ```
- This keeps the narrative readable and avoids code output formatting issues.
- **Use `sprintf()`, not `round()`, so inline values round the way the tables
  round.** `round(3.1, 2)` prints `3.1` while `fmt_number(decimals = 2)` prints
  `3.10`, and the same number appearing two ways reads as two different values.
  The same applies to percentages: `sprintf('%.0f%%', 100 * x)` against
  `fmt_percent(decimals = 0)`.
- Never hard-code a number into prose that a chunk already computes. If the
  seed, the data, or the model changes, hard-coded prose goes silently stale
  while inline values follow.

## Statistical results and interpretive prose

CRITICAL: never write interpretive prose about statistical results you have not
seen.

1. Write the code that produces the results first (tables, model summaries).
2. Render the document, or run the relevant chunk, to obtain the actual numbers.
3. Read the rendered output to see what the results actually are.
4. Only then write the text describing and contextualising them.

Guessing what results will look like leads to incorrect characterisations that
are difficult to catch. The same applies after any change to a seed, a filter,
or a model: re-read the rendered output before trusting prose written against
the previous version.

- Check every sentence that summarises a table against the rendered table.
  Rhetorically parallel summaries ("X is more sensitive to A, Y is not more
  sensitive to B") are where prose most often drifts from the data.

## Tabsets

- Use `.panel-tabset` divs to show alternative views side by side (e.g.,
  different plots, subgroup breakdowns):
  ```
  ::: {.panel-tabset}

  ## View A
  ```{r}
  plot_a()
  ```

  ## View B
  ```{r}
  plot_b()
  ```

  :::
  ```

## Parameterized reports

- Use `params:` in the YAML header when the same report should render with
  different inputs (e.g., per-study or per-outcome):
  ```yaml
  params:
    study: "study1"
    alpha: 0.05
  ```
  Access in code as `params$study`. Render with overrides via
  `quarto render report.qmd -P study:study2`.

## Caching / freeze

- For computationally expensive reports, set `execute: freeze: auto` in
  `_quarto.yml` so chunks only re-run when their source changes.

## File paths (R-specific)

- Always use `here::here()` for file paths. Never use `setwd()` or rely on
  the working directory.

# Writing Introductions -- Wallrich Style Reference

These are patterns observed across papers. Apply what fits the paper at hand.

## Overall arc
- **Funnel structure**: broad societal relevance (1-2 paragraphs) --> define key constructs --> review competing theories/existing evidence --> identify limitations of prior work --> present contribution
- Arguments are built **incrementally**, moving from established findings to the novel contribution
- Each claim is **supported by citations**, often with specific quantitative details from cited work
- Counterarguments are **genuinely engaged with**, not strawmanned

## Presenting competing theories
- When two theoretical perspectives make opposing predictions, both are laid out with their logic and evidence before taking a position
- Avoids strawmanning the weaker theory; both get a fair hearing

## Gap identification
- Gaps are framed constructively: "there has only been one study that explicitly considered...", "to date, there has not been...", "little is known regarding..."
- Prior work's limitations are treated as structural problems in the field, not as criticism of individual papers

## The "present research" transition
- Explicitly marked, often as a sub-heading or clear paragraph break
- Contribution language is understated: "We address this in two studies", "Here, we summarized the growing literature...", "We offer X as a simple, interpretable..."
- Avoids: "novel contribution", "important contribution", "groundbreaking"

## Theory-to-hypothesis transitions (where applicable)
- **Directional hypotheses** only when theory provides a clear basis. When evidence is mixed, **research questions** are used instead.
- Explicitly states when a directional prediction is not warranted: "we refrain from stating a directional hypothesis. Instead, we ask:"
- Derivation sequence: *theoretical reasoning --> supporting evidence --> qualifying evidence --> prediction*
- Bridge phrases to hypotheses: "Therefore, we hypothesize that:", "Together, these developments lead us to hypothesize that:"
- Bridge phrases to research questions: "Considering these contradictions, we ask:", "Therefore, we ask:"
- Hypotheses and RQs are set apart from the main text, stated as complete propositions.

## Argumentation
- Even in technical papers, implications are drawn for practitioners or for the broader field
- Real-world examples and illustrations embedded to ground abstract arguments
- Concrete numerical examples make methodological points tangible
- Speculation is clearly flagged: "Here we would speculate that...", paired with a call for further evidence
# Writing Methods -- Wallrich Style Reference

These are patterns observed across papers. Apply what fits the paper at hand.

## General approach
- **Thorough and transparent**
- Justifies methodological choices with citations
- Explains analytical decisions in enough detail for replication
- Acknowledges limitations of methods directly
- Software and packages are named and cited: "the lavaan 0.6-6 package (Rosseel, 2012) in R 4.0.1"

## Reporting statistical results
- Precise reporting with **confidence intervals** where available (not just p-values)
- Where appropriate, uses **equivalence testing** alongside significance testing to distinguish "no evidence of effect" from "evidence of no effect"
- Reports effect sizes with appropriate context and interpretation
- Candid about null or weak results: "significant and positive, but insubstantial (|r| < .1)"
- Standard APA notation: "F(2, 2635) = 5.84, p = .003"

## Open science and transparency (where applicable)
- Pre-registration and open data are **motivated by field-wide problems**, not presented as virtue
- Where pre-registered, deviations are reported openly and justified under a dedicated sub-heading
- Data, code, and materials availability stated prominently
- AI use is declared transparently where applicable

# Writing Introductions -- Wallrich Style Reference

These are patterns observed across papers. Apply what fits the paper at hand.

## Overall arc
- **Funnel structure**: broad societal relevance (1-2 paragraphs) --> define key constructs --> review competing theories/existing evidence --> identify limitations of prior work --> present contribution
- Arguments are built **incrementally**, moving from established findings to the novel contribution
- Each claim is **supported by citations**, often with specific quantitative details from cited work
- Counterarguments are **genuinely engaged with**, not strawmanned

## Presenting competing theories
- When two theoretical perspectives make opposing predictions, both are laid out with their logic and evidence before taking a position
- Avoids strawmanning the weaker theory; both get a fair hearing

## Gap identification
- Gaps are framed constructively: "there has only been one study that explicitly considered...", "to date, there has not been...", "little is known regarding..."
- Prior work's limitations are treated as structural problems in the field, not as criticism of individual papers

## The "present research" transition
- Explicitly marked, often as a sub-heading or clear paragraph break
- Contribution language is understated: "We address this in two studies", "Here, we summarized the growing literature...", "We offer X as a simple, interpretable..."
- Avoids: "novel contribution", "important contribution", "groundbreaking"

## Theory-to-hypothesis transitions (where applicable)
- **Directional hypotheses** only when theory provides a clear basis. When evidence is mixed, **research questions** are used instead.
- Explicitly states when a directional prediction is not warranted: "we refrain from stating a directional hypothesis. Instead, we ask:"
- Derivation sequence: *theoretical reasoning --> supporting evidence --> qualifying evidence --> prediction*
- Bridge phrases to hypotheses: "Therefore, we hypothesize that:", "Together, these developments lead us to hypothesize that:"
- Bridge phrases to research questions: "Considering these contradictions, we ask:", "Therefore, we ask:"
- Hypotheses and RQs are set apart from the main text, stated as complete propositions.

## Argumentation
- Even in technical papers, implications are drawn for practitioners or for the broader field
- Real-world examples and illustrations embedded to ground abstract arguments
- Concrete numerical examples make methodological points tangible
- Speculation is clearly flagged: "Here we would speculate that...", paired with a call for further evidence
# Writing Methods -- Wallrich Style Reference

These are patterns observed across papers. Apply what fits the paper at hand.

## General approach
- **Thorough and transparent**
- Justifies methodological choices with citations
- Explains analytical decisions in enough detail for replication
- Acknowledges limitations of methods directly
- Software and packages are named and cited: "the lavaan 0.6-6 package (Rosseel, 2012) in R 4.0.1"

## Reporting statistical results
- Precise reporting with **confidence intervals** where available (not just p-values)
- Where appropriate, uses **equivalence testing** alongside significance testing to distinguish "no evidence of effect" from "evidence of no effect"
- Reports effect sizes with appropriate context and interpretation
- Candid about null or weak results: "significant and positive, but insubstantial (|r| < .1)"
- Standard APA notation: "F(2, 2635) = 5.84, p = .003"

content.content:
Anchoring without scale distortion
Abstract The scale distortion theory of anchoring argues that people are influenced by a previously considered numeric value, an anchor, because the anchor distorts the scale on which a subsequent judgment is made. The distortion of the scale due to the anchor is a momentary effect that would be overridden if the scale was distorted again, for example, by consideration of a different value on the same scale. In the present study, participants compared thirteen random anchors on the same scale to thirteen different objects. Subsequent numeric estimates of objects’ attributes were influenced by the corresponding anchors even though the anchors were divided from the estimates by twelve questions pertaining to different values on the same scale. The numeric value considered immediately before the estimate did not have a considerable effect on the judgment. While the anchoring effect was robust, it cannot be easily explained by scale distortion. Other possible theories of the anchoring effect are compatible with the results.

Decision making can be improved through observational learning
