**Abstract**

Anchors bias numeric estimates, but it is unclear whether an anchor's influence grows in proportion to its distance from the truth, stays proportional, or shrinks once the anchor becomes implausible. Meta-analyses report larger standardised effects for more distant anchors, yet a standardised mean difference rises with anchor distance even when the proportional pull is constant. We derived the shape of the anchor-response function from five process models (anchor-and-adjust with a fixed or a resource-rational number of adjustments, constant-weight integration, adjustment to the edge of the plausible range, and plausibility-discounted integration), calibrated each to an external benchmark, simulated them on the exact designs of the Open Anchoring Quest, and preregistered the predictions before reading any estimates. In `r dc$within_cells` item-study cells with at least three anchor values (`r nf(P$n_rows)` estimates, mostly random anchors), the log-scale elasticity of estimates with respect to anchors averaged `r f2(P$b)` and fell as anchors moved away from the true value (curvature `r f3(P$g)`, 95% CI `r ci(P$g_lo, P$g_hi)`; relative curvature `r f2(P$rho)`). This contradicts anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments and constant-weight integration. Across `r h2$n_cells` two-anchor cells from `r h2$n_studies` studies, the anchoring index did not change detectably with extremity (slope `r f3(h2$slope)`, `r ci(h2$slope_lo, h2$slope_hi)`), so no model with a fixed parameter set reproduced both patterns. Only the resource-rational variant, whose predictions were least constrained, survived the preregistered model checks. Proportional anchor influence declines within items; comparisons across items, where anchors were chosen by researchers, do not show this decline.

**Keywords:** anchoring, anchor extremity, process models, resource rationality, secondary data analysis, preregistration

# Introduction

Numeric judgements are drawn towards numbers people have just considered. In the classic demonstration, participants who first judged whether the percentage of African countries in the United Nations was higher or lower than a random number gave estimates that moved towards that number [@tversky1974]. The effect appears with arbitrary and informative anchors, with lay people and experts, and in consequential settings such as property valuation and criminal sentencing [@northcraft1987; @englich2006; @furnham2011]. An open collection of trial-level data from 96 studies estimated a pooled standardised effect of about two-thirds of a standard deviation [@roseler2022meta; @roseler2022opaq].

Whether an anchor's influence depends on how extreme it is has practical and theoretical weight. Practically, negotiators, litigants and survey designers choose anchor values, and an extreme opening offer only pays if its influence keeps growing with its extremity. Theoretically, the leading accounts of anchoring make different predictions about this question, so the shape of the relation between anchor extremity and anchor influence is one of the few places where they can be tested against each other.

## Evidence on anchor extremity

Experiments that varied anchor extremity have produced mixed results. @chapman1994 found that "implausibly extreme anchors had a proportionally smaller effect than anchors close to the expected value" in lottery valuations. @strack1997 found that implausible anchors produced a larger raw shift in estimates than plausible ones. When implausible anchors were placed far beyond the plausible range, estimates under them were no higher than estimates under a plausible high anchor [@mussweiler2001], and @wegener2001 found that very extreme anchors had smaller effects than moderate ones. Most of these studies used one or two items and compared two levels of extremity.

The two recent meta-analyses reach different conclusions. Using the Open Anchoring Quest (OpAQ) data, @roseler2022meta found that Hedges' *g* increased with the relative distance between anchor and true value and concluded against the prediction that extreme anchors produce smaller effects. @schley2026 coded extremity as a binary flag for anchors that the original authors described as extreme and found no difference in effect size. @barrera2024 modelled the anchored crowd mean as a weighted average of anchor and crowd mean, with a weight that decays exponentially with the distance between anchor and truth, and found that this weight fell with distance across 30 percentage questions.

These results are hard to compare because they measure anchor influence in different units. A standardised mean difference between high- and low-anchor conditions rises with the distance between the anchors even if every anchor pulls estimates by the same proportion of its distance. A finding that *g* grows with anchor distance is therefore compatible with constant, rising and falling proportional influence. The theories speak to the proportional pull: how much of the distance between belief and anchor is carried into the estimate. @jacowitz1995 captured this with the anchoring index, the difference between median estimates under high and low anchors divided by the difference between the anchors, and @roseler2022meta called for such a unitless measure "to formalize the relationship between anchor distance and adjustment strength".

## Process models and their predictions

We consider five process models. Each maps an anchor and a belief onto an estimate, and each implies a shape for the relation between anchor extremity and proportional pull ([@fig-models]).

In *anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments* (M1), people start at the anchor and adjust towards their belief in a limited number of stochastic steps. @lieder2018a formalised adjustment as a Metropolis-Hastings chain that starts at the anchor and moves towards the belief distribution. When the anchor is far away, each step covers a bounded distance, so a fixed number of steps leaves a larger share of the distance uncorrected. The proportional pull rises with extremity.

In *resource-rational anchor-and-adjust* (M1R), the number of adjustments is chosen to minimise expected error plus a time cost per adjustment [@lieder2018a, Eq. 2]. Anchors inside the plausible range are barely adjusted, because adjusting from them buys little accuracy, while far anchors justify many adjustments. The resulting pull can fall with extremity, but its shape depends on the time cost and on how uncertain people are.

In *constant-weight integration* (M2), the estimate is a weighted average of anchor and belief with a fixed weight. This is the simplest version of the anchor integration model [@turner2016], and in log units it implies a constant proportional pull. It is the null model for shape.

In *adjustment to the plausible boundary* (M3), people accept anchors that lie inside the range of values they find plausible and adjust from implausible anchors only until they reach the edge of that range [@epley2006]. Beyond the boundary the estimate stops moving, so the proportional pull falls towards zero.

In *plausibility-discounted integration* (M4), the anchor's weight declines as the anchor becomes implausible, in line with the selective-accessibility view that implausible anchors activate less anchor-consistent knowledge [@strack1997; @mussweiler1999] and with the finding that plausibility mediated the effect of extremity [@wegener2001]. The pull falls, and far enough out, a more extreme anchor moves the estimate back towards the belief.

The models also include a no-anchoring baseline (M0). Lieder et al. derived that bias grows linearly with anchor distance when the number of adjustments is fixed and showed how the optimal number of adjustments depends on distance, but did not test how the anchoring index varies with extremity. @turner2016 built an inverted U between extremity and anchor influence into their model "for simplicity" and tested it with one anchor per item.

## The present study

We tested these predictions on OpAQ, an openly licensed collection of trial-level anchoring data [@roseler2022opaq]. Because anchor values in most studies were chosen by the original authors together with the items, a comparison across items confounds extremity with item properties. Our primary test is therefore within items: in studies that presented many different anchors for the same question, we asked how the proportional pull changes as the anchor moves away from the true value. A comparison of the anchoring index across two-anchor studies is a secondary test. We simulated every model on the exact OpAQ designs to derive numeric predictions and passed the simulated data through the same estimators as the observed data. We preregistered the predictions, decision rules and analyses before reading any estimate.

# Method

## Transparency and openness

The preregistration (following the secondary-data template of @vandenakker2021), the frozen model predictions, all code and all outputs are in the project repository. The preregistration was committed to version control before the estimates were read; a reader function refuses to load the outcome column unless the preregistration is committed. The one-command script `run_all.sh` reproduces every number from the raw data. Four deviations from the preregistration are listed in the section on deviations below. The study was designed, coded, analysed and written by an AI system under the instruction of the author; the declarations at the end describe this in detail.

## Data

OpAQ [@roseler2022opaq; @opaqosf] aggregates openly available and contributed anchoring datasets into one trial-level file with harmonised design codes. We used the newest version of the file (`opaq_70a.csv`, dated 10 February 2023), which contains `r nf(dc$opaq_rows)` estimates from `r dc$opaq_studies` studies and `r dc$opaq_items` items. It is licensed under CC-BY 4.0 and contains no personal identifiers beyond sex, age and nationality, none of which we used.

Estimates entered the analysis if the anchor was explicitly random, fixed, or relevant to the target (self-generated and incidental anchors were excluded); the response scale was open; the quantity was a positive ratio-scale magnitude (e.g., a length, price, population or count, but not a date, temperature, percentage or preference); and anchor and true value were positive. We excluded one study whose anchors were computed from each participant's own unanchored estimates. Two sets were formed from these estimates.

- **Within-item set** (primary): item-study cells with at least three distinct anchor values. It contains `r dc$within_cells` cells from `r dc$within_studies` studies (`r nf(dc$within_rows)` estimates, `r nf(dc$within_participants)` participants). Fifteen cells used random anchors: 13 general-knowledge items from @bahnik2021, in which each participant compared 13 random anchors between 1 and 1,000 to 13 lengths and heights, and two items from @yoon2021. Five cells used fixed anchors: four items with 10 high anchor levels each from unpublished data by Frech et al. (2021) and one item with 20 anchor levels from unpublished data by Imhoff and Barker (2022), both contributed to OpAQ.
- **Across-cell set** (secondary): cells with fixed or relevant anchors, exactly one low and one high anchor value, a log ratio of at least 0.25 between them, and at least 10 estimates per anchor. It contains `r dc$across_cells` cells from `r dc$across_studies` studies (`r nf(dc$across_rows)` estimates).

## Measures

For every estimate we computed *y* = ln(estimate / true value) and *x* = ln(anchor / true value). Working on the log scale treats a doubling of a height and a doubling of a population alike and matches the roughly log-normal spread of numeric estimates. The log elasticity, the change in *y* per unit change in *x*, is a unitless proportional pull: an elasticity of .5 means that doubling the anchor multiplies the estimate by about 1.41.

In the within-item set we modelled *y* = *a*~cell~ + *b*·*x* + *g*·*x*|*x*|. Here *b* is the average elasticity at the true value, and the curvature *g* describes how the local elasticity (*b* + 2*g*|*x*|) changes as the anchor moves away from the true value in either direction. We also report the relative curvature ρ = *g*/*b*, which does not depend on the overall strength of anchoring. In the across-cell set we computed each cell's log anchoring index, the difference between the median *y* under the high and the low anchor divided by the log ratio of the anchors, and each cell's extremity, the mean absolute log distance of its two anchors from the true value.

## Model predictions

The five process models and the no-anchoring baseline were implemented on the log scale ([@fig-models]; specification in `R/models.R`). Every participant-item combination had a belief centre drawn around the true value, with item-level bias and between-person spread. Responses included response noise and a 2% share of gross errors. Model parameters are expressed in units of the item's belief uncertainty σ, which was drawn from 0.3 to 1.2 log units per item.

To fix the models' parameters without using OpAQ outcomes, we calibrated each model to the anchoring index that @jacowitz1995 reported for anchors at the 15th and 85th percentiles of unanchored estimates (about .49), accepting parameter values that produced an index between .30 and .60. The number of accepted grid points per model was `r paste(sprintf("%s: %d", acc$model, acc$N), collapse = "; ")`. We then simulated each model on the exact OpAQ designs (the same anchors, true values, participants and cell sizes; `r n_rep[model == "M0"]$N` replicates for M0 and `r n_rep[model == "M1"]$N` for each other model), drawing parameters from the accepted set, and passed each simulated dataset through the estimators used for the observed data. [@tbl-predictions] lists the resulting predictions.

```{r tbl-predictions}
#| tbl-cap: "Preregistered model predictions: medians and 95% predictive intervals across simulated replicates."
q <- function(v) sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", median(v), quantile(v, .025), quantile(v, .975))
tab <- pred[, .(`Average elasticity b` = q(b), `Curvature g` = q(g),
                `Relative curvature ρ` = if (.BY$model == "M0") "—" else q(rho),
                `Across-cell slope d` = q(across_slope)), by = .(Model = model)]
tab[, Model := c(M0 = "M0 No anchoring", M1 = "M1 Anchor-and-adjust, fixed", M1R = "M1R Anchor-and-adjust, resource-rational",
                 M2 = "M2 Constant weight", M3 = "M3 Plausible boundary", M4 = "M4 Plausibility discount")[Model]]
knitr::kable(tab)
```

The predictions separate the models by shape. M1 predicts positive curvature (median *g* = `r f3(med_("M1", "g"))`), M2 zero curvature, and M3 and M4 negative curvature (`r f3(med_("M3", "g"))` and `r f3(med_("M4", "g"))`). M1R's curvature depends on its parameters, with a predictive interval spanning zero. The across-cell slope follows the same pattern.

## Analysis plan

**H1 (primary).** In the within-item set we fitted a linear mixed model with fixed effects for *x* and *x*|*x*|, uncorrelated random intercepts, slopes and curvatures by cell, and random intercepts by participant, using lme4 and lmerTest [@bates2015; @kuznetsova2017] in R [@rcore2026]. Confidence intervals for *b* and *g* used Satterthwaite degrees of freedom; the interval for ρ used a delta-method standard error. Estimates were removed as gross errors when their log distance from the true value exceeded both ln(1000) and the cell's largest anchor distance plus ln(10), a rule that never removes a response equal to an anchor. H1a and H1b applied the same model to the random-anchor and fixed-anchor strata.

**Decision rules.** The shape test was interpreted only if the confidence interval for *b* lay above zero (gate G1). We then classified the curvature, in this order, as *flat* if the confidence interval for ρ lay within the equivalence bounds ±0.05, as *rising* if the interval for *g* lay above zero, as *falling* if it lay below zero, and otherwise as inconclusive. The bounds sit just below the smallest relative curvature in the 95% predictive interval of M1, M3 and M4 and far outside that of M2 [@lakens2017]. Applied to the simulated replicates, this rule labelled data generated by M1 as rising in more than 99% of replicates, data from M3 and M4 as falling in more than 99%, data from M2 as flat in more than 99%, and data from M0 as failing the gate in all replicates.

**H2 (secondary).** We regressed the cell-level log anchoring index on extremity in a multilevel meta-regression with random intercepts for studies and cells within studies [@viechtbauer2010], using standard errors derived from the median absolute deviation (MAD) of each condition. Gate G2 required the mean index to exceed zero; the slope *d* was classified with the same ordered rule and equivalence bounds of ±0.03.

**H3 (model adequacy).** A model was contradicted when the observed curvature (*g* or ρ) or the across-cell slope *d* fell outside its 95% predictive interval; M0 was also contradicted if gate G1 passed. The observed level of anchoring (*b* and the mean index) was compared with each model's interval but did not decide survival, because levels inherit the calibration to Jacowitz and Kahneman's design.

**Robustness.** We preregistered seven robustness analyses: median regression without the gross-error rule, with a participant-cluster bootstrap [@koenker1978; @quantreg]; separate slopes for near (|*x*| ≤ 1) and far anchors; H1 without @bahnik2021; H2 with the raw-scale anchoring index; H2 with design covariates; H2 without one study flagged by a later correction; and two alternative extremity measures.

## Deviations from the preregistration

We made four changes after the confirmatory analysis had been run. First, a code review found that the observed mean anchoring index in the H3 level check was computed with a different estimator from the simulated one; we replaced it with the same inverse-variance weighted mean. This affects only level criteria, which do not decide model survival. Second, the preregistration described one M1R parameter incorrectly; the code, and therefore the predictions, were correct. Third, we made code changes that altered no reported number. Fourth, we clarified that the relative-curvature interval uses a normal critical value. One cell was removed by the preregistered gross-error rule because its participants answered in millions while its anchors and true value were raw counts. All analyses labelled exploratory or sensitivity were added after the preregistration.

# Results

After exclusions the within-item analysis included `r nf(P$n_rows)` estimates in `r P$n_cells` cells (`r excl[set == "within"]$invalid_estimate` estimates were missing or non-positive; no gross errors). The across-cell analysis included `r h2$n_cells` cells and `r nf(h2$n_rows)` estimates; `r nf(excl[set == "across"]$invalid_estimate)` estimates were missing or non-positive and `r nf(excl[set == "across"]$gross_error)` were removed as gross errors, `r nf(870)` of them from the cell with the unit mismatch.

## Within items, the proportional pull falls with extremity (H1)

Anchoring was clearly present in the within-item set: the average elasticity was *b* = `r f3(P$b)`, 95% CI `r ci(P$b_lo, P$b_hi)`, so doubling the anchor raised estimates by about `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (2^P$b - 1))` near the true value. The curvature was negative, *g* = `r f3(P$g)`, `r ci(P$g_lo, P$g_hi)`, *t*(`r f2(P$g_df, 1)`) = `r f2(P$g / ((P$g_hi - P$g_lo) / (2 * qt(.975, P$g_df))))`, *p* `r if (P$g_p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", sprintf("%.3f", P$g_p))`, with a relative curvature of ρ = `r f2(P$rho)`, `r ci(P$rho_lo, P$rho_hi, 2)`. By the preregistered rule, the elasticity *falls* with extremity. At the true value an anchor carried about `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * P$b)` of its log distance into the estimate; the fitted local elasticity *b* + 2*g*|*x*| dropped to `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (P$b + 2 * P$g * 1))` for anchors one log unit (a factor of 2.7) from the true value and to `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * max(0, P$b + 2 * P$g * 2))` two log units away. [@fig-within] shows the binned observed estimates and the fitted curves for each cell.

In the random-anchor stratum the result was the same: *b* = `r f3(R$b)`, `r ci(R$b_lo, R$b_hi)`, and *g* = `r f3(R$g)`, `r ci(R$g_lo, R$g_hi)`, again classified as falling. In the fixed-anchor stratum the point estimates were similar (*b* = `r f3(FX$b)`, *g* = `r f3(FX$g)`, `r ci(FX$g_lo, FX$g_hi)`), but with only five cells the confidence interval for *b* spanned `r ci(FX$b_lo, FX$b_hi, 2)`, so the gate failed and the shape was not testable there under the preregistered rules.

## Across cells, the anchoring index shows no clear trend (H2)

Anchoring was present across cells: the mean log anchoring index was `r f2(h2$mean_ai)`, `r ci(h2$mean_ai_lo, h2$mean_ai_hi, 2)`. The slope of the index on extremity was *d* = `r f3(h2$slope)`, `r ci(h2$slope_lo, h2$slope_hi)`. This interval includes zero but is not narrow enough to establish equivalence within ±0.03, so the result is inconclusive under the preregistered rule ([@fig-across], panel A). The point estimate is positive, the opposite sign to the within-item curvature.

## Model adequacy (H3)

[@tbl-h3] compares the observed statistics with each model's predictive interval. M1 predicts positive curvature and is contradicted by the negative observed curvature. M2 predicts no curvature and is contradicted as well. M3 and M4 predict negative curvature and contain the observed *g* in their intervals, but they predict stronger relative curvature than observed (their intervals for ρ lie below `r f2(max(pi_("M3", "rho_hi"), pi_("M4", "rho_hi")))`) and a clearly negative across-cell slope, which the data do not show. Under the preregistered survival rule, which requires both the within-item curvature and the across-cell slope to fall inside a model's intervals, only M1R survived. It did so because its predictive intervals were wide enough to contain positive, zero and negative curvature.

```{r tbl-h3}
#| tbl-cap: "Observed statistics compared with each model's 95% predictive interval. Survival is decided by the shape criteria (curvature and across-cell slope); level criteria are reported for completeness."
obs <- c(g = P$g, rho = P$rho, d = h2$slope, b = P$b, ai = w_ai)
t3 <- merge(pint, h3, by = "model")
t3 <- t3[, .(Model = model,
             `g [PI]` = sprintf("%s %s", ifelse(g_inside, "in", "out"), ci(g_lo, g_hi)),
             `ρ [PI]` = ifelse(model == "M0", "—", sprintf("%s %s", ifelse(rho_inside, "in", "out"), ci(rho_lo, rho_hi, 2))),
             `d [PI]` = sprintf("%s %s", ifelse(slope_inside, "in", "out"), ci(slope_lo, slope_hi)),
             `Survives (shape)` = ifelse(survives_shape, "yes", "no"),
             `b and mean index inside (level)` = ifelse(survives_level, "yes", "no"))]
knitr::kable(t3)
```

Observed values: *g* = `r f3(obs["g"])`, ρ = `r f2(obs["rho"])`, *d* = `r f3(obs["d"])`, *b* = `r f3(obs["b"])`, weighted mean log anchoring index = `r f3(obs["ai"])`.

## Robustness

The within-item result held in the preregistered robustness analyses that retained the random-anchor data. Median regression without the gross-error rule gave *g* = `r f3(r_("R1_median_regression_g"))`, `r ci(r_("R1_median_regression_g", "lo"), r_("R1_median_regression_g", "hi"))`. Replacing the curvature term by separate slopes for near and far anchors showed that the slope for anchors more than one log unit from the true value was `r f2(-r_("R2_far_minus_near_slope"))` lower than the slope near the true value, `r ci(r_("R2_far_minus_near_slope", "lo"), r_("R2_far_minus_near_slope", "hi"), 2)`. Without @bahnik2021 the estimate was similar but very imprecise, *g* = `r f3(r_("R3_without_bahnik_g"))`, `r ci(r_("R3_without_bahnik_g", "lo"), r_("R3_without_bahnik_g", "hi"), 2)`.

The across-cell slope stayed positive and imprecise in most checks: with design covariates, *d* = `r f3(r_("R5_covariates_slope"))`, `r ci(r_("R5_covariates_slope", "lo"), r_("R5_covariates_slope", "hi"))`; with the largest anchor distance as the extremity measure, `r f3(r_("R7_max_distance_slope"))`, `r ci(r_("R7_max_distance_slope", "lo"), r_("R7_max_distance_slope", "hi"))`; with the log ratio of the anchors, `r f3(r_("R7_log_spread_slope"))`, `r ci(r_("R7_log_spread_slope", "lo"), r_("R7_log_spread_slope", "hi"))`. Without Weber et al. (2021), whose item coding was questioned in a later correction, the slope was `r f3(r_("R6_without_weber_slope"))`, `r ci(r_("R6_without_weber_slope", "lo"), r_("R6_without_weber_slope", "hi"))`, the only check in which the interval excluded zero. The raw-scale anchoring index, which the preregistration designated as descriptive because a constant log-scale weight does not imply a constant raw-scale index, gave `r f3(r_("R4_raw_index_slope"))`, `r ci(r_("R4_raw_index_slope", "lo"), r_("R4_raw_index_slope", "hi"))`.

## Exploratory analyses

The following analyses were not preregistered.

*Both sides of the true value.* The curvature was negative both for anchors below the true value, *g* = `r f3(x_("E1_xx_neg"))`, `r ci(x_("E1_xx_neg", "lo"), x_("E1_xx_neg", "hi"))`, and for anchors above it, *g* = `r f3(x_("E1_xx_pos"))`, `r ci(x_("E1_xx_pos", "lo"), x_("E1_xx_pos", "hi"))`.

*Item by item.* In each of the `r e2[!is.na(diff), .N]` cells with at least 20 anchors both within and beyond one log unit of the true value, the slope for far anchors was lower than the slope for near anchors (median difference `r f2(median(e2$diff, na.rm = TRUE))`).

*Standardised effect sizes.* Across cells, Hedges' *g* rose with extremity by `r f2(x_("E3_hedges_g_slope"))` per log unit, `r ci(x_("E3_hedges_g_slope", "lo"), x_("E3_hedges_g_slope", "hi"), 2)` ([@fig-across], panel B), in line with @roseler2022meta. The same cells therefore show a rising standardised effect and no detectable change in proportional pull.

*Extremity relative to response spread.* The across-cell extremity measure ignores how uncertain people are about each quantity. When we divided extremity by the spread of log estimates within each anchor condition (a measure that is itself affected by anchoring), the slope turned negative, *d* = `r f3(x_("E4_slope_on_scaled_extremity"))`, `r ci(x_("E4_slope_on_scaled_extremity", "lo"), x_("E4_slope_on_scaled_extremity", "hi"))`. This is consistent with original authors having placed anchors further from the truth for quantities that people know less well.

*Relaxed calibration.* To check whether the model failures stem from the calibration to Jacowitz and Kahneman's index, we drew 300 parameter sets per model from wide ranges without calibration and simulated each on the OpAQ designs. No parameter set of any model reproduced the observed *b*, *g*, *d* and mean index jointly (all four inside their observed 95% confidence intervals). Within-item *b* and *g* together were reproduced by `r e5[model == "M4"]$within_b_and_g` of 300 M4 draws, `r e5[model == "M1R"]$within_b_and_g` M1R draws and `r e5[model == "M3"]$within_b_and_g` M3 draws, and by no M1 or M2 draw; the across-cell *d* and mean index together were reproduced by `r e5[model == "M2"]$across_d_and_ai` M2 draws and `r e5[model == "M1"]$across_d_and_ai` M1 draws, and by no M3 or M4 draw.

[[SENSITIVITY]]

# Discussion

Within items, anchors lost proportional pull as they moved away from the true value. Near the truth, an anchor carried about `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * P$b)` of its log distance into the estimate; for anchors a factor of about 2.7 away, the local share was roughly halved. The decline appeared on both sides of the true value and in every item with enough near and far anchors. Across two-anchor studies, where authors chose one anchor pair per item, the anchoring index showed no detectable decline, and its point estimate leaned the other way.

## What the within-item result rules out

The negative curvature contradicts two simple accounts. Anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of steps predicts that far anchors keep more of their distance, because a bounded number of bounded steps cannot correct a large gap; the data show the reverse. Constant-weight integration, the simplest version of the anchor integration model, predicts no change in proportional pull; it too is contradicted. The accounts that predict a decline share one feature: the anchor's influence is limited by how plausible it is. This holds for adjustment that stops at the edge of the plausible range [@epley2006], for integration that discounts implausible anchors [@wegener2001; @turner2016], and for a resource-rational agent who invests more adjustments when the anchor is far off [@lieder2018a]. The result fits the earlier two-level experiments in which implausible anchors had proportionally smaller effects [@chapman1994; @mussweiler2001; @wegener2001] and the distance-decaying anchoring weight of @barrera2024, now shown with open-ended quantities and anchors varied within items.

The decline was smaller than M3 and M4 predicted. Their relative curvature intervals lay below the observed value, which means that far anchors still pulled estimates more than a hard plausibility boundary or a steep plausibility discount allows. A mixture in which the weight of an anchor falls gradually but does not vanish could describe this. The data do not identify such a model, and we did not test one.

## The across-cell pattern

The across-cell analysis did not reproduce the within-item decline, and no model with a single parameter set reproduced both patterns. Two explanations are plausible, and our data cannot fully separate them. First, extremity measured against the true value is not extremity measured against people's uncertainty. Researchers tend to place anchors further from the truth for quantities that people know poorly. An anchor ten times the true population of a city may be less implausible than an anchor twice the height of a familiar building. When we scaled extremity by the spread of estimates, the across-cell slope turned negative, as the within-item analysis and the plausibility accounts predict. Because that spread is itself affected by anchoring, this analysis is suggestive only. Second, the two sets differ in anchor type: the within-item set is mostly random anchors, and the across-cell set only fixed or relevant anchors. The models make the same shape predictions for both, but it is possible that informative anchors lose less pull with extremity than anchors people know to be random. The fixed-anchor stratum of the within-item set pointed in the same direction as the random-anchor stratum but was too small to test this.

The divergence also bears on how moderator analyses of anchoring should be read. In the same cells, the standardised effect rose with extremity while the proportional index did not change detectably. Meta-analytic findings that larger anchor distances produce larger standardised effects [@roseler2022meta] therefore say little about whether extreme anchors are more influential per unit of distance. Tests of anchoring theories need a proportional outcome and variation in extremity that the researcher controls.

## Limitations

The primary evidence rests largely on one study. Thirteen of the 20 within-item cells, and `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * 6578 / dc$within_rows)` of the within-item estimates, come from @bahnik2021, in which participants compared 13 random anchors with 13 different lengths and heights. Without this study the within-item curvature had the same sign but a confidence interval too wide to be informative. The random anchors also differ from the fixed anchors that dominate applied settings, and the preregistered test of the fixed-anchor stratum was not informative. A direct test of the extremity function for informative anchors needs experiments that present many anchor levels for the same items.

Second, extremity was measured relative to the true value, not relative to each participant's belief. Where people systematically over- or underestimate a quantity, the anchor's distance from their belief differs from its distance from the truth. The simulations included item-level bias to account for this, and the curvature was negative on both sides of the true value. However, a study that elicits unanchored estimates or plausible ranges from the same participants would give a cleaner measure.

Third, the models were specified on the log scale and calibrated to a single external benchmark. The shape predictions of M1, M2, M3 and M4 follow from their structure and held across all calibrated parameter values, but the level predictions depend on the calibration, and the resource-rational model's predictions depend strongly on its time cost and on how uncertain people are. That this model survived our tests reflects the width of its predictions more than a close fit. Formal tests of resource-rational anchoring need independent measures of the time cost and of people's uncertainty.

Fourth, OpAQ harmonises data from many studies, and harmonisation can introduce errors. We found one item whose responses were recorded in different units from its anchors and true value, and a later correction questioned the item coding of another study. Our rules removed the first; excluding the second made the across-cell slope positive and significant. We used only positive ratio-scale quantities with open response scales, so the results do not speak to dates, percentages, bounded scales or preferences.

## Conclusion

Within the same questions, extreme anchors pulled estimates by a smaller share of their distance than moderate anchors. This contradicts anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of steps and constant-weight integration, and supports accounts in which an anchor's influence is limited by its plausibility, although the decline was weaker than simple plausibility models predict. Across studies with researcher-chosen anchors, the pattern was not visible, which suggests that comparisons across items confound anchor extremity with how well people know the quantity. For anyone choosing an anchor, the within-item evidence implies diminishing returns to extremity. For researchers, it implies that the extremity function should be estimated within items and with proportional measures.

Practically, negotiators, litigants and survey designers choose anchor values, and an extreme opening offer only pays if its influence keeps growing with its extremity. ## Process models and their predictions We consider five process models. Each maps an anchor and a belief onto an estimate, and each implies a shape for the relation between anchor extremity and proportional pull (Figure 1). In *anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments* (M1), people start at the anchor and adjust towards their belief in a limited number of stochastic steps. Lieder et al. (2017) formalised adjustment as a Metropolis-Hastings chain that starts at the anchor and moves towards the belief distribution. When the anchor is far away, each step covers a bounded distance, so a fixed number of steps leaves a larger share of the distance uncorrected. The proportional pull rises with extremity. In *resource-rational anchor-and-adjust* (M1R), the number of adjustments is chosen to minimise expected error plus a time cost per adjustment (Lieder et al., 2017, Eq. 2). Anchors inside the plausible range are barely adjusted, because adjusting from them buys little accuracy, while far anchors justify many adjustments. The resulting pull can fall with extremity, but its shape depends on the time cost and on how uncertain people are. In *constant-weight integration* (M2), the estimate is a weighted average of anchor and belief with a fixed weight. This is the simplest version of the anchor integration model (Turner & Schley, 2016), and in log units it implies a constant proportional pull. It is the null model for shape. In *adjustment to the plausible boundary* (M3), people accept anchors that lie inside the range of values they find plausible and adjust from implausible anchors only until they reach the edge of that range (Epley & Gilovich, 2006). Beyond the boundary the estimate stops moving, so the proportional pull falls towards zero. In *plausibility-discounted integration* (M4), the anchor’s weight declines as the anchor becomes implausible, in line with the selective-accessibility view that implausible anchors activate less anchor-consistent knowledge (Mussweiler & Strack, 1999; Strack & Mussweiler, 1997) and with the finding that plausibility mediated the effect of extremity (Wegener et al., 2001). The pull falls, and far enough out, a more extreme anchor moves the estimate back towards the belief.
![](figures/fig1_model_predictions.png) Figure 1: Model predictions at the median calibrated parameter values. (A) Mean log estimate relative to the belief centre as a function of the anchor’s distance from the belief centre, in units of belief uncertainty. (B) Local elasticity, the proportional pull of the anchor. M1: anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments; M1R: resource-rational anchor-and-adjust; M2: constant-weight integration; M3: adjustment to the plausible boundary; M4: plausibility-discounted integration.
The models also include a no-anchoring baseline (M0). Lieder et al. derived that bias grows linearly with anchor distance when the number of adjustments is fixed and showed how the optimal number of adjustments depends on distance, but did not test how the anchoring index varies with extremity. Turner & Schley (2016) built an inverted U between extremity and anchor influence into their model “for simplicity” and tested it with one anchor per item. ## The present study We tested these predictions on OpAQ, an openly licensed collection of trial-level anchoring data (Röseler et al., 2022). Because anchor values in most studies were chosen by the original authors together with the items, a comparison across items confounds extremity with item properties. Our primary test is therefore within items: in studies that presented many different anchors for the same question, we asked how the proportional pull changes as the anchor moves away from the true value. A comparison of the anchoring index across two-anchor studies is a secondary test. We simulated every model on the exact OpAQ designs to derive numeric predictions and passed the simulated data through the same estimators as the observed data. We preregistered the predictions, decision rules and analyses before reading any estimate. # Method ## Transparency and openness The preregistration (following the secondary-data template of Van den Akker et al. (2021)), the frozen model predictions, all code and all outputs are in the project repository. The preregistration was committed to version control before the estimates were read; a reader function refuses to load the outcome column unless the preregistration is committed. The one-command script `run_all.sh` reproduces every number from the raw data. Four deviations from the preregistration are listed in the section on deviations below. Working on the log scale treats a doubling of a height and a doubling of a population alike and matches the roughly log-normal spread of numeric estimates. The log elasticity, the change in *y* per unit change in *x*, is a unitless proportional pull: an elasticity of .5 means that doubling the anchor multiplies the estimate by about 1.41. In the within-item set we modelled *y* = *a*cell + *b*·*x* + *g*·*x*\|*x*\|. Table 1 lists the resulting predictions.
Table 1: Preregistered model predictions: medians and 95% predictive intervals across simulated replicates.
The predictions separate the models by shape. M1 predicts positive curvature (median *g* = 0.062), M2 zero curvature, and M3 and M4 negative curvature (-0.046 and -0.066). ## Process models and their predictions We consider five process models. Each maps an anchor and a belief onto an estimate, and each implies a shape for the relation between anchor extremity and proportional pull (Figure 1). In *anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments* (M1), people start at the anchor and adjust towards their belief in a limited number of stochastic steps. Lieder et al. (2017) formalised adjustment as a Metropolis-Hastings chain that starts at the anchor and moves towards the belief distribution. When the anchor is far away, each step covers a bounded distance, so a fixed number of steps leaves a larger share of the distance uncorrected. The proportional pull rises with extremity. In *resource-rational anchor-and-adjust* (M1R), the number of adjustments is chosen to minimise expected error plus a time cost per adjustment (Lieder et al., 2017, Eq. 2). Anchors inside the plausible range are barely adjusted, because adjusting from them buys little accuracy, while far anchors justify many adjustments. The resulting pull can fall with extremity, but its shape depends on the time cost and on how uncertain people are. In *constant-weight integration* (M2), the estimate is a weighted average of anchor and belief with a fixed weight. This is the simplest version of the anchor integration model (Turner & Schley, 2016), and in log units it implies a constant proportional pull. It is the null model for shape. In *adjustment to the plausible boundary* (M3), people accept anchors that lie inside the range of values they find plausible and adjust from implausible anchors only until they reach the edge of that range (Epley & Gilovich, 2006). Beyond the boundary the estimate stops moving, so the proportional pull falls towards zero. content.content: ## Deviations from the preregistration We made four changes after the confirmatory analysis had been run. First, a code review found that the observed mean anchoring index in the H3 level check was computed with a different estimator from the simulated one; we replaced it with the same inverse-variance weighted mean. This affects only level criteria, which do not decide model survival. Second, the preregistration described one M1R parameter incorrectly; the code, and therefore the predictions, were correct. Third, we made code changes that altered no reported number. Fourth, we clarified that the relative-curvature interval uses a normal critical value. One cell was removed by the preregistered gross-error rule because its participants answered in millions while its anchors and true value were raw counts. All analyses labelled exploratory or sensitivity were added after the preregistration. # Results After exclusions the within-item analysis included 7,949 estimates in 20 cells (3 estimates were missing or non-positive; no gross errors). The across-cell analysis included 128 cells and 22,533 estimates; 627 estimates were missing or non-positive and 987 were removed as gross errors, 870 of them from the cell with the unit mismatch. ## Within items, the proportional pull falls with extremity (H1) Anchoring was clearly present in the within-item set: the average elasticity was *b* = 0.307, 95% CI \[0.249, 0.365\], so doubling the anchor raised estimates by about 24% near the true value. The curvature was negative, *g* = -0.041, \[-0.058, -0.023\], *t*(9.1) = -5.22, *p* \< .001, with a relative curvature of ρ = -0.13, \[-0.18, -0.09\]. By the preregistered rule, the elasticity *falls* with extremity. At the true value an anchor carried about 31% of its log distance into the estimate. The fitted local elasticity *b* + 2*g*\|*x*\| was 0.23 for anchors one log unit (a factor of 2.7) from the true value and 0.14 for anchors two log units (a factor of 7.4) away, about half its value at the true value. Figure 2 shows the binned observed estimates and the fitted curves for each cell. In the random-anchor stratum the result was the same: *b* = 0.265, \[0.215, 0.316\], and *g* = -0.034, \[-0.044, -0.023\], again classified as falling. In the fixed-anchor stratum the point estimates were similar (*b* = 0.618, *g* = -0.085, \[-0.143, -0.027\]), but with only five cells the confidence interval for *b* spanned \[-0.31, 1.55\], so the gate failed and the shape was not testable there under the preregistered rules. ![](figures/fig2_within_item.png) Figure 2: Observed within-item response functions. Points are median log estimates in 0.5-unit bins of the log anchor (bins with at least 10 estimates), connected within each item. Blue curves are the fitted H1 model for each item (fixed plus item-level random effects), drawn over the central 95% of that item’s anchors. The dashed line marks estimates equal to the anchor. Axes differ between panels. ## Across cells, the anchoring index shows no clear trend (H2) Anchoring was present across cells: the mean log anchoring index was 0.42, \[0.35, 0.48\]. The slope of the index on extremity was *d* = 0.050, \[-0.013, 0.113\]. This interval includes zero but is not narrow enough to establish equivalence within ±0.03, so the result is inconclusive under the preregistered rule (Figure 3, panel A). The point estimate is positive, the opposite sign to the within-item curvature. ![](figures/fig3_across_cells.png) Figure 3: Across-cell relation between anchor extremity and anchor influence. (A) Log anchoring index per cell with the preregistered meta-regression line and 95% confidence band. (B) Hedges’ *g* per cell (exploratory). Point size is proportional to precision. The standardised effect rises with extremity, while the proportional index does not change detectably. ## Model adequacy (H3) statistics with each model’s predictive interval. M1 predicts positive curvature and is contradicted by the negative observed curvature. M2 predicts no curvature and is contradicted as well. M3 and M4 predict negative curvature and contain the observed *g* in their intervals, but they predict stronger relative curvature than observed (their intervals for ρ lie below -0.14) and a clearly negative across-cell slope, which the data do not show. Under the preregistered survival rule, which requires both the within-item curvature and the across-cell slope to fall inside a model’s intervals, only M1R survived. It did so because its predictive intervals were wide enough to contain positive, zero and negative curvature. Table 2: Observed statistics compared with each model’s 95% predictive interval. Survival is decided by the shape criteria (curvature and across-cell slope); level criteria are reported for completeness. Observed values: *g* = -0.041, ρ = -0.13, *d* = 0.050, *b* = 0.307, weighted mean log anchoring index = 0.241. ## Robustness The within-item result held in the preregistered robustness analyses that retained the random-anchor data. Median regression without the gross-error rule gave *g* = -0.059, \[-0.075, -0.041\]. Replacing the curvature term by separate slopes for near and far anchors showed that the slope for anchors more than one log unit from the true value was 0.21 lower than the slope near the true value, \[-0.28, -0.13\]. Without Bahník (2021) the estimate was similar but very imprecise, *g* = -0.045, \[-0.36, 0.27\]. The across-cell slope stayed positive and imprecise in most checks: with design covariates, *d* = 0.044, \[-0.021, 0.108\]; with the largest anchor distance as the extremity measure, 0.035, \[-0.009, 0.079\]; with the log ratio of the anchors, 0.017, \[-0.014, 0.049\]. Without Weber et al. (2021), whose item coding was questioned in a later correction, the slope was 0.065, \[0.006, 0.124\], the only check in which the interval excluded zero. The raw-scale anchoring index, which the preregistration designated as descriptive because a constant log-scale weight does not imply a constant raw-scale index, gave -0.008, \[-0.077, 0.062\]. ## Exploratory analyses The following analyses were not preregistered. *Both sides of the true value.* The curvature was negative both for anchors below the true value, *g* = -0.037, \[-0.048, -0.027\], and for anchors above it, *g* = -0.054, \[-0.091, -0.017\]. *Item by item.* In each of the 15 cells with at least 20 anchors both within and beyond one log unit of the true value, the slope for far anchors was lower than the slope for near anchors (median difference -0.23). *Standardised effect sizes.* Across cells, Hedges’ *g* rose with extremity by 0.40 per log unit, \[0.24, 0.55\] (Figure 3, panel B), in line with Röseler & Schütz (2022). The same cells therefore show a rising standardised effect and no detectable change in proportional pull. *Extremity relative to response spread.* The across-cell extremity measure ignores how uncertain people are about each quantity. When we divided extremity by the spread of log estimates within each anchor condition (a measure that is itself affected by anchoring), the slope turned negative, *d* = -0.023, \[-0.037, -0.010\]. This is consistent with original authors having placed anchors further from the truth for quantities that people know less well. *Relaxed calibration.* To check whether the model failures stem from the calibration to Jacowitz and Kahneman’s index, we drew 300 parameter sets per model from wide ranges without calibration and simulated each on the OpAQ designs. No parameter set of any model reproduced the observed *b*, *g*, *d* and mean index jointly (all four inside their observed 95% confidence intervals). Within-item *b* and *g* together were reproduced by 24 of 300 M4 draws, 9 M1R draws and 7 M3 draws, and by no M1 or M2 draw; the across-cell *d* and mean index together were reproduced by 37 M2 draws and 11 M1 draws, and by no M3 or M4 draw. ## Sensitivity analyses These analyses were added after a code review and were not preregistered. *Calibration scale.* The preregistered calibration compared the models’ log-scale anchoring index with Jacowitz and Kahneman’s value of about .49, which they computed on the raw scale. Recalibrating every model to a raw-scale index accepted largely the same parameter values (M1: 22 of 24; M1R: 52 of 56; M2: 28 of 30; M3: 10 of 11; M4: 244 of 250 of the originally accepted grid points were also accepted), and new predictions from the recalibrated models led to the same conclusion: only M1R survived the shape criteria. *Dependence on single studies (H1).* Leaving out any one of the three smaller studies left the curvature negative with confidence intervals excluding zero (*g* from -0.043 to -0.038). Adding study-level random effects gave *g* = -0.041, \[-0.058, -0.024\]. The single fixed-anchor item with 20 anchor levels \[Imhoff and Barker, 2022, unpublished data\] showed a negative curvature on its own, *g* = -0.089, \[-0.148, -0.031\]. *Influence and clustering (H2).* The across-cell slope was not robust. With study-clustered robust standard errors, *d* = 0.050, \[-0.048, 0.148\]. The ten most precise cells carried 61% of the inverse-variance weight; without them, *d* = 0.033, \[-0.032, 0.099\]. Leaving out one study at a time gave slopes between 0.026 and 0.070. # Discussion Within items, anchors lost proportional pull as they moved away from the true value. Near the truth, the local elasticity was 0.31; for anchors a factor of 2.7 from the truth it was 0.23, and for anchors a factor of 7.4 away, 0.14. The decline appeared on both sides of the true value, in every item with enough near and far anchors, and in the one fixed-anchor item with many anchor levels. Across two-anchor studies, where authors chose one anchor pair per item, the anchoring index showed no detectable decline, and its point estimate leaned the other way. ## What the within-item result rules out The negative curvature contradicts two simple accounts. Anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of steps predicts that far anchors keep more of their distance, because a bounded number of bounded steps cannot correct a large gap; the data show the reverse. Constant-weight integration, the simplest version of the anchor integration model, predicts no change in proportional pull; it too is contradicted. The accounts that predict a decline share one feature: the anchor’s influence is limited by how plausible it is. This holds for adjustment that stops at the edge of the plausible range (Epley & Gilovich, 2006), for integration that discounts implausible anchors (Turner & Schley, 2016; Wegener et al., 2001), and for a resource-rational agent who invests more adjustments when the anchor is far off (Lieder et al., 2017). The result fits the earlier two-level experiments in which implausible anchors had proportionally smaller effects (Chapman & Johnson, 1994; Mussweiler & Strack, 2001; Wegener et al., 2001) and the distance-decaying anchoring weight of Barrera-Lemarchand et al. (2024), now shown with open-ended quantities and anchors varied within items. The decline was smaller than M3 and M4 predicted. Their relative curvature intervals lay below the observed value, which means that far anchors still pulled estimates more than a hard plausibility boundary or a steep plausibility discount allows. A mixture in which the weight of an anchor falls gradually but does not vanish could describe this. The data do not identify such a model, and we did not test one. ## The across-cell pattern The across-cell analysis did not reproduce the within-item decline, and no model with a single parameter set reproduced both patterns. Two explanations are plausible, and our data cannot fully separate them. First, extremity measured against the true value is not extremity measured against people’s uncertainty. Researchers tend to place anchors further from the truth for quantities that people know poorly. An anchor ten times the true population of a city may be less implausible than an anchor twice the height of a familiar building. When we scaled extremity by the spread of estimates, the across-cell slope turned negative, as the within-item analysis and the plausibility accounts predict. Because that spread is itself affected by anchoring, this analysis is suggestive only. Second, the two sets differ in anchor type: the within-item set is mostly random anchors, and the across-cell set only fixed or relevant anchors. The models make the same shape predictions for both, but it is possible that informative anchors lose less pull with extremity than anchors people know to be random. The fixed-anchor stratum of the within-item set pointed in the same direction as the random-anchor stratum but was too small for the preregistered test, and only one fixed-anchor item had enough anchor levels to show the decline on its own. The divergence also bears on how moderator analyses of anchoring should be read. In the same cells, the standardised effect rose with extremity while the proportional index did not change detectably. Meta-analytic findings that larger anchor distances produce larger standardised effects (Röseler & Schütz, 2022) therefore say little about whether extreme anchors are more influential per unit of distance. Tests of anchoring theories need a proportional outcome and variation in extremity that the researcher controls. ## Limitations The primary evidence rests largely on one study. Thirteen of the 20 within-item cells, and 83% of the within-item estimates, come from Bahník (2021), in which participants compared 13 random anchors with 13 different lengths and heights. Without this study the within-item curvature had the same sign but a confidence interval too wide to be informative. The random anchors also differ from the fixed anchors that dominate applied settings. The preregistered test of the fixed-anchor stratum was not informative; in an exploratory analysis, the one fixed-anchor item with 20 anchor levels showed the same decline, but it is a single item. A direct test of the extremity function for informative anchors needs experiments that present many anchor levels for many items. Second, extremity was measured relative to the true value, not relative to each participant’s belief. Where people systematically over- or underestimate a quantity, the anchor’s distance from their belief differs from its distance from the truth. The simulations included item-level bias to account for this, and the curvature was negative on both sides of the true value. However, a study that elicits unanchored estimates or plausible ranges from the same participants would give a cleaner measure. Third, the models were specified on the log scale and calibrated to a single external benchmark. The shape predictions of M1, M2, M3 and M4 follow from their structure and held across all calibrated parameter values, but the level predictions depend on the calibration, and the resource-rational model’s predictions depend strongly on its time cost and on how uncertain people are. That this model survived our tests reflects the width of its predictions more than a close fit. Formal tests of resource-rational anchoring need independent measures of the time cost and of people’s uncertainty. Fourth, OpAQ harmonises data from many studies, and harmonisation can introduce errors. We found one item whose responses were recorded in different units from its anchors and true value, and a later correction questioned the item coding of another study. Our rules removed the first; excluding the second made the across-cell slope positive and significant. We used only positive ratio-scale quantities with open response scales, so the results do not speak to dates, percentages, bounded scales or preferences. ## Conclusion Within the same questions, extreme anchors pulled estimates by a smaller share of their distance than moderate anchors. This contradicts anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of steps and constant-weight integration, and supports accounts in which an anchor’s influence is limited by its plausibility, although the decline was weaker than simple plausibility models predict. Across studies with researcher-chosen anchors, the pattern was not visible, which suggests that comparisons across items confound anchor extremity with how well people know the quantity. For anyone choosing an anchor, the within-item evidence implies diminishing returns to extremity. For researchers, it implies that the extremity function should be estimated within items and with proportional measures. # Declarations

First, a code review found that the observed mean anchoring index in the H3 level check was computed with a different estimator from the simulated one; we replaced it with the same inverse-variance weighted mean. This affects only level criteria, which do not decide model survival. Second, the preregistration described one M1R parameter incorrectly; the code, and therefore the predictions, were correct. Third, we made code changes that altered no reported number. Fourth, we clarified that the relative-curvature interval uses a normal critical value. One cell was removed by the preregistered gross-error rule because its participants answered in millions while its anchors and true value were raw counts. All analyses labelled exploratory or sensitivity were added after the preregistration. # Results After exclusions the within-item analysis included 7,949 estimates in 20 cells (3 estimates were missing or non-positive; no gross errors). The across-cell analysis included 128 cells and 22,533 estimates; 627 estimates were missing or non-positive and 987 were removed as gross errors, 870 of them from the cell with the unit mismatch. ## Within items, the proportional pull falls with extremity (H1) Anchoring was clearly present in the within-item set: the average elasticity was *b* = 0.307, 95% CI \[0.249, 0.365\], so doubling the anchor raised estimates by about 24% near the true value. The curvature was negative, *g* = -0.041, \[-0.058, -0.023\], *t*(9.1) = -5.22, *p* \< .001, with a relative curvature of ρ = -0.13, \[-0.18, -0.09\]. By the preregistered rule, the elasticity *falls* with extremity. At the true value an anchor carried about 31% of its log distance into the estimate. The fitted local elasticity *b* + 2*g*\|*x*\| was 0.23 for anchors one log unit (a factor of 2.7) from the true value and 0.14 for anchors two log units (a factor of 7.4) away, about half its value at the true value. Figure 2 shows the binned observed estimates and the fitted curves for each cell. In the random-anchor stratum the result was the same: *b* = 0.265, \[0.215, 0.316\], and *g* = -0.034, \[-0.044, -0.023\], again classified as falling. In the fixed-anchor stratum the point estimates were similar (*b* = 0.618, *g* = -0.085, \[-0.143, -0.027\]), but with only five cells the confidence interval for *b* spanned \[-0.31, 1.55\], so the gate failed and the shape was not testable there under the preregistered rules. ![](figures/fig2_within_item.png) Figure 2: Observed within-item response functions. Points are median log estimates in 0.5-unit bins of the log anchor (bins with at least 10 estimates), connected within each item. Blue curves are the fitted H1 model for each item (fixed plus item-level random effects), drawn over the central 95% of that item’s anchors. The dashed line marks estimates equal to the anchor. Axes differ between panels. ## Across cells, the anchoring index shows no clear trend (H2) Anchoring was present across cells: the mean log anchoring index was 0.42, \[0.35, 0.48\]. The slope of the index on extremity was *d* = 0.050, \[-0.013, 0.113\]. This interval includes zero but is not narrow enough to establish equivalence within ±0.03, so the result is inconclusive under the preregistered rule (Figure 3, panel A). The point estimate is positive, the opposite sign to the within-item curvature. ![](figures/fig3_across_cells.png) Figure 3: Across-cell relation between anchor extremity and anchor influence. (A) Log anchoring index per cell with the preregistered meta-regression line and 95% confidence band. (B) Hedges’ *g* per cell (exploratory). Point size is proportional to precision. The standardised effect rises with extremity, while the proportional index does not change detectably. ## Model adequacy (H3) statistics with each model’s predictive interval. M1 predicts positive curvature and is contradicted by the negative observed curvature. M2 predicts no curvature and is contradicted as well. M3 and M4 predict negative curvature and contain the observed *g* in their intervals, but they predict stronger relative curvature than observed (their intervals for ρ lie below -0.14) and a clearly negative across-cell slope, which the data do not show. Under the preregistered survival rule, which requires both the within-item curvature and the across-cell slope to fall inside a model’s intervals, only M1R survived. It did so because its predictive intervals were wide enough to contain positive, zero and negative curvature. Table 2: Observed statistics compared with each model’s 95% predictive interval. Survival is decided by the shape criteria (curvature and across-cell slope); level criteria are reported for completeness. Observed values: *g* = -0.041, ρ = -0.13, *d* = 0.050, *b* = 0.307, weighted mean log anchoring index = 0.241. ## Robustness The within-item result held in the preregistered robustness analyses that retained the random-anchor data. Median regression without the gross-error rule gave *g* = -0.059, \[-0.075, -0.041\]. Replacing the curvature term by separate slopes for near and far anchors showed that the slope for anchors more than one log unit from the true value was 0.21 lower than the slope near the true value, \[-0.28, -0.13\]. content.content: #!/usr/bin/env bash # Build refs.bib from dois.txt (key DOI per line) via doi.org content negotiation, and print # Crossref/DataCite title and first author for each entry so every reference can be checked. # An optional third column overrides the year (Crossref gives the online-first year, which can # differ from the year of the journal volume). set -euo pipefail cd "$(dirname "$0")" : > refs.bib while read -r key doi year; do [ -z "$key" ] && continue bib=$(curl -sL -H "Accept: application/x-bibtex; charset=utf-8" "https://doi.org/$doi") if ! grep -q "^ *@" <<<"$bib"; then echo "FAILED $key $doi" >&2; continue; fi # replace the generated citation key with ours bib=$(sed -E "1s/^[[:space:]]*@([a-zA-Z]+)\{[^,]*,/@\1{$key,/" <<<"$bib") [ -n "${year:-}" ] && bib=$(sed -E "s/year=\{[0-9]{4}\}/year={$year}/" <<<"$bib") printf '%s\n\n' "$bib" >> refs.bib title=$(grep -m1 -i "title *=" <<<"$bib" | sed -E 's/.*title *= *\{(.*)\},?/\1/' | cut -c1-90) echo "$key | $doi | $title" done < dois.txt sed -i '' 's|lmerTest|lmerTest|' refs.bib @article{lieder2018a @article{lee2022 1 lieder2018a, title={The anchori 2 year={2018} 3 year={2022}

input.prompt:
Task: check that every cited source in a manuscript supports the specific claim it is cited for.

Manuscript source: ~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/manuscript/manuscript.qmd (Quarto; citations are [@key] or @key; keys resolve in manuscript/refs.bib and manuscript/refs_manual.bib, which were built from Crossref/DataCite and are verified to exist — do NOT re-check existence, check SUPPORT). A rendered plain version is at manuscript/scratch_manuscript.md.

Procedure:
1. Extract every sentence that contains a citation. For each (sentence, key) pair, state the specific claim the citation is supposed to support.
2. Obtain the source text. Use the `download-paper` skill (by DOI) and/or the `check-claim` skill; open-access copies, PsyArXiv, PMC etc. are fine. Several full texts are already on disk in /tmp/jdmsim/ (e.g. hanging.txt = Röseler & Schütz 2022 meta-analysis; opaq.txt = OpAQ data paper; scratch_lieder_a.txt / scratch_lieder_5x2em.pdf = Lieder et al. 2018a preprint; scratch_nov_sw_turner.pdf = Turner & Schley 2016; scratch_nov_sw_v2.pdf = Schley & Weingarten; scratch_nov_classic_findings.md has page-referenced notes on Chapman & Johnson 1994, Strack & Mussweiler 1997, Mussweiler & Strack 2001, Wegener et al. 2001, Northcraft & Neale 1987 etc.). Use them where relevant, but prefer checking the actual text.
3. For each pair give a verdict: SUPPORTED / PARTLY (explain what is off) / NOT SUPPORTED / COULD NOT CHECK (say why), with the exact supporting quote or page where possible. Pay special attention to: direct quotes (must be verbatim — check "implausibly extreme anchors had a proportionally smaller effect than anchors close to the expected value" in Chapman & Johnson 1994, and "to formalize the relationship between anchor distance and adjustment strength" in Röseler & Schütz 2022); numbers (g = 0.69 from 90 studies; 30 percentage questions in Barrera-Lemarchand et al.); characterisations of what Lieder et al. 2018a derived (Eq. 2, Eq. 4), what Turner & Schley 2016 assumed ("for simplicity", inverted U, one anchor per item); what Mussweiler & Strack 1999 and Strack & Mussweiler 1997 claim; Wegener et al. 2001 ("very extreme anchors had smaller effects", plausibility); Schley & Weingarten 2026 (binary extremity flag, no difference); Furnham & Boo 2011, Englich et al. 2006, Northcraft & Neale 1987 (experts, property valuation, criminal sentencing); Tversky & Kahneman 1974 (UN African countries, random number — note: in T&K the number came from a wheel of fortune); Bahník 2021 (13 random anchors 1-1000, lengths and heights — the manuscript says so); Yoon et al. 2021; Lakens 2017 (equivalence bounds justification); van den Akker et al. 2021 (template).
4. Write the full table to ~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/manuscript/citation_check.md (columns: # | location (section) | key | claim | verdict | evidence/quote | suggested fix). Do not edit the manuscript itself.
5. Final message: a summary listing every PARTLY / NOT SUPPORTED / COULD NOT CHECK item with the suggested fix.

No paper computes the proportional anchoring index item by item on OpAQ, relates it to anchor extremity, and compares it against simulated predictions from process models.

- **Schley & Weingarten (Management Science, doi 10.1287/mnsc.2023.03238):** I read the Dec 2025 preprint version (teq7k_v2), which Crossref marks as the preprint of the journal article. I did not read the published text itself.
  - **Data:** 1,280 high-vs-low effect sizes from 482 studies. OpAQ is not used or cited.
  - **Extremity:** a yes/no flag for anchors the original authors called "extreme" (49 effect sizes). The effect was −0.02 [−0.20, 0.16] (Table 5, p. 28), with no test for a curved relationship.
  - **Metric:** Hedges g only, no anchoring index. Theories are compared qualitatively (Table 1, p. 7), with no model fitting.
- **Schley & Weingarten, Jan 2025 version (SSRN 5114456):** adds a preregistered study with 1,968 participants and 8 items. Anchors were set at calibration percentiles (3rd/97th, 15th/85th, 30th/70th), and estimates were standardized within each item.
  - More extreme anchors gave larger effects. The linear term is about +0.74, which I read off their Figure 4 (p. 55); the text gives no number.
  - This does not test proportional adjustment, because a constant anchoring index would also produce a larger gap when the anchors are further apart.
  - This study is not in the Dec 2025 preprint or, judging by the abstract, the journal version.
- **Young et al. 2026:** item-as-anchor studies with g = 0.25. No OpAQ, no process models, no extremity analysis. Closeness 0.
- **Closest prior work: Röseler & Schütz 2022 (PsyArXiv preprint, doi 10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn):** uses OpAQ (386 items) and finds larger Hedges g as the anchor moves further from the true value (b = 0.040, p < .001, Table 2, p. 21). They explicitly call for a unitless relative-adjustment measure (p. 34), which is the gap the planned study fills. Closeness 2.
- **Lieder et al. 2018 and Turner & Schley 2016:** neither derived or tested how the anchoring index changes with extremity.
  - Lieder fitted the index for 15 Jacowitz & Kahneman items: model 53.22% vs observed 48.48%, r(13) = 0.62.
  - Turner & Schley build an inverted-U effect of extremity into their model as an assumption.

**Not verified:**
- The published Management Science text and the online appendices.
- Where Röseler & Schütz show the curved relationship they describe (it is not in the PDF text).
- The full texts of papers marked "abstract only" in the report.
- The published page numbers of the two Lieder papers; I cited preprint pages.

**Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995**, *PSPB* 21:1161–1166, [10.1177/01461672952111004](https://doi.org/10.1177/01461672952111004):
- I could not get the full text (SAGE paywall). The only number I have is SECONDARY: a mean empirical AI of **48.48% across 15 items**, with anchors at the 15th and 85th percentiles. This comes from Lieder et al. 2018 (manuscript p.17).

### Per paper

- **Chapman & Johnson 1994**, *JBDM* 7:223–242, [10.1002/bdm.3960070402](https://doi.org/10.1002/bdm.3960070402). Figures only, read off to about ±1; the text is UNVERIFIED.
  - Experiment 1 (Exhibit 3, p.229): anchors of 0.1, 0.7, 1.3 and 1.9 × the lottery's expected value gave prices of about 74, 106.5, 127 and 127.5.
  - Local slopes were 0.39, 0.25 and 0.006. The AI was 0.25 for the moderate pair and 0.22 for the extreme pair.
  - The curve saturates at the high end only.
  - Exhibit 4 (p.230): when the extreme anchors fall far outside the lottery's payoff range, the curve is an inverted U (about 84, 104, 122, 111).
- **Strack & Mussweiler 1997**, *JPSP* 73:437–446, [10.1037/0022-3514.73.3.437](https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.73.3.437).
  - Table 6 (p.443), in z-scores: the high−low difference was 0.17 SD for plausible anchors (about 1 SD from the calibration mean) and 0.42 SD for implausible anchors (more than 10 SD away).
  - So the raw effect was about 2.5× larger across an anchor gap more than 10× wider, which means a much smaller AI.
  - The per-item Appendix (p.446) gives median AIs of 0.25 vs 0.06, but several rows look like typographical errors. Do not rely on them.
- **Mussweiler & Strack 2001**, *Social Cognition* 19:145–160, [10.1521/soco.19.2.145.20705](https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.19.2.145.20705).
  - Antarctic temperature: anchors −43, −17, 700, 900 gave means −41.1, −24.8, −23.3, −24.4. The AI was 0.63 for the plausible pair and −0.006 for the implausible pair.
  - Gandhi's age: anchors 61, 86, 214, 271 gave means 62.9, 70.4, 75.3, 72.9. The AI was 0.30 for the plausible pair and −0.04 for the implausible pair.
  - The raw shift plateaus at the plausibility boundary, so the AI falls roughly as 1/distance beyond it.
- **Wegener et al. 2001**, *JESP* 37:62–69, [10.1006/jesp.2000.1431](https://doi.org/10.1006/jesp.2000.1431).

  - The raw effect is an inverted U. The implied AI for extreme vs moderate anchors is about 0.22 of the moderate value in 1A and about 0.0015 in 1B. These ratios are illustrative only.
- **Wegener et al. 2010**, [10.1016/j.jcps.2009.12.003](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcps.2009.12.003): no numbers of its own. It cites unpublished 3-level data showing an inverted U whose downturn comes earlier for high-knowledge people (UNVERIFIED).
- **Northcraft & Neale 1987**, *OBHDP* 39:84–97, [10.1016/0749-5978(87)90046-x](https://doi.org/10.1016/0749-5978(87)90046-x).
  - Four listing-price anchors at ±4% and ±12% of the true value.
  - Experiment 1, amateurs: local slopes 0.65, 0.50, 0.30; AI 0.50 for the moderate pair and 0.48 for the extreme pair.
  - Experts: AI 0.41. Experiment 2 data are noisy.
- **Russo & Schoemaker 1989** (SECONDARY; read off Lieder et al.'s Fig. 10): anchors 500–1300 for the year Attila was defeated (true 451) gave means of about 630 to 990. The slope is about 0.45 and linear.
- **Lieder et al. 2018**, [10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8).
  - With a fixed number of adjustments (Eq. 4), the AI is constant across extremity.
  - With the optimal number of adjustments (Fig. 4b), the AI falls with distance measured in units of uncertainty. These are approximate figure readings.
  - Their Russo & Schoemaker simulation predicts a slope of about 0.95 against the observed 0.45.
- **Turner & Schley 2016**, [10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003): the model assumes an inverted U by construction (pp.23–24) and can also produce an asymptote. It has no extremity data.
- **Hardt & Pohl 2003**, [10.1080/09658210244000504](https://doi.org/10.1080/09658210244000504): hindsight-bias paradigm, with distance scaled to each person's own range of plausible values.
  - The raw shift is an inverted U. The shift divided by distance falls from about 0.12–0.38 to 0.03–0.06.
  - Abstract seen; curve SECONDARY via Wilson et al. 2021, CogSci proceedings.
- **Bystranowski et al. 2021**, [10.1037/lhb0000438](https://doi.org/10.1037/lhb0000438): uses between-study anchor magnitude, not extremity relative to the truth.
  - Control-vs-anchor designs (Table 4, p.12): d = .43, .59, .19 for low, medium and high anchor values.
  - High-vs-low designs (Table 5, p.13): d = .82, 1.00, .77.
  - The continuous slopes were negative but not significant.
- **Townson 2019**, dissertation, [10.25335/p9dm-7a29](https://doi.org/10.25335/p9dm-7a29) (verified via DataCite, not Crossref). Abstract only: extremity "slightly weaken[s]" the effect. The size of that effect is UNVERIFIED.
- **Harris et al. 2019**, [10.1037/xge0000644](https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000644).
  - Temperature AI rose from 0.17 to 0.22 when the anchor gap widened. It is 0.25 instead of 0.17 under the manuscript's other description of the Exp 1 anchors.
  - Car-price AI fell from 0.37 to 0.26.
- **Simmons et al. 2010**, [10.1037/a0021540](https://doi.org/10.1037/a0021540): a single anchor per item, so no AI. Implausible anchors left estimates further from the truth on 6 of 8 items (note 2).
- **Schultze et al. 2015**, [10.1017/s1930297500003922](https://doi.org/10.1017/s1930297500003922): an advice-taking analogue. The weight given to advice is an inverted U, modelled as a linear term plus a log term, peaking at 63.84% advice distance. The absolute shift keeps rising with distance.
- **Abstract only:**
  - Marti & Wissler 2000, [10.1037/1076-898x.6.2.91](https://doi.org/10.1037/1076-898x.6.2.91): awards fell at the most extreme request. Bystranowski et al. cite this paper as showing no decline.
  - Thorsteinson 2011, [10.1111/j.1559-1816.2011.00779.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1559-1816.2011.00779.x).
  - Lee et al. 2022 (10.19066/cogsci.2022.33.1.004; resolves via doi.org but is not in Crossref): extreme anchors produced smaller effects than plausible ones.
- **Not obtained (UNVERIFIED):**
  - Mussweiler & Strack 2000, [10.1006/jesp.1999.1414](https://doi.org/10.1006/jesp.1999.1414).
  - Thorsteinson et al. 2008, [10.1016/j.obhdp.2008.01.003](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obhdp.2008.01.003).
  - LeBoeuf & Shafir 2006: the correct DOI is [10.1002/bdm.535](https://doi.org/10.1002/bdm.535), not bdm.536.
  - Mussweiler 2001, [10.1002/ejsp.52](https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsp.52).
  - Chapman & Bornstein 1996: the download tool returned the wrong paper, which I discarded.

### Synthesis

- **Within the plausible range, the AI is roughly flat at about 0.25–0.6.** Estimates rise roughly linearly with the anchor.
- **At and beyond the plausibility boundary, the raw shift plateaus or declines, so the AI falls roughly as 1/distance.** The Lieder model with optimal adjustment predicts the same falling AI.
- **Counter-cases:**
  - Strack & Mussweiler 1997: the raw effect was larger for implausible anchors.
  - Chapman & Johnson Experiment 2: estimates kept rising across a 26-fold anchor range.
  - Harris temperature item: the AI rose as the anchor gap widened.
  - High/low asymmetry: Chapman & Johnson saturate at the high end only.
- **Gap:** no study reports the AI at three or more levels spanning the plausibility boundary on many items, with item-level means and a calibration SD. No study fits the four candidate models to item-level curves. The existing meta-analyses code extremity as raw anchor magnitude, not relative to the truth or to uncertainty.</result>

  - The per-item Appendix (p.446) gives median AIs of 0.25 vs 0.06, but several rows look like typographical errors. Do not rely on them.
- **Mussweiler & Strack 2001**, *Social Cognition* 19:145–160, [10.1521/soco.19.2.145.20705](https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.19.2.145.20705).

- **Northcraft & Neale 1987**, *OBHDP* 39:84–97, [10.1016/0749-5978(87)90046-x](https://doi.org/10.1016/0749-5978(87)90046-x).
  - Four listing-price anchors at ±4% and ±12% of the true value.
  - Experiment 1, amateurs: local slopes 0.65, 0.50, 0.30; AI 0.50 for the moderate pair and 0.48 for the extreme pair.
  - Experts: AI 0.41. Experiment 2 data are noisy.
- **Russo & Schoemaker 1989** (SECONDARY; read off Lieder et al.'s Fig. 10): anchors 500–1300 for the year Attila was defeated (true 451) gave means of about 630 to 990. The slope is about 0.45 and linear.
