  - With a fixed number of adjustments (Eq. 4), the AI is constant across extremity.
  - With the optimal number of adjustments (Fig. 4b), the AI falls with distance measured in units of uncertainty. These are approximate figure readings.
  - Their Russo & Schoemaker simulation predicts a slope of about 0.95 against the observed 0.45.
- **Turner & Schley 2016**, [10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003): the model assumes an inverted U by construction (pp.23–24) and can also produce an asymptote. It has no extremity data.
- **Hardt & Pohl 2003**, [10.1080/09658210244000504](https://doi.org/10.1080/09658210244000504): hindsight-bias paradigm, with distance scaled to each person's own range of plausible values.
  - The raw shift is an inverted U. The shift divided by distance falls from about 0.12–0.38 to 0.03–0.06.
  - Abstract seen; curve SECONDARY via Wilson et al. 2021, CogSci proceedings.
- **Bystranowski et al. 2021**, [10.1037/lhb0000438](https://doi.org/10.1037/lhb0000438): uses between-study anchor magnitude, not extremity relative to the truth.
  - Control-vs-anchor designs (Table 4, p.12): d = .43, .59, .19 for low, medium and high anchor values.
  - High-vs-low designs (Table 5, p.13): d = .82, 1.00, .77.
  - The continuous slopes were negative but not significant.
- **Townson 2019**, dissertation, [10.25335/p9dm-7a29](https://doi.org/10.25335/p9dm-7a29) (verified via DataCite, not Crossref). Abstract only: extremity "slightly weaken[s]" the effect. The size of that effect is UNVERIFIED.
- **Harris et al. 2019**, [10.1037/xge0000644](https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000644).
  - Temperature AI rose from 0.17 to 0.22 when the anchor gap widened. It is 0.25 instead of 0.17 under the manuscript's other description of the Exp 1 anchors.
  - Car-price AI fell from 0.37 to 0.26.
- **Simmons et al. 2010**, [10.1037/a0021540](https://doi.org/10.1037/a0021540): a single anchor per item, so no AI. Implausible anchors left estimates further from the truth on 6 of 8 items (note 2).
- **Schultze et al. 2015**, [10.1017/s1930297500003922](https://doi.org/10.1017/s1930297500003922): an advice-taking analogue. The weight given to advice is an inverted U, modelled as a linear term plus a log term, peaking at 63.84% advice distance. The absolute shift keeps rising with distance.
- **Abstract only:**
  - Marti & Wissler 2000, [10.1037/1076-898x.6.2.91](https://doi.org/10.1037/1076-898x.6.2.91): awards fell at the most extreme request. Bystranowski et al. cite this paper as showing no decline.
  - Thorsteinson 2011, [10.1111/j.1559-1816.2011.00779.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1559-1816.2011.00779.x).
  - Lee et al. 2022 (10.19066/cogsci.2022.33.1.004; resolves via doi.org but is not in Crossref): extreme anchors produced smaller effects than plausible ones.

  - Mussweiler & Strack 2000, [10.1006/jesp.1999.1414](https://doi.org/10.1006/jesp.1999.1414).
  - Thorsteinson et al. 2008, [10.1016/j.obhdp.2008.01.003](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obhdp.2008.01.003).
  - LeBoeuf & Shafir 2006: the correct DOI is [10.1002/bdm.535](https://doi.org/10.1002/bdm.535), not bdm.536.
  - Mussweiler 2001, [10.1002/ejsp.52](https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsp.52).
  - Chapman & Bornstein 1996: the download tool returned the wrong paper, which I discarded.

### Synthesis

- **Within the plausible range, the AI is roughly flat at about 0.25–0.6.** Estimates rise roughly linearly with the anchor.
- **At and beyond the plausibility boundary, the raw shift plateaus or declines, so the AI falls roughly as 1/distance.** The Lieder model with optimal adjustment predicts the same falling AI.
- **Counter-cases:**
  - Strack & Mussweiler 1997: the raw effect was larger for implausible anchors.
  - Chapman & Johnson Experiment 2: estimates kept rising across a 26-fold anchor range.
  - Harris temperature item: the AI rose as the anchor gap widened.
  - High/low asymmetry: Chapman & Johnson saturate at the high end only.
- **Gap:** no study reports the AI at three or more levels spanning the plausibility boundary on many items, with item-level means and a calibration SD. No study fits the four candidate models to item-level curves. The existing meta-analyses code extremity as raw anchor magnitude, not relative to the truth or to uncertainty.</result>

- **Within the plausible range, the AI is roughly flat at about 0.25–0.6.** Estimates rise roughly linearly with the anchor.

  - Strack & Mussweiler 1997: the raw effect was larger for implausible anchors.
  - Chapman & Johnson Experiment 2: estimates kept rising across a 26-fold anchor range.
  - Harris temperature item: the AI rose as the anchor gap widened.
  - High/low asymmetry: Chapman & Johnson saturate at the high end only.
- **Gap:** no study reports the AI at three or more levels spanning the plausibility boundary on many items, with item-level means and a calibration SD. No study fits the four candidate models to item-level curves. The existing meta-analyses code extremity as raw anchor magnitude, not relative to the truth or to uncertainty.</result>

# AI disclosure

## Summary

This study was conceived, designed, preregistered, coded, analysed, written and reviewed by AI systems. The human author, Lukas Wallrich, set the task and its constraints in a single instruction and did not intervene in the work that followed. He is accountable for the content under the policies of the target journal. The AI's role is disclosed here in full so that readers and editors can judge the work with that knowledge.

## What the human author did

- On 27 September 2026, gave one instruction: produce a complete, novel judgement-and-decision-making paper without collecting new data, working autonomously, recording decisions, preregistering before analysis, reviewing with other AI systems, and not submitting anything or contacting anyone.
- Provided the working environment (Claude Code with access to R, Quarto, the web, OpenAlex and Crossref, and the codex and agy command-line tools) and his writing style guide.
- Did not choose the research question, dataset, models, analyses or wording, and did not review the work before this record was written.

Before any submission, the author would need to read and verify the work, take responsibility for every claim, and decide whether to submit. None of that has happened yet.

## What the AI systems did

| System | Version | Access | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude (Anthropic) | Claude Opus 5.5 (model id claude-opus-5-5, 1M-token context), run in Claude Code | Anthropic API / Claude Code | Lead agent. Scoped the literature and datasets (through subagents running the same model), chose the study, wrote the preregistration, the simulation models and all R code, ran all analyses, made the figures, wrote the manuscript, cover letter and all project documents, and responded to reviews. Every decision and its reason is in `decision_log.md`. |
| Claude subagents | Claude Opus 5.5 | Claude Code Agent tool | Parallel literature searches, dataset licence checks, novelty checks, journal-policy extraction, citation-support checks. |
| OpenAI Codex CLI | codex-cli 0.155.1 (default model) | `codex exec`, read-only sandbox | Critique of the study shortlist; review of code and results; manuscript reviews. Outputs in `reviews/`. |
| Google Gemini via Antigravity CLI | Gemini 3.8 Flash (High) | `agy -p`, sandboxed | Critique of the study shortlist; manuscript reviews. Outputs in `reviews/`. |
| coarse-review pipeline | local Claude Code skill running Claude models headlessly | `coarse-review` skill | Full structured peer review of the manuscript. Output in `reviews/`. |

Dates of use: 27-28 September 2026.

## Safeguards

- **Preregistration before data contact.** The preregistration, frozen model predictions and analysis code were committed to git (tag `prereg-v1`, commit a40911b) before any outcome variable was read. The data reader (`R/read_opaq.R`) refuses to load the outcome column until the preregistration is committed. Only design columns were read before that commit; `prereg/preregistration.md` (Q18) lists them.
- **Numbers come from code.** Every number in the manuscript is computed inline from files in `output/`, which `run_all.sh` regenerates from the raw data.
- **References.** The bibliography was built by script from DOIs through doi.org content negotiation (Crossref and DataCite metadata); no reference was typed from memory. A separate agent checked each citation against the source text for support of the claim it is attached to (`manuscript/citation_check.md`).
- **Independent review.** Two non-Anthropic AI systems reviewed the design, code and manuscript; all comments and responses are in `review_log.md`.

## Known risks of AI authorship in this project

- The same model family that wrote the paper also judged which reviewer comments to accept. Rejected comments and the reasons are listed in `review_log.md` so that a human can second-guess them.
- Literature knowledge from model training may be out of date or wrong. Literature claims were therefore checked against retrieved texts, not recalled.
- The AI chose the research question under an instruction to produce a paper. Scoping reports (`scoping/`) and the decision log show the alternatives considered.

## Compliance with the target journal's policy

Judgment and Decision Making applies the Cambridge University Press policy (`scoping/journals/jdm.md`): AI tools may not be listed as authors; AI use in analysis is described in the Methods; AI-generated text is declared in the Acknowledgements; AI-generated figures are declared in their captions; each declaration names the tool and version, the dates, how others can access it, and a full description of the use. The manuscript follows these rules. No AI system is listed as an author.

<result>I found 24 works that cite OpAQ or the meta-analysis. None relates the two-anchor proportional anchoring index (AI) to anchor extremity on OpAQ's human item-level estimates, and none fits process models to them. Only one citer reuses OpAQ's human estimates: the 2024 reliability paper (row 2 below). Two LLM papers reuse OpAQ items only.

**How I searched.** I used OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar (the OpAQ DOI only), Google Scholar "cited by" via SerpAPI, and web searches. Semantic Scholar does not find the meta-analysis by its DOI (10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn), so I used Google Scholar's two clusters for it (14 + 3 citers, all retrieved). The meta-analysis has not been published: I found no journal version in OpenAlex, Crossref or Google Scholar. I opened no data files; reading covered papers, OSF node metadata, wiki text and file names. Page numbers are PDF pages.

## Priority 1: Barrera-Lemarchand et al. 2024, Psych Sci
DOI [10.1177/09567976241252138](https://doi.org/10.1177/09567976241252138). **Classification: CITED-ONLY, own data.**

I read the accepted Word manuscript (49 pp., April 2024; preprint [10.31234/osf.io/wvfm3](https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/wvfm3)). The typeset version was blocked, so page numbers are manuscript pages and I could not check the published wording.

- **OpAQ items or data: not used.**
  - OpAQ is cited only as a reference (MS p. 31). "Röseler et al., 2022" is cited in the text as the source of the "anchoring extremeness effect" (pp. 6, 8, 15).
  - Exp 2 items are 30 Argentina-specific survey percentages (SI Table S4).
  - Barrera-Lemarchand, Navajas and Freira are OpAQ co-authors under the 2024 Correction, so their data are probably in OpAQ.
- **Model (MS p. 8, Eq. 4):** the anchored mean is w·A + (1−w)·μ, where μ is the unanchored crowd mean and w = w₀·e^(−β|A_j − θ|).
  - θ is the true value. β is described as sensitivity to anchor–truth distance, "the anchoring extremeness effect".
  - Simulation values: θ = 324, μ = 250, A_L = 10, A_H = 1000, w₀ = 1, β = 0.0017.
- **Exp 2 design (MS pp. 13–14):**
  - N = 396 recruited online in Argentina (119 in Group 1, 277 in Group 2).
  - 30 general-knowledge percentage questions, split into two sets of 15, bounded 0–100.
  - The anchors were the same for every question: 5% (low) and 95% (high). Low or high was assigned at random per question. The control group gave estimates without anchors.
  - Preregistered: aspredicted RYC_4Y5.
- **Distance:** raw |A_j − θ| in percentage points, not normalised.
  - Because the anchors are fixed, distance varies only through the true value θ. Anchor position was never manipulated.
  - The Fig. 3D caption (MS p. 17) plots each question's weight (low-anchor dots, high-anchor dots) against distance, with a log scale on the weight axis and a linear fit.
- **Anchoring weight:** one-sided, per anchor and per question: w_j = (μ_j − μ)/(A_j − μ), measured against the unanchored mean μ (SI p. 43, Eq. 16).
  - The authors call it "very similar" to the Jacowitz–Kahneman anchoring index (MS p. 15).
  - It is 0 when the anchor has no effect and 1 when the mean equals the anchor.
  - It is **not** the two-anchor AI (high − low)/(A_H − A_L).
- **Main result:** the weight correlates with distance at **r = −0.56, p = 3×10⁻⁶** (MS p. 16).
  - The text gives no n; about 60 points (30 questions × 2 anchors) is my inference, not stated.
  - Supporting pattern: for true values below 50% (17 questions), the low-anchor group's estimates did not differ from the truth (t(16) = 0.95, p = .36, BF₀₁ = 2.7). The mirror pattern held for the 13 questions above 50% (MS pp. 14–15).
- **Model comparison (MS p. 16):** the exponential form fits best, but the margins are small.
  - Against linear: ΔAIC = ΔBIC = 1.9.
  - Against hyperbolic w₀/(1 + β|A − θ|) (their Eq. 7): ΔAIC = ΔBIC = 0.59.
  - One weight per question beats separate low and high weights (ΔAIC = 1.6, ΔBIC = 5.7).

## Priority 2: Mayer & Rebholz 2024 (does not cite OpAQ)
PsyArXiv [10.31234/osf.io/69jwr](https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/69jwr), full text read. No journal version found.

- **Task and design:** random-dot estimation (100–599 dots, 25 anchoring images) in a 2 (expertise) × 2 (anchor relevance) × 2 (anchor extremity) design (p. 11).
  - Extremity: anchors deviate ±35% ("low") or ±70% ("high") from the true value, coded −0.5/0.5 (p. 14).
  - Preregistered: aspredicted GZQ_48M.
- **Outcome:** absolute relative error = |judgment/correct × 100 − 100|, i.e. percent deviation from the truth (p. 14).
- **Results:**

| Experiment | Extremity effect (percentage points) | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Exp 1 | β = 4.88, 95% CI [2.80, 6.97], t(23.79) = 4.60, p < .001 | p. 15 |
| Exp 2 | β = 7.37, 95% CI [4.53, 10.20], t(24.00) = 5.09, p < .001 | p. 21 |

- **Exploratory slope (Exp 1):** relative error on signed anchor deviation, β = 0.15 [0.09, 0.21], t(23.08) = 5.13 (page not pinned; around p. 17).
- **My reading, not the authors':** doubling the anchor's distance (35% → 70%) raises absolute error by only about 5–7 points. That is a pull of roughly 0.14–0.21 per unit of extra distance, i.e. a roughly constant proportional pull. "Stronger anchoring" here is absolute, not proportional.

## Full list of citing works

| # | Work (where found) | Class | Summary |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Correction to OpAQ, JOPD 2024, [10.5334/jopd.92](https://doi.org/10.5334/jopd.92) (OpenAlex, S2, GS) | n/a | Author list only: 10 co-authors were omitted "due to an administrative error" (p. 2). No item, trial or variable changes. |
| 2 | Röseler et al. 2024, Meta-Psychology 8, [10.15626/MP.2022.3236](https://doi.org/10.15626/MP.2022.3236) | **REUSED-OPAQ (human estimates)** | Reliability of person-level scores: 41 studies, N = 9,825 (p. 5). Mean interitem r = .126 (REML .137 [.078, .197]); 0-1 score .131; restricted 0-1 score .164; adjustment .154 (pp. 5–6). The "0-1 score" (estimate − anchor)/(true − anchor) is proportional but per person, and never related to distance (p. 4). One aside says nonlinear models for extreme anchors would be "more precise" (p. 11). |
| 3 | Röseler, Incerti, Rebholz, Seida, Papenmeier, published Meta-Psychology 9 (2025), [10.15626/MP.2024.4137](https://doi.org/10.15626/MP.2024.4137) (Crossref-verified; preprint jztk2) | CITED-ONLY (contributes data) | Formalises insufficient adjustment as a step model of discrete jumps (p. 3). Four studies, N = 898: time effect r = 0.02 [−.045, .086]; anchoring r = 0.191 [−.211, .594], Q(8) = 177.61 (p. 22). Proposes that adjustment can go both ways (p. 22). Data from Studies 1, 2 and 4 are in OpAQ (p. 24). |
| 4 | Mayer & Heck 2025, PBR, [10.3758/s13423-024-02619-9](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-024-02619-9) | CITED-ONLY (meta-analysis) | Computational model of sequential collaboration. Anchoring term A = E_i·(y_prev − T): a fixed fraction of the anchor–truth gap, so the AI does not change with distance (p. 1147, Eq. 9). No OpAQ data. |
| 5 | Fischer, Mayer, Kimmerle 2026, JBDM, [10.1002/bdm.70063](https://doi.org/10.1002/bdm.70063) | CITED-ONLY | Judgment invariance in sequential collaboration. Cites the meta-analysis for "informative anchors induce a higher anchoring effect". |
| 6 | Onuki & Ueda 2025, Commun Psychol, [10.1038/s44271-025-00276-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44271-025-00276-9) | CITED-ONLY (OpAQ co-authors) | Range nudges. The meta-analysis's g = 0.59 ("speed") and g = 0.94 ("duration") set the power analyses (pp. 2–5). |
| 7 | Barrera-Lemarchand et al. 2024 | CITED-ONLY | See Priority 1. |
| 8 | Reimer et al. 2024, Sustainability, [10.3390/su16062540](https://doi.org/10.3390/su16062540) | CITED-ONLY | Thermostat scales: current temperature, midpoint and range affect setpoints (abstract). The meta-analysis is a general citation. |
| 9 | Navarre, Didierjean, Thomas 2024, Année psychologique, [10.3917/anpsy1.244.0591](https://doi.org/10.3917/anpsy1.244.0591) | CITED-ONLY (review) | Claims the anchor/effect relation is nonlinear beyond the plausible range, **for high anchors only**; low anchors stay linear (p. 597, again p. 602). Cites Chapman & Johnson 1994, Thorsteinson 2011 and the reliability paper (row 2), which does not show this. |
| 10 | Young, Speekenbrink et al. 2026, Cogn Psychol, [10.1016/j.cogpsych.2026.101796](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2026.101796) | CITED-ONLY | Cites the meta-analysis only (pp. 1, 18). No OpAQ data. |
| 11 | Stöcker 2024 thesis, [10.20378/irb-96573](https://doi.org/10.20378/irb-96573) | CITED-ONLY | Advice taking; the meta-analysis cited on p. 23. |
| 12 | Shiddieqi et al. 2024, Scientax, [10.52869/st.v5i2.667](https://doi.org/10.52869/st.v5i2.667) | CITED-ONLY | Tax compliance; the meta-analysis is in the reference list only. |
| 13 | Owusu, Wiegreffe, Feldman 2026, arXiv [2606.12818](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.12818) (S2) | **REUSED-OPAQ (items only)** | 100 OpAQ questions turned into multiple-choice items to locate anchoring pathways inside LLMs (pp. 1, 3). No extremity analysis. |
| 14 | Owusu & Feldman 2026, ACL, [10.18653/v1/2026.acl-short.16](https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2026.acl-short.16) (S2) | **REUSED-OPAQ (items only)** | 50 OpAQ items, replicated on 99 (1,188 observations). Anchoring falls with model confidence, β ≈ −0.05, p < .001 (pp. 2–3). |
| 15 | Vaccaro 2026, SSRN, [10.2139/ssrn.6732238](https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6732238) (S2) | CITED-ONLY | LLM specification curve over 2,430 configurations; anchor distance is one factor. OpAQ cited for a "human range 0.3–0.6" (pp. 13–14). |
| 16 | Rebholz, Groß, Röseler, registered report PsyArXiv 5u8br (v2 read; v3 Feb 2026) | CITED-ONLY | Anchoring data from Weber & Röseler 2025 (p. 20). OpAQ meta-analytic d = 0.60 used for power (p. 28). |
| 17 | Rebholz, Biella, Hütter, JBDM 2024, [10.1002/bdm.2369](https://doi.org/10.1002/bdm.2369) (GS only) | Probably a Google Scholar mis-link | OpAQ is absent from the text and the reference list. Relevant method point: ratio indices such as the anchoring index assume linearity; mixed-effects regression weights can take nonlinear distance terms. |
| 18 | Weber & Röseler 2025, EJOP, [10.5964/ejop.9891](https://doi.org/10.5964/ejop.9891) | Contributes data | OpAQ score correlations used for the power analysis (p. 2). A corrected version (Jan 2026, OSF component sz5b9) reassigns item effect sizes (published p. 4 vs corrected p. 10); see the item-mapping note in the Röseler list. |
| 19–22 | Röseler 2023 z-curve (MetaArXiv ewb2t); Haidinger 2026 EJOR [10.1016/j.ejor.2026.06.002](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejor.2026.06.002); Edmar et al. 2025 misinformation meta-analysis; Röseler et al. 2024 JCRE [10.18718/81781.38](https://doi.org/10.18718/81781.38) | CITED-ONLY | JCRE is a replication of anchoring moderators. The other three were **not read**; their titles show unrelated topics. |

## Röseler anchoring works 2022–2026
- **OpAQ:** JOPD 2022 (10.5334/jopd.67); Correction 2024 (10.5334/jopd.92).
- **Meta-analysis:** preprint only (wf2tn). OSF file qswer is `OpAQ_metaanalysis_v1.pdf`.
- **Reliability paper:** preprint b6t35, published Meta-Psychology 2024.
- **EJOP reliability study:** preprint 2kfh3, published EJOP 2025. An unpublished corrected version exists (Jan 2026). Its corrected table moves effect sizes between items. Examples: Danube −0.32 → 1.12; Russia–US distance 1.24 → −0.32. I cannot tell whether the OpAQ master file has the corrected item mapping. That matters for an item-level analysis.
- **Insufficient adjustment model:** preprint jztk2, published Meta-Psychology 2025.
- **Epley & Gilovich replication:** preprint bgp3m, published JCRE 2024.

- **Model (MS p. 8, Eq. 4):** the anchored mean is w·A + (1−w)·μ, where μ is the unanchored crowd mean and w = w₀·e^(−β|A_j − θ|).
  - θ is the true value. β is described as sensitivity to anchor–truth distance, "the anchoring extremeness effect".
  - Simulation values: θ = 324, μ = 250, A_L = 10, A_H = 1000, w₀ = 1, β = 0.0017.
- **Exp 2 design (MS pp. 13–14):**
  - N = 396 recruited online in Argentina (119 in Group 1, 277 in Group 2).
  - 30 general-knowledge percentage questions, split into two sets of 15, bounded 0–100.
  - The anchors were the same for every question: 5% (low) and 95% (high). Low or high was assigned at random per question. The control group gave estimates without anchors.
  - Preregistered: aspredicted RYC_4Y5.
- **Distance:** raw |A_j − θ| in percentage points, not normalised.
  - Because the anchors are fixed, distance varies only through the true value θ. Anchor position was never manipulated.
  - The Fig. 3D caption (MS p. 17) plots each question's weight (low-anchor dots, high-anchor dots) against distance, with a log scale on the weight axis and a linear fit.
- **Anchoring weight:** one-sided, per anchor and per question: w_j = (μ_j − μ)/(A_j − μ), measured against the unanchored mean μ (SI p. 43, Eq. 16).
  - The authors call it "very similar" to the Jacowitz–Kahneman anchoring index (MS p. 15).
  - It is 0 when the anchor has no effect and 1 when the mean equals the anchor.
  - It is **not** the two-anchor AI (high − low)/(A_H − A_L).
- **Main result:** the weight correlates with distance at **r = −0.56, p = 3×10⁻⁶** (MS p. 16).
  - The text gives no n; about 60 points (30 questions × 2 anchors) is my inference, not stated.
  - Supporting pattern: for true values below 50% (17 questions), the low-anchor group's estimates did not differ from the truth (t(16) = 0.95, p = .36, BF₀₁ = 2.7). The mirror pattern held for the 13 questions above 50% (MS pp. 14–15).
- **Model comparison (MS p. 16):** the exponential form fits best, but the margins are small.
  - Against linear: ΔAIC = ΔBIC = 1.9.
  - Against hyperbolic w₀/(1 + β|A − θ|) (their Eq. 7): ΔAIC = ΔBIC = 0.59.
  - One weight per question beats separate low and high weights (ΔAIC = 1.6, ΔBIC = 5.7).

## Priority 2: Mayer & Rebholz 2024 (does not cite OpAQ)
PsyArXiv [10.31234/osf.io/69jwr](https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/69jwr), full text read. No journal version found.

- **Task and design:** random-dot estimation (100–599 dots, 25 anchoring images) in a 2 (expertise) × 2 (anchor relevance) × 2 (anchor extremity) design (p. 11).
  - Extremity: anchors deviate ±35% ("low") or ±70% ("high") from the true value, coded −0.5/0.5 (p. 14).
  - Preregistered: aspredicted GZQ_48M.
- **Outcome:** absolute relative error = |judgment/correct × 100 − 100|, i.e. percent deviation from the truth (p. 14).
- **Results:**

| Experiment | Extremity effect (percentage points) | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Exp 1 | β = 4.88, 95% CI [2.80, 6.97], t(23.79) = 4.60, p < .001 | p. 15 |
| Exp 2 | β = 7.37, 95% CI [4.53, 10.20], t(24.00) = 5.09, p < .001 | p. 21 |

- **Exploratory slope (Exp 1):** relative error on signed anchor deviation, β = 0.15 [0.09, 0.21], t(23.08) = 5.13 (page not pinned; around p. 17).
- **My reading, not the authors':** doubling the anchor's distance (35% → 70%) raises absolute error by only about 5–7 points. That is a pull of roughly 0.14–0.21 per unit of extra distance, i.e. a roughly constant proportional pull. "Stronger anchoring" here is absolute, not proportional.

Dear Editors of *Judgment and Decision Making*,

Please consider the enclosed manuscript, "Extreme anchors lose proportional pull: A preregistered, model-based test of how anchoring scales with anchor extremity in open trial-level data", as an Empirical Article.

**What the paper does.** Anchoring theories disagree about how an anchor's influence changes as the anchor becomes more extreme, and the two recent meta-analyses reach different conclusions on this question. Much of the disagreement comes from measuring anchor influence as a standardised mean difference, which grows with anchor distance even when anchors pull estimates by a constant proportion. We derived the shape of the anchor-response function from five process models, including two versions of Lieder et al.'s (2018) resource-rational account. We then simulated these models on the exact designs of the Open Anchoring Quest, an openly licensed collection of trial-level anchoring data, and tested the predictions in a preregistered secondary analysis.

**Main findings.** Within items, the proportional pull of an anchor fell as the anchor moved away from the true value. This contradicts anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments and constant-weight integration. Across two-anchor studies, where authors chose the anchor values, the anchoring index showed no detectable decline, and no model reproduced both patterns with one parameter set. We report the limits openly: the within-item evidence comes mostly from one study with random anchors, and the across-cell result is sensitive to influential cells.

**Fit with the journal.** The journal's aims name the analysis of existing data and process models, and the journal published one of the studies we analyse (Bahník, 2021). The paper should interest readers who work on anchoring, on process models of judgement, and on how moderator analyses in meta-analyses are read.

**Transparency.** The preregistration (following van den Akker et al.'s secondary-data template) was committed to version control before any outcome variable was read, together with frozen model predictions and the analysis code. All deviations are listed in the manuscript and in a separate file. Code, outputs and the preregistration are openly available, and one script reproduces every number from the openly licensed raw data (CC-BY 4.0). The study used only anonymised secondary data. No new data were collected, and no ethics approval was sought; we can provide further information if the editors require it.

**Use of artificial intelligence.** The study was designed, analysed and written by an AI system (Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic) working autonomously under my instruction, and reviewed by two other AI systems. This is declared in the Methods and Acknowledgements, as the Cambridge University Press policy requires, and documented in full in the repository. No AI system is listed as an author, and I take responsibility for the content of the manuscript.

The manuscript is not under consideration elsewhere. I declare no competing interests and no funding.

Yours sincerely,

Lukas Wallrich
Birkbeck, University of London, United Kingdom
ORCID [ORCID redacted]

time in advance.

                             2.2 Materials
                             The study consisted of two parts. In the ﬁrst part of the study, participants were given 13
                             objects that they compared with a random anchor. The objects were selected to be either
                             known to the participants (e.g., related to well-known Prague locations) or speciﬁed in a
                             way that their characteristics could be reasonably estimated (e.g., “highest waterfall Angel
                             Falls”). For each item, participants ﬁrst generated a random number and then answered
                             whether the given object was smaller or larger in terms of size in meters than the generated
                             random number. The dimension of size was always speciﬁed to be length, height, or
                             distance. The random generation was emphasized by a mechanism similar to a slot machine
                             with three “wheels”, each with a single digit, that spun and then stopped on the number of
                                1Pre-registration, software used for data collection, data, and analysis scripts can be found on: https://osf.
                             io/mf4bc/wiki/home/ and https://osf.io/3t2hw/.


                                                                                                   134
Downloaded from https://www.cambridge.org/core. 27 Sep 2026 at 22:58:24, subject to the Cambridge Core terms of use.
                              Judgment and Decision Making, Vol. 16, No. 1, January 2021 Anchoring without scale distortion


                             the anchor. The anchors therefore ranged from 1 to 1000 (“000” on the wheels corresponded
                             to 1000). The true size of all the objects in meters fell within this range. After this ﬁrst
                             part of the study, which presented comparison questions, participants made an absolute
                             judgment of size of each object in meters in the second part. The order of objects was
                             randomized for each participant, but it stayed constant between the two parts of the study.


                             3 Results
                             Based on a pre-registered exclusion criterion, 13 absolute judgments higher than 3000
                             were excluded as outliers. The analysis was conducted with the remaining 6635 answers.
                             Mixed-eﬀect linear regression with absolute judgment as the dependent variable and anchor
                             as the independent variable was used in analysis. Random intercepts for participants and
                             items were included in the model. Random slopes for the anchor value for items were also
                             included in the model to take into account that the anchoring eﬀect could diﬀer between
                             items. The anchor value was scaled to a range −0.5 to 0.5. The results showed a strong
                             anchoring eﬀect (t = 7.56, b = 233.82, Wald 95% CI [173.2, 294.4]).
                                 Inﬂuence of an anchor or a judgment from a preceding trial may show a possible eﬀect
                             of scale distortion caused by a previously considered value. An exploratory analysis showed
                             that, absolute judgments were inﬂuenced by neither the anchor value on the previous trial (t
                             = 1.27, b = 18.1, CI [-9.7, 46.0]), nor the preceding absolute judgment (t = 2.05, b = 34.7,
                             CI [1.6, 67.8]),3 nor the median of absolute judgments for the previous item (t = 1.39, b =
                             28.5, CI [−11.7, 68.7]. The eﬀect of the preceding absolute judgment was clearly positive
                             when random slopes for the eﬀect of the preceding judgment was not included in the model,
                             that is, assuming that the eﬀect is the same for all items (t = 3.20, b = 35.1, CI [13.6, 56.7]).
                                 In an exploratory analysis, the trial number (scaled to range from −0.5 to 0.5) and its
                             interaction with the anchor value were added in the model of possible order eﬀects.4 The
                             resulting model suggested that judgments were generally lower in later trials (t = 1.93, b =
                             23.7, CI [−0.4, 47.8]), and that the anchoring eﬀect was somewhat smaller in later trials
                             t = −1.91, b = −82.9, CI [-168.0, 2.2]); however, neither of the eﬀects was at all robust.
                             A visual inspection of the results (Figure 1B) suggested a possible quadratic eﬀect of trial
                             order. Correspondingly, the interaction of the squared centered trial number with the anchor
                             value was clearly present (t = 3.50, b = 550.1, CI [242.2, 858.0]), showing that the anchoring
                             eﬀect was larger for initial and later trials than for trials in the middle. Nevertheless, the
                                 2Slope of the judgment in meters as a function of the full range of anchors, −.5 to .5.
                                 3The preceding absolute judgment was divided by 1000 before analysis to make the coeﬃcients comparable
                             with the reported anchoring eﬀect.
                                 4This and some other models did not include the full random-eﬀects structure because the models with
                             full random-eﬀects structure led to a singular ﬁt, suggesting overﬁtting of the data. In such cases, random
                             eﬀects were iteratively removed until a better ﬁt was obtained. The ﬁnal reported models are better than the
                             original “maximal” models according to the Akaike information criterion.

            Connecting the dots: Nonlinear patterns in the presence
            of symbolic and nonsymbolic numerical standards
            Roland Imhoff           1,2 and Paul Barker1
            1 Social Cognition Center Cologne, University of Cologne, Cologne, Germany and 2 Social and Legal Psychology, Johannes
            Gutenberg University Mainz, Mainz, Germany
            Corresponding author: Roland Imhoff; Email: [email redacted]
            Received: 9 March 2023; Revised: 23 May 2023; Accepted: 17 July 2023
            Keywords: anchoring; contrast; enumeration; numerical representations
            Abstract
            Much like other social and nonsocial evaluations, estimates of numerical quantities are susceptible to comparative
            inﬂuences. However, numerical representations can take either a nonsymbolic (e.g., a grouping of dots) or a
            symbolic numerical form (e.g., Hindu–Arabic numerals), which each produce comparative biases in opposite
            directions. The current work takes a ﬁne-grained curve ﬁtting approach across a wide range of values to the
            investigation of their potential nonlinear inﬂuence in the context of a numerical estimation task. A series of 3
            experiments (N = 1,613) showed how nonsymbolic standards produce linear contrastive patterns (Study 1), whereas
            symbolic numerical anchors show a cubic assimilative effect with a leveling off in strength for more extreme
            standards (Study 2). Sequential contrast from the previous patterns and assimilation to the previous response were
            found to be present and additive in the presence of both representations but were larger in absence of the symbolic
            numerical anchors (Study 3).
            1. Introduction
            Imagine, you have the task to estimate the number of political supporters at the presidential inauguration
            ceremony of Donald Trump. As virtually any judgment, your exact estimate will be susceptible to
            potentially irrelevant inﬂuences such as a more or less arbitrarily chosen comparison standards (e.g.,
            supporters on Barack Obama’s 2009 inauguration). Importantly, this standard could be presented
            as a merely numerical symbolic representation (i.e., the number 1.8 million) or non-symbolically

3. Study 2
           In this second study, exact symbolic numerical anchors were included underneath the image of the
           standard, offering immediate nonsymbolic and symbolic numerical information while the estimate is
           given. Thereby, the current study assessed if the visual information in the nonsymbolic representation
           still exerted their contrastive inﬂuence, or whether anchoring to the symbolic numerical representations

                                                                                                   Judgment and Decision Making   9
            dominated in the responses. We also investigated potential nonlinearity of the resulting pattern, as
            was done for the contrastive patterns. Any insufﬁcient adjustment type process would predict that the
            anchoring effects would level off as the anchor value becomes more extreme (Mussweiler and Strack,
            2001). We expected to see this pattern expressed as a cubic function with positive linear and a slight
            negative cubic term.
               The scale distortion theory (Frederick and Mochon, 2012) on the other hand does not directly predict
            this leveling off, but a purely linear effect in which the sequential anchors would be expected to work in
            an additive way (Mochon and Frederick, 2013). Finally, the study also probed if the sequential contrast
            from previous standards still occurred when concrete symbolic numerical representations are available
            within each the trial. In other words, the study was designed to provide insight whether a clear numeric
            anchor will overrule the inﬂuence of the previous trial.
            3.1. Method
            3.1.1. Participants
            The number of participants for this study was increased as a shortened online format was implemented.
            The necessary sample size of 800 participants was again determined using simulations based on the
            effect sizes and parameters found in previous work in the social comparative domain that used a similar
            paradigm (Barker and Imhoff, 2021). Therefore, 803 participants recruited via Proliﬁc Academic
            completed the study for a reward of £1.25. This ﬁnal sample consisted of 59% females and was aged
            between 18 and 74 years (M = 35.48, SD = 13.31).
            3.1.2. DJT-41
            As in the previous experiment, each trial consisted of a target image (indicated by “judgment target”)
            for which the number of dots had to be estimated horizontally next to a standard image (both images
            300 × 300 pixel) without any time constraints. For half of the trials, the target image was on the left and
            the standard on the right, for the other half it was vice versa. In order to rule out confusion regarding
            which image to estimate, participants had to click a radio button to indicate what they thought the target
            image was (trials with wrong clicks were excluded). Different from the previous study, the nonsymbolic
            dot pattern of the standard was now accompanied by the symbolic numeric information displaying the
            actual number of dots presented in this standard (“This image contains [between 93 and 901] dots.”).
            A visual display of the trials can be found on OSF.
               For better use online and to reduce strain on participants, the DJT was shortened to include just
            41 trials per participant. In order to keep a similar granularity in measurement steps, however, 2
            counterbalancing conditions were created so that half of the participants were randomly assigned to
            either estimate 41 dot patterns of around 500 dots (±10 dots) next to standards that varied between
            400 dots above or below the target image in intervals of 20 dots. The second group judged 40 similar
            dot images in the presence of standards at each 20-dot-interval between 390 dots below or above
            the target image as well as one in which the both images had an equal number of dots. In effect,
            this counterbalancing offers the same 81-step precision in measurement that was also included in the
            previous study.
            3.1.3. Additional measures
            Again, some basic demographics were recorded, including age, sex, and education, although the
            INCOM was no longer administered in this study. An additional item was included at the start of the
            survey to check for correct image display by asking participants to describe what they saw on a simple
            image containing 3 shapes of different colors. A small traditional anchoring task, closely modeled on
            the task and one of the questions in Strack and Mussweiler’s work (1997), was also included after the
            main task for exploratory purposes not directly related to this line of research. This task and its analysis
            are described in detail in the additional materials available online. After this, an open-ended item
            was included to gauge participant’s suspicions regarding the goal of the current study. Finally, a new

           Again, the main analysis took the form of a mixed model regression with REML that included ﬁxed
           effects for the number of dots present in the target, as well as the standard (and additionally given as
           a numeric anchor below the standard) in hundreds and modeled up to the third polynomials term. We
           included random slopes of the 3 polynomials as well as the actual number of dots for participants to
           account for participant level variation in patterns (no random intercept was estimated due to singular
           ﬁt issues). As in Study 1, participants were above-chance accurate in detecting subtle differences in the

start=s.index('# Declarations'); end=s.index('# References')

# Ethics

The study used only openly licensed, anonymised secondary data. No new data were collected, and no ethics approval was sought.

# Financial support

This research received no specific grant from any funding agency, commercial or not-for-profit sectors.

'''
s=s[:start]+decl+s[end:]

s=s.replace('''#| fig-cap: "Observed within-item response functions.''','''#| fig-alt: "Four panels, one per source study, plotting the median log estimate against the log anchor relative to the true value. #| fig-cap: "Observed within-item response functions.''')
s=s.replace('''drawn over the central 95% of that item's anchors. The dashed line marks estimates equal to the anchor. #| fig-cap: "Across-cell relation between anchor extremity and anchor influence.''')
s=s.replace('''The standardised effect rises with extremity, while the proportional index does not change detectably."''','''The standardised effect rises with extremity, while the proportional index does not change detectably. Figure produced with R code written by an AI system (see Method)."''')
s=s.replace('''#| fig-cap: "Model predictions at the median calibrated parameter values.''','''#| fig-alt: "Two line charts of five models against anchor distance from the belief centre. Left: mean estimate; M1 and M2 rise linearly, M1R, M3 and M4 flatten beyond about one unit. Right: local elasticity; M1 rises with distance, M2 is flat, M1R, M3 and M4 fall to zero or below."
#| fig-cap: "Model predictions at the median calibrated parameter values.''')
s=s.replace('''M3: adjustment to the plausible boundary; M4: plausibility-discounted integration."''','''M3: adjustment to the plausible boundary; M4: plausibility-discounted integration. Figure produced with R code written by an AI system (see Method)."''')
open(p,'w').write(s)

AI below means the anchoring index: (estimate under high anchor − estimate under low anchor) / (high anchor − low anchor). I computed it on means unless a paper gave medians.

**How AI changes with anchor extremity:**
- **Within the plausible range, AI stays roughly flat.**
  - Russo & Schoemaker 1989: slope about 0.45. This is read off a figure in Lieder et al. 2018, so it is secondary.
  - Northcraft & Neale 1987: 0.48–0.50.
  - Mussweiler & Strack 2001, plausible anchor pairs: 0.30–0.63.
  - Chapman & Johnson 1994, moderate anchor pair: 0.25.
  - Harris et al. 2019: 0.17–0.37.
- **At and beyond the plausibility boundary, AI falls roughly as 1/distance.** The raw shift in estimates stops growing or shrinks.
  - Mussweiler & Strack 2001: implausible anchors gave AI of −0.006 and −0.04 on the two items. These values are within noise.
  - Wegener et al. 2001: the raw effect shrank for extreme anchors in three studies.
  - Chapman & Johnson 1994: the curve flattens at the high end only (local slopes 0.39, 0.25, 0.006).
  - Bystranowski et al. 2021: the high-anchor bin had the smallest effect (d = .19).
  - Abstracts only: Marti & Wissler 2000, Townson 2019 and Hardt & Pohl 2003 report the same kind of downturn.
- **Counter-cases:**
  - Strack & Mussweiler 1997: implausible anchors gave a larger raw effect (0.42 vs 0.17 SD). The implied AI is still smaller.
  - Chapman & Johnson 1994, Experiment 2: prices kept rising across anchors from 1.08 to 28.16 times the lottery's expected value.
  - Harris et al. 2019: the temperature item's AI rose when the anchor gap widened; the car-price item's AI fell.
- **Model predictions:**
  - Lieder et al. 2018 predicts two different shapes. With a fixed number of adjustments, AI is constant across extremity. With the optimal number of adjustments, AI falls as the anchor moves further out relative to the person's uncertainty.
  - Turner & Schley 2016 build an inverted U into their model by assumption, citing Wegener et al. 2001.

**Gaps the planned study would fill:**
- No study reports AI at three or more extremity levels on both sides of the plausibility boundary, across many items, with item-level means and a calibration SD.
- Only Hardt & Pohl 2003 scale distance to each person's own uncertainty. That study measures hindsight bias, and I have its numbers only secondhand.
- No study fits the four candidate models to item-level curves of AI against extremity.

**Coverage and quality:**
- **Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995:** I could not get the full text. The only number is a mean AI of 48.48% across 15 items, as reported by Lieder et al. 2018. Their per-item AIs and any high/low asymmetry are UNVERIFIED.
- **Chapman & Johnson 1994:** figures only. The numbers are read off the figures to within about ±1.
- **Strack & Mussweiler 1997:** several per-item rows in the Appendix look like typographical errors. Use only the study's summary z-scores.
- **Not obtained:** Mussweiler & Strack 2000, Thorsteinson et al. 2008, LeBoeuf & Shafir 2006, Mussweiler 2001 and Chapman & Bornstein 1996. For Chapman & Bornstein the download tool returned the wrong paper, which I discarded.
- **Correction to the brief:** the correct DOI for LeBoeuf & Shafir 2006 is 10.1002/bdm.535; 10.1002/bdm.536 is a different paper.</result>

# Review log

Every reviewer comment and the response to it. Raw reviewer outputs are in `reviews/` (scoping critiques in `reviews/scoping/`, code review in `reviews/code/`, manuscript reviews in `reviews/manuscript/`). "Accepted" means the change was made; "Rejected" gives the reason.

## Round 0: Code and results review (codex, after the confirmatory analysis)

Source: `reviews/code/codex_answer_code_review_1.txt`. Codex confirmed that the preregistered rules produce the committed verdicts, that the inclusion rules reproduce the registered design counts, and that the models implement their stated equations.

| # | Severity | Comment | Response |
|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | Major | The external benchmark (Jacowitz & Kahneman's index of about .49) is a raw-scale quantity, but the calibration used a log-scale index. | Accepted as a sensitivity analysis. S1 (`R/05b_sensitivity.R`) recalibrates all models to a raw-scale index; the accepted parameter sets overlap almost completely and model survival is unchanged. The frozen predictions stay as preregistered; the manuscript reports both. |
| C2 | Major | M1R's parameter kappa does not have the meaning stated in the preregistration (the code multiplies sigma, not the 0.6 sigma spread of belief centres). | Accepted as a documentation correction (deviation D2). The code, and hence the predictions, are unchanged; the description in the manuscript follows the code. |
| C3 | Major | H3 compares a weighted mean index (simulation) with a multilevel intercept (observed). | Accepted (deviation D1). The observed level statistic now uses the same inverse-variance weighted mean as the simulation. Survival is decided by shape criteria and does not change. |
| C4 | Major | H1 rests largely on one study (13 of 20 cells); no study-level effect; R3 without Bahník is uninformative. | Accepted. Added S2: leave-one-study-out, a study random effect, and single-study fits. The manuscript presents study dependence as the first limitation and in the abstract ("mostly random anchors"). |
| C5 | Major | 870 of 987 gross errors come from one cell (Shanks et al., 2020, Study 3, Chicago) with a unit mismatch; the cell drops out. | Accepted. Documented in `deviations.md` and in the Method and Results; no change to the rule, which was applied as preregistered. |
| C6 | Minor | Stratum-level model simplifications (Q23 fallback) not logged. | Accepted; listed in `deviations.md` under contingency rules. |
| C7 | Minor | Operating characteristics use normal critical values and the full random structure, unlike Q22. | Accepted; described as approximations in `deviations.md`. The manuscript reports them as rounded shares (above 99%). |
| C8 | Minor | Rho CI uses a normal quantile while b and g use Satterthwaite t. | Accepted as a clarification (deviation D4); stated in the Method. |
| C9 | Minor | H2 has an extreme range of sampling variances; ten cells hold about 61% of the weight; participants appear in several cells. | Accepted. S3 adds study-clustered robust SEs, a fit without the ten most precise cells, and leave-one-study-out; the manuscript now says the across-cell slope is not robust. |
| C10 | Minor | H2 fallback did not check whether clubSandwich is installed. | Accepted; fixed in code (not triggered). |
| C11 | Minor | R2 fit has no convergence check; unlabelled warnings in the log. | Accepted; warnings from R2 and R3 are now labelled. The unlabelled convergence warning came from a fit that the preregistered fallback discarded. |
| C12 | Minor | Present the positive-leaning across-cell slope as an unresolved design difference, not a sign change within the same items. | Accepted; the Discussion describes two candidate explanations and says the data cannot separate them. |
| C13 | Nitpick | Misspelt task type "quantitity" in the inclusion list. | Accepted; removed (no analysed rows affected). |
| C14 | Nitpick | R4 silently drops cells with zero SE; MAD floor not registered. | Accepted as documentation: neither rule affected the observed cell set (noted in `deviations.md`, D3). |
| C15 | Nitpick | Data hash check used only the first 16 characters. | Accepted; now checks the full SHA-256. |

<task-notification>

<summary>Agent "Schley/Weingarten + computational models" finished</summary>
<note>A task-notification fires each time this agent stops with no live background children of its own. The user can send it another message and resume it, so the same task-id may notify more than once.</note>
<result>I found no 2022–2026 paper that computes the proportional anchoring index (AI) item by item on OpAQ, relates it to anchor extremity, and compares it against simulated process-model predictions. The complete report, with all page references, is at `/tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_sw_REPORT.md`, and I've sent the requesting agent that path.

Three works come closest:
- **Röseler & Schütz (2022, PsyArXiv, doi 10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn):** uses OpAQ (386 items). The outcome is Hedges g, and extremity is the anchor's distance from the true value relative to that value. Effects grew with that distance: b = 0.040, k = 312, p < .001 (Table 2, p. 21). On p. 34 they explicitly call for a unitless "relative strength of adjustment" measure, which is the gap the planned study fills. Closeness 2.
- **Schley & Weingarten meta-study (Jan 2025 version only, SSRN doi 10.2139/ssrn.5114456):** 1,968 participants, 8 items, anchors at calibration percentiles, estimates z-scored within item. More extreme anchors gave larger effects. Closeness 2.
- **Lieder et al. (2018a):** fitted the AI for 15 Jacowitz & Kahneman items but never tested how it changes with extremity.

Both empirical extremity findings measure a larger absolute or standardized gap between high- and low-anchor estimates. A constant AI would also produce that, because the anchors themselves are further apart. So neither tests proportional adjustment, and an AI-based analysis is what can tell the models apart.

Evidence tiers:
- **full text:** read in full.
- **figure-read:** my estimate from a plot.
- **abstract only:** only the abstract was read.
- **UNVERIFIED:** not read.

Closeness to the planned study is rated 0–3. I checked every DOI against Crossref, and all titles and authors match. I opened no data files.

## A. Schley & Weingarten

**It is one paper in several versions.**
- **Management Science:** doi 10.1287/mnsc.2023.03238, "Fifty Years of Anchoring Effects: A Theoretical Reintegration and Meta-Analysis". Crossref lists it online since 2026-05-19, with no volume, issue or pages yet. I did not read the published text (UNVERIFIED).
- **PsyArXiv teq7k_v2 (2025-12-09):** Crossref marks it as the preprint of the journal article. Its abstract matches the journal abstract, and SSRN doi 10.2139/ssrn.5893864 is the same version. Read in full (48 pp.); the page numbers below refer to it.
- **Jan 2025 version (PsyArXiv teq7k v1, file revision 5; SSRN doi 10.2139/ssrn.5114456):** titled "…A Meta-Analysis and Meta-Study of Anchoring Effects". Read in full (88 pp.). It adds the preregistered meta-study. The meta-study is not in v2 and, judging by the abstract, not in the journal version.
- **SSRN doi 10.2139/ssrn.4605057 (2023):** earlier version with 1,283 effect sizes (abstract only).
- **Online appendices (osf.io/d583s):** not read (UNVERIFIED).

**(1) Data sources**
- 1,280 high-vs-low effect sizes, from 482 studies in 178 papers (v2, pp. 17 and 23). The total across all their databases is 2,601.
- Database searches were run in Dec 2017, Feb 2019 and Feb 2024, plus Many Labs 1 and 2 and the Reproducibility Project (pp. 15–16).
- **OpAQ is not used or cited.**

**(2) How extremity was coded**
- **Meta-analysis:** a yes/no flag for anchors the original authors called "extreme" or "implausible", or that sat beside more moderate anchor levels. 49 of 1,280 effect sizes are flagged (Table 2, pp. 20–21).
  - There is no measure relative to the true value, the SD or percentiles.
  - Only 8.3% of studies (40 of 482) ran a calibration pretest (p. 39).
- **Meta-study:** anchors at the 3rd/97th, 15th/85th and 30th/70th percentiles of a Prolific calibration sample, varied within participants across 8 items (Table 7, p. 50). This amounts to extremity relative to uncertainty.

**(3) Level of testing and results**

In the meta-analysis, extremity was tested at the effect-size level in a 3-level model (effect sizes nested in studies; p. 22). Results from Table 5 (p. 28):

| Model | Estimate |
|---|---|
| Multivariate | −0.02 [−0.20, 0.16] |
| Univariate | 0.01 |
| Studies that manipulated extremity | 0.09 [−0.14, 0.31] |

- Table 6 (p. 29): g = 0.84 for extreme anchors vs 0.82 for the rest.
- There is no test for a curved relationship.
- The authors say (p. 31) the coefficient implies "not that the anchoring effect is proportional to the anchor extremity but that the total magnitude of the anchoring effect appears no larger or smaller for anchors defined by their study's authors as 'extreme.'"

The meta-study was tested at the trial level, with linear and quadratic extremity terms (pp. 52–54):
- The text gives no numbers. From their Figure 4 (p. 55, figure-read), the linear term is about +0.74 and the quadratic term about +0.10.
- From Figure 3 (p. 53, figure-read), the high-minus-low gap is about 0.2 SD at 30/70, 0.5 SD at 15/85 and 1.0 SD at 3/97.
- The distance between the two anchors widens several-fold across these levels, so the AI cannot be computed from the paper.

**(4) Effect-size metric**
- Hedges g only.
- The paper uses no AI or other unitless adjustment measure.

**(5) Theories compared, and how**
- Seven theories get qualitative predictions in Table 1 (p. 7).
- Extremity predictions (p. 12):
  - anchoring-and-adjustment: increases up to a threshold;
  - selective accessibility: increases up to a threshold;
  - attitudinal perspective: inverted U;
  - extremeness aversion: increases;
  - noise theory: increases.
- There is no model fitting. The authors explicitly decline to tally which theories win (p. 33).

**(6) Random or uninformative anchors**
- Transparently random anchors: −0.19** [−0.33, −0.05] (Table 5, p. 28). The Jan 2025 version reports −0.27*** (its p. 42).
- Primed or incidental anchors: −0.72***.

**Closeness:** meta-analysis 1; meta-study 2 (extremity relative to uncertainty, but only 8 items, a z-scored outcome, no AI and no model simulations).

## B. Young et al. 2026

"Anchoring the anchor: judgments of both items assimilate in item-based anchoring", Cognitive Psychology 164, 101796, doi 10.1016/j.cogpsych.2026.101796. Full text read.

- **Design:** 10 studies, N = 1,353, where the anchors are items rather than numbers ("torch vs laptop"). The outcome is each estimate's percentile rank within an unanchored calibration sample.
- **Result:** g = 0.25 [0.05, 0.45] (p. 11).
- **OpAQ:** not used.
- **Models:** none fitted. The authors favour selective accessibility.
- **Extremity:** only a remark in the discussion (pp. 15–16).
- **Discrepancy:** they cite Schley & Weingarten as d = 0.876 (p. 2) and 0.88 (p. 15), whereas every Schley & Weingarten version I read reports 0.824 or 0.825. I did not resolve this.
- **Closeness: 0.**

## C. Searches, 2022–2026

I screened the 2022–2026 citers of Lieder 2018a (164), Lieder 2018b (21), Turner & Schley 2016 (54) and OpAQ (4) in OpenAlex, and ran keyword and web searches. The OpAQ citer list misses papers that use OpAQ, so that route has low recall. None of the citers fits process models to multi-item anchoring data or relates the proportional AI to extremity.

| Paper | What it did | Closeness |
|---|---|---|
| Röseler & Schütz 2022 | See the summary above. | 2 |
| Wu et al. 2026, Cognitive Science, doi 10.1111/cogs.70229 | Full text. VR height estimation with anchors offset 2, 4 or 8 m (N = 127). The anchoring score is linear in the subjective offset (β = 0.66). One quantity only. | 1 |
| Lee & Morewedge 2022, Psychological Science, doi 10.1177/09567976211024254 | Abstract only. Anchoring increases with stimulus magnitude, attributed to noise. | 1 |
| Röseler et al. 2024, Meta-Psychology, doi 10.15626/mp.2022.3236 | Abstract only. Uses OpAQ to show that individual anchoring scores are unreliable. | 1 |
| Röseler, Incerti, Rebholz & Seida 2025, PsyArXiv, doi 10.31234/osf.io/jztk2_v3 | Abstract only. A formalized insufficient-adjustment model; less adjustment time did not move estimates closer to the anchor. | 1 |
| Spicer et al. 2022, Psychological Science, doi 10.1177/09567976221089599 | Abstract only. Anchoring and repulsion occur together; background for sampling models. | 1 |
| Rebholz, Biella & Hütter 2024, JBDM, doi 10.1002/bdm.2369 | Abstract only. Regression weights as an alternative to ratio-based indices such as the AI; a methods point. | 1 |
| Yasseri & Reher 2022, J Comput Soc Sci, doi 10.1007/s42001-021-00158-0 | Abstract only. Large online experiment reporting a "positive, yet complex" link between anchors and bias. | 1 |
| Zhu et al. 2024, Psychological Review, doi 10.1037/rev0000427 | Abstract only. A general sampling model for estimates. | 0–1 |
| Mayer & Rebholz 2024, PsyArXiv, doi 10.31234/osf.io/69jwr | Abstract only. Tests how expertise affects anchoring, contrasting three theories. | 0–1 |
| Honda et al. 2024, Cognition, doi 10.1016/j.cognition.2024.105758 | Abstract only. | 0 |
| Bixter & Luhmann 2025, Acta Psychologica, doi 10.1016/j.actpsy.2024.104646 | Abstract only. | 0 |
| Li et al. 2025, Economic Inquiry, doi 10.1111/ecin.13279 | Abstract only. | 0 |

## D. What Lieder 2018 and Turner & Schley 2016 fitted

Lieder page numbers are from the 2017 PsyArXiv preprints; I did not check the published journal pagination.

**Lieder et al. 2018a (doi 10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8)**
- Fitted two parameters to the Jacowitz & Kahneman AI for 15 quantities (p. 25).
- Mean AI: 53.22% predicted vs 48.48% observed; across items r(13) = 0.62 (p. 26).
- Other data fitted:
  - self-generated anchors (Epley & Gilovich 2006): r(17) = 0.61;
  - Russo & Schoemaker: compared on mean estimates only (pp. 30–31);
  - Simmons Study 3b: ρ(22) = 0.72 (p. 39).
- The stated prediction is a constant relative adjustment: bias is proportional to the anchor–truth distance (Eqs. 3–4, p. 20).
- Their Fig. 4 (p. 19) implies a remaining bias that is non-monotonic in distance at some time costs. That is my reading of the figure; the authors do not say it.
- They never tested how the AI varies with extremity.

**Lieder et al. 2018b (doi 10.3758/s13423-017-1288-6)**
- Bus-delay predictions with a single quantity (N = 30 and 60).
- Relative adjustment was 41.3% (p. 10), and 29.86% vs 27.25% for low vs high anchors (p. 16).

**Turner & Schley 2016 (doi 10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003)**
- Exp 1: N = 589, 6 items, one anchor per item, so no AI is possible (pp. 12–14).
- Exp 2: N = 189, each participant gave an estimate before and after the anchor (p. 26).
- The inverted-U effect of extremity is built into the model as an assumption ("for simplicity", p. 23). The curved pattern in their Fig. 14 (p. 31) is across participants for a single anchor.

**Closeness:** Lieder 2018a 1–2; Lieder 2018b 0–1; Turner & Schley 2016 1.

## Not verified
- The published Management Science text and the online appendices.
- Where Röseler & Schütz show the curved relationship they describe; the PDF text contains only a linear coefficient.
- Full texts of the papers marked abstract only.
- The published page numbers of the two Lieder papers.</result>

## Answer

### Peer Review for *Judgment and Decision Making*

**Manuscript Title:** *Extreme anchors lose proportional pull: A preregistered, model-based test of how anchoring scales with anchor extremity in open trial-level data*  
**Author:** Lukas Wallrich  

---

### Overview

This manuscript addresses an important, long-standing theoretical and empirical question in judgment and decision making: how does an anchor's proportional influence scale with its extremity? The paper makes notable methodological contributions: it formalizes five cognitive process models on a common log-elasticity metric, simulates their predictions across the exact empirical designs of the Open Anchoring Quest (OpAQ) dataset, preregisters the predictions and analytical decision rules before accessing outcome data, and reports analyses with exemplary computational reproducibility.

However, several substantial issues regarding the calibration of conclusions, theoretical framing, selective reporting of exploratory analyses, and missing descriptive information must be addressed. Below is a detailed list of major and minor comments.

---

### Numbered Comments

#### 1. [MAJOR] Overgeneralized conclusions versus narrow empirical base (Dependence on Bahník, 2021)
* **Location:** Title, Abstract (lines 6–28), Discussion (lines 606–614, 726–738).
* **Problem:** The manuscript titles itself *"Extreme anchors lose proportional pull"* and presents this as a general empirical property of numeric anchoring. However, 83% of the within-item estimates (6,578 out of 7,949) and 13 of the 20 cells come from a single study: Bahník (2021a). Furthermore, all 13 items in that study are physical lengths, heights, and distances measured in metres (e.g., football field, Cheops pyramid, Eiffel tower, Burj Khalifa), evaluated using uniformly generated random anchors between 1 and 1,000. In robustness check R3, when Bahník (2021a) is excluded, the curvature estimate becomes completely uninformative: $g = -0.045$, 95% CI $[-0.358, 0.268]$, spanning zero widely. Thus, the confirmatory within-item evidence is essentially an observation about a single experimental paradigm using physical dimensions with random anchors. While this limitation is mentioned in the Discussion (lines 683–688), the Title, Abstract, and Conclusion state the finding as an established general rule.
* **Suggested Fix:** Calibrate the claims throughout the Title, Abstract, and Discussion. The title should be tempered (e.g., *"Do extreme anchors lose proportional pull? Diminishing elasticity for random anchors in physical estimation and an across-study puzzle"*). The Abstract and Introduction must state upfront that the confirmatory within-item evidence is dominated by a single study and domain.

---

#### 2. [MAJOR] Unwarranted extrapolation from random anchors to strategic applied anchoring
* **Location:** Introduction (lines 46–50), Discussion (lines 662–670, 734–736).
* **Problem:** In the Introduction, the paper motivates the research by arguing that *"negotiators, litigants and survey designers choose anchor values, and whether an extreme opening offer buys proportionally more influence than a moderate one depends on this relation"* (lines 47–50), and concludes: *"For anyone choosing an anchor, the within-item evidence implies diminishing returns to extremity"* (lines 734–735). This is an unjustified leap. The within-item evidence is 85% explicitly random numbers (and 100% random among the items showing significant within-item curvature). In contrast, in the across-cell analysis of 128 cells—where anchors were deliberate, fixed, or informative—the slope was *positive* ($d = +0.050$, and $d = +0.065$, $p < .05$ without Weber et al.). Strategic opening offers in negotiations or legal claims are intentional communicative acts laden with conversational implicatures (Gricean relevance), not arbitrary lottery spins. Advising practitioners that opening offers suffer diminishing returns based on random anchors for physical heights directly contradicts the paper's own across-cell findings on fixed anchors.
* **Suggested Fix:** Remove or heavily qualify all practical advice to negotiators and litigants. Explicitly discuss that diminishing returns may be restricted to anchors perceived as arbitrary or uninformative, and highlight that deliberate, communicative anchors might behave very differently (as hinted by the across-cell slope).

---

#### 3. [MAJOR] Theoretical framing of M1 as a strawman and artifactual "survival" of M1R
* **Location:** Abstract (lines 24–25), Process Models (lines 107–126), Model Adequacy / Table 2 (lines 488–492, 505), Discussion (lines 618–629, 709–713).
* **Problem:**
  1. *Strawman status of M1:* Model M1 ("anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments") is framed as a leading cognitive account. However, no theorist defends fixed-step adjustment across arbitrary anchor distances. Lieder et al. (2018) specifically introduced resource rationality (M1R) precisely because a fixed number of adjustments is psychologically implausible. Classical anchoring-and-adjustment (Epley & Gilovich, 2001, 2006) posits adjustment to the edge of a plausible range (M3), not a fixed step count. Presenting M1 as a serious competing theory to be "contradicted" sets up a computational strawman.
  2. *Artifactual survival of M1R:* The Abstract states that *"Only the resource-rational variant... survived the preregistered model checks."* This implies superior descriptive validity, but the survival is purely an artifact of model flexibility. In Table 2, M1R's predicted curvature was $g \in [-0.029, 0.082]$ (median $+0.003$); the observed curvature ($g = -0.041$) actually fell *outside* M1R's 95% predictive interval. M1R "survived" solely because the preregistered survival rule allowed a disjunction (`g_inside | rho_inside`), and M1R's predictive interval for relative curvature $\rho = g/b$ was pathologically diffuse ($[-0.37, 1.39]$) due to simulation replicates where $b \approx 0$. Furthermore, M3 and M4 accurately predicted the observed curvature ($g = -0.041$ was squarely inside both M3's $[-0.071, -0.022]$ and M4's $[-0.110, -0.017]$ intervals), but were eliminated because they failed on the across-cell slope $d$—which the author argues is confounded by item properties!
* **Suggested Fix:**
  1. Clarify in the theoretical introduction that M1 is a baseline mechanistic null, not a model advocated in the literature.
  2. Explicitly clarify in the Abstract, Results, and Discussion that M1R failed to predict the observed curvature $g$, and that its technical survival was purely a function of diffuse predictive intervals under an "OR" rule.
  3. Note that for the within-item curvature $g$, plausibility-discounting and boundary models (M3 and M4) were empirically accurate.

---

#### 4. [MAJOR] Selective reporting of Exploratory Analysis E4 (Extremity scaled by response spread)
* **Location:** Results (lines 558–564), Discussion (lines 658–661), Analysis script (`R/05_exploratory.R`, lines 60–67).
* **Problem:** In the Results section, the manuscript reports: *"When we divided extremity by the spread of log estimates within each anchor condition... the slope turned negative, d = -0.023, [-0.037, -0.010]. This is consistent with original authors having placed anchors further from the truth for quantities that people know less well."* However, inspection of `R/05_exploratory.R` reveals that a multivariable meta-regression was also estimated (`m4b`, adjusting for spread as an independent predictor: `mods = ~ extremity + spread`). In that model, the extremity slope remained *positive*: $d = +0.028$, 95% CI $[-0.050, 0.106]$ (`E4_slope_adjusting_spread` in `output/exploratory/exploratory_results.csv`). Dividing extremity by spread creates a ratio variable ($X / Y$) where the denominator is correlated with the outcome's standard error denominator, introducing well-known spurious ratio artifacts (Kronmal, 1993). Reporting only the ratio specification while omitting the simultaneous regression presents a selectively tidy narrative that the across-cell discrepancy is resolved.
* **Suggested Fix:** Transparently report both exploratory specifications in the Results text: the ratio model ($d = -0.023$) and the multivariable model ($d = +0.028$). Discuss that when controlling for spread without forming a ratio, the extremity slope remains positive, and urge appropriate caution regarding ratio artifacts.

---

#### 5. [MAJOR] Missing descriptive table of the 20 within-item cells
* **Location:** Method (lines 251–265).
* **Problem:** The entire confirmatory test of H1 rests on 20 item-study cells. Currently, the manuscript describes these cells only in a brief narrative paragraph (lines 253–260). A JDM reader has no direct way to examine the items, target quantities, true values, anchor ranges, number of anchor levels, sample sizes, or anchor types without inspecting raw data files. This obscures essential design characteristics (e.g., that 13 items are lengths from Bahník, 4 are high-anchor-only items from Frech et al., 2 are from Yoon et al., and only 1 item has 20 anchor levels from Imhoff & Barker).
* **Suggested Fix:** Add a comprehensive descriptive table of the 20 within-item cells to the main manuscript (or as Table 1, shifting subsequent tables). Include columns for: Study citation, Item text/target, Unit/dimension, True value ($t$), Number of participants, Number of distinct anchor levels, Range of anchors used, Anchor type (random vs. fixed), and Anchor side (high only vs. both).

---

#### 6. [MINOR] Quadratic model turnover artifact ($x|x|$)
* **Location:** Measures (lines 276–281), Results (lines 421–424).
* **Problem:** The quadratic specification $y = a_{\text{cell}} + b x + g x|x|$ implies a local elasticity of $b + 2g|x|$. With $b = 0.307$ and $g = -0.041$, the implied elasticity becomes negative when $|x| > b / (2|g|) = 0.307 / 0.082 \approx 3.74$ log units (an anchor differing from the true value by a factor $> 42$). In Bahník (2021a), anchors as low as 1 were used for Salto Angel ($t = 979$, $|x| = 6.89$) and Cheops pyramid ($t = 139$, $|x| = 4.93$). Beyond $|x| = 3.74$, this polynomial model mechanically forces estimates to move in the opposite direction of the anchor (a contrast effect).
* **Suggested Fix:** Explicitly acknowledge this mathematical property of the $x|x|$ model. State the turnover threshold ($|x| \approx 3.74$) and emphasize that the piecewise linear model (robustness check R2), which does not force a contrast turnaround, confirms the flattening without this polynomial artifact.

---

#### 7. [MINOR] Degrees of freedom jump in random-anchor stratum due to model step-down
* **Location:** Results (lines 427–428), `output/confirmatory/h1_within.csv`.
* **Problem:** In the pooled H1 model, Satterthwaite degrees of freedom for $g$ are $df = 9.10$ ($p < .001$), reflecting cell-level clustering across 20 cells. In the random-anchor stratum, however, the degrees of freedom jump to $df = 3936.38$ ($p = 1.17 \times 10^{-9}$). This occurred because the full model failed to converge, triggering the preregistered fallback to drop the random curvature variance `(0 + xx | cell)`. Dropping this variance treats cell curvature as fixed across cells, shifting the effective denominator from the cell level to the observation level.
* **Suggested Fix:** Add a brief note in the text clarifying that the random-effects step-down for the random-anchor stratum eliminated the between-cell curvature variance, which accounts for the dramatic jump in degrees of freedom and anticonservatively small $p$-value.

---

#### 8. [MINOR] Weighting artifacts in across-cell meta-regression (H2)
* **Location:** Method (lines 365–371), Results / Sensitivity (lines 598–603).
* **Problem:** The sampling variance of the anchoring index is $SE(AI)^2 \propto 1 / (x_{\text{high}} - x_{\text{low}})^2$. By definition, cells with more extreme anchors have wider anchor spreads, resulting in smaller $SE(AI)$ and higher inverse-variance weights. Sensitivity analysis S3 confirms that the 10 most precise cells carried 60.6% of the total meta-regression weight. This mathematical coupling between the predictor (extremity) and precision creates an inherent weighting artifact.
* **Suggested Fix:** Note in the Method or Discussion that the formulation of $SE(AI)$ naturally assigns greater weight to cells with wider anchor separations, explaining why precision is strongly tied to extremity.

---

#### 9. [MINOR] Reporting two divergent "mean anchoring indices" without explanation
* **Location:** Results (lines 453–454, 514–515).
* **Problem:** In line 453, the text reports: *"the mean log anchoring index was 0.42, [0.35, 0.48]"*, whereas in line 514, it reports: *"weighted mean log anchoring index = 0.241"*. Readers will be confused by this substantial difference (0.42 vs. 0.24) without an explanation in the text.
* **Suggested Fix:** Explain in the text that 0.42 is the multilevel meta-regression intercept (REML, accounting for study- and cell-level variance), whereas 0.241 is the fixed-effects inverse-variance weighted mean across cells (used to match the simulation estimator, per Deviation D1).

---

#### 10. [MINOR] Citation and reporting inconsistencies
* **Location:** References, Method, Results.
* **Problem:**
  1. *Imhoff & Barker year:* Cited as 2023 in the manuscript text and references (lines 67, 186, 260, 846), but referenced as "2022" in `preregistration.md` (lines 59, 73), `deviations.md` (line 37), and output tables (`S2_without_Imhoff & Barker, 2022, Study 2`).
  2. *Bahník citation:* Cited as "Bahník (2021)" in the text (lines 254, 525, 685, 779), but as "Bahník (2021a)" in the preregistration, code, and `design_cells.csv`.
  3. *Participant counts:* Line 253 reports 1,492 participants before exclusion; Results (line 406) reports 7,949 estimates after dropping 3 rows, but omits the final post-exclusion participant count (1,491, per `h1_within.csv`).
* **Suggested Fix:** Harmonize the citation years (clarify that OpAQ labeled Imhoff & Barker as 2022, but the final published paper is 2023) and report the final sample size consistently (7,949 estimates from 1,491 participants).

---

#### 11. [MINOR] Intuitive interpretation of elasticity and curvature units for JDM readers
* **Location:** Measures (lines 271–285), Results (lines 420–424).
* **Problem:** While log elasticity ($b$) and curvature ($g$) are mathematically principled, many behavioral decision-making researchers think in terms of percentage adjustments or raw anchoring indices.
* **Suggested Fix:** Provide a brief concrete example in the text (e.g., estimating a quantity whose true value is 100 with anchors of 25, 50, 200, 400, and 1,000), showing the predicted median estimates and implied local anchoring indices across those anchor levels. This will make the practical meaning of $b = 0.31$ and $g = -0.041$ immediately transparent.

---

### Overall Recommendation

**Recommendation:** **Major Revision**

**Summary of Recommendation:**
The paper addresses a core theoretical puzzle in JDM with exemplary computational rigor, code transparency, and preregistration discipline. However, several **MAJOR** issues remain that prevent immediate acceptance:
1. The empirical finding of diminishing proportional pull rests almost entirely (83% of data) on a single study (Bahník, 2021a) involving random anchors on physical lengths, requiring substantive recalibration of the Title, Abstract, and Conclusions.
2. The generalization from random anchors to strategic, deliberate anchors (negotiations, litigation) is ungrounded and contradicts the paper's own across-cell results.
3. The theoretical framing sets up M1 as a strawman and declares M1R as having "survived" despite failing on curvature, solely due to diffuse predictive intervals under a disjunctive evaluation rule.
4. Exploratory analysis E4 selectively reported a ratio specification while omitting the simultaneous multivariable model where the extremity slope remained positive.
5. A comprehensive descriptive table of the 20 within-item cells is missing.

Once these major issues are thoroughly addressed, this manuscript will represent an exceptionally strong, nuanced, and transparent contribution to the journal.
