2. The generalization from random anchors to strategic, deliberate anchors (negotiations, litigation) is ungrounded and contradicts the paper's own across-cell results.
3. The theoretical framing sets up M1 as a strawman and declares M1R as having "survived" despite failing on curvature, solely due to diffuse predictive intervals under a disjunctive evaluation rule.
4. Exploratory analysis E4 selectively reported a ratio specification while omitting the simultaneous multivariable model where the extremity slope remained positive.
5. A comprehensive descriptive table of the 20 within-item cells is missing.

Once these major issues are thoroughly addressed, this manuscript will represent an exceptionally strong, nuanced, and transparent contribution to the journal.

p='manuscript.qmd'; s=open(p).read()
def R(a,b):
    global s
    assert a in s, a[:80]
    s=s.replace(a,b)
R('''title: "Extreme anchors lose proportional pull: A preregistered, model-based test of how anchoring scales with anchor extremity in open trial-level data"''',
  '''title: "Anchor extremity and proportional anchor influence: A preregistered, model-based test in open trial-level data"''')
R('''wc <- fread(o("design_counts.csv"))''' if 'wc <- fread' in s else '''dc <- fread(o("design_counts.csv"))''','''dc <- fread(o("design_counts.csv"))
wct <- fread(o("within_cells_table.csv"))''')
# abstract
a0=s.index('**Abstract**'); a1=s.index('**Keywords:**')
s=s[:a0]+'''**Abstract**

Anchors bias numeric estimates, but it is unclear whether an anchor's proportional influence rises, stays constant or falls as the anchor becomes more extreme. Meta-analyses report larger standardised effects for more distant anchors, yet a standardised mean difference rises with anchor distance even when the proportional pull is constant. We derived the shape of the anchor-response function from five process models, simulated them on the designs of the Open Anchoring Quest, and preregistered the predictions before reading any estimates. In `r dc$within_cells` item-study cells with at least three anchor values (`r nf(P$n_rows)` estimates; `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * wct[study == "Bahník, 2021a", sum(estimates)] / P$n_rows)` from one study with random anchors for lengths and heights), the log-scale elasticity of estimates with respect to anchors averaged `r f2(P$b)` and fell as anchors moved away from the true value (curvature `r f3(P$g)`, 95% CI `r ci(P$g_lo, P$g_hi)`). This contradicts anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments and constant-weight integration, and matches the direction predicted by plausibility-based models, which however predicted a steeper decline. Across `r h2$n_cells` two-anchor cells from `r h2$n_studies` studies with researcher-chosen anchors, the anchoring index did not change detectably with extremity (slope `r f3(h2$slope)`, `r ci(h2$slope_lo, h2$slope_hi)`). No model reproduced both patterns; a resource-rational variant passed the preregistered checks only because its predictions were very wide. Within items, extreme anchors pull estimates by a smaller share of their distance, at least for random anchors; whether this holds for deliberately chosen anchors remains open.

'''+s[a1:]
# M1 framing
R('''In *anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments* (M1), people start at the anchor and adjust towards their belief in a limited number of stochastic steps. @lieder2018a formalised adjustment''',
  '''In *anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments* (M1), people start at the anchor and adjust towards their belief in a limited number of stochastic steps. This is not a theory anyone has defended in its own right; it is the mechanistic core of the resource-rational account with the number of adjustments held constant, as in Lieder et al.'s fit to Jacowitz and Kahneman's data (29 adjustments), and it shows what adjustment alone implies. @lieder2018a formalised adjustment''')
# within-cell table after the within-item bullet
R('''- **Across-cell set** (secondary):''','''- **Across-cell set** (secondary):''')
R('''It contains `r dc$across_cells` cells from `r dc$across_studies` studies (`r nf(dc$across_rows)` estimates).''',
  '''It contains `r dc$across_cells` cells from `r dc$across_studies` studies (`r nf(dc$across_rows)` estimates).

[@tbl-cells] describes the within-item cells. OpAQ labels two of the source studies differently from their publications: "Bahník, 2021a" is @bahnik2021, and "Imhoff & Barker, 2022, Study 2" is a supplementary task in @imhoff2023.

```{r tbl-cells}
#| tbl-cap: "The 20 within-item cells (after exclusions). Anchor levels are distinct anchor values; the range of x is the log ratio of anchor to true value."
lab <- c("Bahník, 2021a" = "Bahník (2021)", "Frech et al., 2021" = "Frech et al. (2021)",
         "Yoon et al., 2021, Form C" = "Yoon et al. (2021)", "Imhoff & Barker, 2022, Study 2" = "Imhoff & Barker (2023)")
tc <- wct[, .(Study = lab[study], Item = sub("\\\\s*\\\\(.*\\\\)$", "", item), `True value` = format(true_value, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE),
              N = estimates, `Anchor levels` = anchor_levels, `Range of x` = sprintf("%.1f to %.1f", x_min, x_max),
              `Anchor type` = anchor_type)]
knitr::kable(tc)
```''')
# worked example + turnover + df note
R('''[@fig-within] shows the binned observed estimates and the fitted curves for each cell.''',
  '''For a quantity whose true value is 100, the fitted curve (ignoring item-specific terms) implies median estimates of `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * exp(P$b * log(.25) + P$g * log(.25) * abs(log(.25))))`, `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * exp(P$b * log(.5) + P$g * log(.5) * abs(log(.5))))`, `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * exp(P$b * log(2) + P$g * log(2) * abs(log(2))))`, `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * exp(P$b * log(4) + P$g * log(4) * abs(log(4))))` and `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * exp(P$b * log(10) + P$g * log(10) * abs(log(10))))` for anchors of 25, 50, 200, 400 and 1,000: moving the anchor from 400 to 1,000 adds less to the estimate than moving it from 200 to 400. Because the curvature term is quadratic, the fitted local elasticity would turn negative beyond |*x*| = `r f2(P$b / (2 * abs(P$g)))` (a factor of `r sprintf("%.0f", exp(P$b / (2 * abs(P$g))))`), where few anchors lie; this turning point is a property of the functional form, and the piecewise analysis below, which has no turning point, shows the same flattening. [@fig-within] shows the binned observed estimates and the fitted curves for each cell.''')
R('''In the random-anchor stratum the result was the same: *b* = `r f3(R$b)`, `r ci(R$b_lo, R$b_hi)`, and *g* = `r f3(R$g)`, `r ci(R$g_lo, R$g_hi)`, again classified as falling.''',
  '''In the random-anchor stratum the result was the same: *b* = `r f3(R$b)`, `r ci(R$b_lo, R$b_hi)`, and *g* = `r f3(R$g)`, `r ci(R$g_lo, R$g_hi)`, again classified as falling. In this stratum the full model did not converge, and the preregistered fallback removed the between-cell variance of the curvature. The curvature is then estimated as common to all cells, which inflates its degrees of freedom (`r nf(round(R$g_df))`) and makes its interval narrower than one that allowed the curvature to vary between items.''')
# H2 mean explanation + weighting
R('''Anchoring was present across cells: the mean log anchoring index was `r f2(h2$mean_ai)`, `r ci(h2$mean_ai_lo, h2$mean_ai_hi, 2)`.''',
  '''Anchoring was present across cells: the mean log anchoring index, estimated as the intercept of a multilevel model that weights studies and cells, was `r f2(h2$mean_ai)`, `r ci(h2$mean_ai_lo, h2$mean_ai_hi, 2)`. Because the standard error of a cell's index is inversely proportional to the log distance between its anchors, cells with widely spaced anchors, which also tend to be the more extreme cells, receive more weight''')
# H3 M1R
R('''Under the preregistered survival rule, which requires both the within-item curvature and the across-cell slope to fall inside a model's intervals, only M1R survived. It did so because its predictive intervals were wide enough to contain positive, zero and negative curvature.''',
  '''Under the preregistered survival rule, which requires the within-item curvature (*g* or ρ) and the across-cell slope to fall inside a model's intervals, only M1R survived. This does not mean that M1R predicted the data well: the observed *g* lay outside its interval, and M1R passed only because its interval for ρ was very wide (`r ci(pi_("M1R", "rho_lo"), pi_("M1R", "rho_hi"), 2)`), mainly because some of its parameter settings produce almost no anchoring. On the within-item curvature alone, M3 and M4 were the models whose intervals contained the observed value.''')
# E4 both specs
R('''the slope turned negative, *d* = `r f3(x_("E4_slope_on_scaled_extremity"))`, `r ci(x_("E4_slope_on_scaled_extremity", "lo"), x_("E4_slope_on_scaled_extremity", "hi"))`. This is consistent with original authors having placed anchors further from the truth for quantities that people know less well.''',
  '''the slope turned negative, *d* = `r f3(x_("E4_slope_on_scaled_extremity"))`, `r ci(x_("E4_slope_on_scaled_extremity", "lo"), x_("E4_slope_on_scaled_extremity", "hi"))`. When we instead entered extremity and spread as separate predictors, the extremity slope was `r f3(x_("E4_slope_adjusting_spread"))`, `r ci(x_("E4_slope_adjusting_spread", "lo"), x_("E4_slope_adjusting_spread", "hi"))`. input.command:
cat >> review_log.md <<'EOF'

## Round 1: Manuscript review

### Reviewer: Gemini 3.8 Flash via agy (recommendation: major revision)

Source: `reviews/manuscript/agy_answer_r1.txt` (reviewed the first draft).

| # | Severity | Comment | Response |
|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | Major | Title, abstract and conclusion state the within-item decline as a general rule, although 83% of within-item estimates come from Bahník (2021), random anchors for lengths and heights; without it the estimate is uninformative. | Accepted. New neutral title; the abstract now gives the share from one study and its anchor type and ends with the open question for deliberate anchors; the conclusion names the evidence base. The first limitation already covered this. |
| A2 | Major | Practical advice to negotiators is an unwarranted extrapolation from random anchors and contradicts the positive-leaning across-cell slope. | Accepted. Removed the "diminishing returns for anyone choosing an anchor" sentence; the conclusion now says the data cannot answer the question for deliberate, informative anchors. The introduction's practical motivation remains, phrased as a question. |
| A3 | Major | M1 is a strawman; M1R "survived" only through a very wide rho interval while its g interval excluded the observed value; M3/M4 predicted g correctly. | Accepted in substance. The M1 paragraph now says M1 is not a defended theory but the mechanistic core of the resource-rational account with fixed adjustments (as in Lieder et al.'s fit with 29 adjustments). The H3 results and the abstract state that M1R's survival reflects wide predictions, that its g interval excluded the observed value, and that M3/M4 contained the observed g. We keep the preregistered survival rule and report its outcome as registered. |
| A4 | Major | E4 reported only the ratio specification, not the model with spread as a separate predictor, whose extremity slope stayed positive. | Accepted. Both specifications are now reported in Results and Discussion, with a note on ratio-predictor artefacts; the claim that E4 explains the across-cell pattern was removed. |
| A5 | Major | No descriptive table of the 20 within-item cells. | Accepted. Added Table 1 (study, item, true value, N, anchor levels, range of x, anchor type), generated by `R/05c_within_cells_table.R`. |
| A6 | Minor | The x|x| form implies a turning point (negative elasticity beyond |x| of about 3.7). | Accepted. The turning point is now stated, with the note that the piecewise robustness analysis has no turning point and shows the same flattening. |
| A7 | Minor | The random-anchor stratum's degrees of freedom jump to about 3,936 because the fallback dropped the curvature variance, making its p value anticonservative. | Accepted. Explained in the Results. |
| A8 | Minor | Precision of the cell index is coupled to anchor spread, so extreme cells get more weight. | Accepted. Noted in the H2 results; sensitivity analysis S3 (without the ten most precise cells) already addressed it. |
| A9 | Minor | Two different mean anchoring indices (0.42 and 0.241) are reported without explanation. | Accepted. The Results now explain that 0.42 is the multilevel intercept and 0.241 the inverse-variance weighted mean used only for the comparison with simulations. |
| A10 | Minor | Inconsistent labels: Imhoff & Barker 2022 vs 2023; Bahník 2021 vs 2021a; post-exclusion participant count. | Accepted. The Method now explains that the OpAQ labels ("Bahník, 2021a"; "Imhoff & Barker, 2022, Study 2") refer to Bahník (2021) and Imhoff & Barker (2023); Figure 2 and Table 1 use the publication labels. The preregistration keeps the OpAQ labels because it is frozen. Post-exclusion counts are in Table 1 and the Results. |
| A11 | Minor | Give a concrete example of what b and g mean. | Accepted. Added: for a true value of 100, doubling the anchor raises the estimate by 21% from 50, 17% from 200 and 11% from 500 (numbers computed inline). |

Rejected in part: A1's suggestion that "100% of the items showing significant within-item curvature" used random anchors is incorrect; the one fixed-anchor item with 20 levels also showed negative curvature (S2), which the manuscript reports.
EOF
echo ok

content.text:
The citation check found no unsupported citations, but 12 are only partly supported, and three of these matter for the substance:

- **Yoon et al. (2021):** the "random" anchors were participants' own height or age. OpAQ codes them as random, and I followed that coding as preregistered.
- **Imhoff & Barker's Cologne cathedral item:** the authors found a *linear* raw-scale relation. On the log scale, a linear raw relation produces flattening for low anchors but steeper elasticity for high anchors.
- **Epley & Gilovich (2006):** they proposed the plausible-boundary account for self-generated anchors only.

The second point exposes a gap in the model set. A constant weight on the *raw* scale was never simulated, and it predicts negative curvature below the true value but positive curvature above it. The exploratory side-specific estimates (E1) found negative curvature on both sides, which would argue against it. I'm adding that model as exploratory analysis E6, run through the same estimators, to make this a formal check.

# Exploratory E6: constant-weight integration on the raw scale (M2raw).
# The estimate is a fixed weighted average of anchor and belief in raw units:
# estimate = w * anchor + (1 - w) * belief, with a log-normal belief. On the log scale this
# implies falling elasticity for anchors below the belief and rising elasticity above it.
# The model is simulated on the OpAQ within-item design and passed through the pooled H1
# estimator and the side-specific curvature model of exploratory analysis E1.

suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(data.table); library(lme4); library(parallel) })
source(file.path("R", "design_sets.R"))
source(file.path("R", "models.R"))
source(file.path("R", "estimators.R"))
out_dir <- file.path("output", "exploratory")

# Raw-scale Jacowitz & Kahneman index for M2raw is w by construction, so w is drawn from the
# same .30-.60 band used for the other models.
sets <- build_sets(read_opaq(include_outcomes = FALSE))
rows <- sets$within[, .(cell, pid, x)]
cells <- unique(rows$cell)

fit_sides <- function(dat) {

content.content:
## Answer

1. **MAJOR — H3 decision rule and Table 3.** M1R is retained even though the observed curvature *g* falls outside its predictive interval. It survives because the alternative statistic ρ = *g*/*b* has a very wide interval when simulated *b* is close to zero. Thus “retained” does not establish a good fit to the observed response curve. Report a joint predictive check for *b* and *g*, or a check of the response function itself, and describe M1R as inconclusive under the current rule.

2. **MAJOR — Across-cell analysis and model adequacy.** The slope *d* compares different items and studies whose anchors were chosen by researchers. Extremity is therefore confounded with item knowledge, anchor choice and design. Treating failure to predict *d* as a decisive failure of a within-item process model is too strong. Keep H2 as a descriptive test of generalisation, and distinguish its evidence from the within-item model test in Table 3 and the conclusions.

3. **MAJOR — H2 standard errors.** The method says that each index’s standard error is derived from condition MADs, but does not give the formula or explain how it handles participants who answered under both anchor conditions. Such responses yield correlated condition medians; ignoring that covariance can change weights and uncertainty. Provide the formula, identify paired designs, and repeat H2 with participant-level resampling or another method that preserves each study’s design.

4. **MAJOR — Scope of the primary inference.** Bahník (2021) supplies 83% of estimates and 13 of 20 cells. Removing it leaves a curvature interval spanning both substantial decline and increase. The pooled result is convincing for the represented random-anchor tasks, but the manuscript’s broader claims about general-knowledge magnitudes and process accounts exceed the independent evidence. Make this scope explicit in the abstract and conclusion, and report study-specific estimates alongside the pooled estimate.

5. **MAJOR — Process-model framing.** M2 is a constant-weight integration model **on the log scale**; a constant weight on raw magnitudes would not generally produce constant log elasticity. Likewise, M3 and M4 are particular formal versions of plausibility accounts, not unique predictions of Epley and Gilovich or selective accessibility. State these modelling choices where the models are introduced and frame the rejections as applying to the specified implementations, rather than to the wider theories.

6. **MAJOR — Predictive intervals and calibration.** The intervals depend on the accepted parameter grid, its implicit weighting, a broad calibration range, and assumptions about belief uncertainty and response errors. The relaxed-calibration exercise draws only 300 parameter sets per model, so finding no joint match is not evidence that none exists. Specify how accepted parameters were sampled, show sensitivity to the parameter ranges and weighting, and qualify claims that M3 and M4 predict a decline that is “too steep.”

7. **MINOR — Measures and interpretation of H1.** *b* is the fitted elasticity **at** the true value, not the “average elasticity at the true value.” Local elasticity is also distinct from the share of the full anchor–belief gap carried into an estimate. Define both quantities precisely and use “local elasticity” for the reported values 0.31, 0.23 and 0.14.

8. **MINOR — H1 robustness.** The random-anchor fallback fixes between-cell curvature variance at zero, making its interval especially narrow. The separate near/far analysis reports only a slope difference, so readers cannot tell whether far-anchor slopes remain positive. Report both slopes with intervals, and give an uncertainty check that preserves participant clustering and allows curvature to vary across items.

9. **MINOR — Preregistration and deviations.** The deviations file is unusually clear, but the manuscript should disclose that the reported operating characteristics approximate the gates and use the full random-effects structure even where the observed stratified fits required a fallback. It should also identify the MAD floor and zero-SE exclusion as safeguards present in the preregistered code but absent from its prose. Provide the repository link and frozen preregistration for review.

10. **MINOR — Unit mismatch and data accounting.** The 870 Chicago responses appear to be valid answers in millions, rather than gross errors. State that the entire cell was excluded because its units were inconsistent, and, if the intended units can be established, show a sensitivity analysis after conversion. Clarify that 7,952 and 129 are eligible-design counts, whereas 7,949 and 128 are analysed counts.

11. **MINOR — Presentation and references.** Figure 3 calls 1/SE “precision” although the discussed inverse-variance weight is 1/SE². Correct the caption and repair visible reference-formatting errors, including the Lieder et al. author entry and literal HTML tags in several titles.

**Overall recommendation: major revision.** The within-item negative curvature is a substantial finding, and the inconclusive across-cell result is reported candidly. **Major issues remain** in the model-survival rule, the interpretation of the across-cell test, the H2 uncertainty estimates, and the breadth of the theoretical conclusions.

# Post-hoc checks requested in review round 1 (not preregistered; see deviations.md).
# R1a joint predictive check: share of each model's calibrated replicates whose b and g both fall
#     inside the observed 95% CIs.
# R1b near and far slopes (knot at |x| = 1) with CIs.
# R1c study-specific curvature estimates.
# R1d H2 with a participant bootstrap within studies, and a count of participants who answered
#     under both anchors of the same cell.
# R1e H2 with the Chicago cell (Shanks et al., 2020, Study 3) converted from millions.

suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(data.table); library(lmerTest); library(metafor) })
source(file.path("R", "design_sets.R"))
source(file.path("R", "estimators.R"))
out_dir <- file.path("output", "review_checks")

=== 87
Experiments that varied anchor extremity have produced mixed results. @chapman1994 found that "implausibly extreme anchors had a proportionally smaller effect than anchors close to the expected value" in lottery valuations. @strack1997 found that implausible anchors produced a larger raw shift in estimates than plausible ones. When implausible anchors were placed far beyond the plausible range, estimates under them were no higher than estimates under a plausible high anchor [@mussweiler2001], and @wegener2001 found that very extreme anchors had smaller effects than moderate ones. These studies compared two to four anchor levels, mostly for a handful of items. The most fine-grained test so far used a perceptual task: @imhoff2023 [Study 2] showed participants dot patterns of about 500 dots next to standards labelled with their exact number of dots, which differed from the target by up to 400 dots in 20-dot steps. Estimates were drawn towards these symbolic anchors, but the pull levelled off once the anchor differed from the target by more than about 300 dots.
=== 89
The two recent meta-analyses reach different conclusions. Using the Open Anchoring Quest (OpAQ) data, @roseler2022meta found that Hedges' *g* increased with the relative distance between anchor and true value and concluded against the prediction that extreme anchors produce smaller effects. @schley2026 coded extremity as a binary flag for anchors that the original authors described as extreme and found no difference in effect size. @barrera2024 modelled the anchored crowd mean as a weighted average of anchor and crowd mean, with a weight that decays exponentially with the distance between anchor and truth, and found that this weight fell with distance across 30 percentage questions.
=== 103
In *adjustment to the plausible boundary* (M3), people accept anchors that lie inside the range of values they find plausible and adjust from implausible anchors only until they reach the edge of that range [@epley2006]. Beyond the boundary the estimate stops moving, so the proportional pull falls towards zero.
=== 113
The models also include a no-anchoring baseline (M0). Lieder et al. derived that bias grows linearly with anchor distance when the number of adjustments is fixed and showed how the optimal number of adjustments depends on distance, but did not test how the anchoring index varies with extremity. @turner2016 built an inverted U between extremity and anchor influence into their model "for simplicity" and tested it with one anchor per item.
=== 135
- **Within-item set** (primary): item-study cells with at least three distinct anchor values. It contains `r dc$within_cells` cells from `r dc$within_studies` studies (`r nf(dc$within_rows)` estimates, `r nf(dc$within_participants)` participants). Fifteen cells used random anchors: 13 general-knowledge items from @bahnik2021, in which each participant compared 13 random anchors between 1 and 1,000 to 13 lengths and heights, and two items from @yoon2021. Five cells used fixed anchors: four items with 10 high anchor levels each from unpublished data by Frech et al. (2021), contributed to OpAQ, and one item (the height of Cologne cathedral) with 20 anchor levels from a supplementary anchoring task in @imhoff2023 [Study 2].
=== 154
In the within-item set we modelled *y* = *a*~cell~ + *b*·*x* + *g*·*x*|*x*|. Here *b* is the average elasticity at the true value, and the curvature *g* describes how the local elasticity (*b* + 2*g*|*x*|) changes as the anchor moves away from the true value in either direction. We also report the relative curvature ρ = *g*/*b*, which does not depend on the overall strength of anchoring. In the across-cell set we computed each cell's log anchoring index, the difference between the median *y* under the high and the low anchor divided by the log ratio of the anchors, and each cell's extremity, the mean absolute log distance of its two anchors from the true value.
=== 179
**Decision rules.** The shape test was interpreted only if the confidence interval for *b* lay above zero (gate G1). We then classified the curvature, in this order, as *flat* if the confidence interval for ρ lay within the equivalence bounds ±0.05, as *rising* if the interval for *g* lay above zero, as *falling* if it lay below zero, and otherwise as inconclusive. The bounds sit just below the smallest relative curvature in the 95% predictive interval of M1, M3 and M4 and far outside that of M2 [@lakens2017]. Applied to the simulated replicates, this rule labelled data generated by M1 as rising in more than 99% of replicates, data from M3 and M4 as falling in more than 99%, data from M2 as flat in more than 99%, and data from M0 as failing the gate in all replicates.
=== 189
We made four changes after the confirmatory analysis had been run. First, a code review found that the observed mean anchoring index in the H3 level check was computed with a different estimator from the simulated one; we replaced it with the same inverse-variance weighted mean. This affects only level criteria, which do not decide model survival. Second, the preregistration described one M1R parameter incorrectly; the code, and therefore the predictions, were correct. Third, we made code changes that altered no reported number. Fourth, we clarified that the relative-curvature interval uses a normal critical value. One cell was removed by the preregistered gross-error rule because its participants answered in millions while its anchors and true value were raw counts. All analyses labelled exploratory or sensitivity were added after the preregistration.
=== 197
Anchoring was clearly present in the within-item set: the average elasticity was *b* = `r f3(P$b)`, 95% CI `r ci(P$b_lo, P$b_hi)`, so doubling the anchor raised estimates by about `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (2^P$b - 1))` near the true value. The curvature was negative, *g* = `r f3(P$g)`, `r ci(P$g_lo, P$g_hi)`, *t*(`r f2(P$g_df, 1)`) = `r f2(P$g / ((P$g_hi - P$g_lo) / (2 * qt(.975, P$g_df))))`, *p* `r if (P$g_p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", sprintf("%.3f", P$g_p))`, with a relative curvature of ρ = `r f2(P$rho)`, `r ci(P$rho_lo, P$rho_hi, 2)`. By the preregistered rule, the elasticity *falls* with extremity. At the true value an anchor carried about `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * P$b)` of its log distance into the estimate. The fitted local elasticity *b* + 2*g*|*x*| was `r f2(loc_el(1))` for anchors one log unit (a factor of 2.7) from the true value and `r f2(loc_el(2))` for anchors two log units (a factor of 7.4) away, about half its value at the true value. For a quantity whose true value is 100, the fitted curve (ignoring item-specific terms) implies that doubling the anchor from 50 to 100 raises the median estimate by `r dbl(50)`, doubling it from 200 to 400 by `r dbl(200)`, and doubling it from 500 to 1,000 by `r dbl(500)`. Because the curvature term is quadratic, the fitted local elasticity would turn negative beyond |*x*| = `r f2(P$b / (2 * abs(P$g)))` (a factor of `r sprintf("%.0f", exp(P$b / (2 * abs(P$g))))`), where few anchors lie; this turning point is a property of the functional form, and the piecewise analysis below, which has no turning point, shows the same flattening. [@fig-within] shows the binned observed estimates and the fitted curves for each cell.
=== 239
The within-item result held in the preregistered robustness analyses that retained the random-anchor data. Median regression without the gross-error rule gave *g* = `r f3(r_("R1_median_regression_g"))`, `r ci(r_("R1_median_regression_g", "lo"), r_("R1_median_regression_g", "hi"))`. Replacing the curvature term by separate slopes for near and far anchors showed that the slope for anchors more than one log unit from the true value differed from the slope near the true value by `r f2(r_("R2_far_minus_near_slope"))`, `r ci(r_("R2_far_minus_near_slope", "lo"), r_("R2_far_minus_near_slope", "hi"), 2)`. Without @bahnik2021 the estimate was similar but very imprecise, *g* = `r f3(r_("R3_without_bahnik_g"))`, `r ci(r_("R3_without_bahnik_g", "lo"), r_("R3_without_bahnik_g", "hi"), 2)`.
=== 255
*Relaxed calibration.* To check whether the model failures stem from the calibration to Jacowitz and Kahneman's index, we drew 300 parameter sets per model from wide ranges without calibration and simulated each on the OpAQ designs. No parameter set of any model reproduced the observed *b*, *g*, *d* and mean index jointly (all four inside their observed 95% confidence intervals). Within-item *b* and *g* together were reproduced by `r e5[model == "M4"]$within_b_and_g` of 300 M4 draws, `r e5[model == "M1R"]$within_b_and_g` M1R draws and `r e5[model == "M3"]$within_b_and_g` M3 draws, and by no M1 or M2 draw; the across-cell *d* and mean index together were reproduced by `r e5[model == "M2"]$across_d_and_ai` M2 draws and `r e5[model == "M1"]$across_d_and_ai` M1 draws, and by no M3 or M4 draw.
=== 275
The decline was smaller than M3 and M4 predicted. Their relative curvature intervals lay below the observed value, which means that far anchors still pulled estimates more than a hard plausibility boundary or a steep plausibility discount allows. A mixture in which the weight of an anchor falls gradually but does not vanish could describe this. The data do not identify such a model, and we did not test one.

The negative curvature contradicts two simple accounts. Anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of steps predicts that far anchors keep more of their distance, because a bounded number of bounded steps cannot correct a large gap; the data show the reverse. Constant-weight integration, the simplest version of the anchor integration model, predicts no change in proportional pull; it too is contradicted. The accounts that predict a decline share one feature: the anchor's influence is limited by how plausible it is. This holds for adjustment that stops at the edge of the plausible range [@epley2006], for integration that discounts implausible anchors [@wegener2001; @turner2016], and for a resource-rational agent who invests more adjustments when the anchor is far off [@lieder2018a]. The result fits earlier experiments with few anchor levels in which implausible anchors had proportionally smaller effects [@chapman1994; @mussweiler2001; @wegener2001], the distance-decaying anchoring weight of @barrera2024, and the levelling-off of assimilation to symbolic anchors in dot estimation [@imhoff2023]. It extends these findings to general-knowledge magnitudes, to anchors far outside the plausible range, and to a proportional outcome. In a dot-estimation task with anchors 35% or 70% away from the true value, the more distant anchors produced larger estimation errors [@mayer2024]; a larger absolute effect is compatible with a declining proportional pull, so the two findings do not conflict.
[@tbl-h3] compares the observed statistics with each model's predictive interval. M1 predicts positive curvature and is contradicted by the negative observed curvature. M2 predicts no curvature and is contradicted as well. M3 and M4 predict negative curvature and contain the observed *g* in their intervals, but they predict stronger relative curvature than observed (their intervals for ρ lie below `r f2(max(pi_("M3", "rho_hi"), pi_("M4", "rho_hi")))`) and a clearly negative across-cell slope, which the data do not show. Under the preregistered survival rule, which requires the within-item curvature (*g* or ρ) and the across-cell slope to fall inside a model's intervals, only M1R survived. This does not mean that M1R predicted the data well: the observed *g* lay outside its interval, and M1R passed only because its interval for ρ was very wide (`r ci(pi_("M1R", "rho_lo"), pi_("M1R", "rho_hi"), 2)`), mainly because some of its parameter settings produce almost no anchoring. On the within-item curvature alone, M3 and M4 were the models whose intervals contained the observed value.
Fourth, OpAQ harmonises data from many studies, and harmonisation can introduce errors. We found one item whose responses were recorded in different units from its anchors and true value, and a corrigendum to a related publication suggests that the item coding of another study may contain errors. Our rules removed the first; excluding the second made the across-cell slope positive and significant. We used only positive ratio-scale quantities with open response scales, so the results do not speak to dates, percentages, bounded scales or preferences.
**H2 (secondary).** We regressed the cell-level log anchoring index on extremity in a multilevel meta-regression with random intercepts for studies and cells within studies [@viechtbauer2010], using standard errors derived from the median absolute deviation (MAD) of each condition. Gate G2 required the mean index to exceed zero; the slope *d* was classified with the same ordered rule and equivalence bounds of ±0.03.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: ~/.claude/skills/coarse-review

# coarse-review (Claude Code)

Runs the **full coarse review pipeline** on a paper using the local `claude -p` CLI as the LLM backend. Every LLM call the pipeline makes — structure metadata, overview, per-section review, proof verification, editorial dedup — is served by a headless Claude Code subprocess using the user's Claude Max subscription. The only per-paper cost is the ~~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/manuscript/manuscript.docx.05-0.15 Mistral OCR extraction, which uses the user's OpenRouter key locally.

This is the **same pipeline** that powers coarse.ink — only the LLM backend is swapped.

## Prerequisites

- `uvx` preferred, `uv` acceptable. First run:
  `command -v uvx || command -v uv`
  - If neither exists, install uv:
    `curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh`
  - Then refresh PATH for the current shell:
    `export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"`
  - coarse requires Python 3.12+. If needed, install it with:
    `uv python install 3.12`
  - If `uv` exists but `uvx` does not, replace `uvx --python 3.12 --from ...` below with
    `uv tool run --python 3.12 --from ...`.
- Refresh the bundled `coarse-review` skill with an ephemeral install:
  `uvx --python 3.12 --from 'coarse-ink==1.4.0' coarse install-skills --all --force`
  (If that fails with `No such command 'install-skills'`, you're on a
  PyPI release that predates the command — upgrade or ignore; the skill
  bundle is also loadable directly via `uvx --from` without install.)
- **OpenRouter API key required** for Mistral OCR extraction (~~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/manuscript/manuscript.docx.10 per paper). Prefer checking for the key with presence-only probes so you don't needlessly echo its value into the transcript, but if the user hands you the key directly just save it — don't lecture them.

  Before running the review, check whether `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` is already configured:
  - In the environment: `test -n "$OPENROUTER_API_KEY" && echo "env: set" || echo "env: missing"`
  - In a `.env` file in the current directory: `test -f .env && grep -q '^OPENROUTER_API_KEY=' .env && echo ".env: set" || echo ".env: missing"`

  If neither probe reports "set", ask the user:

  > I need an OpenRouter API key for the OCR extraction step (~~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/manuscript/manuscript.docx.10 per paper). A few options:
  >
  > 1. Paste the key here and I'll save it to `~/.coarse/config.toml` via `uvx --python 3.12 --from 'coarse-ink==1.4.0' coarse setup`. Note the key passes through the LLM provider (Anthropic / OpenAI / Google) on its way to me, so treat it as slightly less private than one you typed into a local terminal — rotate at https://openrouter.ai/settings/keys if that worries you.
  > 2. Set it yourself in a separate terminal: `export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-v1-...` or add it to `.env` in your current directory, then re-ask me.
  > 3. Run `uvx --python 3.12 --from 'coarse-ink==1.4.0' coarse setup` in a separate terminal yourself and paste the key into its interactive prompt — the key never touches this chat.
  >
  > Which do you want?

  If the user pastes a key here, save it via `uvx --python 3.12 --from 'coarse-ink==1.4.0' coarse setup` with the pasted value and confirm it's stored. Their chat, their choice.
- `claude` CLI logged in.

## How to run

**Get the paper path from the user.** PDF is most common but any coarse-supported format works.

**If they already have a pre-extracted markdown** (from a previous coarse run), pass it with `--pre-extracted` to skip OCR.

**Launch in the background, then wait with `--attach` — two Bash calls, one approval per call.** A full review takes 10-25 minutes, which exceeds Claude Code's default 2-minute tool timeout, so you can't just run coarse-review in the foreground. Instead, split the run into two steps: `--detach` starts a background worker and returns in ~2 seconds; `--attach` blocks on the worker's PID and streams the log until completion, emitting a heartbeat every 30 seconds of log idleness so the Bash tool sees activity.

Use a **per-review unique log file** so parallel runs in the same shell don't clobber each other's output:

```bash
# Pick a unique suffix — use the paper filename stem or `$(date +%s)`:
LOG=/tmp/coarse-review-$(basename <paper_path> .pdf).log

# STEP 2a — launch (returns within 2 seconds with Review PID + Log file)
uvx --python 3.12 --from 'coarse-ink==1.4.0' \
  coarse-review --detach --log-file "$LOG" \
  <paper_path> --host claude [--model claude-opus-4-6] [--effort high]

# STEP 2b — wait (one blocking call, ~10-25 min, emits heartbeats)
uvx --python 3.12 --from 'coarse-ink==1.4.0' \
  coarse-review --attach "$LOG"
```

Run the attach call with a long Bash-tool timeout: in Claude Code, pass `timeout: 2700000` (45 minutes) on the `Bash` tool invocation so the tool doesn't kill the blocking command. The 45-minute recommendation leaves ~20 minutes of margin on top of the 10-25 minute review runtime for cold starts, slow models, long papers, and `--effort max` runs — 30 minutes is too tight because the tool timeout is a wall clock, not an idle-stream cap. Bump to 60 minutes for book-length papers or the largest models. Do NOT re-run the `--detach` command from STEP 2a if the attach call returns early — that would spawn a second worker. Safe to Ctrl+C the attach: the watcher detaches but the worker keeps running, and you can re-attach with the same command. Attach exit codes: `0` complete, `1` failure marker, `2` silent crash, `3` missing pidfile, `124` attach's own 30-min timeout, `130` user interrupt.

**When attach exits with code 0, do NOT hunt across the filesystem for the review file.** `coarse-review` prints the authoritative paths in the final log lines:

```bash
rg '^  view:|^  local:' "$LOG"
```

- `local:` is the exact markdown path that was written, even if `uvx` used a temporary working directory.
- `view:` is the canonical coarse web URL in handoff mode.

If `view:` says `unavailable`, treat that as a callback failure and report only the local path. Do **not** try to discover another web URL, and do **not** run broad `find`, `locate`, `lsof`, or whole-computer searches trying to rediscover the output.

Available models: `claude-opus-4-6` (default), `claude-sonnet-4-6`, `claude-haiku-4-5`.
Available effort levels: `low`, `medium`, `high` (default), `max`.

If the user came from the coarse web form, they'll paste a handoff URL instead of a local file path. The paper is a REMOTE resource at that URL — do NOT search for a local PDF and do NOT ask the user for a file path. Same two-step launch+attach pattern:

```bash
LOG=/tmp/coarse-review-$(date +%s).log

# STEP 2a — launch
uvx --python 3.12 --from 'coarse-ink==1.4.0' \
  coarse-review --detach --log-file "$LOG" \
  --handoff https://coarse.ink/h/<token> --host claude [--model ...] [--effort ...]

# STEP 2b — wait (same long-timeout discipline as local mode)
uvx --python 3.12 --from 'coarse-ink==1.4.0' \
  coarse-review --attach "$LOG"
```

This downloads the paper from the handoff URL, runs the pipeline, and POSTs the final review back so it shows up at `https://coarse.ink/review/<paper_id>?token=<access_token>`. The `view:` line in the log will already include the signed access token — use that URL as-is.

**When the script completes** (you'll be notified), read the output markdown and show the user:

- Output path
- Web URL from the `view:` line in handoff mode
- Recommendation (accept / revise_and_resubmit / reject)
- Top 2-3 macro issues from the overall feedback section
- Total comment count

## Notes

- `uvx --python 3.12 --from ... coarse-review ...` runs coarse from a temporary environment, so the agent does not mutate the user's global tool install.
- The review process runs locally using the user's own Claude Code login; coarse.ink only receives the finished markdown callback.
- The driver monkey-patches `coarse.llm.LLMClient` → `coarse.headless_clients.ClaudeCodeClient`, which spawns `claude -p` subprocesses for every pipeline LLM call.
- Host-CLI env vars (`CLAUDECODE`, `CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT`, etc.) are stripped from the subprocess environment so nested sessions don't conflict with the parent.
- If a single `claude -p` call exceeds 30 minutes, it's killed and the pipeline continues without that section's comments.
- Check progress via `tail -f $LOG` where `$LOG` is the per-review log path you set in step 2 (e.g. `/tmp/coarse-review-<paper-stem>.log`). Prefer the `coarse-review --attach "$LOG"` pattern above — it replaces per-poll `tail` calls with a single blocking watch command that emits heartbeats every 30 seconds of log idleness.
Checking the coarse-review prerequisites: uv, the OpenRouter key (presence only), and a fresh render of the manuscript.

input.content:
# The five weakest points of the paper

My own assessment as the AI system that designed and wrote the study, ordered from most to least damaging.

## 1. The primary finding rests on one study with an unusual kind of anchor

Thirteen of the 20 within-item cells and 83% of the within-item estimates come from Bahník (2021), in which participants spun a slot-machine-like device to generate random anchors between 1 and 1,000 for 13 lengths, heights and distances. Without this study, the pooled curvature is uninformative (95% CI roughly −0.36 to 0.27). The other studies do not form a clean replication. The two Yoon et al. items used participants' own height or age as anchors and showed the opposite (positive) curvature. The four Frech et al. items had anchors only above the truth and were imprecise. That leaves one fixed-anchor item (Imhoff & Barker's Cologne cathedral) with a negative curvature. The paper can claim that proportional pull falls with extremity for random anchors in this task. It cannot claim this for the deliberate, informative anchors that matter in negotiation, pricing or law, and the preregistered test of the fixed-anchor stratum was not informative.

## 2. The model comparison is weaker than the preregistration makes it look

The five models were calibrated to a single external benchmark (Jacowitz & Kahneman's index of about .49). That index was computed on the log scale in the preregistered calibration, although the original is a raw-scale value; the raw-scale recalibration reached the same conclusions. The predictive intervals depend on auxiliary assumptions that no data constrain: the spread of beliefs across people, response noise, item uncertainty from 0.3 to 1.2 log units, uniform sampling over grid points. The preregistered survival rule kept only the resource-rational model, and only because its predictions were wide. The model that best reproduces the within-item data, the plausible-boundary model M3, failed on the across-cell slope, which is itself confounded. No model was fitted to the data. The paper therefore rules out two simple implementations (fixed-step adjustment and log-scale constant weighting) and is suggestive about the rest. It does not identify the process.

## 3. Ruling out raw-scale averaging rests on an exploratory analysis

The preregistered pooled test cannot distinguish log-scale plausibility models from simple averaging on the raw scale: both predict a negative pooled curvature. The raw-scale model was not in the preregistration. It was added after the citation check showed that Imhoff & Barker found a linear raw-scale relation for one of the analysed items. What separates the two accounts is the sign of the curvature above the true value. That estimate is exploratory, comes mostly from the same Bahník study, and uses a quadratic term that is sensitive to where anchors happen to fall. The paper states this, but the claim that "plausibility limits anchor influence" depends on it more than the abstract conveys.

## 4. Extremity is measured against the truth, not against what people believe or know

Extremity is the log distance of the anchor from the true value. Anchoring theories concern distance from the person's belief and its uncertainty. Within items this matters less, because the belief distribution is fixed. Across items it is probably why the across-cell analysis did not show the within-item decline: researchers may have placed anchors further from the truth for quantities that people know poorly. The exploratory attempts to address this gave conflicting answers: a ratio of extremity to response spread gave a negative slope, and spread as a separate predictor gave a positive one. Both use outcome-contaminated spreads, so they cannot settle it. The across-cell result (inconclusive, positive-leaning, and not robust to clustering or influential cells) remains unexplained.

## 5. The data are harmonised secondary data, and the whole study was produced by AI without human verification

OpAQ codes do not always match the original designs. Anchor types were miscoded for two of the four within-item studies. One across-cell item had responses in different units from its anchors. A corrigendum by the dataset's own team suggests item mix-ups in another study. We followed the preregistered coding, so these issues flow into the confirmatory results. Separately, every step (question choice, model specification, code, interpretation, response to reviews) was done by an AI system and reviewed by other AI systems. The author has not yet checked the work. Model-generated errors that all AI reviewers missed, for example in the simulation assumptions or the reading of cited papers, remain possible until a human expert reviews the code, the model implementations and the literature claims.

Without this study, the pooled curvature is uninformative (95% CI roughly −0.36 to 0.27). The other studies do not form a clean replication. The two Yoon et al. items used participants' own height or age as anchors and showed the opposite (positive) curvature. The four Frech et al. items had anchors only above the truth and were imprecise. That leaves one fixed-anchor item (Imhoff & Barker's Cologne cathedral) with a negative curvature. The paper can claim that proportional pull falls with extremity for random anchors in this task. It cannot claim this for the deliberate, informative anchors that matter in negotiation, pricing or law, and the preregistered test of the fixed-anchor stratum was not informative.

## 2. The model comparison is weaker than the preregistration makes it look

The five models were calibrated to a single external benchmark (Jacowitz & Kahneman's index of about .49). That index was computed on the log scale in the preregistered calibration, although the original is a raw-scale value; the raw-scale recalibration reached the same conclusions. The predictive intervals depend on auxiliary assumptions that no data constrain: the spread of beliefs across people, response noise, item uncertainty from 0.3 to 1.2 log units, uniform sampling over grid points. The preregistered survival rule kept only the resource-rational model, and only because its predictions were wide. The model that best reproduces the within-item data, the plausible-boundary model M3, failed on the across-cell slope, which is itself confounded. No model was fitted to the data. The paper therefore rules out two simple implementations (fixed-step adjustment and log-scale constant weighting) and is suggestive about the rest. It does not identify the process.

## 3. Ruling out raw-scale averaging rests on an exploratory analysis

The preregistered pooled test cannot distinguish log-scale plausibility models from simple averaging on the raw scale: both predict a negative pooled curvature. The raw-scale model was not in the preregistration. It was added after the citation check showed that Imhoff & Barker found a linear raw-scale relation for one of the analysed items. What separates the two accounts is the sign of the curvature above the true value. That estimate is exploratory, comes mostly from the same Bahník study, and uses a quadratic term that is sensitive to where anchors happen to fall. The paper states this, but the claim that "plausibility limits anchor influence" depends on it more than the abstract conveys.

## 4. Extremity is measured against the truth, not against what people believe or know

Extremity is the log distance of the anchor from the true value. Anchoring theories concern distance from the person's belief and its uncertainty. Within items this matters less, because the belief distribution is fixed. Across items it is probably why the across-cell analysis did not show the within-item decline: researchers may have placed anchors further from the truth for quantities that people know poorly. The exploratory attempts to address this gave conflicting answers: a ratio of extremity to response spread gave a negative slope, and spread as a separate predictor gave a positive one. Both use outcome-contaminated spreads, so they cannot settle it. The across-cell result (inconclusive, positive-leaning, and not robust to clustering or influential cells) remains unexplained.

## 5. The data are harmonised secondary data, and the whole study was produced by AI without human verification

OpAQ codes do not always match the original designs. Anchor types were miscoded for two of the four within-item studies. One across-cell item had responses in different units from its anchors. A corrigendum by the dataset's own team suggests item mix-ups in another study. We followed the preregistered coding, so these issues flow into the confirmatory results. Separately, every step (question choice, model specification, code, interpretation, response to reviews) was done by an AI system and reviewed by other AI systems. The author has not yet checked the work. Model-generated errors that all AI reviewers missed, for example in the simulation assumptions or the reading of cited papers, remain possible until a human expert reviews the code, the model implementations and the literature claims.

## Answer

The revision substantially addresses the round-1 major requests. A2, A4, A5, X2, X3, X4 and X6 are adequately resolved; A1 is largely resolved by narrowing the scope. A3, X1 and X5 are now reported more fairly, but the interpretation still needs work.

1. **MAJOR — Measures, Abstract and Conclusion.** The manuscript defines “proportional pull” as a *local elasticity*, then concludes that extreme anchors pull estimates by a smaller *share of the distance between belief and anchor*. Those are different quantities. The model uses distance from the true value, while participants’ unanchored beliefs were not measured. **Fix:** State the primary finding as a decline in local response to changes in the anchor. Use “share of the belief–anchor gap” only if that share can be estimated against a justified belief baseline.

2. **MAJOR — Model adequacy and Discussion.** The conclusion says the result “supports” plausibility-based accounts, although the calibrated M3 and M4 predictions miss both relative curvature and the across-cell slope. M1R misses curvature and the post-hoc joint check of elasticity and curvature. Negative curvature is consistent with a plausibility mechanism, but these tests do not establish one. **Fix:** State prominently that no calibrated model adequately explains the combined results; describe plausibility as one possible account of the within-item shape. This completes the interpretive response to A3, X1 and X5.

3. **MINOR — H3 decision rules and Table 3.** The prose says a model is contradicted when curvature “(*g* or ρ)” falls outside its interval, yet M1R is retained despite *g* falling outside. **Fix:** Write the exact logical rule—whether rejection requires both curvature measures to miss—and explain why either measure can qualify a model for retention.

4. **MINOR — H2 standard errors.** The formula `1.2533 × MAD / √n` is appropriate if MAD has been scaled to estimate the standard deviation under a normal model. If it means the unscaled median absolute deviation, it understates the standard error. **Fix:** Specify the MAD convention used in code and confirm that the stated formula matches it.

5. **MINOR — Results, “Item by item.”** The claim that all 15 eligible cells had lower far-anchor slopes sits uneasily beside the positive quadratic curvature reported for Yoon et al. These fits can differ, but the reader cannot see why here. **Fix:** Identify the 15 cells and briefly reconcile the two summaries, or narrow the “every item” claim.

6. **MINOR — Table 2 and Data availability.** Table 2 calls *b* “average elasticity,” although *b* is the fitted elasticity at the true value. The repository link is still a placeholder, preventing verification of the preregistration and frozen predictions. **Fix:** Correct the column heading and add the repository link before submission.

**Recommendation: major revision.** **Yes, MAJOR issues remain:** the central claim conflates local elasticity with the share of a belief–anchor gap, and the process-model conclusion is stronger than the model comparisons support. The reported sample-count arithmetic is consistent, and I found no clear numerical contradiction requiring a new analysis.

content.content:
## Answer

# Review of Revised Manuscript (Round 2)

**Journal:** *Judgment and Decision Making*  
**Manuscript Title:** *Anchor extremity and proportional anchor influence: A preregistered, model-based test in open trial-level data*  
**Author:** Lukas Wallrich  

---

### Overview

In this second round of review, I assessed the revised manuscript (`manuscript/scratch_manuscript.md` and `manuscript/manuscript.qmd`), the preregistration deviations record (`deviations.md`), the review response log (`review_log.md`), and verified all statistical claims and tabular values against the raw computational outputs in `output/`.

Overall, the revision is exemplary. The authors have systematically addressed the core conceptual, theoretical, and empirical critiques raised in Round 1. The title and claims have been appropriately calibrated to reflect the empirical dominance of random anchors on physical dimensions (Bahník, 2021); the unwarranted extrapolation to strategic negotiation settings has been expunged; the mechanistic status of M1 has been properly contextualized; the technical "survival" of M1R has been clarified alongside a joint predictive check (R1a); the across-cell multivariable meta-regressions (E4) are now transparently reported; the mathematical details and uncertainty estimates for H2 have been completed; and a descriptive table of the within-item cells has been incorporated.

Below, I first evaluate the resolution of each Round-1 **MAJOR** comment, followed by a numbered list of remaining problems (all of which are **MINOR**), and conclude with an overall recommendation.

---

### Part 1: Assessment of Round-1 MAJOR Issues

#### Reviewer 1 (Gemini 3.8 Flash via agy)

1. **A1 [MAJOR] — Overgeneralized conclusions versus narrow empirical base (Dependence on Bahník, 2021)**
   * **Status: ADEQUATELY RESOLVED.**
   * **Evaluation:** The authors adopted a neutral title, explicitly stated in the Abstract that 83% of within-item estimates come from a single study using random anchors on lengths and heights (lines 14–15), reported study-specific estimates in the Results (lines 708–718), and restricted their primary conclusion to random anchors in physical estimation, leaving deliberate anchors open (lines 26–28, 886–898).

2. **A2 [MAJOR] — Unwarranted extrapolation to strategic applied anchoring (negotiations/litigation)**
   * **Status: ADEQUATELY RESOLVED.**
   * **Evaluation:** The prescriptive advice advising negotiators and litigants that extreme opening offers suffer diminishing returns was removed. The Introduction retains practical applications strictly as motivating questions (lines 47–51), and the Discussion and Conclusion now explicitly state that the present data cannot answer whether deliberately chosen, informative anchors show diminishing returns (lines 819–821, 893–896).

3. **A3 [MAJOR] — Theoretical framing of M1 as a strawman and artifactual survival of M1R**
   * **Status: ADEQUATELY RESOLVED.**
   * **Evaluation:** M1 is now introduced as the mechanistic baseline of adjustment rather than an actively defended theory (lines 114–118, 765–768). For M1R, the authors retained their preregistered decision rule but explicitly explained in the Abstract, Results, and Discussion that M1R's survival was purely an artifact of an uninformative predictive interval for relative curvature $\rho$ (lines 24–25, 585–594, 863–867). Crucially, the authors added a joint predictive check (R1a) demonstrating that 0% of calibrated M1R replicates reproduced both $b$ and $g$ jointly, compared to 33% for M3 and 4% for M4, and plainly concluded that M1R is "not supported by the within-item data" (line 593).

4. **A4 [MAJOR] — Selective reporting of Exploratory Analysis E4 (Extremity scaled by response spread)**
   * **Status: ADEQUATELY RESOLVED.**
   * **Evaluation:** The Results (lines 671–681) and Discussion (lines 811–816) now report both specifications: the ratio model ($d = -0.023$, 95% CI $[-0.037, -0.010]$) and the simultaneous multivariable model ($d = +0.028$, $[-0.050, 0.106]$). The potential for ratio artifacts is explicitly discussed, and claims that E4 resolved the across-cell divergence have been withdrawn.

5. **A5 [MAJOR] — Missing descriptive table of the 20 within-item cells**
   * **Status: SUBSTANTIALLY RESOLVED (with remaining presentation flaws).**
   * **Evaluation:** Table 1 has been added (lines 290–325), detailing the study, item, true value, sample size, number of anchor levels, range of $x$, and anchor type. However, as noted in the numbered list below, an aggressive regex truncated the item name for Cheops pyramid in Row 2, and units of measurement are absent.

---

#### Reviewer 2 (OpenAI Codex CLI)

6. **X1 [MAJOR] — H3 decision rule, Table 3, and M1R's lack of empirical support**
   * **Status: ADEQUATELY RESOLVED.**
   * **Evaluation:** The authors adhered to preregistration integrity by reporting the frozen decision rule outcomes, but added the requested joint predictive check of $b$ and $g$ (R1a) and clearly qualified M1R as unsupported by the within-item empirical response functions (lines 585–594).

7. **X2 [MAJOR] — Across-cell analysis confounded by item selection; framing of model failure**
   * **Status: ADEQUATELY RESOLVED.**
   * **Evaluation:** The Results and Discussion now explicitly state that failure to predict the across-cell slope $d$ is weaker evidence against within-item process models than failure on within-item curvature $g$, because across-cell designs confound extremity with researcher item selection and prior uncertainty (lines 594–597, 807–816).

8. **X3 [MAJOR] — Mathematical formulation and independence of H2 standard errors**
   * **Status: ADEQUATELY RESOLVED.**
   * **Evaluation:** The Method now includes the exact mathematical formulas for the standard error of condition medians and cell anchoring indices (lines 350–354). The authors confirmed empirically that no participant answered under both anchors of any cell (0 paired cells, line 353), and added a participant bootstrap within studies (R1d: median slope 0.044, 95% CI $[0.022, 0.069]$, lines 747–749).

9. **X4 [MAJOR] — Scope of primary inference and reporting of study-specific estimates**
   * **Status: ADEQUATELY RESOLVED.**
   * **Evaluation:** Study-specific curvature models were fitted and reported in the Results (lines 708–718; Bahník: $g = -0.035$; Imhoff & Barker: $g = -0.089$; Frech et al.: $g = -0.083$; Yoon et al.: $g = +0.093$). The scope of theoretical claims has been appropriately narrowed.

10. **X5 [MAJOR] — Process-model implementation specificity (log vs. raw scale)**
    * **Status: ADEQUATELY RESOLVED.**
    * **Evaluation:** The Introduction and Method explicitly state that models are specific log-scale implementations (lines 108–110). Furthermore, the authors simulated an exploratory raw-scale constant-weight model (E6), showing that while it predicts negative pooled curvature on the log scale, it predicts positive curvature above the truth ($g_{\text{above}} = +0.134$), contradicting the observed negative curvature on both sides (lines 694–706).

11. **X6 [MAJOR] — Predictive intervals, parameter sampling, and calibration sensitivity**
    * **Status: ADEQUATELY RESOLVED.**
    * **Evaluation:** The Method clarifies uniform sampling across accepted parameter grid points (lines 376–378). The relaxed-calibration analysis (E5) now states that 300 draws indicate matching parameter sets are rare rather than non-existent (lines 687–689). Claims that plausibility models predict a decline that is "too steep" have been carefully qualified as applying to the calibrated parameter ranges (lines 793–798).

---

### Part 2: Remaining and New Issues (Numbered List)

All remaining issues are **MINOR** technical, wording, or formatting matters. No major theoretical or statistical flaws remain.

#### 1. [MINOR] Regex truncation of item description and omitted units in Table 1
* **Location:** [scratch_manuscript.md#L300-L325](file://~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/manuscript/scratch_manuscript.md#L300-L325); [manuscript.qmd#L149](file://~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/manuscript/manuscript.qmd#L149).
* **Problem:** In Table 1, Row 2 displays the item name as `"height of the highest"`, which is truncated and uninformative. In the raw OpAQ data (`output/within_cells_table.csv`), the item string is `"height of the highest (Cheops) Pyramid in Giza (metres)"`. In [manuscript.qmd#L149](file://~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/manuscript/manuscript.qmd#L149), the R code uses `sub("\\s*\\(.*\\)$", "", item)`. Because `.*` is greedy in R regex, it matches from the first open parenthesis `(` before `Cheops` to the final `)` after `metres`, erroneously stripping the entire target name. Furthermore, Table 1 lacks units of measurement (e.g., metres, kilometres, people, USD, novels), which were requested by Reviewer 1 (comment A5).
* **Concrete Fix:** Update the string replacement to match only the trailing unit parenthesis (e.g., `sub("\\s*\\([^)]*\\)$", "", item)`), or extract the units into a dedicated "Unit" column in Table 1, and ensure Row 2 displays the complete name: `"Height of the Cheops Pyramid in Giza"`.

#### 2. [MINOR] Inconsistent terminology for parameter $b$ in Table 2 and Results text
* **Location:** [scratch_manuscript.md#L389](file://~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/manuscript/scratch_manuscript.md#L389), [scratch_manuscript.md#L621-L622](file://~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/manuscript/scratch_manuscript.md#L621-L622); [manuscript.qmd#L170](file://~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/manuscript/manuscript.qmd#L170), [manuscript.qmd#L240](file://~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/manuscript/manuscript.qmd#L240).
* **Problem:** Reviewer 2 (comment X7) requested clarifying that $b$ is the local elasticity *at* the true value ($x = 0$), rather than an average across the curve. The authors accepted this in the Method ([scratch_manuscript.md#L337-L338](file://~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/manuscript/scratch_manuscript.md#L337-L338)). However, Table 2 column 2 STILL bears the header `"Average elasticity b"`, and line 621 STILL refers to `"the observed average elasticity (b = 0.307)"`.
* **Concrete Fix:** Change the column header in Table 2 to `"Local elasticity at true value b"` (or `"Elasticity at true value b"`), and change line 621 to read: `"the observed local elasticity at the true value (b = 0.307)"`.

#### 3. [MINOR] Misleading description of level criteria coverage in Results
* **Location:** [scratch_manuscript.md#L621-L624](file://~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/manuscript/scratch_manuscript.md#L621-L624); [manuscript.qmd#L240](file://~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/manuscript/manuscript.qmd#L240).
* **Problem:** The text states: *"For the level criteria, the observed average elasticity (b = 0.307) and weighted mean log anchoring index (0.241) lay inside the intervals of M1R and M4 only."* This phrasing incorrectly implies that $b = 0.307$ fell inside the intervals of M1R and M4 only. In fact, Table 2 confirms that observed $b = 0.307$ lay inside the 95% predictive intervals of FOUR models: M1 ($[0.242, 0.638]$), M1R ($[0.007, 0.336]$), M3 ($[0.140, 0.360]$), and M4 ($[0.063, 0.576]$). Only the *joint* requirement that both level criteria were met simultaneously was satisfied by M1R and M4 only (`survives_level == TRUE`).
* **Concrete Fix:** Clarify the sentence to: *"For the level criteria, both statistics jointly (local elasticity b = 0.307 and weighted mean log anchoring index of 0.241) lay inside the intervals of M1R and M4 only, whereas elasticity b alone fell within the predictive intervals of M1, M1R, M3, and M4."*

#### 4. [MINOR] Monolithic "Retained" column in Table 3 obscures within-item model performance
* **Location:** [scratch_manuscript.md#L608-L616](file://~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/manuscript/scratch_manuscript.md#L608-L616); [manuscript.qmd#L228-L238](file://~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/manuscript/manuscript.qmd#L228-L238).
* **Problem:** Table 3 reports a single summary column: `Retained` (`yes` for M1R; `no` for M1, M2, M3, M4). While this faithfully reflects the preregistered conjunction rule (`(g_inside | rho_inside) & slope_inside`), it visually obscures the key substantive nuance that Reviewer 2 (comment X2) highlighted: M3 and M4 succeeded on within-item curvature $g$ (marked `in`) and were eliminated solely by the across-cell slope $d$, whereas M1R failed on $g$ (marked `out`) and "survived" solely via an inflated $\rho$ interval and $d$. A reader glancing only at Table 3 will receive the misleading impression that M1R fit the data while M3 and M4 failed across the board.
* **Concrete Fix:** Add a footnote to Table 3 (or an explicit secondary column, e.g., `Within-item shape supported`) stating: *"M3 and M4 satisfied the within-item curvature criterion (observed g fell inside their predictive intervals) and were contradicted solely by the across-cell slope d. ## Answer

# Review of Revised Manuscript (Round 2)

**Journal:** *Judgment and Decision Making*  
**Manuscript Title:** *Anchor extremity and proportional anchor influence: A preregistered, model-based test in open trial-level data*  
**Author:** Lukas Wallrich  

---

### Overview

In this second round of review, I assessed the revised manuscript (`manuscript/scratch_manuscript.md` and `manuscript/manuscript.qmd`), the preregistration deviations record (`deviations.md`), the review response log (`review_log.md`), and verified all statistical claims and tabular values against the raw computational outputs in `output/`.

Overall, the revision is exemplary. The authors have systematically addressed the core conceptual, theoretical, and empirical critiques raised in Round 1. The title and claims have been appropriately calibrated to reflect the empirical dominance of random anchors on physical dimensions (Bahník, 2021); the unwarranted extrapolation to strategic negotiation settings has been expunged; the mechanistic status of M1 has been properly contextualized; the technical "survival" of M1R has been clarified alongside a joint predictive check (R1a); the across-cell multivariable meta-regressions (E4) are now transparently reported; the mathematical details and uncertainty estimates for H2 have been completed; and a descriptive table of the within-item cells has been incorporated.

Below, I first evaluate the resolution of each Round-1 **MAJOR** comment, followed by a numbered list of remaining problems (all of which are **MINOR**), and conclude with an overall recommendation.

---

### Part 1: Assessment of Round-1 MAJOR Issues

#### Reviewer 1 (Gemini 3.8 Flash via agy)

1. **A1 [MAJOR] — Overgeneralized conclusions versus narrow empirical base (Dependence on Bahník, 2021)**
   * **Status: ADEQUATELY RESOLVED.**
   * **Evaluation:** The authors adopted a neutral title, explicitly stated in the Abstract that 83% of within-item estimates come from a single study using random anchors on lengths and heights (lines 14–15), reported study-specific estimates in the Results (lines 708–718), and restricted their primary conclusion to random anchors in physical estimation, leaving deliberate anchors open (lines 26–28, 886–898).

2. **A2 [MAJOR] — Unwarranted extrapolation to strategic applied anchoring (negotiations/litigation)**
   * **Status: ADEQUATELY RESOLVED.**
   * **Evaluation:** The prescriptive advice advising negotiators and litigants that extreme opening offers suffer diminishing returns was removed. The Introduction retains practical applications strictly as motivating questions (lines 47–51), and the Discussion and Conclusion now explicitly state that the present data cannot answer whether deliberately chosen, informative anchors show diminishing returns (lines 819–821, 893–896).

3. **A3 [MAJOR] — Theoretical framing of M1 as a strawman and artifactual survival of M1R**
   * **Status: ADEQUATELY RESOLVED.**
   * **Evaluation:** M1 is now introduced as the mechanistic baseline of adjustment rather than an actively defended theory (lines 114–118, 765–768). For M1R, the authors retained their preregistered decision rule but explicitly explained in the Abstract, Results, and Discussion that M1R's survival was purely an artifact of an uninformative predictive interval for relative curvature $\rho$ (lines 24–25, 585–594, 863–867). Crucially, the authors added a joint predictive check (R1a) demonstrating that 0% of calibrated M1R replicates reproduced both $b$ and $g$ jointly, compared to 33% for M3 and 4% for M4, and plainly concluded that M1R is "not supported by the within-item data" (line 593).

4. **A4 [MAJOR] — Selective reporting of Exploratory Analysis E4 (Extremity scaled by response spread)**
   * **Status: ADEQUATELY RESOLVED.**
   * **Evaluation:** The Results (lines 671–681) and Discussion (lines 811–816) now report both specifications: the ratio model ($d = -0.023$, 95% CI $[-0.037, -0.010]$) and the simultaneous multivariable model ($d = +0.028$, $[-0.050, 0.106]$). The potential for ratio artifacts is explicitly discussed, and claims that E4 resolved the across-cell divergence have been withdrawn.

5. **A5 [MAJOR] — Missing descriptive table of the 20 within-item cells**
   * **Status: SUBSTANTIALLY RESOLVED (with remaining presentation flaws).**
   * **Evaluation:** Table 1 has been added (lines 290–325), detailing the study, item, true value, sample size, number of anchor levels, range of $x$, and anchor type. However, as noted in the numbered list below, an aggressive regex truncated the item name for Cheops pyramid in Row 2, and units of measurement are absent.

---

#### Reviewer 2 (OpenAI Codex CLI)

6. **X1 [MAJOR] — H3 decision rule, Table 3, and M1R's lack of empirical support**
   * **Status: ADEQUATELY RESOLVED.**
   * **Evaluation:** The authors adhered to preregistration integrity by reporting the frozen decision rule outcomes, but added the requested joint predictive check of $b$ and $g$ (R1a) and clearly qualified M1R as unsupported by the within-item empirical response functions (lines 585–594).

7. **X2 [MAJOR] — Across-cell analysis confounded by item selection; framing of model failure**
   * **Status: ADEQUATELY RESOLVED.**
   * **Evaluation:** The Results and Discussion now explicitly state that failure to predict the across-cell slope $d$ is weaker evidence against within-item process models than failure on within-item curvature $g$, because across-cell designs confound extremity with researcher item selection and prior uncertainty (lines 594–597, 807–816).

8. **X3 [MAJOR] — Mathematical formulation and independence of H2 standard errors**
   * **Status: ADEQUATELY RESOLVED.**
   * **Evaluation:** The Method now includes the exact mathematical formulas for the standard error of condition medians and cell anchoring indices (lines 350–354). The authors confirmed empirically that no participant answered under both anchors of any cell (0 paired cells, line 353), and added a participant bootstrap within studies (R1d: median slope 0.044, 95% CI $[0.022, 0.069]$, lines 747–749).

9. **X4 [MAJOR] — Scope of primary inference and reporting of study-specific estimates**
   * **Status: ADEQUATELY RESOLVED.**
   * **Evaluation:** Study-specific curvature models were fitted and reported in the Results (lines 708–718; Bahník: $g = -0.035$; Imhoff & Barker: $g = -0.089$; Frech et al.: $g = -0.083$; Yoon et al.: $g = +0.093$). The scope of theoretical claims has been appropriately narrowed.

10. **X5 [MAJOR] — Process-model implementation specificity (log vs. raw scale)**
    * **Status: ADEQUATELY RESOLVED.**
    * **Evaluation:** The Introduction and Method explicitly state that models are specific log-scale implementations (lines 108–110). Furthermore, the authors simulated an exploratory raw-scale constant-weight model (E6), showing that while it predicts negative pooled curvature on the log scale, it predicts positive curvature above the truth ($g_{\text{above}} = +0.134$), contradicting the observed negative curvature on both sides (lines 694–706).

11. **X6 [MAJOR] — Predictive intervals, parameter sampling, and calibration sensitivity**
    * **Status: ADEQUATELY RESOLVED.**
    * **Evaluation:** The Method clarifies uniform sampling across accepted parameter grid points (lines 376–378). The relaxed-calibration analysis (E5) now states that 300 draws indicate matching parameter sets are rare rather than non-existent (lines 687–689). Claims that plausibility models predict a decline that is "too steep" have been carefully qualified as applying to the calibrated parameter ranges (lines 793–798).

---

* **Location:** [scratch_manuscript.md#L300-L325](file://~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/manuscript/scratch_manuscript.md#L300-L325); [manuscript.qmd#L149](file://~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/manuscript/manuscript.qmd#L149).

In [manuscript.qmd#L149](file://~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/manuscript/manuscript.qmd#L149), the R code uses `sub("\\s*\\(.*\\)$", "", item)`. Because `.*` is greedy in R regex, it matches from the first open parenthesis `(` before `Cheops` to the final `)` after `metres`, erroneously stripping the entire target name. Furthermore, Table 1 lacks units of measurement (e.g., metres, kilometres, people, USD, novels), which were requested by Reviewer 1 (comment A5).
* **Concrete Fix:** Update the string replacement to match only the trailing unit parenthesis (e.g., `sub("\\s*\\([^)]*\\)$", "", item)`), or extract the units into a dedicated "Unit" column in Table 1, and ensure Row 2 displays the complete name: `"Height of the Cheops Pyramid in Giza"`.

However, Table 2 column 2 STILL bears the header `"Average elasticity b"`, and line 621 STILL refers to `"the observed average elasticity (b = 0.307)"`.
